1113400090000.title_en: Five-story Stone Pagoda at Jeongnimsa Temple Site, Buyeo
1113400090000.description: This stone pagoda stands at the Jeongnimsa Temple site in Buyeo and consists of a single low base with a five-story body above it. Its form closely follows wooden architecture, with slightly swelling corner columns, thin broad roof stones, and a restrained yet refined appearance. It is valued as one of only two surviving Baekje stone pagodas, together with the stone pagoda at Mireuksa Temple Site in Iksan.

1113500100000.title_en: Three-story Stone Pagoda at Baekjangam Hermitage, Ssanggyesa Temple, Namwon
1113500100000.description: This pagoda stands in the field below Baekjangam Hermitage, a small hermitage affiliated with Ssanggyesa Temple. It has a low base and three-story body, but unlike most pagodas its proportions remain nearly uniform, and its surfaces are richly decorated with carvings from the base to the roof stones. The style and sculpture suggest it was built in the late Unified Silla period.

1113500110000.title_en: Stone Pagoda at Mireuksa Temple Site, Iksan
1113500110000.description: This stone pagoda is the western one of the three pagodas at Mireuksa Temple, the largest temple of Baekje, which was founded during King Mu's reign. It is the largest surviving stone pagoda in Korea and the earliest surviving pagoda with a clearly known construction date; an inscription found in 2009 confirmed that it was built in 639. The pagoda preserves features derived from wooden architecture, including a central interior space and a vertical central pillar.

1113600120000.title_en: Stone Lantern in Front of Gakhwangjeon Hall, Hwaeomsa Temple, Gurye
1113600120000.description: This stone lantern stands in front of Gakhwangjeon Hall at Hwaeomsa Temple and is 6.4 meters tall, making it the largest stone lantern in Korea. It is an octagonal lantern with a three-tiered base, a jar-shaped central shaft, a fire chamber with four openings, and a roof stone with prominent corner ornaments. It is thought to have been made sometime between 860 and 873 in the late Unified Silla period.

1113600130000.title_en: Geukrakbojeon Hall of Muwisa Temple, Gangjin
1113600130000.description: Geukrakbojeon Hall is the oldest building at Muwisa Temple and was built in 1430 during the reign of King Sejong. It is a three-bay by three-bay wooden hall with a gabled roof and a simple yet refined bracket structure placed only on the tops of the columns. The hall once contained Amitabha Buddha triad images and 29 wall paintings, of which one large painting remains in place and the others are kept separately.

1113700140000.title_en: Yeongsanjeon Hall of Geojosa Temple, Yeongcheon
1113700140000.description: Yeongsanjeon Hall is the main building of Geojosa Temple and was first built in 1375. It houses a seated image of Sakyamuni Buddha and 526 stone arhat statues. The building is a seven-bay by three-bay wooden hall with a gabled roof and a bracket system applied only above the columns, showing the style of the late Goryeo and early Joseon periods.

1113700150000.title_en: Geukrakjeon Hall of Bongjeongsa Temple, Andong
1113700150000.description: Geukrakjeon Hall at Bongjeongsa Temple is traditionally associated with the temple's founding in the seventh century, but its present structure is estimated to date from the early 13th century. It is a three-bay by four-bay wooden hall with a gabled roof, swelling columns, and a bracket system placed only on the columns. The interior includes a richly decorated canopy above the main Buddha image and vine motifs carved on the altar sides.

1113700160000.title_en: Seven-story Brick Pagoda at Beopheungsa Temple Site, Andong
1113700160000.description: This pagoda is believed to have belonged to Beopheungsa Temple, which was founded in the Unified Silla period. It stands on a single base and has a seven-story body built of dark gray bricks, with stone carvings of the Eight Guardian Deities and the Four Heavenly Kings on the base. The pagoda is one of the largest and oldest surviving brick pagodas in Korea.

1111100010000.description: This gate was the main south gate of Hanyang Fortress, the Joseon capital, and is also called Namdaemun. It was begun in 1396 and completed in 1398, and is the oldest surviving wooden building in Seoul. The gate was severely damaged in a 2008 arson attack and later restored, reopening in 2013.

1111100020000.title_en: Ten-Story Stone Pagoda at Wongaksaji Site, Seoul
1111100020000.description: This pagoda stood at the site of Wongaksa Temple, which was founded in 1465 at the present Tapgol Park site. It was completed in 1467 and is the only extant stone pagoda of its kind from the Joseon period. The pagoda is made of marble and is notable for its rich carved decoration and unusual form.

1111100030000.title_en: Stele of King Jinheung's Royal Tour, Bukhansan Mountain, Seoul
1111100030000.description: This is one of the boundary-inspection steles erected by King Jinheung of Silla to commemorate his visit after the Han River basin had been incorporated into the kingdom. The inscription is carved in regular script on a rectangular stele set on a two-tiered base, and the monument is now kept at the National Museum of Korea. It was discovered and read by Chusa Kim Jeong-hui in 1816.

1113100040000.title_en: Stupa at Godalsa Temple Site, Yeoju
1113100040000.description: This is a Goryeo-period monk's stupa standing at the site of Godalsa Temple. It has an octagonal plan and a richly carved base, body, roof stones, and finial, with decorative motifs including lotus petals, clouds, dragons, and the Four Heavenly Kings. The stupa is believed to have been built in the early Goryeo period.

1113300050000.title_en: Twin-Lion Stone Lantern of Beopjusa Temple, Boeun
1113300050000.description: This stone lantern at Beopjusa Temple is a Unified Silla-period lantern supported by two carved lions facing each other. The lantern has an octagonal lamp chamber and a plain roof stone, and is regarded as one of the finest surviving stone lions. It is thought to have been made around 720.

1113300060000.title_en: Seven-Story Stone Pagoda at Tapwongri, Chungju
1113300060000.description: This Unified Silla stone pagoda, also called Jungangtap, is the largest pagoda built in its time and stands on two-tiered foundations. It has seven stories, with elaborately carved pillars and upturned roof corners, and was likely erected in the late 8th century. Relics and a reliquary were found during repairs in 1917.

1113400070000.title_en: Stele of Bongseon Honggyeongsa Temple, Cheonan
1113400070000.description: This stele records the founding of Bongseon Honggyeongsa Temple, which was established in 1021 during the reign of King Hyeonjong of Goryeo. The inscription says the stele was erected in 1026 and was written by the scholar Choe Chung, with the text calligraphed by Baek Hyeon-rye. The stele has a turtle-shaped base and a dragon-decorated headstone.

1113400080000.title_en: Stele for State Preceptor Nanghye at Seongjusa Temple Site, Boryeong
1113400080000.description: This is the stele of the monk Nanghye Hwasang Muyeom at the site of Seongjusa Temple. It was likely erected in 890, two years after his death, and preserves a detailed inscription by Choe Chiwon with calligraphy by his cousin Choe Ingon. The monument is especially noted for its large turtle base and elaborate dragon-and-cloud carving.

1113700170000.title_en: Stone Lantern in Front of Muryangsujeon Hall, Buseoksa Temple, Yeongju
1113700170000.description: This Unified Silla stone lantern stands in front of Muryangsujeon Hall at Buseoksa Temple. It has a square base, a three-tiered pedestal, an octagonal light chamber with four windows and four reliefs of bodhisattvas, and an octagonal roof stone with a finial base remaining at the top.

1113700180000.description: Muryangsujeon Hall is the main hall of Buseoksa Temple and houses an image of Amitabha Buddha. The present building was rebuilt in 1376 after the earlier hall burned down in 1358, and it is a representative example of the Jusimpo style with a gabled-hip roof.

1113700190000.description: Josadang Shrine enshrines the portrait of the monk Uisang. It was built in 1377 and repaired in 1490 and 1493; the shrine also preserved late Goryeo murals of the Four Heavenly Kings and bodhisattvas, which are now kept in the Buseoksa Sacred Relics Museum.

1113700200000.description: Dabotap Pagoda stands east of the main hall courtyard at Bulguksa Temple, opposite Seokgatap Pagoda. It is thought to have been built when Bulguksa was founded in 751, and it combines square, octagonal, and circular forms in one structure.

1113700210000.description: Seokgatap Pagoda stands west of Dabotap Pagoda in the main courtyard of Bulguksa Temple. It is a three-story stone pagoda believed to have been made in 751, and the reliquary found during repair work in 1966 included the Mugujeonggwang Daedaranigyeong.

1113700220000.title_en: Yeonhwagyo Bridge and Chilbogyo Bridge, Bulguksa Temple, Gyeongju
1113700220000.description: Yeonhwagyo Bridge and Chilbogyo Bridge form the western stairway leading to Anyangmun Gate and Geuknakjeon Hall at Bulguksa Temple. They are believed to have been built in 751 and are arranged in 18 steps, with lotus reliefs carved on the steps of Yeonhwagyo Bridge.

1113700230000.title_en: Cheongungyo Bridge and Baegungyo Bridge, Bulguksa Temple, Gyeongju
1113700230000.description: Cheongungyo Bridge and Baegungyo Bridge form the eastern stairway leading to Jahamun Gate and Daeungjeon Hall at Bulguksa Temple. They are believed to have been built in 751 and are arranged in 34 steps, with the arched stone structure preserved in a complete form.

1113700240000.description: Seokguram Grotto was begun by Gim Daeseong in 751 and completed in 774 during the Unified Silla period. It is an artificial stone grotto on Mount Tohamsan with a main chamber centered on a seated Buddha and surrounding sculptures of bodhisattvas, disciples, heavenly beings, and guardian figures.

1113800330000.title_en: Stele Commemorating King Jinheung’s Territorial Expansion, Changnyeong
1113800330000.description: This stele was erected by King Jinheung of Silla to commemorate his inspection of the area after incorporating Bitbeolgaya, now Changnyeong, into Silla territory. Although its inscription is heavily worn, the remaining text includes the names and ranks of officials who accompanied the king, making it an important source for Silla’s local administration and social organization.

1113800340000.title_en: East Three-story Stone Pagoda of Suljeong-ri, Changnyeong
1113800340000.description: This three-story stone pagoda stands on a two-tiered base and represents the standard form of Unified Silla stone pagodas. It was dismantled and restored in 1965, when relics including a bronze reliquary with a lid were found in the third-story body stone.

1113600350000.title_en: Three-story Stone Pagoda with Four Lions at Hwaeomsa Temple, Gurye
1113600350000.description: This pagoda stands on a high terrace at the northwest side of Hwaeomsa Temple, facing a stone lantern. The upper base is supported at each corner by four lion figures, and the first-story body stone is carved with door-like designs, guardians, and bodhisattvas.

1113200360000.description: This bronze bell at Sangwonsa Temple was made in 725, during the reign of King Seongdeok of Silla. It is one of the three surviving complete Unified Silla bells, and is decorated with dragon-shaped suspension, music-playing figures, flying apsaras, and lotus motifs.

1113700370000.title_en: Three-story Stone Pagoda Site of Hwangboksa Temple, Gyeongju
1113700370000.description: This pagoda was erected by King Hyoso to pray for the repose of his father, King Sinmun, and was later reopened with reliquaries and Buddhist images added in 706. Excavation during dismantling revealed a gilt-bronze reliquary and other objects, helping confirm the pagoda’s date and purpose.

1113700380000.title_en: Three-story Stone Pagoda Site of Goseonsa Temple, Gyeongju
1113700380000.description: This pagoda originally stood at the site of Goseonsa Temple, where Wonhyo is said to have served as head monk, and was moved to the National Museum of Gyeongju when the temple site was submerged by the construction of Deokdong Dam. It is a typical early Unified Silla stone pagoda, and its third-story body stone was made as a single stone to hold a reliquary chamber.

1113700390000.title_en: Five-story Stone Pagoda of Nawon-ri, Gyeongju
1113700390000.description: This large stone pagoda remains at a former temple site in Nawon-ri and is also called the "Nawon White Pagoda" because of its pale granite color. It has a two-tiered base and five stories, with most major parts carved from single stones, and is thought to date to the 8th century.

1113700400000.title_en: Thirteen-story Stone Pagoda Site of Jeonghye-sa Temple, Gyeongju
1113700400000.description: This pagoda stands at the site of Jeonghye-sa Temple and has a unique form with 13 stories built on a single earthen base. Its first story is large, while the upper stories become rapidly smaller, making the upper section appear almost like an added finial.

1113300410000.title_en: Iron Flagpole Site of Yongdusa Temple, Cheongju
1113300410000.description: This is the iron flagpole that stood at the former site of Yongdusa Temple in Sangdang-gu, Cheongju. The stone base and two supporting stone posts remain intact, and the iron shaft is composed of 20 cylindrical sections locked together; an inscription on the third section records the reason and process of its erection. It is dated to 962, during the reign of King Gwangjong of Goryeo, and is a rare surviving example of an iron flagpole.

1113600420000.title_en: Wooden Shrine for the Seated Triad of Buddhas, Songgwangsa Temple, Suncheon
1113600420000.description: This small wooden Buddhist shrine houses a seated triad of Buddha images and is said to have been brought back from China by Jinul, though no documentary record survives. It is made in three sections with side doors, and when closed it forms an octagonal, rounded upper shape. The carving is detailed and precise, showing a combination of Indian- and Tang Chinese-influenced features.

1113600430000.description: This document records the approval, in 1216, of granting the title of Dae Seonsa to Hyeseim, the second state preceptor of Songgwangsa Temple. It is written in ink on a scroll made by joining seven sheets of brocade in red, yellow, and white with a diamond-flower pattern. It is a rare surviving example of an official certificate bestowed on a Buddhist monk in the Goryeo period.

1113600440000.title_en: South and North Three-story Stone Pagodas and Stone Lantern of Borimsa Temple, Jangheung
1113600440000.description: At Borimsa Temple, two three-story stone pagodas and a stone lantern stand side by side in the temple courtyard. The pagodas are typical Unified Silla stone pagodas with a two-tiered base, three-story body, and finial, while the stone lantern has an octagonal shaft and a square flame chamber with four openings. An inscription found inside one pagoda shows that the pagodas were made around 870, and the lantern is believed to be from the same period.

1113700450000.title_en: Clay Seated Buddha, Buseoksa Temple, Yeongju
1113700450000.description: This large clay seated Buddha, 2.78 meters high, is enshrined in Muryangsujeon Hall at Buseoksa Temple. It is formed over a wooden framework with applied clay and is regarded as one of the oldest and largest surviving clay Buddha images in Korea. The formalized robe folds and restrained expression suggest an early Goryeo date.

1113700460000.title_en: Mural Paintings of Joseodang Hall, Buseoksa Temple
1113700460000.description: These six wall paintings were created on the interior walls of Joseodang Hall at Buseoksa Temple and depict the Four Heavenly Kings, Indra, and Brahma. They were painted in green, red, white, and gold on a mud wall, and are now kept separately after being detached during the Japanese colonial period. Based on records found in the building, they are believed to date to around 1377 and are considered the oldest surviving murals in Korea.
1113700460000.material: Ink and color on mud wall

1113800470000.title_en: Stele for National Preceptor Jingamseonsa at Ssanggyesa Temple, Hadong
1113800470000.description: This stele commemorates Jingamseonsa, a renowned late Unified Silla monk who introduced and popularized Buddhist chant. It consists of a tortoise pedestal, body stone, and capstone; the pedestal has a dragon head and six-sided patterns, and the capstone is carved with a pair of dragons contesting a jewel. The inscription was written by Choe Chi-won, and the stele was erected in 887.

1113200480000.title_en: Eight-sided Nine-story Stone Pagoda, Woljeongsa Temple, Pyeongchang
1113200480000.description: This pagoda stands at Woljeongsa Temple, with a stone bodhisattva seated in an attitude of offering in front of it. It has an octagonal two-tiered base, a nine-story body, and a finial with a stone lower part and gilt-bronze upper part; wind bells are hung from the corners of the roofs. It represents an important example of early Goryeo polygonal multi-story pagodas and preserves valuable evidence of metalcraft.

1113700250000.title_en: Stele for King Taejong Muyeol's Tomb, Gyeongju
1113700250000.description: This stone stele was erected in front of the tomb of King Taejong Muyeol, the 29th king of Silla. It is the earliest known Unified Silla stele to show the turtle-shaped base and dragon-decorated capstone influenced by Tang China; the stele body is now lost, leaving only the base and capstone. The inscription records the tomb stele of Taejong Muyeol, and the stele was erected in 661.

1113700260000.title_en: Gilt-bronze Seated Vairocana Buddha of Bulguksa Temple, Gyeongju
1113700260000.description: This seated Buddha image is enshrined in the Vairocana Hall of Bulguksa Temple and stands 1.77 m tall. It represents Vairocana Buddha, who is understood to rule over the world of truth, and shows the refined and idealized form typical of Unified Silla sculpture. The statue is dated to 750.

1113700270000.title_en: Gilt-bronze Seated Amitabha Buddha of Bulguksa Temple, Gyeongju
1113700270000.description: This seated Buddha image is enshrined in the Geungnakjeon Hall of Bulguksa Temple and stands 1.66 m tall. The figure shows the dignified body, broad shoulders, and stable seated pose associated with Unified Silla Buddhist sculpture. It is one of the three great gilt-bronze Buddha statues of Unified Silla and is dated to the 8th century.

1113700280000.title_en: Gilt-bronze Standing Medicine Buddha of Baekryulsa Temple, Gyeongju
1113700280000.description: This standing Buddha image was originally at Baekryulsa Temple in northern Gyeongju and was moved to the Gyeongju National Museum in 1930. It represents the Medicine Buddha, who heals all beings, and stands 1.77 m tall. The statue is dated to the 8th century and is regarded as one of the three great gilt-bronze Buddha statues of Unified Silla.

1113700290000.description: This is the largest surviving bell in Korea and one of the three complete Unified Silla bells that remain. It was completed in 771 during the reign of King Hyegong, after an earlier plan begun by King Gyeongdeok to honor the virtues of his father, King Seongdeok. The bell is known for its distinctive sound tube at the top, dragon-shaped suspension loop, floral ornament, and long inscription on the body.

1113700300000.description: This is the oldest surviving Silla stone pagoda and is built by shaping stone blocks like bricks. Although records say it originally had nine stories, only three remain today. The pagoda stands on a wide base with lion figures at the corners and includes guardian figures on the first story, making it an important example of 7th-century Silla stone sculpture.

1113700310000.description: This Silla-period astronomical observatory was used to observe the movement of celestial bodies. It is built in the form of a stone cylinder on a square base with a window opening on the southeast side, and it is about 9 m high. It is believed to have been built during the reign of Queen Seondeok.

1113800320000.title_en: Tripitaka Koreana Woodblocks, Haeinsa Temple, Hapcheon
1113800320000.description: These woodblocks contain the Buddhist canon, consisting of the sutras, vinaya, and treatises. They were carved between 1237 and 1248 during the Goryeo dynasty as a new edition after the earlier Tripitaka Koreana was destroyed in the Mongol invasions. The woodblocks are now kept at Haeinsa Temple and are known for their completeness and accuracy.

1113200480200.title_en: Stone Bodhisattva Statue at Woljeongsa Temple, Pyeongchang
1113200480200.description: This stone bodhisattva statue stands south of the Octagonal Nine-story Stone Pagoda at Woljeongsa Temple and is seated in a kneeling posture with both hands gathered before the chest as if making an offering to the pagoda. It is generally identified as the Bodhisattva Medicine King, based on the account in Odaesan Sajik and on its iconography and setting. The statue is notable for its balanced proportions, stable posture, and finely carved ornaments such as the crown, earrings, bracelets, and chest jewelry.

1113400490000.title_en: Daeungjeon Hall of Sudoksa Temple, Yesan
1113400490000.description: This hall enshrines a Sakyamuni Buddha image and was built in 1308, making it one of the oldest wooden buildings in Korea whose date of construction is known. It is a three-bay by four-bay building with a gabled roof and a bracket system placed only on the tops of the columns. The hall is valued as an important example of Goryeo-period wooden architecture that inherited the Baekje architectural tradition.

1113600500000.title_en: Haetalmun Gate of Dogapsa Temple, Yeongam
1113600500000.description: This gate is the oldest surviving structure at Dogapsa Temple and stands at the temple entrance as a mountain gate. It is a three-bay by two-bay building with guardian Vajra figures standing in the side bays and a central passage in the middle bay. The gate is an unusual example of a mountain gate and is considered an important comparison to the Hojeonmun Gate of Cheongpyeongsa Temple.

1113200510000.title_en: Sammun Gate of Imyeonggwan Guesthouse, Gangneung
1113200510000.description: This is the surviving main gate of the Goryeo-period guesthouse in Gangneung, while the guesthouse building itself no longer remains. The gate is a three-bay by two-bay structure with a gabled roof and a simple bracket system placed only on the column tops. Its plain form and refined carved details reflect characteristic features of Goryeo architecture.

1113800520000.title_en: Janggyeong Panjeon Hall, Haeinsa Temple, Hapcheon
1113800520000.description: These storage halls preserve the woodblocks of the Tripitaka Koreana, and the complex is the oldest surviving structure at Haeinsa Temple. The halls were rebuilt in 1457 and again in 1488 under royal patronage, and their placement and design were adjusted to protect the woodblocks through ventilation and humidity control. The buildings are noted for their rational use of natural conditions and for their role as the only surviving storage facility for the Tripitaka woodblocks in the world.

1113600530000.title_en: East Stupa of Yeongoksa Temple, Gurye
1113600530000.description: This octagonal monk’s stupa stands on a square base on the east side of Yeongoksa Temple and is regarded as one of the finest examples among the temple’s stupa group. The base is carved with dragons, lions, the Eight Classes of Being, and garuda, while the body is decorated with the Four Heavenly Kings and the roof stone is carved with rafters, roof tiles, and end tiles. It is traditionally said to be the stupa of Monk Doseon, though this has not been confirmed.

1113600540000.title_en: North Stupa of Yeongoksa Temple, Gurye
1113600540000.description: This octagonal monk’s stupa stands on a square base in the northern slope area of Yeongoksa Temple. It closely follows the form of the East Stupa at the temple, though it differs slightly in decorative details. The stupa is traditionally attributed to a monk but the record is lost, so its dedicatee is unknown.

1113300550000.title_en: Palsangjeon Hall of Beopjusa Temple, Boeun
1113300550000.description: This is the only surviving five-story wooden pagoda in Korea, and the present building was rebuilt after the Japanese invasions and later dismantled and repaired in 1968. The hall takes its name from the Palsangdo paintings of the Buddha’s life displayed on its walls. Its structure changes by story, with a four-sided hip roof and a pagoda-style finial on top, making it an important example of Korean wooden pagoda architecture.

1113600560000.title_en: State Preceptor Hall, Songgwangsa Temple, Suncheon
1113600560000.description: This hall at Songgwangsa Temple enshrines portraits of 16 great monks and was originally used as a place for meditation. It was first built in 1369 and later repaired twice. The building is a 4-bay by 3-bay structure with a gable roof and single-bracket system, preserving early Joseon architectural features.

1113600570000.title_en: Stupa of State Preceptor Cheolgam, Ssangbongsa Temple, Hwasun
1113600570000.description: This octagonal stone stupa was erected for the monk Cheolgam, who died at this temple in 868. The base, body, and roof stones are all richly carved, including lions, celestial beings, and guardian figures. It is regarded as a masterpiece of Unified Silla stone sculpture.

1113400580000.title_en: Seated Iron Medicine Buddha with Stone Base, Janggoksa Temple, Cheongyang
1113400580000.description: This seated iron Buddha is placed on a large stone pedestal inside the upper Daeungjeon Hall of Janggoksa Temple. The figure shows the restrained, calm style of late Unified Silla Buddhist sculpture, and the stone base has a distinctive three-tiered form. The original stone halo appears to have been replaced with a wooden one during the Joseon period.

1113200590000.title_en: Stele for State Preceptor Jinggwang at the Site of Beopcheonsa Temple, Wonju
1113200590000.description: This stele was erected at the former site of Beopcheonsa Temple to honor State Preceptor Jinggwang, who died in 1070. It consists of a turtle-shaped base, a stele shaft, and a crown-shaped capstone, all decorated with elaborate carvings. The inscription was written to commemorate the monk’s life and achievements.

1111100600000.title_en: Celadon Incense Burner with Lion-shaped Cover
1111100600000.description: This Goryeo celadon incense burner was made in the first half of the 12th century. It consists of a body supported by three beast-form legs and a cover shaped like a seated lion. The pale green glaze and fine inlaid and carved details show the high level of celadon craftsmanship of the period.

1111100610000.title_en: Celadon Ewer in the Form of a Fish-Dragon
1111100610000.description: This Goryeo celadon ewer was made in the 12th century and takes the form of an imagined creature combining a dragon’s head and a fish’s body. Details such as the scales, fins, handle, and tail-shaped lid are rendered with fine carved work and white slip accents. Its form and glaze show the inventive skill of Goryeo celadon artisans.

1113500620000.description: This three-story hall enshrines the Great Maitreya Buddha and is also called Yonghwajeon, Sanhojeon, or Jangnyukjeon. It was rebuilt in 1635 after being burned during the Japanese invasions, and has been repaired several times since. The building is notable for its large scale, double-eaved hip-and-gable roof, and dapo bracket system.

1113200630000.title_en: Seated Iron Vairocana Buddha, Dopiaesa Temple, Cheorwon
1113200630000.description: This iron seated Vairocana Buddha at Dopiaesa Temple was made in 865, as recorded on the back of the figure. The Buddha is paired with an iron pedestal, which is rare, and represents the late Unified Silla style of iron Buddhist images. The serene face and simplified drapery show the characteristic forms of the period.

1111100720000.title_en: Gilt-bronze Triad Buddha with an Inscription of Gyesin Year
1111100720000.description: This gilt-bronze triad shows the main Buddha seated with two attendant bodhisattvas against a single large halo. An inscription on the back of the halo indicates that it was made in 563, during the 10th year of King Wideok of Baekje. The style follows Northern and Southern Dynasties Chinese Buddhist sculpture.

1111100730000.description: This small gilt-bronze Buddhist shrine contains a central Buddha and two bodhisattvas inside a house-shaped cover with windows on the front and sides. It is believed to date to the 11th or 12th century, showing the influence of northern Chinese Buddhist styles. The shrine also preserves important evidence for early Korean wooden architecture and Buddhist sculpture.

1111100740000.title_en: Celadon Water Dropper in the Shape of a Duck
1111100740000.description: This Goryeo celadon water dropper is modeled as a duck floating on water and holding a lotus stem in its beak. The back has an opening for filling water and a small lotus-bud-shaped stopper. It is noted for its realistic carving and refined celadon glaze.

1113800750000.title_en: Bronze Incense Burner with Silver Inlay from Pyochungsa Temple
1113800750000.description: This bronze incense burner was made in 1177, during the reign of King Myeongjong of Goryeo, and is decorated with silver inlay. Its form, with a flaring foot and broad rim, is typical of Goryeo incense burners. The inscription inside the rim provides important evidence for dating Goryeo metalwork.

1113400760000.title_en: Nanjung Ilgi and Letters, Imjin Jangcho by Yi Sun-sin
1113400760000.description: This set consists of seven volumes of Yi Sun-sin's handwritten war diary kept during the Imjin War. It includes the drafts of reports and other military records related to naval command and battle conditions. The work is an important source for studying the military system of the period.

1113700770000.title_en: Five-story Stone Pagoda at Tapriri, Uiseong
1113700770000.description: This five-story stone pagoda in Tapriri, Uiseong, dates to the Unified Silla period. It combines features of brick pagodas and wooden architecture, including a low single-tier base, a tall first story, and roof stones with layered undersides and upturned corners. It is an important example for studying early Unified Silla stone pagodas.

1111100780000.description: This bodhisattva statue sits in the pensive pose with one leg crossed and a hand touching the cheek, and it is 80 cm high. Scholars consider it a work from the mid-6th century or shortly afterward because of its balanced pose, elegant drapery, and calm facial expression. It is now kept at the National Museum of Korea.

1111100790000.title_en: Gilt-bronze Seated Buddha from Guhwang-dong, Gyeongju
1111100790000.description: This seated Buddha was found in a reliquary discovered during repairs to the three-story stone pagoda at Hwangboksa Temple Site in Gyeongju. An inscription in the reliquary states that a six-cun gold Amitabha image was placed there in 706, during the reign of King Seongdeok. The statue is important for studying early eighth-century Buddhist sculpture in Unified Silla.

1113700880000.description: This Silla gold belt and its hanging ornaments were excavated from Geumgwanchong Tomb in Noseo-dong, Gyeongju. The belt is made of 39 pure-gold plates, with gold-wire circular ornaments on the plates and multiple hanging pendants attached below.

1111100890000.title_en: Gold Belt Hook from Seokam-ri, Pyongyang
1111100890000.description: This gold belt hook was excavated from Tomb No. 9 at Seokam-ri in Daedong-gun, Pyongyang. It is decorated with fine gold-wire work showing one large dragon and six smaller dragons, with jade inlays set between floral motifs.

1111100900000.title_en: Gold Earrings from Bubu Tomb, Gyeongju
1111100900000.description: These paired Silla gold earrings were excavated from Bubu Tomb in Bomun-dong, Gyeongju. They are hollow ring earrings decorated with floral and leaf-shaped pendants, using delicate granulation and gold-wire techniques throughout.

1111100910000.description: This pair of pottery funerary figurines was excavated from Geumnyeongchong Tomb in Gyeongju. The two figures depict a rider and a servant on small horses, and were likely made for ritual use in guiding the dead to the afterlife.

1111100920000.title_en: Bronze Ewer with Silver Inlay and Waterfowl Design
1111100920000.description: This Goryeo-period ritual ewer is a representative metalwork piece with silver inlay. Its surface shows a lyrical landscape of reeds, willow trees, water birds, and a boatman, all executed by inlaying silver into engraved bronze.

1111100930000.title_en: White Porcelain Jar with Iron-Painted Grape and Monkey Design
1111100930000.description: This late Joseon white porcelain jar has a rounded shoulder and a form narrowing gradually toward the base. Its body is decorated with vigorous iron-painted grape vines, and the brushwork suggests the hand of a professional painter rather than a potter.

1111100940000.title_en: Celadon Bottle in the Shape of a Quince
1111100940000.description: This Goryeo celadon bottle was found with a dated book in the tomb of King Injong in Jangdan-gun, Gyeonggi-do. It has a quince-shaped body with a floral mouth and a tall flared foot, and is coated with a thin, even bluish-green glaze.

1111100950000.title_en: Celadon Incense Burner with Openwork Seven Treasures Design Cover
1111100950000.description: This early Goryeo celadon incense burner is composed of a cover and a body. The cover is openworked for the incense to rise, and the base is supported by three rabbits, with floral and vine designs decorating the surface.

1113300640000.title_en: Stone Lotus Basin of Beopjusa Temple, Boeun
1113300640000.description: This is a small stone basin shaped like a lotus pond, located east of Cheonwangmun Gate at Beopjusa Temple. It is supported by an octagonal base and a central shaft, and the basin is carved in the form of a half-open lotus blossom with decorative lotus petals and floral motifs. It is generally dated to the 8th century of Unified Silla.

1111100650000.title_en: Celadon Censer with Lid in the Form of a Qilin
1111100650000.description: This celadon incense burner was made in the 12th century, when Goryeo celadon was at its peak, and stands about 20 cm high. It consists of a body with three beast-shaped legs and a lid carved in the form of a kneeling qilin; the incense smoke was designed to pass through the animal's mouth. The vessel has a soft jade-green glaze and is an example of auspicious animal-shaped celadon.

1111100660000.title_en: Celadon Ewer with Inlaid Lotus Pond, Mandarin Duck, and Reed Design
1111100660000.description: This Goryeo celadon ewer is 37.0 cm high and was used in Buddhist ritual washing ceremonies. The body is decorated with inlaid willow, reed, lotus, and a pair of mandarin ducks in white clay, with peony motifs on the neck. The spout is octagonal and stands vertically above the neck, and the vessel retains the refined style of early inlaid celadon.

1113600670000.title_en: Gakhwangjeon Hall of Hwaeomsa Temple, Gurye
1113600670000.description: Gakhwangjeon Hall at Hwaeomsa Temple is a two-story Buddhist hall built on a stone platform believed to date from the Silla period. The present building was rebuilt after the hall was destroyed in the Japanese invasions of the late 16th century, and it has a seven-bay front, five-bay sides, and a multi-bracketing system. The interior is open through both floors and enshrines three Buddha statues and four bodhisattva statues.

1111100680000.title_en: Celadon Maebyeong with Inlaid Cloud and Crane Design
1111100680000.description: This late-12th-century Goryeo maebyeong shows the graceful curves typical of Korean maebyeong vessels. The body is decorated with inlaid clouds and cranes in black and white, with cranes flying upward inside circles and downward outside them. Flowers are placed around the mouth and lotus motifs around the foot.

1112100690000.title_en: Record of Merit for Shim Jibaek as a Founding Allied Meritorious Subject
1112100690000.description: This document was issued in 1397 by the Office of Meritorious Subjects, under royal command, to Shim Jibaek as proof of his status as a meritorious subject. It is a scroll printed with wooden type and is an important surviving early Joseon printed document. The text is valuable because it preserves details about the Founding Allied Meritorious Subject system and uses many early Korean idu expressions.

1111100700000.description: This book is a Hanmun commentary on the newly created Hunminjeongeum, compiled under royal order by scholars of the Hall of Worthies and published in 1446. It consists of a main text, explanations of the letters, and a preface by Jeong In-ji, and is also called the Hunminjeongeum Haeryebon. The work explains the principles of the Korean script and records its creation and publication.

1111100710000.description: Dongguk Jeongun was compiled under King Sejong and published in 1448 as Korea's first book on standardized pronunciation. It was intended to correct and unify the pronunciation of Chinese characters in Korea, and the extant copies preserve only volumes 1 and 6 of the original six-volume set. The text is important for the study of Korean phonology and for understanding the background of Hunminjeongeum.

1111100800000.title_en: Gilt-bronze Standing Buddha from Guhwang-dong, Gyeongju
1111100800000.description: This gilt Buddha was found inside the reliquary placed in Hwangboksa Temple Site Three-story Stone Pagoda, together with the gilt-bronze seated Buddha from Guhwang-dong, Gyeongju. It is 14 cm high, made of pure gold, and has both a pedestal and a halo. The inscription in the reliquary suggests it was placed there in 692, making it an important benchmark for the study of early Unified Silla Buddhist sculpture.

1111100810000.title_en: Stone Standing Maitreya Bodhisattva, Gamsansa Temple Site, Gyeongju
1111100810000.description: This stone statue was made in 719 by Kim Ji-seong at Gamsansa Temple to pray for his parents and for the peace of the king and royal family. It wears an elaborate crown and necklace, and the halo and pedestal are carved with decorative motifs. An inscription on the back of the halo records the date of its creation.

1111100820000.title_en: Stone Standing Amitabha Buddha, Gamsansa Temple Site, Gyeongju
1111100820000.description: This statue was made in 719 at Gamsansa Temple, which was founded by Kim Ji-seong in the name of King Seongdeok of Silla. It is a balanced and realistic stone Buddha figure with a rounded face, stylized drapery folds, and a boat-shaped halo. An inscription on the back of the halo identifies its date and maker.

1111100830000.description: This gilt-bronze pensive bodhisattva, now in the National Museum of Korea, is one of the largest surviving gilt-bronze pensive bodhisattvas in Korea at 93.5 cm high. It wears a three-peaked crown and sits in a contemplative pose with one leg crossed over the other and a hand resting on the raised knee. It is generally dated to the late Three Kingdoms period.

1113400840000.description: This cliff-carved Buddhist triad is cut into a rock face in Gayasan Valley, Seosan, with a standing Buddha in the center, a bodhisattva on the right, and a pensive figure on the left. The main Buddha is known for its rounded, gentle expression, often called the "smile of Baekje." It is thought to have been made in the late 6th or early 7th century and is associated with the cultural exchange between Baekje and China.

1111100850000.title_en: Gilt-bronze Triad Buddha with Sinmyo Inscription
1111100850000.description: This small gilt-bronze triad Buddha was unearthed in 1930 in Bongsan-ri, Hwachon-myeon, Goksan-gun, Hwanghae-do, and is now displayed at the Leeum Museum of Art. The main Buddha stands at the center of a large halo with attendant bodhisattvas on either side, and an inscription on the back records that it was made in the Sinmyo year, identified as 571. Its style is generally regarded as Goguryeo.

1111100860000.title_en: Ten-story Stone Pagoda of Gyeongcheonsa Temple Site, Gaeseong
1111100860000.description: This pagoda originally stood at Gyeongcheonsa Temple Site in Gaepung-gun and was returned after being taken to Japan during the Japanese colonial period. It is a ten-story marble pagoda with elaborate carvings of Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and floral motifs, and an inscription on the first story records its construction in 1348. Its structure reflects wooden architecture and influenced later Joseon stone pagodas.

1113700870000.title_en: Gold Crown and Gold Crown Ornaments from Geumgwanchong Tomb
1113700870000.description: This gold crown was excavated from Geumgwanchong Tomb in Noseo-dong, Gyeongju, and is a representative example of Silla gold crowns. It has a headband with three vertical tree-like ornaments in front, antler-shaped ornaments at the back, and numerous jade and bead pendants. A separate inner cap made of thin gold sheet was also found outside the coffin.

1111100960000.title_en: Celadon Ewer in the Shape of a Tortoise and Dragon
1111100960000.description: This Goryeo celadon ewer was made in the first half of the 12th century, during the height of celadon production. It is modeled as a tortoise-like creature seated on a lotus, with a water inlet, spout, body, and handle all integrated into the form. The back is inscribed with the character for king (王), and the glaze is a soft grayish blue-green.

1111100970000.title_en: Celadon Meiping Vase with Incised Lotus and Arabesque Design
1111100970000.description: This Goryeo celadon meiping vase was made in the 12th century and has the characteristic rounded shoulders, narrow neck, and balanced curves of Goryeo pottery. The body is decorated with bold incised lotus-vine designs, and the surface is covered with a clear grayish blue-green glaze with fine crackle. It is thought to have been fired at the Sacheong-ri kiln site in Gangjin, Jeollanam-do.

1111100980000.title_en: Celadon Jar with Inlaid Peony Design
1111100980000.description: This Goryeo celadon jar was made in the 12th century and is decorated on both sides with large peony sprays. The flowers are inlaid in white and the leaves in black, creating a strong contrast on the grayish blue-green glaze. The vessel shows the refined quality of inlaid celadon techniques.

1111100990000.title_en: East and West Three-Story Stone Pagodas from Galhangsa Temple Site, Gimcheon
1111100990000.description: These two stone pagodas originally stood east and west of the Galhangsa Temple site in Gimcheon, Gyeongsangbuk-do. The inscription on the east pagoda records that they were built in 758, the 17th year of King Gyeongdeok of Unified Silla, by the three members of the monk Ueonbeop. Both pagodas survive in a nearly complete state except for the finials.

1111101000000.title_en: Seven-Story Stone Pagoda at Nammgyewon Site, Gaeseong
1111101000000.description: This stone pagoda stood at the Namgyewon site near Gaeseong and was long known under a different name before its site was identified. It is a seven-story pagoda on a two-tiered base, showing the general form of Goryeo stone pagodas while retaining strong influence from Unified Silla styles. A copy of the Lotus Sutra found inside the pagoda indicates that it was repaired in 1283.

1111101010000.title_en: Stupa of National Preceptor Jigwang from Beopcheonsa Temple Site, Wonju
1111101010000.description: This stupa commemorates the Goryeo monk Jigwang Guksa Hae-rin (984–1070). Unlike the typical octagonal stupas of later periods, it uses a square-plan form and has richly carved details, including lion figures at the corners of the base and carved Buddhist figures and phoenixes on the roof stone. It is thought to have been built soon after the monk's death, between 1070 and 1085.

1111101020000.title_en: Stupa of National Preceptor Hongbeop from Jeongtosa Temple Site, Chungju
1111101020000.description: This stupa was made for the monk Hongbeop Guksa and dates to 1017, the 8th year of King Hyeonjong of Goryeo. It has an octagonal base with carved dragons and lotus motifs, and its most distinctive feature is the round main body with crossed decorative bands. The structure preserves the basic octagonal stupa form of Silla while introducing new Goryeo-period experimentation.

1112401030000.title_en: Twin-Lion Stone Lantern from Jungheungsanseong Fortress, Gwangyang
1112401030000.description: This stone lantern from the Unified Silla period stands on a lower base carved with large lotus petals and uses two lions instead of a central shaft. The two lions brace themselves back to back and support the upper structure with their bodies, showing a naturalistic style. The lantern has an octagonal fire chamber with four openings and a roof stone with gracefully upturned corners.

1111101040000.title_en: Stupa of Buddhist Monk Yeomgeo from the Former Heungbeopsa Temple Site, Wonju
1111101040000.description: This reliquary stupa of the Silla-period monk Yeomgeo was made in 844, the 6th year of King Munseong’s reign. The structure has an octagonal plan and shows a refined, well-preserved example of early stone stupa design; a gilt-bronze stupa inscription found inside confirmed its date. It is regarded as the earliest extant reliquary stupa and as a model that influenced later stupa forms.

1111101050000.description: This three-story stone pagoda was originally found in the ruins of an old temple in Sancheong, Gyeongsangnam-do, and is now kept at the Jinju National Museum. It stands on a two-tiered base and is decorated with column-like reliefs, Eight Classes of Deities on the upper base, and Bodhisattva figures on the first-story body. Its ornate carving is considered a representative example of late Unified Silla pagoda style.

1113301060000.title_en: Inscribed Stele-like Stone Buddhist Triad of the Gye-yu Year
1113301060000.description: This stone triad was found at Biamsa Temple in Yeongi and is carved on the faces of a tall, four-sided stone pillar. The front shows an Amitabha triad, while the other sides are filled with many small Buddha figures, figures of guardians, heavenly beings, and inscriptions. It is thought to date to 673, shortly after the unification of the Three Kingdoms.

1111101070000.title_en: White Porcelain Jar with Iron-Painted Grape Design
1111101070000.description: This Joseon-period white porcelain jar is decorated with grape vines painted in iron pigment. The form is broad and stable, and the painting shows the rich pictorial quality typical of 18th-century white porcelain. It is a representative mid-Joseon jar in both size and shape.

1113401080000.title_en: Inscribed Stele-like Stone Buddhist Triad of the Gye-yu Year
1113401080000.description: This carved stone work was discovered at Seogwangam Hermitage near Jochiwon, and its four-sided surface is filled with Buddha images and inscriptions. The front centers on a triad, while the remaining surfaces are densely covered with small Buddhas, apparently intended to represent a thousand Buddhas. The inscription suggests that it was made in 673, and it is historically significant as a work created by descendants of Baekje to pray for the repose of their ancestors.

1113701090000.description: This early Unified Silla cave temple was made in a natural cave on a cliff of Palgongsan in Gunwi, Daegu, and predates the Seokguram Grotto. It houses a stone Amitabha triad dated to around 700. The main Buddha sits with the soles of the feet turned upward, and the attendant bodhisattvas show Tang-dynasty style proportions and dress.

1111101100000.description: This portrait depicts the Goryeo scholar-official Yi Je-hyeon (1287–1367) seated on a silk background. It was painted in 1319 by the Yuan dynasty painter Chen Jinyu when Yi accompanied King Chungsuk to Yuan, and it is considered one of only two surviving original Goryeo portraits. The work preserves the left-facing pose, detailed accessories, and composed structure characteristic of Goryeo portrait painting.

1113701110000.description: This half-length portrait shows the Goryeo scholar An Hyang (1243–1306), who helped introduce Neo-Confucian learning to Korea. The composition is divided into an upper inscription and a lower image, with the figure shown wearing a flat-topped cap and facing left. It is one of the oldest surviving Korean portraits and is an important work for the study of Goryeo portrait style.

1113701120000.title_en: Gyeongju Gameunsa Temple Site East and West Three-story Stone Pagodas
1113701120000.description: These paired stone pagodas stand side by side in the wide forecourt of the Gameunsa Temple site. They were built in 682, when King Sinmun completed the temple founded by King Munmu to protect the nation after the unification of the Three Kingdoms.

1111101130000.title_en: Celadon Bottle with Iron-painted Willow Design
1111101130000.description: This Goryeo celadon bottle has a long cylindrical body and willow trees painted on both sides in iron pigment. Its simple form and restrained decoration are balanced by the subtle color changes in the glaze, which create a pictorial effect.

1111101140000.title_en: Celadon Inlaid Peony and Chrysanthemum Design Melon-shaped Bottle
1111101140000.description: This melon-shaped Goryeo celadon bottle was made in the 12th century during the height of celadon production. It has an inlaid decoration of peonies, chrysanthemums, lotus flowers, and floral bands arranged around the body and neck.

1111101150000.description: This celadon bowl was found with the tomb inscription of Mun Gong-yu, who died in 1159, and is the oldest dated inlaid celadon known. The inside and outside are decorated with scrolls and chrysanthemum motifs using white and black inlay.

1111101160000.title_en: Celadon Inlaid Peony Design Gourd-shaped Ewer
1111101160000.description: This 12th-century Goryeo celadon ewer has a gourd-shaped body, a spout, and a handle. The neck is decorated with cloud and crane motifs in black and white inlay, and the lower body is filled with peony patterns and buds.

1113601170000.title_en: Seated Iron Vairocana Buddha, Borimsa Temple, Jangheung
1113601170000.description: This iron Buddha statue is enshrined in Daejeokgwangjeon Hall at Borimsa Temple, Jangheung, and only the body remains. An inscription on the back records that it was made in 858 by Kim Su-jong, a deputy official of Muju Jangsa.

1111101180000.title_en: Gilt-bronze Maitreya Bodhisattva in Half-seated Contemplation (1964)
1111101180000.description: This small bodhisattva statue was unearthed in 1944 at Pyeongcheon-ri, Pyongyang, and is attributed to the late 6th century. Its half-seated contemplative pose, three-peaked crown, and slender body make it an important example of a Goguryeo Buddhist sculpture.

1111101190000.title_en: Gilt-bronze Standing Buddha with Inscription of the Seventh Year of Yeonga
1111101190000.description: This gilt-bronze standing Buddha bears an inscription connected to Goguryeo and was found in Uiryeong, in the former Silla region. The inscription says it was made by monks of Dongsa Temple in Pyongyang as one of a set of thousand Buddhas, and the date corresponds to the mid-6th century.

1113101280000.description: This small standing bodhisattva image, said to have been unearthed in Gongju, Chungcheongnam-do, is a fine example of Baekje-style Buddhist sculpture. It is 15.2 cm high and shows a dignified face, a slender body draped in thin robes, and a hexagonal lotus pedestal with wide, soft lotus petals.

1111101290000.description: This gilt-bronze standing bodhisattva, 54.5 cm high, shows the characteristic style of bodhisattva images popular in Unified Silla. The work is missing its pedestal, crown, and left forearm, and is thought to date to the late 8th century.

1113701300000.title_en: Five-story Stone Pagoda at Jukjang-ri, Gumi
1113701300000.description: This stone pagoda stands on the former temple site of Jukjangsa, where building stones and roof tiles were found nearby. It is a large five-story pagoda made of more than 100 stones and is the tallest brick-style stone pagoda in Korea, reaching about 10 m.

1111101310000.title_en: Old Document Related to the Household Register of Hwaryeongbu in the Late Goryeo Period
1111101310000.description: This household register was prepared in Yeongheung, the ancestral home of Yi Seong-gye, in 1390, the second year of King Gongyang of Goryeo. It records Yi Seong-gye’s official position and stipend, and also lists household members, relatives, sons-in-law, and slaves living with him.

1113701320000.description: This manuscript records the circumstances of the Japanese invasions of Korea written by the Joseon statesman Yu Seong-ryong. It was later published in 1647 as a 16-volume, 7-volume-set edition, and is valued as an important source for studying the years before and after the Imjin War.

1111101330000.title_en: Celadon Ewer with Copper-oxide Lotus Design in the Shape of a Gourd
1111101330000.description: This Goryeo celadon ewer is 33.2 cm high and was likely made in the reign of King Gojong. The gourd-shaped body is decorated with lotus leaves, a flower-bud stopper, a handle formed like a bent vine with a frog, and red copper-oxide decoration along the lotus leaf edges and veins.

1111101340000.description: This work, said to have been found in Chuncheon, Gangwon-do, is a rare form in which a triad is arranged on a single halo, with the Buddha image, halo, and pedestal attached together. The central bodhisattva is flanked by two standing arhats, and the X-shaped drapery and lotus-decorated pedestal suggest a Three Kingdoms-period style, possibly Baekje.

1111101350000.title_en: Album of Genre Paintings by Sin Yun-bok
1111101350000.description: This album contains more than 30 genre paintings by the late Joseon artist Sin Yun-bok, including works such as Dano Pungjeong and Wolhajeongin. The paintings focus on love, romance, and aristocratic leisure, and are noted for their delicate brushwork and refined color.

1113101200000.description: This large Buddhist temple bell was made in the early Goryeo period and preserves the style of Silla-period bells. It is 1.44 meters high, 0.87 meters in mouth diameter, and weighs about 1.5 tons. The bell is decorated with celestial figures, a triad image, dragon-shaped features, and lotus-bud bosses, and is regarded as one of the masterpieces of Goryeo bells.

1113701210000.description: These are wooden masks handed down in Hahoe Village and Byeongsan Village in Andong, and they are the oldest surviving masks used for mask dramas in Korea. The Hahoe masks include 11 types, while only 2 Byeongsan masks remain. They were carved from willow wood and coated with several layers of lacquer; the lower jaw is separately made so it can move during performances.

1113201220000.title_en: Three-story Stone Pagoda at Jinjeonsa Temple Site, Yangyang
1113201220000.description: This three-story stone pagoda stands at the site of Jinjeonsa Temple, which is said to have been founded in the late 8th century during Unified Silla. It sits on a two-tiered base and has carvings of heavenly beings and guardian deities on the lower sections. The pagoda is a representative Unified Silla stone pagoda noted for its balanced form and refined carving.

1113501230000.title_en: Reliquary from the Five-story Stone Pagoda at Wanggung-ri, Iksan
1113501230000.description: These relics were found in 1965 during the disassembly and repair of the Five-story Stone Pagoda at Wanggung-ri, Iksan. They include a gilt-bronze standing Buddha, a bronze bell, glass reliquary vessels, a Diamond Sutra plaque, and containers made of gilt bronze. The objects are thought to date from the period spanning Baekje to Unified Silla.

1111101240000.title_en: Stone Seated Bodhisattva from Hansongsa Temple Site, Gangneung
1111101240000.description: This bodhisattva statue originally stood at the site of Hansongsa Temple in Gangneung and was returned from Japan in 1965. It is carved from white marble, which is unusual for Korean Buddhist sculpture, and is almost complete apart from damage from rejoining the head and loss of the urna on the forehead. Its refined carving, serene expression, and elaborate ornamentation suggest a date in the 10th century.

1111101250000.title_en: Green-glazed Bone Jar with Stone Outer Case
1111101250000.description: This bone jar was used in Buddhist cremation burials to hold bones after cremation. It was found inside a flower-shaped granite outer case, and both the body and lid are coated with green glaze. The surface is decorated with stamped dot lines and floral motifs, making it one of the finest surviving glazed bone jars.

1113701260000.title_en: Reliquary from the Three-story Stone Pagoda at Bulguksa Temple
1113701260000.description: These reliquary objects were discovered in 1966 in the relic chamber of the pagoda during repair work at Bulguksa Temple. The assemblage includes silver and gilt-bronze reliquaries, the Mugujeonggwang Great Dharani Sutra, beads, bronze Buddhist images, and other small objects. The outer case and containers are finely decorated with openwork scroll motifs, lotus designs, and inlaid details, and the Dharani Sutra is considered one of the oldest surviving woodblock prints in the world.
1113701260000.material: Silver, gilt bronze, bronze, gold, paper, silk, wood

1111101270000.title_en: Gilt-bronze Standing Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva from Samyang-dong, Seoul
1111101270000.description: This 20.7-centimeter-tall bodhisattva image was discovered in Samyang-dong, Seoul, in 1967 and is now housed at the National Museum of Korea. It shows Avalokitesvara with a triangular crown, a gently smiling face, a water bottle in the right hand, and a distinctive left hand gesture. Based on its form and style, it is thought to date to the first half of the 7th century.

1111101360000.description: A small banner pole ornament, 73.8 cm high, with two uprights on a two-tiered base and a pole set between them. The pole is made of eight joined cylindrical sections, and the top section is decorated with a dragon head; traces of dark brown lacquer and gilding remain on the surface. It is thought to be a Goryeo-period object that preserves the style and craftsmanship of banner poles developed since Silla.

1111101370100.title_en: Bronze Weapons from Bisandong, Daegu - Sword and Scabbard Fittings
1111101370100.description: This group of artifacts was excavated from an early Iron Age tomb site in Bisandong, northern Daegu. It includes a slender bronze short sword with a fish-bird design on the hilt pommel, along with hilt ornaments, scabbard fittings, a sword-end ornament, and other fragments. The sword is notable for showing a separate construction of blade and hilt ornament, suggesting production in the southern Korean Peninsula.

1113101370200.title_en: Bronze Weapons from Bisandong, Daegu - Socketed Spears and Polearms
1113101370200.description: This group consists of bronze weapons excavated from an early Iron Age tomb site in Bisandong, northern Daegu. It includes three socketed spearheads, one of which is 67.1 cm long and among the largest found in Korea, and another broad-bladed example that appears to have been used for ritual rather than practical purposes. The group is notable for its fully localized Korean form rather than a simple imitation of Chinese examples.

1111101380000.title_en: Gold Crown and Ornaments from Goryeong, Said to Be from Goryeong
1111101380000.description: This set is said to have been excavated in Goryeong, Gyeongsangbuk-do, and includes a gold crown and associated gold ornaments of the Gaya region. The crown has a broad band with four flower-shaped upright ornaments, circular gold plaques, and traces of curved jade pendants added later. The associated ornaments are mixed in form, so their original positions on the crown are not certain.

1111101390000.title_en: Kim Hong-do, Immortals Gathering Folding Screen
1111101390000.description: This is a Daoist-figure painting by the late Joseon artist Kim Hong-do (1745–?). The original work was an eight-panel folding screen, now separated into three hanging scrolls, and it was painted in 1776. It depicts groups of immortals and attendants, including Laozi riding an ox and Dong Fangshuo holding a peach, rendered with bold ink lines and lively brushwork on paper.

1111101400000.description: This bronze mirror, said to have been excavated in the Gaya region, is made with mother-of-pearl inlay and measures 18.6 cm in diameter. The back is decorated with a beaded border, floral motifs with amber inlays, peony designs, and figures of a lion and a bird, with blue jade pieces set between the motifs. It is considered one of the earliest mother-of-pearl craft objects in Korea and is thought to date to the 8th to 10th century.

1111101410000.description: A Jeongmun mirror is a bronze mirror of the early Iron Age, also called a fine-pattern mirror, with two handles on one side for suspension. This example has a diameter of 21.2 cm and is divided into inner, middle, and outer zones filled with finely engraved geometric patterns based on small triangles. It is one of the largest and most elaborate surviving mirrors of its type in Korea.

1111101420000.description: Compiled by Shin Suk-ju, Choe Hang, and Park Paeng-nyeon by royal order and printed in 1448, this 6-volume book was Korea's first work on standard pronunciation. It was produced to correct and unify Chinese-character pronunciation in Korea, with large main text printed in wooden type and smaller text in Gapsinja type. The book is an important source for the study of Korean phonology and the history of Hangul.

1112401430000.description: This assemblage was excavated from a Bronze Age tomb site on a hill in Daegok-ri, Hwasun, Jeollanam-do. It includes three slender bronze daggers, two bronze bells with eight-sided star-shaped frames, two double bronze bells, one bronze knife, one bronze axe, and two fine-line bronze mirrors. The variety and workmanship of the objects show a high level of metalworking in the Korean Bronze Age.

1113601440000.title_en: Rock-Carved Seated Buddha on Wolchulsan Mountain, Yeongam
1113601440000.description: This large seated Buddha was carved by cutting deeply into the rock face northwest of Gujeongbong Peak on Wolchulsan Mountain in Yeongam, Jeollanam-do. A child figure kneeling in worship is carved beside the Buddha’s right knee, and the figure is 8.6 meters high. The style suggests a date in the late Unified Silla period or the early Goryeo period.

1111101450000.description: This Goryeo-period bronze vessel is shaped like a cauldron resting on a stand and is 12.9 cm high. A demon face is modeled on the body, and the lower part has three beast-head legs. It may have been used as an incense burner, brazier, or tea stove because the body has ventilation openings.

1111101460000.title_en: Bronze Bells from Nonsan, Preserved as a Set
1111101460000.description: This set consists of Bronze Age ritual bells reportedly found in Nonsan, Chungcheongnam-do. It includes two eight-sided star-shaped bells, two bullet-shaped bells, one combined double-headed bell with an X-shaped frame, and two dumbbell-shaped double bells. Their function and refined casting techniques make them important materials for studying Bronze Age ritual practices.

1112601470000.title_en: Inscription and Rock Carvings at Cheonjeon-ri, Ulju
1112601470000.description: This stone surface at Daegokcheon in Ulju, Ulsan, is covered with carvings and inscriptions made in different periods and techniques. The upper section has Bronze Age geometric motifs, animals, and abstract human figures, while the lower section contains horse-riding processions, animals, a dragon, boats, and more than 800 characters of Silla-period inscription. The carvings preserve material from the prehistoric age through the Silla period.

1111101480100.description: This is a fragmentary copy of Volume 16 of Hojingbang’s compiled history of the seventeen standard Chinese dynastic histories, covering the Tang section. It was printed with metal type cast in 1403, known as Gyehae type, and is thought to have been published around 1412. As an early Korean metal-type printing item, it is an important source for the history of type casting and printing.

1111101480200.description: This is a fragmentary copy of Volume 17 of Hojingbang’s compilation of the seventeen standard Chinese dynastic histories, printed with Gyehae type cast in 1403. It was likely published around 1412 and is valuable for studying the development of metal type casting and printing in early Joseon and late Goryeo. The surviving copy is incomplete and shows significant wear.

1111101490100.title_en: Dongnae Seonsaeng Gyojeong Buksa Sangjeol, Volumes 4 and 5
1111101490100.description: This book was printed in the reign of King Taejong using Gyehae type cast in 1403. Volume 4 is incomplete, while Volume 5 survives intact. It is an important source for studying early Joseon metal-type printing and the history of typefaces.

1111101490200.description: This book was printed in the reign of King Taejong using Gyemija, the earliest metal type cast in Joseon in 1403. It is a rare surviving copy and an important source for the study of metal-type casting, typesetting, and typefaces in Goryeo and early Joseon. The volume originally consisted of 32 leaves, but one leaf is missing.

1111101500000.description: This is a surviving fragment of a book compiled from selected memorials and letters presented to the Song emperor by prominent officials on matters of governance. It was printed with Gyemija, the first metal type cast in Joseon in 1403, during the reign of King Taejong. Because Gyemija was used for only a short time, surviving editions are rare and are valuable for research on early Joseon printing technology and typefaces.

1111101510100.title_en: Annals of the Joseon Dynasty, Jeongjoksan Sago Copy
1111101510100.description: The Annals of the Joseon Dynasty record the history of 25 reigns from King Taejo to King Cheoljong over 472 years, from 1392 to 1863. This Jeongjoksan Sago copy consists of 1,187 volumes and is a continuation of the early Joseon annals preserved at the Jeonju Sago. The text was compiled from official records such as draft histories, court diaries, and other government documents, and the annals are now recognized as UNESCO Memory of the World.

1112101510200.title_en: Annals of the Joseon Dynasty, Taebaeksan Sago Copy
1112101510200.description: The Annals of the Joseon Dynasty record the history of 25 reigns from King Taejo to King Cheoljong over 472 years, from 1392 to 1863. This Taebaeksan Sago copy consists of 848 volumes and was one of the four copies newly printed from the Jeonju Sago edition between 1603 and 1606. It was kept at Taebaeksan Sago until 1910 and later transferred to the National Archives of Korea.

1111101510300.title_en: Annals of the Joseon Dynasty, Odaesan Sago Copy
1111101510300.description: The Annals of the Joseon Dynasty record the history of 25 reigns from King Taejo to King Cheoljong over 472 years, from 1392 to 1863. This Odaesan Sago copy consists of 75 volumes; for the annals from King Taejo to King Myeongjong, it preserves corrected proof copies, while later annals are in standard printed form. Most of the copy was lost in the Great Kanto Earthquake, and the surviving volumes were later returned to Korea.

1111101510400.title_en: Annals of the Joseon Dynasty, Jeoksangsan Sago Copy
1111101510400.description: The Jeoksangsan Sago copy of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty includes four surviving volumes: one volume of the Annals of King Gwanghaegun and three volumes from the Annals of Kings Seongjong, Injo, and Hyojong. These volumes were once kept at Jeoksangsan Sago in Muju and were identified through surviving ownership seals and labels. The item confirms the existence of Joseon annals copies preserved at the Jeongsongsan, Odaesan, Jeoksangsan, and Taebaeksan archives.

1113101510500.title_en: Annals of the Joseon Dynasty, Bongmodang Copy
1113101510500.description: This set consists of six supplementary volumes of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty now held by the Jangseogak Archives of the Academy of Korean Studies. They bear the ownership seal "Bongmodang," the building in Changdeokgung where royal materials such as the king's writings and genealogical records were kept in the late Joseon period. The copy is significant as evidence of special royal-viewing editions of the annals preserved at Bongmodang.

1111101510600.title_en: Annals of the Joseon Dynasty, Missing-leaf and Scattered-leaf Copies
1111101510600.description: This designation covers 99 volumes of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty, divided into 69 missing-leaf copies and 30 scattered-leaf copies. The missing-leaf copies include many later reprinted editions, while the scattered-leaf copies are gathered leaves from Jeongjoksan Sago editions. These materials are valuable for studying corrections made during reprinting and the transmission of the annals.

1111101520000.description: A register recording the daily business of the Bibyeonsa, the highest state council responsible for major government affairs in the mid- and late Joseon period. The earlier registers were lost before the Japanese invasions of 1592, and 273 volumes survive from 1617 to 1892. These records were an important source for compiling the Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty and for studying late Joseon social and economic change.

1111101530000.description: This chronicle records various state affairs from January 1760 to August 1910 over 151 years of the late Joseon period. It began as King Jeongjo's personal diary and was later turned into an official court chronicle compiled by Kyujanggak officials and submitted to the king every five days for approval. It is considered a major historical source alongside the Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty, Seungjeongwon Ilgi, and Bibyeonsa Deungnok.

1113401540000.title_en: Gold Crown Ornament of King Muryeong
1113401540000.description: A pair of gold crown ornaments excavated from the tomb of King Muryeong in Gongju. They were found stacked near the king's head inside the coffin in 1971, and are decorated with openwork vine motifs, floral patterns, and flame-like forms. They are important evidence for the level of Baekje culture in the first half of the 6th century.

1113401550000.title_en: Gold Crown Ornament of Queen Muryeong
1113401550000.description: A pair of gold crown ornaments excavated from the tomb of King Muryeong in Gongju and associated with the queen. They were found stacked near the queen's head inside the coffin in 1971, and the openwork design centers on a bottle-shaped motif with vine patterns, a flower, and flame-like decoration. Compared with the king's ornament, it is smaller and more restrained in appearance.

1113401560000.description: A pair of gold earrings excavated from the tomb of King Muryeong in Gongju. Each earring has a thick ring with two long hanging elements, one ending in a large leaf-shaped ornament and the other in bead-like and jade pendants. They were found near the king's head in the coffin.

1113401570000.description: Two pairs of earrings excavated from the tomb of King Muryeong in Gongju and associated with the queen. One pair has two hanging strands of varying length, and the other has a single strand with leaf-shaped ornaments and pale green jade beads. The pieces are now kept at the National Museum of Korea and the Gongju National Museum.

1113401580000.description: Two gold necklaces excavated from the tomb of King Muryeong in Gongju, one with nine segments and the other with seven. They were found overlapped at the time of excavation, and each is made by connecting hexagonal gold bars into a simple but refined form. The pieces were found with only a small fastening ring at one end and no additional decoration.

1113401590000.title_en: Gold Hair Ornament of King Muryeong
1113401590000.description: A gold hair ornament excavated from the coffin of King Muryeong in Gongju. It was found near the king's head and has a broad upper part, a narrow lower part, and three pin-like prongs at the bottom. The form and repoussé decoration suggest it was used as a ceremonial head ornament.

1111101690000.title_en: Celadon Vase with Relief Bamboo-joint Design
1111101690000.description: This Goryeo celadon vase, made in the 12th century, is 33.8 cm high. The neck and lower body are decorated in relief with bamboo stalks, and the joints are expressed with two incised lines. The glaze is a clear light green with slight crackle, and the form has a graceful, balanced curve.

1111101700000.title_en: White Porcelain Covered Jar with Underglaze Cobalt Plum, Bird, and Bamboo Design
1111101700000.description: This Joseon white porcelain covered jar was made in the 15th century and is 16.8 cm high. The lid knob is shaped like a lotus bud, and the body is painted with plum blossoms, birds, and bamboo in underglaze cobalt blue. It is considered an important example for studying early Joseon white porcelain form and decoration.

1111101710000.title_en: Bronze Box with Silver-inlaid Phoenix Design
1111101710000.description: This Goryeo covered box, made in the 12th century, measures 9.9 cm in height and 18.3 cm across the mouth. It was made with the silver-inlay technique, carving designs into bronze and filling them with silver wire. The lid and body are decorated with a phoenix, floral motifs, and arabesque patterns, and it is thought to have been used as an incense box in a temple.

1111101720000.title_en: Artifacts from the Tomb of Yeongin Jeong of Jinyang County
1111101720000.description: These artifacts were excavated from the tomb of Yeongin Jeong in Buk-sang-myeon, Geochang-gun, Gyeongsangnam-do, and include white porcelain vessels, a tomb stele, and other objects. The tomb stele records Jeong's family background, life, and death, showing that she died in 1466. The finds are important for studying early Joseon white porcelain and tomb burial customs.

1111101730000.title_en: Celadon Seated Arhat with Painted Dot Design
1111101730000.description: This Goryeo celadon sculpture, made in the first half of the 12th century, was found in Gukhwa-ri, Ganghwa-do, and later restored from six fragments. The figure sits with arms folded, resting against a small desk on a rock-like pedestal, with the head slightly bowed. Parts of the hair, robes, eyebrows, pupils, and rock base are accented with black pigment and raised white dots.

1111101740000.title_en: Gilt-bronze Candle Stand with Crystal Decoration
1111101740000.description: This pair of candle stands was made in Unified Silla and is 36.8 cm high. The structure has upper and lower flower-petal-shaped supports around a central stem, and the lower support is held up by six animal-shaped legs. The surface is decorated with relief and incised patterns, and crystals were inlaid as ornament.

1111101750000.title_en: White Porcelain Bowl with Inlaid Lotus and Arabesque Design
1111101750000.description: This early Joseon white porcelain bowl, made in the 15th century, is 7.6 cm high and has a thin-walled form. The exterior is divided by bands and filled with inlaid lotus and arabesque patterns, while a simplified vine pattern circles the inner rim. It is an important example of the white porcelain inlay tradition that continued from Goryeo techniques.

1111101760000.title_en: White Porcelain Jar with Underglaze Cobalt Pine and Bamboo Design Inscribed "Hongzhi 2"
1111101760000.description: This Joseon white porcelain jar was made in 1489, the 20th year of King Seongjong's reign, and is painted with pine and bamboo in underglaze cobalt blue. The inscription "Hongzhi 2" on the inside of the mouth gives the date of manufacture. It was reportedly used for holding flowers in court rituals and ceremonies.

1113401600000.description: A pair of silver bracelets was found near the left arm of Queen Muryeong in the wooden coffin of Muryeong Royal Tomb in Gongju. The inner side is finely decorated with sawtooth patterns, and the rounded outer surface is engraved with two three-legged dragons. An inscription on one bracelet records the maker’s name and the weight, and it is regarded as a valuable source for the study of ancient metalcraft.

1113401610000.title_en: Bronze Mirrors from Muryeong Royal Tomb
1113401610000.description: This group consists of three bronze mirrors excavated from Muryeong Royal Tomb in Gongju: a bronze divine-beast mirror, an Ijaseonsudae mirror, and a Sudae mirror. They are imitations of Chinese Han- and Later Han-period mirrors, showing motifs such as figures, inscriptions, bosses, and animal designs. Compared with the originals, the lines are thicker and the decoration is less refined.

1113401620000.title_en: Stone Animal from Muryeong Royal Tomb
1113401620000.description: This stone animal sculpture was made during the Baekje period and excavated from Muryeong Royal Tomb in Gongju. It was placed facing outward in the center of the passage and is shaped with a rounded mouth, a large nose, eyes, ears, a tail, and a realistic excretory opening. It is considered the first such tomb guardian animal discovered in Korea.

1113401630000.title_en: Mourning Tablets of Muryeong Royal Tomb
1113401630000.description: These two stone tablets are the burial documents of King Muryeong and his queen, excavated together with Muryeong Royal Tomb in 1971. They are inscribed with grave-purchase texts, one on each tablet, and the king’s text matches the record in the Samguk sagi. They are the only known grave-purchase documents found in a Three Kingdoms-period tomb and are important evidence for Baekje burial customs and cultural exchange with the Southern Dynasties of China.

1113401640000.description: This wooden funerary pillow was found inside the wooden coffin of Queen Muryeong in Muryeong Royal Tomb. The upper part is cut into a U-shape to support the head, and the surface is lacquered red, gilt, and painted with motifs such as celestial beings, phoenixes, fish-dragons, lotus flowers, and vine scrolls. Wooden phoenix heads were attached to both upper sides of the pillow.

1113401650000.description: This wooden footrest was found inside the wooden coffin of King Muryeong in Muryeong Royal Tomb. A deep W-shaped hollow was carved in the center so that both feet could rest on it, and the front was coated with black lacquer and decorated with gilt turtle-shell patterns and six-petal gold flowers. A ornament resembling a buyo hair decoration was attached to the center of the floral plate.

1111101660000.title_en: White Porcelain Jar with Iron-Black Plum Blossom and Bamboo Design
1111101660000.description: This Joseon-period white porcelain jar is decorated in iron-black underglaze with cloud, petal, wave, plum blossom, and bamboo motifs. Its form is close to 16th-century buncheong ware, and the jar is thought to have been made in the late 16th century at Gwanum-ri kiln site in Gwangju, Gyeonggi Province. It is considered an early example of iron-painted white porcelain.

1111101670000.description: This Goryeo celadon ewer was made in the form of a person wearing a hat and robe and holding a vessel with a peach on it.
