Many parts are missing, including most of the upper stories and the finial, so its original form is only partly preserved. It is regarded as a typical Goryeo-period pagoda that inherited and modified the style of Silla stone pagodas.

1123700110100.title_en: Bronze Bell Made by Saing Bi-gu - Seounam Hermitage, Bogyeongsa Temple, Pohang
1123700110100.description: This Joseon-period bronze bell was made in 1667 by the monk-artisan Saing Bi-gu. It is the earliest surviving bell among his known works and preserves features of his early style, including a ring for suspension, decorative lotus petals around the shoulder, square panels with five bosses, and inscribed mantras between them.

1123700110200.title_en: Bronze Bell Made by Saing Bi-gu - Gilyongsa Temple, Mungyeong
1123700110200.description: This Joseon-period bronze bell was made in 1670 by the monk-artisan Saing Bi-gu. According to the inscription, it was completed three months earlier than the Sutaesa Temple bell made in the same year. It is valued as an important example for studying Saing Bi-gu’s work and the artisan community of late Joseon.

1123200110300.title_en: Bronze Bell Made by Saing Bi-gu - Sutasa Temple, Hongcheon
1123200110300.description: This Joseon-period bronze bell was made in 1670 by the monk-artisan Saing Bi-gu. Together with the Gilyongsa Temple bell, it is notable for its distinctive lotus-flower design around the striking area. The bell was made three months after the Gilyongsa bell in the same year.

1123100110400.title_en: Bronze Bell Made by Saing Bi-gu - Cheongnyongsa Temple, Anseong
1123100110400.description: This Joseon-period bronze bell was made in 1674 by the monk-artisan Saing Bi-gu. It features a dragon engraved on the suspension loop and sound tube, with broad bands of lotus and vine decoration on the shoulder and lower body. The bell is considered an important work from Saing Bi-gu’s mature period.

1121100110500.title_en: Bronze Bell Made by Saing Bi-gu - Hwagyesa Temple, Seoul
1121100110500.description: This Joseon-period bronze bell was made in 1683 by the monk-artisan Saing Bi-gu. Its notable features include two dragons on the suspension loop, broad decorative bands on the shoulder and mouth, and square panels with tablet-shaped ornament. The inscription also provides historical evidence about a monk receiving an official certification document.

1123800110600.title_en: Bronze Bell Made by Saing Bi-gu - Tongdosa Temple
1123800110600.description: This Joseon-period bronze bell was made in 1686 by the monk-artisan Saing Bi-gu. It is distinguished by an Eight Trigrams motif, the only one among his known bells to use this design. The bell also departs from the usual nine-boss arrangement by placing a single boss at the center of each square panel.

1112412260002.title_en: Sakyamuni Buddha’s Three Assemblies Painting, Jikjisa Temple, Gimcheon
1112412260002.description: This three-panel Buddhist painting was completed in 1744 by the monk painters Seogan, Singak, Milgi, Wolin, and others and enshrined in the Daeungjeon Hall of Jikjisa Temple. It consists of an Assembly of Vulture Peak Painting in the center, a Medicine Buddha sermon painting on the left, and an Amitabha Buddha sermon painting on the right, and has been preserved in its original three-panel form.

1112501090001.title_en: Five-story Stone Pagoda of Magoksa Temple, Gongju
1112501090001.description: This stone pagoda at Magoksa Temple is a typical Goryeo-period pagoda in the Baekje-style tradition that was widespread in Chungcheong and Honam during the late Goryeo period. The gilt-bronze finial placed on top of the fifth roof stone, called Bongmadong, reproduces a Llama-style Buddhist stupa form and is the only example of its kind among surviving Korean stone pagodas.

1112503110001.title_en: Stupa of Jikyeon Seonsa, Taeansa Temple, Gokseong
1112503110001.description: This stupa is the memorial pagoda of the Seon master Hyecheol, who founded the Dongnisan branch of the Gusan Seon School in the Unified Silla period. It is an octagonal cylindrical stupa with a separately built base, carved lions on the lower stone, and finely modeled door and Four Heavenly Kings reliefs on the body.

1112504240001.title_en: Maitreya Buddha Hanging Scroll, Muryangsa Temple, Buyeo
1112504240001.description: This large hanging scroll was completed in 1627 and is painted in the standing bodhisattva form with an ornate crown and richly decorated body. It is an early example of the large, splendid hanging paintings used for outdoor Buddhist rites, and the painting record identifies the principal image as Maitreya.

1112506200001.description: These two stone inscriptions stand beside Cheongmot, the reservoir that has been in use since the Silla period, and record the construction, repair, and reinstatement of the embankment over different periods. One inscription records the original construction in 536 and later repair in 798, while the other records its re-erection in 1688.

1112512180001.title_en: Five-story Stone Pagoda at Bowonsa Temple Site, Seosan
1112512180001.description: This pagoda was built in the mid-10th century, during the reign of King Gwangjong of Goryeo, and is an important benchmark for dating Korean stone pagodas. Its two-tiered stylobate has realistically carved lion figures on the lower level and graceful Eight Guardian Deities on the upper level, showing both continuity with late Unified Silla traditions and new Goryeo-period techniques.

1112512180002.title_en: Five-story Stone Pagoda at Gaesimsa Temple Site, Yecheon
1112512180002.description: This Goryeo-period stone pagoda was erected in 1011, and its 190-character inscription provides detailed information on the construction process and historical context. The pagoda is notable for its reliefs of the Twelve Zodiac Deities, Eight Guardian Deities, and Vajra Warriors, which make it an outstanding example of Goryeo stone pagoda sculpture.

1112604220001.title_en: Bronze Bell of Bongseonsa Temple, Namyangju
1112604220001.description: This bell was made in 1469 at the request of King Yejong to pray for the repose of King Sejo, and was originally dedicated to Bongseonsa Temple near Sejo’s royal tomb, Gwangneung. Its form combines elements of Chinese bells, such as the dragon-shaped knop and hemispherical top, with traditional Korean features including bodhisattva reliefs, the six-syllable light mantra, and wave patterns.

1123100110700.title_en: Bronze Bell Made by Sa-in Bi-gu - Uiwang Cheonggyesa Temple Bell
1123100110700.description: This bronze Buddhist temple bell was made in 1701 during the reign of King Sukjong of Joseon by the monk-craftsman Sa-in Bi-gu, who was active in Gyeonggi-do and Gyeongsang-do. It is a large bell with dragon-shaped suspension loops, floral bands, lotus-shaped bosses, and an inscription identifying its maker and date. The bell shows both the traditional Korean bell form and features influenced by Chinese bell styles.

1122300110800.title_en: Bronze Bell Made by Sa-in Bi-gu - Ganghwa Bell
1122300110800.description: This bronze Buddhist temple bell was made in 1711 by the monk-craftsman Sa-in Bi-gu during the reign of King Sukjong of Joseon. It is a large bell with paired dragon-shaped suspension loops, a rounded upper section, lotus bosses, and an inscription recording its date of production. The work shows that in his later years Sa-in Bi-gu also produced bells following Chinese-style bell forms.

1123100120000.title_en: Five-Story Stone Pagoda at Dongsa Temple Site, Hanam
1123100120000.description: This five-story stone pagoda at the Dongsa Temple site in Hanam, Gyeonggi-do stands on a two-tiered base with a five-story body. Its first-story body stone is made in two tiers, and the pagoda uses reduced roof-stone supports and a tapered profile characteristic of early Goryeo stone pagodas. It is thought to date to the late 10th century.

1123100130000.title_en: Three-Story Stone Pagoda at Dongsa Temple Site, Hanam
1123100130000.description: This three-story stone pagoda at the Dongsa Temple site in Hanam, Gyeonggi-do stands on a two-tiered base with a three-story body. The body stones are carved with pillar forms, and the roof stones have sharply upturned corners that give the pagoda a light appearance. Its style preserves typical late Silla stone-pagoda features and suggests a date no later than the middle Goryeo period.

1123100140000.title_en: Stele for King Jingak at Changsungsa Temple Site, Suwon
1123100140000.description: This stele records the life of King Jingak and originally stood at the Changsungsa Temple site. The inscription says that after entering Buddhist life at age 13, he practiced at several temples, repaired Buseoksa Temple, and died at age 76 in Sobaeksan. The stele was erected in 1386, the year after his death, and is a simplified example of late Goryeo stele style.

1123300150000.title_en: Sacheonwang Stone Lantern at Beopjusa Temple, Boeun
1123300150000.description: This stone lantern stands to the west of Palsangjeon Hall at Beopjusa Temple and has an octagonal plan. It consists of a lower base, a middle support, a lantern chamber carved with four guardian kings on four sides, and a roof stone. The refined carving and balanced proportions make it representative of Unified Silla stone lanterns.

1123300160000.title_en: Stele for Grand Master Daegi at Eokjeongsa Temple Site, Chungju
1123300160000.description: This stele commemorates Grand Master Daegi and was preserved at the Eokjeongsa Temple site. It has a simple form with a rectangular base and a stele body whose upper corners are cut diagonally; the four sides of the body bear inscriptions in regular script. The inscription records Daegi's life from his birth in 1328 to his death in 1390 and was written by Bak Euiju, with calligraphy by Seonjin and carving by Hye-gong.

1123300170000.title_en: Stele for Grand Master Beopgyeong at Jeongtosa Temple Site, Chungju
1123300170000.description: This stele was erected at the Jeongtosa Temple site to honor the late Silla and early Goryeo monk Beopgyeong. The monument is well preserved and includes a turtle-shaped base and a dragon carving on the headstone, with the name 'Beopgyeong Daesa' inscribed on the front. It was erected in 943, two years after his death, and the inscription was written by Choe Eon-wi with calligraphy by Gu Juk-dal.

1123400180000.title_en: Nine-Story Stone Pagoda of Seojeong-ri, Cheongyang
1123400180000.description: This stone pagoda stands in an open field about 23 km from Gongju toward Cheongyang. It has a two-tiered base with nine stories above it, and the ornamentation on the lower base shows stylistic features of the Goryeo period. It is thought to have been built in the early Goryeo period.

1123400190000.title_en: Five-Story Stone Pagoda at Seongjusa Temple Site, Boryeong
1123400190000.description: This pagoda stands in front of the presumed site of the main hall at the former Seongjusa Temple, which now remains only as a temple site. It has a two-tiered base and five stories above, with a typical late Unified Silla form and a separate supporting stone under the first story. It is believed to date to the late Unified Silla period.

1123400200000.title_en: Three-Story Stone Pagoda at the Central Site of Seongjusa Temple, Boryeong
1123400200000.description: This is the middle of the three stone pagodas standing side by side at the former Seongjusa Temple site. It has a two-tiered base and three stories above, and the first-story body stone is much larger than those above, with a door design carved on one side. It is considered a work of the late Unified Silla period.

1123400210000.title_en: Stele Commemorating the Merits of Liu Renyuan, Buyeo
1123400210000.description: This stele was erected to honor the achievements of the Tang general Liu Renyuan. The body and capstone are made from a single stone, and the capstone is decorated with six realistic dragon carvings. The inscription says it was set up in 663, during the reign of King Munmu of Unified Silla.

1123500220000.title_en: Stone Pillar of Geumsansa Temple, Gimje
1123500220000.description: This unusual stone pillar stands on the path between Daejeokgwangjeon Hall and the Daejanggak at Geumsansa Temple, and its exact use is unknown. It has a square pedestal-like form with layered supports and lotus ornament, and a finial-like top reminiscent of a pagoda. It is thought to date to the early Goryeo period.

1123500230000.title_en: Stone Lotus Throne of Geumsansa Temple, Gimje
1123500230000.description: This large stone lotus throne is a rare type of stone pedestal for a Buddha image. It is carved from a single stone but is organized into upper, middle, and lower sections, with a flat top, hexagonal middle section, and lotus-patterned lower section. It is believed to have been made around the transition from Unified Silla to Goryeo.

1123500240000.title_en: Stele of Master Hye-deok, Geumsansa Temple, Gimje
1123500240000.description: This memorial stele was erected at Geumsansa Temple to honor Master Hye-deok. The base is carved with a turtle, while the body of the stele is decorated with vine patterns. The inscription states that it was set up in 1111, after Hye-deok's death.

1123500250000.title_en: Five-Story Stone Pagoda of Geumsansa Temple, Gimje
1123500250000.description: This pagoda stands on a high platform called Songdae in the northern part of Geumsansa Temple, with a reliquary platform behind it. It has a two-tiered base and five stories above, and the sixth section functions as a support for the finial, a form not commonly seen in other pagodas. It is a Goryeo-period work that follows the basic form of Unified Silla stone pagodas.

1123500260000.description: This stone stupa-like structure stands in the Songdae precinct of Geumsansa, beside the five-story stone pagoda. It is interpreted as a sarira platform because of the carved figures on the base, the stone railing, and the Four Heavenly Kings placed at the corners. It is believed to be an early Goryeo work and is regarded as the oldest stone bell-shaped pagoda in Korea.

1123500270000.title_en: Gimje Geumsansa Hexagonal Multi-Story Stone Pagoda
1123500270000.description: This pagoda was moved from Bongcheonwon, a Geumsansa-affiliated hermitage, to its present location left of Daejeokgwangjeon. It is made of black and white slate rather than the usual square granite and has a hexagonal plan. Based on the carving style of the body and roof stones, it is thought to date to the early Goryeo period.

1123500280000.description: These stone banner posts stand facing each other inside the Geumsansa precinct and are 3.5 meters high. The posts preserve the foundation stones and the round support for the banner pole between them, and the pole holes are cut at three levels on each post, a feature typical of Unified Silla. They are considered a highly complete example of dangganjiju from the late 8th century.

1123500290000.title_en: Gimje Geumsansa Simwonam Three-Story Stone Pagoda
1123500290000.description: This pagoda stands near the top of a mountain north of Simwonam in Geumsansa. It has a two-tiered base and three stories above it, with broad roof stones and gently upturned eaves that reflect Goryeo-period style. Because it was located deep in the mountains, the pagoda survives in nearly complete condition.

1123500300000.description: This pagoda stands at the site of Manboksa, a temple said to have been founded by the monk Doseon in the Goryeo period. Only the first four stories remain, and the base is buried below the current ground level. A reliquary was found in the first-story body stone during repairs in 1968, and the pagoda is thought to date to the 11th century.

1123500310000.description: This stone pedestal for a Buddhist image stands at the Manboksaji temple site. It is carved from a single large stone into upper, middle, and lower sections, and its hexagonal form is unusual. The ornament of flowers within the pavilions on the lower section reflects a style popular in the Goryeo period, and it is thought to date to around the 11th century.

1123500320000.description: These stone banner posts stand facing east and west at the Manboksaji temple site. The banner pole itself no longer remains, but three holes for fixing it are preserved. The posts are plain and roughly finished, and their simplified form indicates an early Goryeo work.

1123500330000.description: This sarira stupa stands to the right of Geungnakjeon in Silsangsa and enshrines the remains of Master Sucheol. Sucheol, a late Silla monk who became the second founder of Silsangsa, died in 893, and the stupa is believed to have been built around that time. It follows the typical octagonal form of late Silla monk stupas and preserves carvings of clouds, dragons, lions, the Four Heavenly Kings, and roof tiles.

1123700520000.title_en: East and West Three-story Stone Pagodas of Seodong-ri, Bonghwa
1123700520000.description: These two pagodas stand facing each other east and west inside Chunyang Middle School and form a pair. They are built on a two-tier base with three stories of a stone body, and were dismantled and restored in 1962 after being found leaning and partly buried in the ground.

1123700540000.description: These are the two stone posts that supported a temple banner pole at the entrance to a temple site. The outer faces are decorated with vertical bands and recessed panels, while the inner faces are plain except for grooves near the top and bottom for fixing the pole.

1123700560000.title_en: Five-story Brick Pagoda of Unheung-dong, Andong
1123700560000.description: This brick pagoda stands in the precincts of Andong Station and is built of unornamented bricks in five stories. Each storey has a niche, and the second-story south face has two guardian figures carved in relief; it is thought to be the brick pagoda of Beomnimsa mentioned in old records.

1123700570000.title_en: Five-story Brick Pagoda of Jotap-ri, Andong
1123700570000.description: This pagoda is an unusual brick-and-granite structure from the Unified Silla period. A rammed-earth base supports the first story of granite masonry, and the upper stories are built in brick with niches on the south faces of the second and fourth stories.

1123700580000.title_en: Stone Seated Tathagata Buddha of Angi-dong, Andong
1123700580000.description: Only the body and pedestal of this Buddha statue survive; the head was attached later. The right hand rests on the right knee with the fingers touching the ground in bhumisparsha mudra, and the balanced posture and soft drapery suggest a late Unified Silla work.

1123700590000.title_en: Dangganjiju of Suksusa Temple Site, Yeongju
1123700590000.description: These are the stone posts that supported a banner pole at the entrance to a temple. They stand in the pine grove at the entrance to Sosu Seowon, and their simple form and refined carving indicate a Unified Silla-period work.

1123700600000.title_en: Stone Standing Buddha of Yeongjudong, Yeongju
1123700600000.description: This nearly complete Buddhist statue was carved in one stone together with the halo, and it was moved from an old temple site to its present location. Its broad shoulders, thick limbs, and heavy face give it a strong, forceful appearance, and it is generally dated to the late Unified Silla period.

1123700610000.title_en: Sarira Pagoda of Bulguksa Temple, Gyeongju
1123700610000.description: This sarira pagoda is preserved in a protective shelter behind the lecture hall of Bulguksa Temple. Its form resembles a stone lantern, with a pedestal, a cylindrical body containing niches with Buddha and Bodhisattva reliefs, and a roof stone; it was returned from Tokyo in 1933 after being taken out of Korea in 1905.

1123500340000.title_en: Stupa Monument of Sucteol Hwasang, Silsangsa Temple, Namwon
1123500340000.description: This stupa monument at Silsangsa Temple records the life of Sucteol Hwasang, a late Unified Silla Buddhist monk. The inscription says he died in 893, and it records the circumstances of the erection of his reliquary stupa. The monument is heavily worn and damaged, and its construction date is thought to be in the reign of King Hyogong.

1123500350000.title_en: Stone Lantern of Silsangsa Temple, Namwon
1123500350000.description: This stone lantern stands in the front courtyard of Bogwangmyeon Hall at Silsangsa Temple. It has an eight-sided plan with a three-tiered base, a fire chamber with openings on all eight sides, and an ornate roof stone and finial. Its decorative style suggests a mid-9th-century date in the late Unified Silla period.

1123500360000.title_en: Monk's Stupa of Silsangsa Temple, Namwon
1123500360000.description: This stupa was built for the relics of Monk Hongcheok and follows the typical eight-sided, baldachin-type form. Its base and roof stones are simply decorated, and the body stone is plain except for a shallow door on one side. It is generally dated to the early Goryeo period, while continuing the Unified Silla style.

1123500370000.title_en: East and West Three-Story Stone Pagodas of Silsangsa Temple, Namwon
1123500370000.description: These twin pagodas stand to the east and west in the courtyard in front of Bogwangjeon Hall, the main hall of Silsangsa Temple. Both are built on two-tiered bases with three-story bodies, and their finials are unusually well preserved. They are regarded as outstanding late Unified Silla works made at the same time.

1123500380000.title_en: Stupa of Great Master Jeunggak, Silsangsa Temple, Namwon
1123500380000.description: This octagonal stupa enshrines the relics of Monk Hongcheok, who was given the posthumous title Jeunggak. It is a typical octagonal reliquary stupa, with relief figures of the Four Heavenly Kings on the body stones and a roof stone shaped like wooden architecture. It is thought to date to the late 9th century.

1123500390000.title_en: Stupa Monument of Great Master Jeunggak, Silsangsa Temple, Namwon
1123500390000.description: This stupa monument at Silsangsa Temple commemorates Great Master Jeunggak, also known as Hongcheok Guksa or Namhan Josea. Only the tortoise pedestal and capstone remain, and the capstone is noted for its refined carving in the tradition of the King Muyeol stele in Gyeongju. It is considered a mid-9th-century work and a classic form of Korean stone steles.

1123500400000.title_en: Stone Lantern of Baekjangam Hermitage, Silsangsa Temple, Namwon
1123500400000.description: This stone lantern stands near the southern foot of Baekjangam Hermitage at Silsangsa Temple, beside the three-story stone pagoda there. It retains the basic octagonal form of late Unified Silla stone lanterns, with lotus petals carved on the base and a large finial above the roof stone. It is believed to have been built in the 9th century.

1123500410000.title_en: Seated Iron Buddha of Silsangsa Temple, Namwon
1123500410000.description: This seated iron Buddha is a representative late Unified Silla work and has been preserved at Silsangsa Temple since the temple's founding. It shows the characteristic features of 9th-century Buddhist sculpture, including a narrow forehead, downcast eyes, a restrained expression, and heavy robe folds. The statue is considered important as a transitional work between the more energetic 8th-century images and the softer, less tense figures of the 9th century.

1123500420000.title_en: Stone Standing Buddha of Yongdamsaji Temple Site, Namwon
1123500420000.description: This large stone standing Buddha and its halo are carved in high relief on a single stone and reach a height of about 6 meters. The statue has a tall usnisa, broad shoulders and chest, and a natural-stone pedestal, and it belongs to the large-scale Buddha type popular in early Goryeo sculpture.

1123500430000.title_en: Stone Standing Buddha of Manboksaji Temple Site, Namwon
1123500430000.description: This granite standing Buddha at the former site of Manboksa Temple is about 2 meters high and is thought to have been made when the temple was founded. The halo is divided into a head halo and body halo, and the figure shows a gentle face and soft drapery, although some parts of the pose and robe are somewhat awkward.

1123500450000.title_en: Stone Seated Buddha of Yeondong-ri, Iksan
1123500450000.description: This Baekje statue survives with the Buddha body, pedestal, and halo intact, though the head is a modern replacement. It has broad shoulders, a balanced body, and a refined halo with lotus motifs and seven small seated Buddhas on the outer band.

1123500460000.title_en: Stone Standing Buddhas of Godori, Iksan
1123500460000.description: These two stone standing Buddha figures stand about 200 meters apart and are carved into trapezoidal stone pillars with only the face, hands, and pedestal indicated. The statues are highly stylized and resemble stone guardian figures, reflecting the restrained large-scale stone Buddha style of the Goryeo period.

1123400470000.title_en: West Three-story Stone Pagoda at Seongjusa Temple Site, Boryeong
1123400470000.description: This pagoda stands on the western side of a row of three pagodas at the former site of Seongjusa Temple. It has a two-tiered base, a separate supporting stone under the first-story body stone, and a roof stone with slightly upturned corners, showing a late Unified Silla style that anticipates Goryeo pagodas.

1123600490000.title_en: Stone Danggan Outside Dongjeommun Gate, Naju
1123600490000.description: This stone danggan, or flagpole, is a rare example in which the pole itself survives along with the supporting stones. The pole is made of five interlocked stones, narrows upward, and is topped with an octagonal ornamental canopy and jewel finial.

1123600500000.title_en: Three-story Stone Pagoda Outside Bukmangmun Gate, Naju
1123600500000.description: This three-story stone pagoda was moved from its original location outside Naju's north gate to the grounds of Simhyangsa Temple. It has a two-tiered base, three body stories with decreasing proportions, and surviving head components including the lotus-bowl-shaped finial base and lotus-bowl ornament, and it is believed to date to the late Goryeo period.

1123700510000.title_en: Three-story Stone Pagoda of Naehwa-ri, Mungyeong
1123700510000.description: This small and neat three-story stone pagoda stands in a deep mountain valley in Mungyeong. It was found with its parts scattered and was restored in 1960; it has a single-tier base, three body stories, and only the square finial base remaining.

1123700620000.title_en: Rock-carved Standing Triad of Amitabha Buddha, Seoak-dong, Gyeongju
1123700620000.description: This 7th-century triad was carved on a large cliff near the summit of Seondosan, with a tall standing Amitabha Buddha in the center and Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva and Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva on either side. Although the central figure is badly damaged, the work shows the transitional style from the Three Kingdoms period to Unified Silla Buddhist sculpture.

1123700630000.title_en: Stone Standing Triad of Buddha, Baedong, Gyeongju
1123700630000.description: This stone triad was gathered and re-erected at its present location in 1923 after being found scattered at the foot of Namsan, Gyeongju. The central Buddha and the two attendant bodhisattvas share a common style and are believed to have originally been made as a single triad in the 7th century.

1123700640000.title_en: Stone Water Basin of Beomunsa Temple Site, Gyeongju
1123700640000.description: This stone basin remains at the site known as Beomunsa Temple Site, where other Buddhist remains such as a main hall site, twin pagodas, a banner-pole support, and a lantern base were also found. It is a plain, undecorated water container carved from a single block of stone and is thought to date to the Unified Silla period.

1123700650000.title_en: Three-story Stone Pagoda of Seoak-dong, Gyeongju
1123700650000.description: This pagoda belongs to the stone-brick style of pagodas that imitate brick pagodas built of fired clay bricks. It has a distinctive base made of eight cubical stones stacked in two tiers, and its simplified form suggests a late Unified Silla date.

1123700660000.description: This stone ice storage stands on the northern rampart of Banwolseong in Gyeongju and was used to store ice. An inscription records that Jo Myeong-gyeom rebuilt it in stone in 1738 during the reign of King Yeongjo, and moved it to its present location four years later.

1123700670000.title_en: Three-story Stone Pagoda of Hyohyeon-dong, Gyeongju
1123700670000.description: This pagoda stands on a two-tiered stylobate with three stories of the main body above it. Its refined details and the structure of the roof stones are characteristic of stone pagodas from around the 9th century in Unified Silla.

1123700680000.title_en: Stele for Son Si-yang, the Filial Son, Hwangnam-dong, Gyeongju
1123700680000.description: This stele records the circumstances under which a memorial gate was erected to honor Son Si-yang, a Goryeo-period man praised for his filial devotion. The stele dates to 1182 and is unusual in having a simple square-pillar form rather than the more typical stele structure.

1123700690000.title_en: Dangganjiju of Mangdeoksa Temple Site, Gyeongju
1123700690000.description: These two stone banner-pole supports stand facing each other at the west side of the Mangdeoksa Temple Site. They are thought to have been made when the temple was founded in 685 during the reign of King Sinmun of Unified Silla.

1123700700000.description: This turtle pedestal stands across the road south of the King Taejong Muyeol Royal Tomb in Seoak-ri, Gyeongju. Based on records in the Samguk sagi and a stone fragment found at Yeonggyoru of Seoak Seowon, it is thought to have supported a stele commemorating the achievements of Kim Inmun (629–694). It preserves an early form of Korean stele pedestal, with a turtle head rather than a dragon head.

1123800710000.description: Three stone Buddhist figures remain in Daesangol village, forming a single group. The flanking images are believed to have been attendant bodhisattvas, while the central seated figure is identified as a Goryeo-period Buddha by the style of its halo. The group reflects localized Goryeo stone bodhisattva and Buddha sculpture, with a two-tier pedestal and lotus designs.

1123800720000.title_en: East Three-story Stone Pagoda of Dansoksa Temple Site, Sancheong
1123800720000.description: This is the eastern pagoda standing in front of the main hall site at the Dansoksa Temple site. It is a typical Unified Silla stone pagoda with a two-tier base and three-story body. The proportions are balanced and the upper levels diminish appropriately, showing the late Unified Silla style.

1123800730000.title_en: West Three-story Stone Pagoda of Dansoksa Temple Site, Sancheong
1123800730000.description: This is the western pagoda standing in front of the main hall site at the Dansoksa Temple site. Although it follows the typical Unified Silla pattern of a two-tier base and three-story body, it has suffered heavy damage, and the reliquary once enshrined inside was stolen. Details such as the narrow eaves and the gradual reduction in size upward show the late Unified Silla tradition.

1123800740000.title_en: National Jangsaeng Stele of Tongdosa Temple, Yangsan
1123800740000.description: This is one of the jangsaeng markers set up at twelve points around Tongdosa Temple to mark the temple boundary. The inscription states that it was erected by royal order, and it is carved on the rough natural surface of the stone. It was made in 1085, the second year of King Seonjong of Goryeo.

1123800750000.title_en: Maitreya Buddha Seated in Relief on a Cliff, Songhyeon-dong, Changnyeong
1123800750000.description: This Buddha image is carved in relief on a large rock face, using the rock itself as the halo. The rounded face, broad shoulders, and thin robe closely follow the style of the main Buddha of Seokguram, but the form is less realistic and more subdued. The hand gesture is the earth-touching mudra, symbolizing the subjugation of evil.

1123200760000.title_en: Danggan Flagpole Supports of Ghunhwa-dong, Chuncheon
1123200760000.description: These are the two stone supports that held a danggan flagpole at a temple entrance. A two-tier base stands between the supports, and the upper tier is carved with sixteen lotus petals. The simple form and carving style suggest a mid-Goryeo work.

1123200770000.description: This pagoda stands in the center of Chuncheon. Excavation showed that it originally consisted of a two-tier base and a seven-story body, and the upper level was likely associated with Chungwonsa Temple. It was heavily damaged during the Korean War, but later restoration recovered the base section; the style suggests a mid-Goryeo date.

1123200780000.title_en: Wongakguksa Stupa Stele at Geodonsa Temple Site, Wonju
1123200780000.description: This stupa stele at the Geodonsa temple site records the deeds of Wongakguksa, a Goryeo-period monk. The inscription includes his life, accomplishments, and a eulogy praising his virtue. It was erected in 1025, and the inscription was written by Choe Chung and engraved by Kim Geo-ung.

1123200790000.title_en: Three-Story Stone Pagoda at Hoengseong-ri, Hongcheon
1123200790000.description: This is a typical Goryeo-period three-story stone pagoda consisting of a single-tiered base and three bodies. It was moved from behind Hongcheon Elementary School to its present location, and its roof stones have already been broken. The simplified carving style suggests it was made after the middle Goryeo period.

1123200800000.description: These are the two stone posts that supported a temple flagpole at the entrance to a Buddhist temple. No record remains for the site, but many roof tile fragments found nearby suggest it was once a temple site. They are plain in form and are thought to date to the middle Goryeo period.

1123200810000.title_en: Stone Seated Bodhisattva from Hansongsa Temple Site, Gangneung
1123200810000.description: This incomplete bodhisattva statue, now kept at Gangneung Municipal Museum, is missing its head and right arm. Despite the damage, it shows a lively and three-dimensional carving style, and its unusual seated posture is characteristic of bodhisattva images. It is considered an excellent Goryeo work similar in style to the National Treasure bodhisattva from the same temple site.

1123200820000.description: These flagpole supports remain at their original location in central Gangneung, where the area is believed to have been a temple site. No associated records survive, and the supports are simple and unadorned. Their plain form and construction indicate an early stage of development in this type.

1123200830000.description: These flagpole supports stand in what is now a residential area in Okcheon-dong, Gangneung, though the site is thought to have been a temple precinct. An inscription on the east support records repairs made in 1508 and 1817. The supports are rough and simple, with no decorative carving.

1123200840000.title_en: Stone Seated Bodhisattva from Sinboksa Temple Site, Gangneung
1123200840000.description: This bodhisattva statue is shown offering worship toward the three-story stone pagoda at Sinboksa Temple Site. It sits with the left leg raised and the right leg bent beneath the body, and its hands are held at the chest. The rounded, heavy carving style and simplified ornaments reflect early Goryeo features.

1123200850000.title_en: Monk’s Stupa at Gulsansa Temple Site, Gangneung
1123200850000.description: This stupa is believed to enshrine the relics of Beomil Guksa, who founded Gulsansa during the Goryeo period. It is built mainly on an octagonal plan and includes a base, body, roof stone, and finial elements. The middle support stone is carved with eight heavenly musicians playing different instruments.

1123200860000.title_en: Dangganjiju of Gulsansa Temple Site, Gangneung
1123200860000.description: These are the largest dangganjiju in Korea, standing at the former site of Gulsansa Temple, said to have been founded in 847 by Buddhist monk Beomil during the reign of King Munseong of Silla. The two stone pillars are undecorated, with rough tool marks left on the lower surfaces and holes for fixing the banner pole on both upper and lower parts.

1123200870000.title_en: Three-story Stone Pagoda of Sinboksa Temple Site, Gangneung
1123200870000.description: This three-story stone pagoda remains at the former site of Sinboksa Temple, a temple traditionally said to have been founded by Beomil in the Unified Silla period. It stands on a two-tiered base and has unusual features such as lotus-carved upper base stones, three-faced reliefs on the lower base, and a rare, largely intact finial.

1123600880000.title_en: Bronze Bell with Inscription of Tapsansa Temple
1123600880000.description: This bronze bell, made in the Goryeo period, is 79 cm high and 43 cm in mouth diameter. It retains the traditional form inherited from Silla bells while showing late Goryeo features such as a realistic dragon-shaped suspension loop, floral bands, and a decorated body with a triad relief.

1123600890000.title_en: Seated Stone Sakyamuni Buddha of Dogapsa Temple, Yeongam
1123600890000.description: This stone Buddha is enshrined in Mireukjeon Hall at Dogapsa Temple in Yeongam, and the body and mandorla were carved from a single stone. The face is oval with strong features, while the simplified drapery and carved halo with small seated Buddhas reflect mid-Goryeo stone Buddhist sculpture that inherits Unified Silla forms.

1123600900000.title_en: Volume 9–10 of the Commentary on the Mahaparinirvana Sutra
1123600900000.description: This is a woodblock-printed Buddhist text consisting of volumes 9 and 10 bound as one book, printed on paper. It was re-engraved in the Jogyeong Dogam during the reign of King Sejo in 1461 based on the Gyojang edition, and is valued as an important source for both Buddhist scripture studies and Korean print history.

1123100910000.title_en: Three-story Stone Pagoda of Changni, Yeoju
1123100910000.description: This pagoda was moved in 1958 from the site of an old temple in Changni to its present location. It has a two-tiered base, unusually thick components, and features such as reliefs of eye-shaped motifs and three-step supports under the roof stones that are characteristic of mid-Goryeo stone pagodas.

1123100920000.title_en: Three-story Stone Pagoda of Hari, Yeoju
1123100920000.description: This pagoda was moved in 1958 from an old temple site in Hari to its present location. It stands on a single-tier base and has a distinctive reliquary cavity in the first-story body stone, along with four-step supports under the roof stones and a calm, regular form associated with the middle Goryeo period.

1123100930000.title_en: Rock-carved Standing Twin Buddhas of Yongmiri, Paju
1123100930000.description: Two standing Buddhas were carved into a huge natural rock face, each wearing a stone hat that gives the composition a local character. The left figure wears a round hat and holds a lotus, while the right figure wears a square hat and joins both hands; the site is also associated with a birth legend from the Goryeo period.

1123300940000.title_en: Saja Binninsa Temple Site Nine-Story Stone Pagoda, Jecheon
1123300940000.description: This Goryeo-period pagoda stands at the site of Binninsa Temple and was originally a nine-story structure. The surviving pagoda body now retains roof stones up to the fourth tier, and the inscription on the lower base records its construction in 1022. It is notable for the four stone lions on the upper base supporting the pagoda body and for the seated Buddha images placed between them.

1123300950000.description: This pagoda survives at the site where stone Buddhas and a rock-cut cave were once made in the Goryeo period. It has a simple lower base of roughly worked stones, with only the first-story roof stone composed of two stones and the rest made of single stones.

1123300960000.description: This standing Buddha is a large Goryeo-period stone image related in style to other major early Goryeo Buddhas made in the region. It was assembled from five stone blocks, with a thin stone used as the headdress, and shows a round face, arched eyebrows, long eyes, and thick lips.

1123300970000.title_en: Rock-Carved Pair of Seated Buddhas, Wonpung-ri, Goesan
1123300970000.description: This rare rock carving shows two Buddhas seated side by side in a large hollowed-out cliff face about 12 meters high. The faces are rounded and smiling, while the body forms are simplified and formalized; small Buddha figures are carved on the halo behind them.

1123300980000.description: This seated Buddha is an iron image about 0.98 meters high and is related in style to the iron seated Buddha at Dahnosa Temple. Its sharp snail-shell curls, triangular face, and symmetrical robe folds create a severe and restrained appearance, and it is thought to date to the early Goryeo period.

1123400990000.title_en: Dangganjiju of Cheonheungsa Temple Site, Cheonan
1123400990000.description: These are the two stone posts that supported the flagpole used for temple rituals at Cheonheungsa Temple, which was founded in 921. The two uprights stand on a two-tier base, and the outer surfaces are decorated with a central vertical line and lotus-shaped ornamentation around the base.

1123401000000.title_en: Stone Standing Buddha Triad, Anguksa Temple Site, Dangjin
1123401000000.description: This stone triad stands at the site of Anguksa Temple, a ruined temple site that was later rebuilt in 1929 and then abandoned again. The main Buddha and attendant bodhisattvas show a large, block-like style with a large square headdress, simplified bodily form, and unusual arm placement, reflecting a Goryeo regional style.

1123401010000.title_en: Stone Pagoda, Anguksa Temple Site, Dangjin
1123401010000.description: This pagoda stands at the site of Anguksa Temple, which was probably founded in the Goryeo period and later fell into ruin. Only the first-story body remains, while the upper stories have disappeared and the roof stones are stacked above it; the first-story body has pillar motifs, a door on one side, and seated Buddha reliefs on the other sides.

1123401020000.title_en: Stone Water Basin at Bawonsa Temple Site, Seosan
1123401020000.description: This is a rectangular stone water basin carved from a single block of granite at the site of Bawonsa Temple in Seosan. It is large in scale and has no decoration, with only a circular drain hole on one side of the flat bottom. Its plain workmanship and size suggest the scale of the temple in the Unified Silla period.

1123401030000.title_en: Flagpole Supports at Bawonsa Temple Site, Seosan
1123401030000.description: These are the stone supports for a temple flagpole at the former site of Bawonsa Temple. The two pillars stand facing each other with a rectangular base stone between them, and the inner faces have square holes for securing the pole. Their decorated but restrained form is generally dated to the late Unified Silla period.

1123401050000.title_en: Stupa of State Preceptor Beobin at Bawonsa Temple Site, Seosan
1123401050000.description: This stone stupa enshrines the relics of Beobin, the State Preceptor Tanmun, who died at Bawonsa Temple in 975. The octagonal base, body, roof stones, and finial are elaborately carved with lions, dragons, guardian figures, and floral motifs. It is thought to have been built between 975 and 978 and reflects early Goryeo-period style.

1123401060000.title_en: Stele for State Preceptor Beobin at Bawonsa Temple Site, Seosan
1123401060000.description: This stele commemorates Beobin, the State Preceptor, and records that he became a national preceptor in 974 and died the following year. The stele rests on a turtle-shaped pedestal with a dragon-like head, and the stele head is carved with dragons and cloud motifs. It was erected in 978 during the reign of King Gyeongjong.

1123401070000.title_en: Stele for Great Seon Master Daebogwang at Bogwangsa Temple Site, Buyeo
1123401070000.description: This stele was erected to commemorate the reconstruction of Bogwangsa Temple in Imcheon-myeon, Buyeo, and records the achievements of Wonmyeong Guksa Chunggam, who led the project. The inscription was carved on the front in 1358 and later added to on the back in 1750. Only the stele body remains, with vine patterns carved around its edges.

1123401080000.title_en: Stone Seated Tathagata Buddha at Jeongnimsa Temple Site, Buyeo
1123401080000.description: This stone Buddhist statue remains at the Jeongnimsa Temple Site in Buyeo, facing the Five-Story Stone Pagoda. The head and crown were likely re-made later, and much of the body is severely damaged, making detailed style hard to determine. The octagonal pedestal is more carefully made than the statue itself, and the figure is thought to represent Vairocana Buddha.

1122401090000.title_en: Five-Story Stone Pagoda at Seonggeosa Temple Site, Gwangju
1122401090000.description: This early Goryeo stone pagoda stands in Gwangju Park, where the area is said to have been the site of Seonggeosa Temple. It has a single-tiered base and a five-story body, showing the shift from Unified Silla to Goryeo pagoda styles. The first-story body is made from five stones divided into upper and lower sections, a form often seen in Goryeo pagodas.

1122401100000.title_en: Five-Story Stone Pagoda in Jisan-dong, Gwangju
1122401100000.description: This is the eastern of two pagodas standing some distance apart in the city of Gwangju. It is a late Unified Silla pagoda with a two-tiered base and five-story body, preserving the basic form of Silla stone pagodas. A reliquary and reliquary container were discovered during repairs in 1955.

1123601110000.title_en: Stone Lantern of Gaeseonsa Temple Site, Damyang
1123601110000.description: This stone lantern, long buried, was recently reassembled after the ground was excavated and the displaced parts were整理ed. An inscription between the window openings states that it was made in 891, the 5th year of Queen Jinseong of Unified Silla, making it the only surviving Silla stone lantern with an inscription.

1123601120000.title_en: Three-Story Stone Pagoda of Jungheung Mountain Fortress, Gwangyang
1123601120000.description: This three-story stone pagoda stands on the west side of a stream at Jungheung Mountain Fortress and is associated with the site of Jungheungsa Temple. The base, body, and roof stones are richly carved, including figures on the lower platform and Buddha images on the first story, showing a well-preserved Unified Silla pagoda style.

1123701130000.title_en: Three-Story Stone Pagoda of Bonggiri, Cheongdo
1123701130000.description: This pagoda consists of a two-tiered base supporting a three-story body. Its upper and lower base stones each have two central pillars carved on the inner faces, a feature that shows it follows an early stone pagoda form of Unified Silla.

1123701140000.title_en: Three-Story Stone Pagoda of Pyeonghwadong, Andong
1123701140000.description: This three-story stone pagoda stands in Pyeonghwadong, Andong, where the traces of the temple site are no longer visible. The lower base has carved niches, the upper base has a sloping form unlike more conventional pagodas, and the remaining finial elements indicate a later Unified Silla date.

1123701150000.title_en: Rock-Carved Standing Buddha of Icheondong, Andong
1123701150000.description: This large Buddha image is carved into a natural rock face, with the body outlined in line and the head made separately and set above it. Traces of red pigment remain on the head and face, and the figure is considered an important example of the localized large-scale Buddhist sculpture of the Goryeo period.

1123701160000.title_en: Stone Standing Buddha of Seokgori, Yeongju
1123701160000.description: This standing Buddha was found partly buried, but restoration has revealed details such as the rounded feet and flowing robe folds. The figure has a high ushnisha, a refined face, and a form that is considered to belong to the Unified Silla period.

1123701170000.title_en: Three-Story Stone Pagoda of Hwadalli, Sangju
1123701170000.description: This pagoda stands west of the place said to be the royal tomb of ancient Sabalguk and consists of a single-tier base supporting three stories. The first-story body is unusually large, the roof stones have sharply upturned corners, and a headless seated Buddha placed beside the pagoda indicates that the site was once a temple precinct.

1123701180000.title_en: Stone Standing Buddha of Jeungchonri, Sangju
1123701180000.description: This standing Buddha, housed at Yonghwasa Temple in Sangju, is carved together with its halo from a single stone. Although heavily worn, the figure shows a neat body, a large ushnisha, and a restrained, somewhat rigid style characteristic of late Unified Silla stone standing Buddhas.

1123701270000.title_en: Flagpole Supports at Samrangsa Temple Site, Gyeongju
1123701270000.description: These flagpole supports are the stone uprights that held a banner pole at the entrance to a temple during religious ceremonies. The two supports now stand far apart, suggesting that only one may remain in its original position. Their carved vertical lines, curved upper ends, and central grooves are typical of Unified Silla workmanship.

1123801280000.title_en: Wongyeong Wangsa Stele at Banyasa Temple Site, Hapcheon
1123801280000.description: This stele was erected in honor of Wongyeong Wangsa and was moved from the former Banyasa Temple site to its present location at Haeinsa in 1961. It has a turtle-shaped base, stele body, and capstone, and the thin proportions of each part are a notable feature. According to the inscription, the stele was made in 1125, during the reign of King Injong of Goryeo.

1123801290000.title_en: East and West Three-Story Stone Pagodas at Wanggungsa Temple Site, Hapcheon
1123801290000.description: These paired pagodas stand east and west at the site of Wanggungsa Temple. Both are built on a two-tiered base with a three-story body, but the eastern pagoda uses more stone in its base while the western pagoda shows traces of later restoration after collapse. Their similar yet slightly different construction suggests that they were not made at exactly the same time.

1122401310000.title_en: Seated Iron Vairocana Buddha, Jeungsimsa Temple, Gwangju
1122401310000.description: This seated iron image represents Vairocana Buddha and was moved to Jeungsimsa Temple in 1934 from Donggye-ri, Seobang-myeon, Gwangju County. The halo and pedestal are lost, but the figure itself is largely complete, with a high topknot, a gentle smile, and drapery that falls in regular parallel folds. It is thought to date to the late Unified Silla period, around the 9th century.

1123601320000.title_en: East Five-Story Stone Pagoda of Hwaeomsa Temple, Gurye
1123601320000.description: This is the eastern of the paired pagodas standing in front of Daeungjeon Hall at Hwaeomsa Temple. It is a five-story stone pagoda on a single-tier base, and unlike the western pagoda it has no decorative carving. Based on its form and construction, it is thought to date to the 9th century of the Unified Silla period.

1123601330000.title_en: West Five-Story Stone Pagoda of Hwaeomsa Temple, Gurye
1123601330000.description: This pagoda stands to the west of the paired pagodas in front of Daeungjeon Hall at Hwaeomsa Temple. It has a two-tiered base and a five-story body, with elaborate carvings including the Twelve Divine Generals, the Eight Classes of Beings, and the Four Heavenly Kings. These protective figures show a clear intention to guard the relics enshrined within the pagoda, and the work is believed to date to around the 9th century.

1123601340000.description: This is a Buddhist ritual object made to store scripture scrolls. It was constructed by weaving thin bamboo strips with colored thread into a rectangular form, with silk triangular flaps and ties at the ends so the text could be rolled up. It is the only known surviving example of its kind in Korea.

1122201350000.title_en: Lotus, Cloud, and Dragon-Decorated Stupa at Sanggok-dong, Daegu
1122201350000.description: This octagonal monk’s stupa has a base, body, and roof finial, and it is currently displayed at the Kyungpook National University Museum. The lower and middle base stones are carved with lotus and cloud designs and four dragons, while the body has door-like panels and figures of the Four Heavenly Kings. It is thought to date to the early Goryeo period.

1123401500000.description: This pair of stone banner supports stood at the entrance of a temple to support the pole for a Buddhist banner. The inside faces are plain, while the outside faces have raised border bands; the bases and lower part of one pillar were heavily damaged during the Korean War. Based on the carved cushion motifs on the base stones, it is thought to date to Unified Silla.

1123601510000.title_en: Three-story Stone Pagoda of Yeon-goksa Temple, Gurye
1123601510000.description: This stone pagoda stands south of the main hall at Yeongoksa Temple and has a three-tiered base supporting a three-story body. The construction and stonework suggest a late Unified Silla date. The third-story roof stone was displaced and restored during dismantling and repair in 1967, when a gilt-bronze standing Buddha was found inside the upper base.

1123601520000.title_en: Stele for Venerable Hyeon-gak of Yeongoksa Temple, Gurye
1123601520000.description: This stele was erected at Yeongoksa Temple to honor the early Goryeo monk Venerable Hyeon-gak. The stele shaft is now lost, leaving only the pedestal and capstone. The inscription records that it was made in 979, the fourth year of King Gyeongjong of Goryeo.

1123601530000.title_en: East Stele for a Monastic Stupa of Yeongoksa Temple, Gurye
1123601530000.description: This stele stood in front of the eastern stupa at Yeongoksa Temple, which has three monk's reliquary stupas. The stele shaft is missing, and only the pedestal and capstone remain. Its modest scale and unconventional carving style show a Goryeo-period form different from Unified Silla examples.

1123601540000.title_en: Stupa of Venerable Soyo at Yeongoksa Temple, Gurye
1123601540000.description: This octagonal monk's stupa at Yeongoksa Temple houses the relics of Venerable Soyo. It has a three-tiered base with carved lotus motifs, a body stone with a door design and relief images of the Eight Classes of Dharma Protectors, and a roof stone decorated with floral ornaments at the corners. The inscription on the body stone shows that it was erected in 1650, the first year of King Hyojong of Joseon.

1123601550000.title_en: East Monk's Stupa of Borimsa Temple, Jangheung
1123601550000.description: This is the most distinguished of the monk's stupas standing in the forest east of Borimsa Temple. It has an octagonal base, body stone, roof stone, and finial; the body stone has a door design and the roof stone is relatively narrow and low. It was made in the late Unified Silla period and also shows features associated with the early Goryeo period.

1123601560000.title_en: West Monk's Stupas of Borimsa Temple, Jangheung
1123601560000.description: These two octagonal monk's stupas stand to the west of Borimsa Temple and were likely made in the Goryeo period. Both have three-tiered bases, body stones with door designs, roof stones with upturned corners, and complete finials. One was restored in 1944 after the relic container was looted in 1941.

1123601570000.title_en: Stupa of National Preceptor Bojo at Borimsa Temple, Jangheung
1123601570000.description: This octagonal stupa at Borimsa Temple holds the relics of Venerable Bojo. The base has highly relief-carved cloud motifs, the body stone has door designs on the front and back and the Four Heavenly Kings on the sides, and the roof stone shows carved rafters and roof tiles. It is a late Unified Silla work, though it was later restored after the relic container was stolen during the Japanese colonial period.

1123701190000.description: This stone seated Buddha statue was originally located at 358 Bokyong-dong, Sangju, and was moved to its present site in October 1975. The rounded face, narrow eyes, and small lips give it a calm, human expression, while the stylized drapery indicates a Goryeo-period work.

1123701200000.title_en: Stone Seated Medicine Buddha, Jeungchon-ri, Sangju
1123701200000.description: This 1.68-meter-tall stone Buddha statue is housed at Yonghwasa Temple in Sangju. Its left hand holds a medicine bowl, identifying it as a Medicine Buddha, and its compact, angular treatment of the face and body shows the transitional style of the late Unified Silla period.

1123701210000.title_en: Stone Four-directional Buddha, Gulbulsa Temple Site, Gyeongju
1123701210000.description: This rock-cut image at the Gulbulsa Temple Site in Gyeongju depicts the Buddha figures of the four directions: Amitabha to the west, Medicine Buddha to the east, Maitreya to the north, and Śākyamuni to the south. The varied carving techniques, including relief and intaglio, and the arrangement of standing and seated figures make it a distinctive early Unified Silla work.

1123701220000.title_en: Rock-carved Standing Amitabha Triad, Yuldong, Gyeongju
1123701220000.description: This rock-carved triad on the west-facing cliff of Byeokdosan in Gyeongju shows Amitabha in the center with Avalokitesvara and Mahasthamaprapta as attendants. It follows the style of the nearby Stone Four-directional Buddha at Gulbulsa Temple Site, and its rounded faces, slim bodies, and shallow drapery reflect Unified Silla-period sculpture.

1123701230000.title_en: Banner-pole Supports, Bomunsa Temple Site, Gyeongju
1123701230000.description: These stone supports held a banner pole used for Buddhist rites at the entrance of the temple. The pair stands at the southwest side of the Bomunsa Temple Site, and their small, slender, and restrained form is characteristic of Unified Silla stone works.

1123701240000.title_en: East and West Three-story Stone Pagodas, Namsandong, Gyeongju
1123701240000.description: This pair of pagodas in Gyeongju is unusual because the east pagoda follows a brick-style stone pagoda form while the west pagoda is a conventional three-story stone pagoda. They were built as a matched pair during the Unified Silla period, but each was made in a different style.

1123701250000.title_en: Stela for the Creation of Amitabha Buddha Statue, Mujangsa Temple Site, Gyeongju
1123701250000.description: This stele records in detail the creation of an Amitabha Buddha image commissioned by Queen Gyehwa, the wife of King Soseong of Silla, to pray for the king’s repose. The surviving fragments and restored base and headstone at the temple site are important for studying the development of stone stela forms in the early Unified Silla period.

1123701260000.title_en: Three-story Stone Pagoda, Mujangsa Temple Site, Gyeongju
1123701260000.description: This pagoda stands on a two-tiered base with a three-story body and follows the typical stone pagoda style of Unified Silla. The lower base is carved with corner and central pillars on each side, while the upper base has circular eye-shaped reliefs; it was restored in 1963 after having collapsed.

1123701360000.title_en: Stone Seated Buddha at Miriseokgul Valley, Namsan Mountain, Gyeongju
1123701360000.description: This seated stone Buddha, standing 4.36 m tall in total and 2.44 m in height, remains at a site thought to be that of Borisa Temple on Namsan Mountain, Gyeongju. It is one of the most completely preserved Silla stone Buddha statues in Namsan, with a halo carved separately and decorated with small Buddhas, lotus motifs, and vines. The back of the halo is engraved with a Medicine Buddha, a rare feature also seen in only a few other examples.

1123701370000.title_en: Stupa of Jingjeung Daesa, Bongamsa Temple, Mungyeong
1123701370000.description: This stupa enshrines the relics of Jingjeung Daesa, who founded Bongamsa Temple and died in 882. The octagonal base and body are richly carved with lions, clouds, garuda birds, the Four Heavenly Kings, and bodhisattvas, while the stone roof and finial are also carefully decorated. An accompanying stele suggests that it was erected in 883.

1121101410000.title_en: Munmyo Shrine and Seonggyungwan, Seoul (Daeseongjeon Hall, Dongmu Hall, Seomu Hall, Sammun Gate, Myeongnyundang Hall)
1121101410000.description: This complex was originally established in 1398 and rebuilt after being destroyed during the Japanese invasions of Korea. It includes the ancestral shrine area centered on Daeseongjeon, with Dongmu and Seomu, and the educational area centered on Myeongnyundang. The buildings house memorial tablets of Confucius, the Four Sages, the Ten Philosophers, Song dynasty worthies, and Korean Confucian scholars, and served as the main state institution for Confucian rites and education in Joseon.

1121101420000.description: This shrine outside Heunginjimun Gate in Seoul was built to honor Guan Yu, the famous general of the Shu Han kingdom in China. It was begun in 1599 and completed in 1601, and now houses a wooden statue of Guan Yu along with figures of his relatives and retainers. The building has a distinctive T-shaped roof, brick walls on the sides and rear, and lavish interior decoration showing Chinese influence.

1123401430000.description: According to temple records, Gyesimsa was founded in the Baekje period, and the present Daeungjeon Hall was repaired in 1484, as confirmed by a record found during dismantling repairs in 1941. The building is a three-bay by three-bay hall with a front-gabled roof and multi-bracket construction. It is an important example for comparing early Joseon wooden architecture with other major temple halls.

1123801460000.description: This small Buddhist hall is thought to date to the early Joseon period and enshrines the Medicine Buddha, who is believed to cure the suffering of sentient beings. The building is a one-bay by one-bay hall with a front-gabled roof and simple bracket sets only on the columns. Despite its small size, it preserves valuable features of early Joseon temple architecture.

1123401480000.description: This Baekje-period stone basin is preserved in the garden of the Gongju National Museum and was used at a temple to display lotus blossoms. It originally stood at the site of Daetongsa Temple in Banjuk-dong, Gongju, together with the Banjuk-dong Stone Basin. Its form, carving method, and lotus decoration make it an important source for studying Baekje Buddhist art.

1123401490000.description: This Baekje-period stone basin was found at the Daetongsa Temple site in Gongju and is now preserved at the Gongju National Museum. It was likely used for displaying lotus flowers in a temple setting, and it is similar in form and carving technique to the Jungdong Stone Basin. The basin has a rounded body set on a pedestal carved with lotus petals, and its ornamental bands and floral designs are characteristic of Baekje workmanship.

1123601580000.title_en: Bojoseonsa Stupa Monument of Borimsa Temple, Jangheung
1123601580000.description: This stupa monument for the monk Bojoseonsa Jiseon stands at Borimsa Temple, with a tortoise-base stone supporting the stele body and a capstone above. It was erected in 884, in the reign of King Heongang of Unified Silla, and records the life and deeds of Bojoseonsa, with the inscription written by Kim Won and Kim Eon-gyeong and the epitaph composed by Kim Yeong.

1123801590000.title_en: Rock-carved Medicine Buddha Triad Standing Images on Bangeosan Mountain, Haman
1123801590000.description: This rock-carved triad on the cliff of Bangeosan Mountain was made in 801, during the reign of King Aejang of Unified Silla. The main image holds a medicine bowl in the left hand and is flanked by two attendant bodhisattvas, identified as Ilgwang-bosal and Wolgwang-bosal. An inscription gives the date, making it an important work for the study of Unified Silla sculpture.

1123701600000.title_en: Documents of the Yuseong-ryong Family of the Main Lineage
1123701600000.description: This collection consists of manuscripts and related materials preserved by the descendants of Yu Seong-ryong, a leading civil official of the mid-Joseon period. It includes Yu’s own handwritten records from the Imjin War and documents related to the war, and is an important historical source for understanding that period. The collection was formerly designated under another name and was later renamed in 1991.

1122301610000.title_en: Main Hall of Jeongsusa Temple, Ganghwa
1122301610000.description: This building is the Daeungjeon main hall of Jeongsusa Temple, which enshrines a statue of Sakyamuni Buddha. A record found during repairs states that it was newly rebuilt in 1423, during the reign of King Sejong. The hall is a wooden structure with a gabled roof and a single-bracket style on the front and rear, and its carved front door shows fine workmanship.

1123401620000.title_en: Upper Daeungjeon Hall of Janggoksa Temple, Cheongyang
1123401620000.description: This is the upper Daeungjeon hall at Janggoksa Temple, a temple said to have been founded in the late Silla period by Bojo Guksa. The hall has been rebuilt and repaired several times, but its unusual placement above the lower Daeungjeon reflects the temple’s adaptation to the terrain. The interior retains brick flooring, including some lotus-patterned bricks believed to date to Unified Silla.

1123201640000.title_en: Hwajeonmun Gate of Cheongpyeongsa Temple, Chuncheon
1123201640000.description: This gate at Cheongpyeongsa Temple replaced the usual Sacheonwangmun gate and was intended to remind visitors of the Buddhist cycle of rebirth. It was built in the mid-16th century and shows a transitional structure from the jusimpo bracket system to the more elaborate ikgong system. The interior was arranged to hold standing guardian figures, and hongsal were installed above.

1123201650000.description: Ojukheon is the house where Shin Saimdang and her son Yi I were born. It was built by the Joseon official Choi Chi-un and is regarded as one of the older surviving wooden houses in Korea. The building has a mixed floor plan with a wooden hall on one side and an ondol room on the other, and an ikgong-style bracket system.

1121101660000.title_en: Five-Story Stone Pagoda of Hongje-dong, Seoul
1121101660000.description: This pagoda originally stood at the site of Sahyeonsa Temple and was moved to Gyeongbokgung Palace around 1970 before being transferred to the National Museum of Korea. The five-story body is set on a natural stone base, with each story made from a single body stone and roof stone, and the upper stories are carved to imitate wooden architecture. It is thought to date to around 1045, when the temple was founded.

1123501670000.description: This three-story stone pagoda stands in Eunsun-ri Village, Jeongeup, and has an unusually distinctive form. Its lower stylobate and roof stones show features associated with Baekje stone pagodas, suggesting the continuation of Baekje-style pagoda construction in the Goryeo period.

1123701680000.title_en: Gyeongju Cheongung-dong East and West Three-story Stone Pagodas
1123701680000.description: These are a pair of east and west stone pagodas standing on a flat site; they were restored in 1939 after having collapsed. Both pagodas have a two-tier stylobate and three-story body, and a reliquary space was found in the third-story body during excavation.

1123701690000.description: This three-story stone pagoda stands at Bongamsa Temple. It has an unusual one-tier stylobate, while its finial is largely intact and is considered an important example for understanding Korean stone pagodas.

1123601700000.title_en: Stele for Monk Cheolgam at Ssangbongsa Temple, Hwasun
1123601700000.description: This is the stupa stele of the late Unified Silla Buddhist monk Cheolgam (Do-yun, 798–868). Only the tortoise base and the stele crown remain today, and the inscription on the front of the crown records the title of the monument.

1123701710000.title_en: Mungyeong Bongamsa Stupa of Jingjin Daesa
1123701710000.description: This octagonal stupa holds the relics of Jingjin Daesa, Gyoungyang, and stands near the north slope by the temple entrance. It was built in 965 during the reign of King Gwangjong of Goryeo and imitates the style of the nearby stupa of Jijeung Daesa at Bongamsa.

1123701720000.title_en: Stele for the Stupa of Jingjin Daesa, Bongamsa Temple, Mungyeong
1123701720000.description: This early Goryeo stupa stele commemorates Jingjin Daesa, who helped revive Bongamsa Temple. It was erected in 965, and the inscription was written by Lee Mong-yu and calligraphed by Jang Dan-yeol.

1122601730000.title_en: Monk Stupas at Manghaesa Temple Site, Ulsan
1122601730000.description: These two monk stupas stand to the east and west north of the temple hall site at Manghaesa Temple Site, and the east stupa was restored in 1960 after damage. They are octagonal in form, with decorative lotus, cloud, dragon, and door motifs, and are works of the Unified Silla period.

1123401740000.title_en: Iron Seated Vairocana Buddha and Stone Pedestal, Janggoksa Temple, Cheongyang
1123401740000.description: This seated image of Vairocana Buddha is enshrined in Sangdaewoongjeon Hall at Janggoksa Temple in Cheongyang. It has a separate stone pedestal and a wooden halo, and its simple facial features and modest proportions show a style different from mid-9th-century Vairocana images.

1123201910000.title_en: Stupa of Nangwon Daesa, Bohyeonsa Temple, Gangneung
1123201910000.description: This octagonal stupa at Bohyeonsa Temple enshrines the relics of Nangwon Daesa. It was restored near the temple entrance after collapsing, then moved back near its original site in 1991. The stupa is thought to have been built in 940, the same year its stele was erected.

1123201920000.title_en: Stele for the Stupa of Nangwon Daesa, Bohyeonsa Temple, Gangneung
1123201920000.description: This stele at Bohyeonsa Temple records the life of Nangwon Daesa (834–930), including his birth, his appointment as national preceptor under King Gyeongae, and his death. It was erected in 940, ten years after his death, with the text written by Choe Eon-wi and the calligraphy by Gu Juk-dal. The stone stele has a turtle pedestal and a headstone carved with dragons, lotus motifs, and other decorative elements.

1123701930000.title_en: Stone Lantern in Front of the Main Hall of Unmunsa Temple, Cheongdo
1123701930000.description: This octagonal stone lantern stands in front of the main hall of Unmunsa Temple. It consists of a lower base, central shaft, fire chamber, roof stone, and finial. The lower and upper supports are carved with lotus motifs, and the fire chamber has four windows for the light to shine through.

1123401940000.description: This stone basin, kept at the National Buyeo Museum, is believed to be a Baekje relic once used in the area of the former royal palace. It has a simple base and a rounded basin body with eight vertical grooves on the surface. Traces suggest that an inscription may once have been planned on it, but no lotus decoration is present.

1123401960000.title_en: Gilt-bronze Inscribed Seated Sakyamuni Triad of Jeong Ji-won
1123401960000.description: This gilt-bronze Buddhist triad was cast as a single unit with one halo, and is now housed in the National Buyeo Museum. An inscription on the back of the halo states that Jeong Ji-won made the image in gold for his deceased wife so that she could be guided safely to the afterlife. The main Buddha is flanked by two bodhisattvas, and a small Buddha figure is carved above the halo.

1123401970000.title_en: Stone Standing Triad of Sakyamuni Buddha, Eumnae-ri, Cheongyang
1123401970000.description: This stone triad consists of three independent Buddha images with separate halos and pedestals. The main Buddha has a strong, dignified form, and the two attendant bodhisattvas are carved in a similarly formal style. Because of its flat treatment of the body and stylized carving, it is considered an early Goryeo work.

1123701980000.title_en: Rock-Carved Seated Buddha, Bulgok, Namsan Mountain, Gyeongju
1123701980000.description: This seated Buddha is carved inside a stone chamber cut into a rock face in Bulgok Valley on the eastern slope of Namsan Mountain, Gyeongju. The face is round and slightly bowed, with a gentle expression, and the drapery falls smoothly to cover the pedestal. It is regarded as the oldest surviving Silla stone Buddha on Namsan and is thought to date to the late Three Kingdoms period.

1123701990000.title_en: Rock-Carved Half-Sitting Bodhisattva, Sinseonam, Namsan Mountain, Gyeongju
1123701990000.description: This 1.4-meter rock-carved bodhisattva is on a south-facing rock above Chilbulam on Namsan Mountain. It wears a three-faced jeweled crown, holds a flower in the right hand, and raises the left hand as if preaching. The thin robe reveals the body’s contours, and the work is dated to the late 8th century of Unified Silla.

1123201830000.description: A detached pavilion of a yangban residence, said to have been built in 1530 when Seim Eon-gwang served as governor of Gangwon-do. It stands facing south on a three-tier stone embankment, with a three-bay front, two-bay side, and a hipped-and-gabled roof. The plaque reading “Haeunjeong” was written by Song Si-yeol, and the interior displays calligraphy by well-known figures such as Gwon Jin-eung and Yi I.

1123401840000.description: This stone pagoda belongs to the Baekje-style pagodas that copied the form of the Five-story Stone Pagoda at Jeongnimsa Temple Site in Buyeo. It was made in the Goryeo period and has a three-tiered base and a body with niche-like features on all four sides. During dismantling and repair, relics including ivory Buddha images, a wooden pagoda, and a dharani were found inside, and a cavity containing 41 sarira was discovered in the second story.

1123401850000.title_en: Five-story Stone Pagoda, Muryangsa Temple, Buyeo
1123401850000.description: This large five-story stone pagoda stands in front of Geukrakjeon Hall at Muryangsa Temple. It combines Baekje and Unified Silla stone-pagoda traditions, showing a single-tier base, slender body stones, and broad eaves that rise slightly at the corners. During dismantling, a gilt-bronze triad of Amitabha Buddha, Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva, and Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva was found in the first story, along with other Buddhist images and a reliquary.

1123701860000.title_en: Three-story Stone Pagoda in Yongjanggok Valley, Namsan Mountain, Gyeongju
1123701860000.description: This three-story stone pagoda stands on a peak on the eastern rocky ridge overlooking the former site of Yongjangsa Temple in Namsan Mountain, Gyeongju. It was rebuilt in 1922 after having collapsed, and its original reliquary is no longer preserved. The pagoda is regarded as a representative late Unified Silla work for the balanced composition of its parts and its harmony with the surrounding landscape.

1123701870000.title_en: Stone Seated Buddha from Yongjanggok Valley, Namsan Mountain, Gyeongju
1123701870000.description: This stone seated Buddha is located above the former site of Yongjangsa Temple in Namsan Mountain, Gyeongju. The head is missing, but part of the body and hands remain, and the figure is relatively small compared with its pedestal. The statue is believed to date to the mid-eighth century, based on its realistic treatment and its connection with the monk Daehyeon mentioned in Samgukyusa.

1123701880000.description: This three-story stone pagoda was built on a two-tiered base and is richly decorated on each part. The lower base has reliefs of flying apsaras, and the upper base combines guardian figures such as the Four Heavenly Kings and other heavenly beings, an unusual decorative program for a pagoda. The first-story body has bodhisattva images on each side, and the pagoda is thought to date to around the 9th century.

1123701890000.title_en: Five-story Brick Pagoda of Songnimsa Temple, Chilgok
1123701890000.description: This five-story brick pagoda stands in front of Daeungjeon Hall at Songnimsa Temple and was built with fired bricks. Its stone base and brick superstructure preserve a form typical of Unified Silla brick pagodas, and the top finial was restored in a copy based on the original shape in 1959. Its exact date is uncertain, but it is thought to belong to the late 7th to 9th century.

1121101900000.title_en: Stupa of Monk Wongong, Geodonsa Temple Site, Wonju
1121101900000.description: This sarira stupa for the early Goryeo monk Wongong was once kept in a Japanese private house during the Japanese colonial period and moved to Gyeongbokgung Palace in 1948; it is now in the grounds of the National Museum of Korea. It is an octagonal stupa with elaborate relief decoration, including inscriptions, window and door motifs, Four Heavenly Kings, and a roof modeled after wooden architecture. Based on the inscription date, it is believed to have been made in 1025.

1123601750000.title_en: Sutra Tags of Songgwangsa Temple, Suncheon
1123601750000.description: These sutra tags were originally attached to wooden boxes that held Buddhist scriptures and recorded the names of the texts inside. The set preserved at Songgwangsa Temple consists of 43 pieces, including 10 ivory tags and 33 wooden tags, decorated with carved motifs and relief figures on the back. They are thought to be works of the Goryeo period based on their carving technique and refined workmanship.

1123601760000.title_en: Gilt-bronze Ritual Bell of Songgwangsa Temple, Suncheon
1123601760000.description: This ritual bell was used by monks to make sound during ceremonies. It is a bronze object with traces of gilding, and its surfaces are decorated with raised dragon and cloud designs. It is regarded as one of the finest surviving ritual bells in Korea and an especially early example.

1121101770000.title_en: Main Gate of Sajikdan Altar, Seoul
1121101770000.description: This is the main gate of Sajikdan, the altar where rites were performed for the earth and grain deities and for state prosperity and good harvests. The original gate was built in 1394 and burned during the Imjin War; the present structure is believed to have been rebuilt after that and was moved 14 meters in 1962. It is a simple but sturdy gate with a gabled roof and a modest, balanced form.

1122301780000.title_en: Daeungjeon Hall of Jeondeungsa Temple, Ganghwa
1122301780000.description: This hall enshrines the Sakyamuni Buddha triad and is said to have been built in 1621, the 13th year of King Gwanghaegun. It is a three-bay by three-bay building with a hipped-and-gabled roof and the multi-bracket style. Carved human figures at the corners are linked to a local legend about the carpenter who built the hall.

1122301790000.title_en: Yaksajeon Hall of Jeondeungsa Temple, Ganghwa
1122301790000.description: This small hall, located west of Daeungbojeon Hall, enshrines the Healing Buddha. Its exact date is unknown, but it is thought to be a mid-Joseon building because of its construction techniques and similarity to Daeungbojeon Hall. The interior ceiling has a square coffer pattern with painted lotus and vine designs.

1123101800000.title_en: Josadang Shrine of Sinhwonsa Temple, Yeoju
1123101800000.description: Josadang is a hall used to enshrine portraits of eminent monks, and in this building the portraits of Jigong, Muhak, and Naong are placed on the back wall of the altar.
