1123403900000.description: These two manuscripts from Gwangdeoksa Temple are hand-copied Buddhist scriptures from the late Goryeo to early Joseon period. Both volumes are copies of the Lotus Sutra, with illuminated frontispieces and carefully executed gold-letter text. One volume is more finely written, while the other has slightly thicker lines and somewhat less refined calligraphy.

1121103910000.title_en: Painting of the Martyrdom at Busanjin Fortress
1121103910000.description: This painting depicts the battle at Busanjin Fortress over two days in April 1592, during the Japanese invasions of Korea. The surviving work was recopied by the painter Byeon Bak in 1760 from an earlier painting made in 1709, which no longer survives. It is valued as a historical record showing the defense of the country, even though its artistic quality is not considered especially high.

1123104020000.description: Paldalmun is the southern gate of Hwaseong Fortress in Suwon, from which its name is taken. The gate pavilion is a two-story wooden structure with a hipped-and-gabled roof, and a semicircular outer wall was built in front to protect the gate. The gate is connected to the fortress wall on both sides, although those wall sections no longer remain.

1123104030000.description: Hwaseomun is the western gate of Hwaseong Fortress in Suwon. It stands on a high stone platform and has a one-story gate building with a hipped-and-gabled roof, a rainbow-shaped arched opening, and a semicircular outer wall in front. A nearby openwork defensive structure called a gongsimdon is also preserved as part of the fortress defense system.

1123304040000.description: This stele has no inscription, and the person commemorated by it is also unknown. The headstone has only a reserved space for the title, while the base is carved in a form closer to a horse's head than the usual turtle head. The upper part is decorated with nine dragons, and the stele is considered to date to the early Goryeo period based on its style.

1123304050000.title_en: Three-story Stone Pagoda in Hwangsan-ri, Danyang
1123304050000.description: This stone pagoda stands in a field in a mountain valley, where roof tiles and ceramic fragments suggest the site of a temple. It consists of a two-tiered base and three stories of the pagoda body, with each body stone and roof stone made from a single block. It is thought to have been rebuilt by local residents after being destroyed in the 1930s, and its form follows the style of late Unified Silla pagodas.

1123304060000.title_en: Rock-carved Standing Buddha in Deokjusa Temple, Jecheon
1123304060000.description: This large standing Buddha is carved on the eastern cliff of Deokjusa Temple on Mt. Worak. The face is emphasized in high relief while the body is rendered with simple lines, and the large head, emphasized facial features, and flattened body reflect the style of large Buddhist images from the Goryeo period. The figure stands on a lotus pedestal carved into the rock.

1123404070000.title_en: Rock-carved Standing Buddha in Sandae-ri, Cheonan
1123404070000.description: This giant standing Buddha is carved on a large boulder at the foot of Mt. Taehak in Cheonan, and traces of a former building remain above it. The face is carved in high relief while the body is expressed with line carving, a typical feature of late Goryeo rock-cut Buddhas. The figure also shows the Maitreya hand gesture commonly used in Goryeo-period Buddhist sculpture.

1123404080000.title_en: Daeungjeon Hall of Ssanggyesa Temple, Nonsan
1123404080000.description: Daeungjeon is the main Buddha hall of Ssanggyesa Temple and is identified as a late Joseon-period building. It has five bays in front and three bays on the side, with a hipped-and-gabled roof and daepo bracket complexes. The doors are decorated with finely carved floral motifs, and the interior has a coffered ceiling and canopies above the main Buddha images.

1123404090000.title_en: Gilt-bronze Vairocana Buddha Triad Seated Statue of Yeongtapsa Temple, Dangjin
1123404090000.description: This gilt-bronze triad is enshrined at Yeongtapsa Temple and consists of Vairocana Buddha in the center with attendant bodhisattvas on both sides. The main image sits on an octagonal lotus pedestal and shows features associated with mid-Goryeo Buddhist sculpture, including a broad face, stylized robe folds, and a relatively small lower body. The two bodhisattvas are similarly posed and wear elaborate crowns and ornaments.

1121103920000.title_en: Painting of the Righteous Martyrdom at Dongnaebu Government Office
1121103920000.description: This painting depicts the defense of Dongnae Fortress during the Japanese invasions of 1592, focusing on Magistrate Song Sang-hyeon and the townspeople who died fighting the invaders. The work was originally painted in 1709 and was recopied by Byeon Bak in 1760 after viewing the earlier version. It is painted on silk and uses a bird’s-eye composition to show the battle, Song Sang-hyeon’s martyrdom, and the retreat of Yi Gak’s forces.

1122303930000.description: This iron bell is a Chinese bell made in 1097, during the Northern Song dynasty, and bears an inscription identifying it as the bell of Songmyeongsa in Henan Province, China. It was brought to Korea during the Japanese colonial period and later found at the Bupyeong military arsenal before being moved to Jeondeungsa Temple. The bell is notable for its Chinese style in form and decoration, including two dragons at the top and the absence of an inner sound tube.

1123603940000.description: Daeseongjeon Hall is the ritual hall of Naju Hyanggyo, a government-run Confucian school founded in 1398. The hall is arranged in five bays by four bays and has a hip-and-gable roof with a bracket system set only on the pillars. Its layout and details represent a typical mid-Joseon hyanggyo Daeseongjeon and make it an important example of Confucian school architecture.

1123603950000.title_en: East and West Three-story Stone Pagodas of Seonamsa Temple, Suncheon
1123603950000.description: These two three-story stone pagodas stand to the left and right in front of Daeungjeon Hall at Seonamsa Temple. They are built in the same form and technique, with two-tiered bases, single stones for the bodies and roofs of each story, and remaining roof finials. Based on their style, they are thought to date to the 9th century, after the middle of Unified Silla.

1123603960000.title_en: Daeungjeon Hall of Heungguksa Temple, Yeosu
1123603960000.description: This hall is the main Buddha hall of Heungguksa Temple and houses the Sakyamuni triad. The present building was rebuilt in 1624 during the reconstruction of the temple after it was destroyed in the Japanese invasions. It is a three-bay by three-bay building with a hip-and-gable roof, elaborate multi-bracket construction, a coffered ceiling, and a canopy over the altar.

1123403990000.title_en: Daeungjeon Hall of Gosansa Temple, Hongseong
1123403990000.description: This building, now bearing the plaque reading "Daegwangbujeon," serves as the main hall of Gosansa Temple. It is a three-bay by three-bay structure with a hip-and-gable roof and a bracket system placed only on the pillars, showing early Joseon style features. The interior combines a coffered ceiling and an exposed-rafter ceiling, and a finely made altar canopy is installed above the Buddhist image platform.

1123604000000.description: Seungsingyo is a rainbow-shaped stone bridge at Seonamsa Temple, built to cross a stream on the temple grounds. It is founded on natural bedrock and built with carefully joined stones to form a large arch, with stone retaining walls on both sides and a carved dragon head at the center. It is said to have been built during the reconstruction of the temple after the Japanese invasions.

1123104010000.description: This gilt-bronze standing Buddha survives only as the body, without the pedestal or halo, and is 32.3 cm high. It shows late Unified Silla features such as a flat, square face, a compact body, a U-shaped drapery line, and a back with large casting holes. The figure is believed to date to the late Unified Silla period.

1123704110000.description: This building is part of the head family estate of Yi Eonjeok (1491–1553), a Neo-Confucian scholar-official of the Joseon period. It is a mid-Joseon house annex with a 5-bay front and 2-bay side plan, arranged with a large main hall and side ondol rooms. The structure served as an extension of the sarangchae for receiving guests, resting, and reading, and it preserves relics of Yi Eonjeok.

1123704120000.description: Hyangdan is a mid-Joseon house built by Yi Eonjeok (1491–1553) when he served as governor of Gyeongsang Province. Its layout is unusual, combining a body shaped by fengshui principles with an attached servants' quarters to form a U-like composition and two courtyards. The house integrates the servants' quarters, inner quarters, and men's quarters into one complex and shows an efficient use of space.

1123704130000.description: Dokrakdang is the sarangchae behind Oksanseowon, where rites for Yi Eonjeok are held, and is said to have been the residence he used after retiring from office. It was built in 1516, in the 11th year of King Jungjong, and has a 4-bay front, 2-bay side, and paljak roof. The side wall has a narrow lattice window facing the stream, and a pavilion by the water behind the building shows its integration with the surrounding landscape.

1123704140000.description: This house belonged to Yu Seong-ryong (1542–1607), a noted civil official of the mid-Joseon period. The complex consists of a servants' quarters, men's quarters, and inner quarters; the sarangchae and anchae were built by his grandson Yu Won-ji and later expanded and repaired by his great-grandson Yu Ui-ha. It has been well preserved and is considered important for the study of Joseon-period private houses.

1123704150000.title_en: Dry-lacquer Seated Bodhisattva in Half-Lotus Position, Girimsa Temple, Gyeongju
1123704150000.description: This is a Joseon-period dry-lacquer Bodhisattva statue enshrined at Girimsa Temple in Gyeongju. Dry-lacquer images were made by building a wooden core, wrapping it with cloth, applying clay, and removing the core, and surviving examples in Korea are very rare. The base bears a record indicating that it was made in 1501, and the figure is thought to represent Avalokiteshvara.

1121104160000.title_en: Celadon Openwork Stool with Linked Ring Design
1121104160000.description: These four celadon stools were excavated in Gaeseong and date to the 13th century, during the Goryeo period. Two types are distinguished by their decorative technique: one uses openwork with lotus, vine, and chrysanthemum designs, and the other uses incised and openworked linked-ring patterns with vine and almond-shaped motifs. The glaze is grayish blue-green, with uneven coloration and some exposed iron-colored areas at the rim.

1121104170000.description: This is a woodblock-printed edition published in 1455, the 3rd year of King Danjong, based on a project begun in King Sejong's reign. It was compiled to render the Chinese pronunciation of the rhyme dictionary Hongmu Jeongun in Hangul, and the original 16-volume set is now missing volume 1 and volume 2, leaving 14 volumes in 7 books. The text was printed with wood type for Hangul and large Chinese characters, and with gapinja type for the smaller characters.

1123104180000.description: Jewang ungi is a verse history of China and Korea written by Yi Seung-hyu in 1287, during the Goryeo period. The edition here is a later woodblock print identified as a reprint from the 1360 Goryeo engraving, based on matching printing characteristics with another copy. The surviving volume preserves the textual history of the work, which was also reprinted in 1413.

1121104190200.description: This is a single surviving fascicle containing only Volume 2 (Gii) of the Samguk yusa. Of the 49 leaves, four leaves were supplemented with reproductions, and the volume is bound as a five-stitch sewn book with later added covers; the text shows many differences from the Jeongdeok edition and is valuable for correcting textual errors.

1121104190400.description: This bound volume contains Volumes 3 to 5 of the Samguk yusa, though 23 leaves are missing from the beginning of Volume 3 and from Volume 5 to the end of the epilogue. It was printed from the 1512 woodblocks carved in Gyeongju during the reign of King Jungjong, and this copy is one of the early extant Jeongdeok editions with added gugyeol marks to aid reading.

1123504200000.title_en: Bronze Incense Burner with Silver Inlay from Baekjangam Hermitage
1123504200000.description: This incense burner has an oval bowl-shaped body, flaring pedestal, and separate round base, continuing the tradition of Goryeo-style incense burners made with silver inlay. An inscription on the lower part of the rim shows that it was made in 1584, during the reign of King Seonjo.

1123504210000.title_en: Wood-engraved Amitabha Buddha Seated and Preaching, Yaksuam Hermitage, Silsangsa Temple, Namwon
1123504210000.description: This is a wooden carved Buddhist hanging image rather than a painted one, depicting Amitabha Buddha with attendant bodhisattvas and disciples arranged above and below. It was made in 1782, and its balanced composition, carved figures, and detailed workmanship make it an important example of late Joseon wood-carved hanging Buddhist images.

1123504220000.title_en: Iron Seated Buddha, Seonwonsa Temple, Namwon
1123504220000.description: This iron seated Buddha at Seonwonsa Temple in Namwon is a typical Goryeo-period iron Buddha, closely resembling the Iron Seated Shakyamuni Buddha at Chunggung-ri. It has a triangular face, a restrained expression, simplified drapery, and a sturdy body that reflects the characteristics of Goryeo metal Buddhist sculpture.

1123504230000.description: This rock-carved Buddha uses a large boulder as the halo and the natural rock surface as the pedestal, and stands over 3 meters high. Although associated with a legend that Doseon Guksa made it in one night, its rounded face, simplified details, and volumetric body indicate that it was made in the Goryeo period.

1123704240000.title_en: Stone Seated Buddha, Cheongnyongsa Temple, Yecheon
1123704240000.description: This Unified Silla-period stone seated Buddha is enshrined in Cheongnyongsa Temple, Yecheon, alongside the temple's stone seated Vairocana Buddha. It has a small snail-shaped hair arrangement, a narrow face, a thin body, an oval halo, and an octagonal pedestal with lotus motifs.

1123704250000.title_en: Stone Seated Vairocana Buddha, Cheongnyongsa Temple, Yecheon
1123704250000.description: This stone seated Vairocana Buddha at Cheongnyongsa Temple is a Goryeo-period image placed beside the temple's seated Buddha. Its square face, close-set nose and mouth, simplified drapery, and angular pedestal suggest an early Goryeo work that inherited the style of 8th- and 9th-century Vairocana statues.

1123704260000.title_en: Three-story Stone Pagoda in Dongbon-ri, Yecheon
1123704260000.description: This Unified Silla stone pagoda stands on the site of an old temple where a Buddhist statue and the pagoda remain. The base, body, and roof stones are well balanced, and the middle stone of the base is carved with Four Guardian Kings. It is believed to date to the late Unified Silla period.

1123704270000.title_en: Stone Standing Buddha in Dongbon-ri, Yecheon
1123704270000.description: This large Unified Silla-period stone Buddha stands together with the three-story stone pagoda in Dongbon-dong, Yecheon. Carved from a single stone, it shows a calm face, a compact upper body, and drapery that falls in a stylized Y-shape over the legs. Its form suggests a transitional work between Unified Silla and Goryeo styles.

1123704280000.title_en: Stupa and Stele of Buddhist Monk Bogak, Imgaksa Temple, Gunwi
1123704280000.description: This consists of the sarira stupa of the monk Iryeon, known by his posthumous title Bogak Guksa, and a stele recording his life and deeds. Iryeon died in 1289, and the stele was erected in 1295, so the stupa was probably made between those years. The stele inscription was composed by Min Ji and its text is preserved in a copy at Woljeongsa Temple, Odaesan.

1123704290000.title_en: Three-story Stone Pagoda at Bulgulsa Temple, Gyeongsan
1123704290000.description: This pagoda stands in front of the main hall at Bulgulsa Temple, a temple said to have been founded in 690 during King Sinmun's reign. It follows the standard Unified Silla form with a two-tiered base and three-story body, and has simplified but refined stonework. Based on its proportions and details, it is thought to date to the late Unified Silla period.

1123704300000.title_en: Stupa of Monk Wonjin, Bogyeongsa Temple, Pohang
1123704300000.description: This octagonal stupa on the hillside behind Bogyeongsa Temple contains the relics of the monk Wonjin Guksa. Its base, body, and roof are carved in an octagonal form, with flower motifs, lock-shaped carving on the body, and a preserved finial. The overall shape is elongated and simple in style, reflecting Goryeo-period work.

1123704310000.title_en: Stone Seated Buddha at Gwanbong Peak, Palgongsan Mountain, Gyeongsan
1123704310000.description: This seated Buddha was made against a rock backdrop on the summit of Gwanbong Peak in Palgongsan Mountain, where it is popularly called Gatbawi. The figure has a round face, long ears, and a solid body, and its hands are placed on the lap in a pose close to the gesture of touching the earth. Its stylized drapery and rigid form indicate a 9th-century Unified Silla work.

1123304330000.title_en: Stone Seated Vairocana Buddha at Gakyeonsa Temple, Goesan
1123304330000.description: This is a complete stone Buddha image with both the pedestal and halo preserved, representing Vairocana Buddha. The figure shows a simplified robe, highly stylized leg drapery, and a halo decorated with small Buddhas, lotus patterns, clouds, and flames. It is a late Unified Silla work.

1122104340000.title_en: Daeungjeon Hall of Beomeosa Temple, Busan
1122104340000.description: This main Buddha hall at Beomeosa Temple was rebuilt in the 17th century after being destroyed during the Japanese invasions of 1592. It is a three-bay by three-bay building with a gabled roof and multi-bracket construction, and it enshrines Sakyamuni Buddha with Mireuk Bosal and Jehwagara Bosal. The building and its carved interior furnishings show the craftsmanship of mid-Joseon Buddhist architecture.

1123104350000.title_en: Five-Story Stone Pagoda at Bongeopsa Temple Site, Anseong
1123104350000.description: This stone pagoda stands at the former site of Bongeopsa Temple, now turned into farmland. It has a single-base platform and a five-story body, with the first-story body made of four stones and the remaining stories made of single stones.

1123804360000.title_en: Seated Stone Vairocana Buddha of Bulgoksa Temple, Changwon
1123804360000.description: This statue is one of the Vairocana Buddhas made mainly between 850 and 900, and it shows the realistic and natural style of Unified Silla Buddhist sculpture. The figure has a large ushnisha, a round face, clearly marked three neck folds, and an octagonal pedestal carved with lotus motifs and bodhisattvas.

1123504370000.title_en: Royal Certificate of Merit for Kim Hwe-ryeon
1123504370000.description: This document appoints Kim Hwe-ryeon as a meritorious retainer of the founding of Joseon. It is the original scroll of a royal certificate issued in the fourth year of King Taejo's reign, recording the process of selecting meritorious subjects.

1123504380000.description: These two royal decrees appoint Kim Hwe-ryeon to government posts, one in 1395 and the other in 1397. The seals bear the inscription 'Joseon jibo' and the documents are preserved together with the merit certificate.

1123204390000.title_en: Monk Doseun of Jinjeonsa Temple Site Stupa, Yangyang
1123204390000.description: This stupa stands on a small hill inside the former site of Jinjeonsa Temple and is believed to be the tomb stupa of Monk Doseun, who founded the temple. It has a two-tier square base like a stone pagoda, but an octagonal body, and is thought to date to the mid-9th century.

1123804400000.title_en: Eight Bestowed Items of Chungnyeolsa Shrine, Tongyeong
1123804400000.description: This group consists of 15 objects in eight types that were bestowed by the Ming emperor to Admiral Yi Sun-sin for his military achievements during the Imjin War. The set includes items such as a seal, flags, swords, and a trumpet, and was later kept at Chungnyeolsa Shrine.

1122604410000.title_en: Twelve Zodiac Animal Sarira Stupa at Taewha Temple Site, Ulsan
1122604410000.description: This sarira stupa was excavated from the Taewha Temple site in 1962 and is now preserved at the Ulsan Museum. It has a simple form with a bell-shaped body on a broad base, and the twelve zodiac animals are carved in relief around the body.

1123704420000.description: This is the former house of Son Jung-don, a government official known as a clean-handed official in the reign of King Jungjong. The house is arranged around a central courtyard with a men’s quarters and women’s quarters, and its front side opens toward the landscape beyond the low ground.

1123704510000.title_en: Relics of Taesamyo Shrine of the Three Meritorious Subjects, Andong
1123704510000.description: This collection consists of 22 relics in 12 types kept at Taesamyo Shrine, which enshrines the memorial tablets of Gwon Haeng, Kim Seon-pyeong, and Jeong Jeong-pil. The shrine was founded in 1542, destroyed by fire during the Korean War, and restored in 1958. The objects include lacquerware, textiles, garments, metal vessels and implements, a jade ornament, a document thought to be in King Gongmin's hand, and other items from the Goryeo period.

1121104520000.title_en: Celadon Ewer in the Shape of a Turtle and Dragon
1121104520000.description: This Goryeo celadon ewer is shaped like a turtle seated on a lotus flower and measures 17.2 cm in height and 20.2 cm in length. Its surface is decorated with detailed carving, partial gilding, and inlaid or incised motifs including the character "wang" on the shell, showing the characteristics of early-12th-century shaped celadon.

1121104530000.description: This vessel is an earthenware cup with a yellowish-green glaze, accompanied by a saucer-shaped stand and a lid. The cup, stand, and lid are decorated with parallel incised lines, and the form is considered to date to the early Unified Silla period based on comparison with similar Silla and Three Kingdoms examples.

1121104540000.description: This pair of Silla gold bracelets was found in a tomb in Nosodong, Gyeongju. Each bracelet has rows of raised bosses inlaid with jade and four dragon motifs carved on the outer surface, making it a rare and highly accomplished example of Silla metal ornament.

1121104550000.description: These earrings were excavated from Tomb 215 in Nosodong, Gyeongju; one of the original pair was taken to Japan and later returned to Korea in 1966 under the Korea-Japan agreement. They are a typical Silla three-part earrings, consisting of a main ring, pendant section, and terminal ornament, and are dated to the 5th to 6th century.

1121104560000.description: This necklace from Tomb 215 in Nosodong, Gyeongju is made by linking many small gold rings to form hollow spherical beads and attaching forty-four heart-shaped gold pendants linked by gold wire. A jade magatama-shaped pendant hangs at the end, and the piece was also among the cultural properties returned from Japan in 1966.

1123704570000.title_en: Annex of the Chogan Head House of the Yecheon Gwon Clan
1123704570000.description: This building is said to have been constructed by Gwon O-sang, the grandfather of the Joseon scholar Gwon Mun-hae (1534–1591). It is a four-bay by two-bay annex with a hip-and-gable roof, an open front hall, and surrounding railings, and its interior is elaborately decorated with refined ceiling details. The rear study preserves blocks for Gwon Mun-hae's Daedong unbu gunok, an old jade flute, and a complete set of Jizhitongjian gangmu.

1123304590000.title_en: Seven-story Masonry Pagoda of Jangnak-dong, Jecheon
1123304590000.description: This pagoda is a seven-story masonry tower built of slate cut to resemble bricks, imitating a brick pagoda. The base is made with natural stone, the first-story corners use granite pillars, and the pagoda has niches on the north and south sides; it is believed to date to the late Unified Silla period.

1123204430000.title_en: Three-story Stone Pagoda at Hyangseongsa Temple Site, Sokcho
1123204430000.description: This stone pagoda stands at the entrance to Seorak-dong on the way into Seoraksan from Sokcho, and the temple site around it is no longer recognizable. It is a typical Unified Silla stone pagoda built on a two-tiered base with three stories, and it was dismantled and repaired in 1966; remains found at the site suggest it was made around the 9th century.

1123204440000.title_en: Three-story Stone Pagoda at Seonlimwon Temple Site, Yangyang
1123204440000.description: This is a typical Unified Silla stone pagoda restored to its original location south of the main hall site at Seonlimwon Temple Site. It stands on a two-tiered base with three stories, and its form and carving style suggest it was made in the late 9th century.

1123204450000.title_en: Stone Lantern at Seonlimwon Temple Site, Yangyang
1123204450000.description: This stone lantern stands on a western hill within the Seonlimwon Temple Site. It follows the standard Unified Silla octagonal form, but its pedestal arrangement is unusual, and it is thought to have been erected in 886 together with the Honggak Seonsa Stele.

1123204460000.title_en: Stele for Honggak Seonsa at Seonlimwon Temple Site, Yangyang
1123204460000.description: This stele was erected to honor Honggak Seonsa and is thought to date to 886, the first year of King Jeonggang of Silla. The stele body survives only in fragments, while the tortoise base and stele cap remain; the body was restored in 2008.

1123204470000.title_en: Stupa at Seonlimwon Temple Site, Yangyang
1123204470000.description: This monk’s stupa was restored in 1965 after having been completely damaged during the Japanese colonial period, and only the base remains today. Its octagonal structure and decorative carving indicate a late Unified Silla work, likely dating to 886 and associated with Honggak Seonsa.

1123704480000.title_en: Hwaeom Gangdang Hall, Bongjeongsa Temple, Andong
1123704480000.description: Hwaeom Gangdang Hall is the lecture hall where monks studied basic Buddhist doctrine at Bongjeongsa Temple. Documentary evidence suggests it was repaired in the 17th century together with other buildings at the temple, and it is a small gabled wooden hall with a mixed bracket structure.

1123704490000.description: This building stands eastward in front of Geungnakjeon Hall at Bongjeongsa Temple and is thought to have originally served as an auxiliary hall for enshrining a Buddha image. Records found during the 1969 dismantling and repair show that it was rebuilt in 1616 during the reign of King Gwanghaegun.

1123704500000.title_en: Uiseong Kim Clan Head House, Andong
1123704500000.description: This is the head house of the Uiseong Kim clan, said to have been rebuilt by Kim Seong-il after the house burned down during the Imjin War. The complex is arranged around a sarangchae, an inner house, and an attached servants’ quarter, with an unusual layout that reflects Joseon-period Confucian social customs.

1123704600000.title_en: Artifacts from the Yu Seong-ryong Family
1123704600000.description: This collection consists of relics handed down in the eldest-line family of Yu Seong-ryong (1542–1607), a mid-Joseon civil official. It includes items used by Yu himself, materials related to his mother, and official documents bestowed on him by the court. The artifacts are valued as important materials for studying Yu Seong-ryong’s life and the society of his time.

1123604610000.title_en: Rock-Carved Seven Buddhas at Cheolcheon-ri, Naju
1123604610000.description: This is an unusual set of Buddhist figures carved on the surface of a rock shaped like a nearly quadrangular cone. The group originally comprised seven images, including seated and standing Buddhas on the east, north, south, and west faces, though some parts have been lost. The figures show highly stylized features typical of Goryeo stone sculpture.

1123604620000.title_en: Stone Standing Buddha at Cheolcheon-ri, Naju
1123604620000.description: This large standing Buddha, 5.38 meters high, is carved together with the halo from a single stone. The figure has a square face, a prominent ushnisha, three neck folds, and a robe with U-shaped drapery folds down to the ankles. Its fleshy face and stylized treatment indicate an early Goryeo Buddhist image.

1121104630000.title_en: Stele for National Preceptor Jingong at the Site of Heungbeopsa Temple, Wonju
1121104630000.description: This stele was erected at the former site of Heungbeopsa Temple in honor of Jingong Daesa (869–940), a monk active from the late Unified Silla to early Goryeo period. The inscribed body of the stele is broken and kept at the National Museum of Korea, while the turtle pedestal and capstone remain on site. The pedestal is shaped like a dragon-like turtle, and the capstone is carved with dragons and clouds on both sides.

1123204640000.title_en: Three-Story Stone Pagoda at the Site of Heungbeopsa Temple, Wonju
1123204640000.description: This Goryeo-period pagoda stands in a field identified as the site of Heungbeopsa Temple. It has a two-tiered base and three stories of small body stones and roof stones above it, with floral and pillar-like carvings on the base and corners. The pagoda is relatively small in proportion and appears to date to the early Goryeo period.

1123704650000.title_en: Three-Story Stone Pagoda at Sinwol-ri, Yeongcheon
1123704650000.description: This is a ninth-century Unified Silla stone pagoda, 4.75 meters high. It has a two-tiered base with pillar-like carvings and figures of the Eight Deva Kings on the upper base, and three stories of body stones and roof stones above. The pagoda is now preserved at a temple called Sinheungsa.

1123804660000.title_en: Three-Story Stone Pagoda at Maneosa Temple, Miryang
1123804660000.description: This three-story stone pagoda stands near the present Man-eosa Temple grounds, though the original temple site is believed to have been nearby. It has a single-tier base and three stories with body stones and roof stones each carved from one block. The structure is considered a well-balanced Goryeo-period pagoda, probably from the middle of the dynasty.

1123804670000.title_en: Three-Story Stone Pagoda at Pyochungsa Temple, Miryang
1123804670000.description: This three-story stone pagoda stands in front of Daehongwonjeon Hall at Pyochungsa Temple. It has a single-tier base with pillar-like carvings, and each story is made of separate body stones and roof stones; the first-story body stone is unusually tall. The pagoda follows the Unified Silla style and is considered to have been moved from its original location.

1121104770000.title_en: Agreement on the Division of Property Among Yi Yi’s Siblings
1121104770000.description: This document records the agreement made by Yi Yi’s siblings after their parents’ deaths to divide the inherited property. It lists land and slaves assigned for ancestral rites and tomb maintenance, as well as the shares given to the four sons, three daughters, and their stepmother, Gwon. The document is valuable for understanding Yi Yi’s family history and early Joseon inheritance practices.

1123404780000.description: This bell was made in 1584 to pray for the king’s longevity and to be hung at Gapsa Temple. It is 131 cm high with a mouth diameter of 91 cm, and its surface is decorated with lotus motifs, Sanskrit characters, guardian lotus bosses, and a seated Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva among clouds. The bell was taken away during the Japanese colonial period and returned to Gapsa after liberation.

1123804800000.title_en: Three-Story Stone Pagoda of Yeongamsa Temple Site, Hapcheon
1123804800000.description: This pagoda stands at the site of a Silla-period temple on the southern slope of Hwangmaesan Mountain. It was reconstructed in 1969 after the body had collapsed, and it follows the typical form of Unified Silla three-story stone pagodas. Based on its stylistic features, it is believed to date to around the 9th century.

1123604810000.title_en: Collected Old Painting Albums Passed Down in the Haenam Yun Clan
1123604810000.description: This group consists of four albums and maps associated with the calligrapher-painter Yun Du-seo (1668–1715), a leading late Joseon scholar-artist. It includes Yun’s family album, a fan-painting album, and maps of Joseon and Japan. The collection is an important source for studying Yun Du-seo’s diverse painting style and scholarly interests.

1123604820000.title_en: Documents of the Yun Seon-do Head Family
1123604820000.description: This group comprises five manuscripts and documents related to Yun Seon-do, a mid-Joseon statesman and sijo poet. It includes works he copied or compiled himself, such as Gumsaedongjipgo, Gumsaedonggi, and Sansingok, as well as documents concerning royal grants and an adoption approval record. These materials are valuable for studying Yun Seon-do’s personal history.

1123604830000.title_en: Document of Granting Slaves to Yun Dan-hak and Its Certification
1123604830000.description: This document records the transfer of slaves from Yun Gwang-jeon to his son Yun Dan-hak in 1354, during the reign of King Gongmin of Goryeo. It consists of six pages of petition text and two pages of certification issued by the local official. The document is considered an important and rare source for the study of Goryeo social and economic history.

1123704840000.description: This diary was written by the Joseon official Kim Yong while he accompanied King Seonjo during the king’s flight to Uiju in the Imjin War. It covers the period from August 1593 to June 1594 and was later bound into three volumes after its rediscovery in 1925. The diary is a valuable firsthand record of wartime politics, military affairs, diplomacy, and daily life.

1123704850000.title_en: Portrait of the Great Accomplished and Most Holy King Wenshuan at the Throne
1123704850000.description: This painting shows Confucius seated at the center with his disciples arranged in rows before him. Confucius is depicted larger than the other figures, and the composition presents the disciples in profile, wearing formal caps and holding ceremonial tablets. It is a copy made in 1514 of an earlier work and is valued as an important example of record painting used in Joseon court contexts.

1123804680000.description: This stone pagoda stands in the middle of cultivated land, and many roof tiles and pottery shards have been found in nearby fields and a stream. Although no clear traces of a temple remain, it is said to mark the former site of Garisa Temple. The pagoda has a single-tier base with three stories above it, and its simplified form suggests a mid-Goryeo date.

1123704690000.description: This pagoda stands on a site where roof tiles and pottery fragments were found, showing that a temple once stood nearby. It follows the typical Unified Silla form of a three-story stone pagoda on a two-tier base, and the first-story body has a niche for a Buddha image on the south side. Its construction details suggest an early Unified Silla date, around the 8th century.

1123704700000.description: This pagoda stands in the courtyard in front of the main hall at Dorisa, a temple associated with the legend of the monk Ado. It has an unusual five-tier overall form that resembles a brick pagoda, with small squared stones used for the body and stepped roof stones. Because of its distinctive style, it is thought to have been made in the Goryeo period.

1123804710000.description: This structure stands in front of Yonghwadjeon Hall at Tongdosa Temple and is thought to symbolize the handing down of Sakyamuni's robe and begging bowl to Maitreya. It has the rare form of a large lidded bowl placed on a pedestal-like base. Based on the lotus carving and the style of the pedestal columns, it is attributed to the Goryeo period.

1123804720000.title_en: Monk's Stupa at Bocheonsa Temple Site, Uiryeong
1123804720000.description: This monk's stupa stands on the northern slope of a valley at the former site of Bocheonsa Temple, also known as Suwamsa Temple. It follows an octagonal form in both the base and the upper structure, with carved cloud and dragon motifs, lotus petals, and a door-and-lock design on one side of the body. Its heavy roof stones and simplified details suggest an early Goryeo date.

1123804730000.title_en: Three-story Stone Pagoda of Beopgye Temple, Sancheong
1123804730000.description: This pagoda stands on a rock at Beopgye Temple, a high mountain temple on the eastern slope of Jirisan. The body and roof stones of each story are made from single stones, and the base is treated very simply. Its simplified and somewhat rough style indicates that it is a Goryeo-period stone pagoda rather than a typical Silla example.

1123804740000.title_en: Three-story Stone Pagoda of Byeoksongsa Temple, Hamyang
1123804740000.description: This pagoda at Byeoksongsa Temple follows the Unified Silla style of a three-story stone pagoda on a two-tier base, even though the temple itself was founded in 1520. The base, body stones, and roof stones preserve the basic Silla pagoda form, and the finial elements remain only in part. It is considered a Joseon-period work that consciously continued the older Silla tradition.

1123704750000.description: This detached pavilion was built in the reign of King Myeongjong by Seo Hae to use as a study. It is a T-shaped building with a hip-and-gable roof for the main part and a gabled roof for the attached room, combining a daecheong hall, a raised wooden floor, and ondol rooms. The building preserves old construction methods and rare decorative details, including carved dragon motifs on the roof tiles.

1123704860000.title_en: Sumi Altar of Baekheungam Hermitage, Eunhaesa Temple, Yeongcheon
1123704860000.description: This Buddhist altar, made in the late Joseon period, stands in the main hall of Baekheungam Hermitage at Eunhaesa Temple in Yeongcheon. It is 125 cm high and 413 cm wide, and its front is carved in five tiers with a wide variety of birds and animals, including phoenixes, peacocks, cranes, pheasants, dragons, children, fish, frogs, elephants, lions, deer, and goblin faces.

1123704870000.description: This portrait depicts Jeong Tak (1526–1605), a civil official of the mid-Joseon period, seated in full length and wearing official court dress with a headdress and a dark purple robe with a pair of cranes on the chest badge. It was painted in 1604, the 37th year of King Seonjo's reign, and shows the restrained, formal style typical of meritorious subject portraits of the Joseon period.

1123104880000.title_en: Stele of State Preceptor Hyejo at Chiljangsa Temple, Anseong
1123104880000.description: This stele was erected to honor the achievements of State Preceptor Hyejo. The monument, dated 1060, survives today with the tortoise pedestal, stele shaft, and capstone separated; the shaft is made of black marble and has carved dragons on both sides.

1123804890000.title_en: Tortoise Pedestals from the Site of Yeongamsa Temple, Hapcheon
1123804890000.description: These two tortoise pedestals remain on the east and west sides of the main hall site at the former Yeongamsa Temple grounds. They are considered to be 9th-century Unified Silla works, and both have hexagonal shell patterns, dragon-like heads, and detailed pedestal surfaces with cloud or lotus motifs.

1123704900000.title_en: Rock-carved Standing Buddha of Geumosan Mountain, Gumi
1123704900000.description: This Goryeo-period standing Buddha is carved into a cliff face and stands 5.5 meters high. The composition places the figure around the corner of the rock wall, and the face, body, drapery, pedestal, and halo show more formalized features than earlier Silla examples.

1123804910000.title_en: Stone Seated Buddha of Yonghwasa Temple, Yangsan
1123804910000.description: This complete seated Buddha, with pedestal and halo, was originally from a temple site in Sangdong-myeon, Gimhae, and was later moved to its present location. Its form reflects the style of the mid- to late Unified Silla period, with a strong body structure but increasingly formalized details in the face, hands, and robe folds.

1123704920000.title_en: Stone Seated Buddha of Haepyeong-ri, Gumi
1123704920000.description: This seated Buddha was the main image of Bocheonsa Temple and retains both its halo and pedestal despite minor damage to the face and body. The elaborate halo and three-part pedestal, decorated with lotus, cloud, and celestial figures, show the typical style of 9th-century Unified Silla Buddhist sculpture.

1123804930000.title_en: Stone Seated Buddha of Mubongsa Temple, Milyang
1123804930000.description: This 0.97-meter-high Buddha is enshrined in the main hall of Mubongsa Temple, which is said to have been founded in 733 during the reign of King Hyegong of Silla. The figure has a compact body, simplified drapery, and a richly decorated halo, and the reverse side of the halo is carved with another seated Buddha, a rare feature.

1123705020000.description: This portrait depicts Jang Mal-seon (1431–1486), a civil official of the Joseon period who distinguished himself in suppressing the Rebel Yi Si-ae's Uprising in 1467. It is a seated full-length portrait composed of three joined panels and is believed to have been painted after he was granted the title of meritorious subject in 1482. The work preserves early Joseon portrait style and is considered an important source for the study of meritorious-subject portraits.

1123605030000.title_en: Haenam Monument to the Victory at Myeongnyang
1123605030000.description: This stele was erected to commemorate Admiral Yi Sun-sin's victory at the Battle of Myeongnyang during the Imjin War. The inscription records the battle in detail, including the defeat of a large Japanese fleet with a small number of ships after the Battle of Chilcheollyang. The text was written in 1686, and the monument was erected in 1688 by Park Sin-ju.

1123605040000.title_en: Three-Story Stone Pagoda of Sincheon-ri, Yeonggwang
1123605040000.description: This three-story stone pagoda stands on the former site of Iheungsa Temple. It has a two-tiered base, with separate stones used for the bodies and roof stones of the pagoda, and only the support stone for the finial remains at the top. It is thought to have been built in the early Goryeo period and shows an inheritance of Unified Silla stone pagoda style.

1123605050000.title_en: Stone Danggan Pole of Gaeksa-ri, Damyang
1123605050000.description: This stone danggan pole stands in a rice field about 1 km from Damyang toward Sunchang. A flagpole is set on a lotus-carved stone and supported by posts on both sides, with the pole made of three connected octagonal stone sections bound with iron bands. Based on the nearby stele, the present structure was rebuilt in 1839.

1123605060000.title_en: Five-Story Stone Pagoda of Namsan-ri, Damyang
1123605060000.description: This pagoda stands alone in an open field where traces of a temple site no longer remain. It has a one-tiered base and five stories of the pagoda body, with a low base and a distinctive upper base stone narrower than the first roof stone. It is a Goryeo-period work that appears to have been modeled on the five-story stone pagoda at Jeongnimsa Temple Site in Buyeo.

1123605070000.title_en: Stele for Master Seonggak at Muwisa Temple, Gangjin
1123605070000.description: This stele was erected in 946 to honor Seonggak Daesa Hyeongmi, a monk of the late Silla period. The stele is complete, with a tortoise-shaped base, a body stone, and a capstone decorated with clouds and dragons; the inscription records the monk's life and the authorship and calligraphy of the text. Its carvings are noted for being especially realistic for the period.

1123405080000.description: This stone Buddhist image is carved from two joined stones and stands on the slope of Sumaesan Mountain in Yesan. The bodhisattva wears a head covering and a broad, hexagonal headdress stone, and the body is rendered in a simple pillar-like form with minimal modeling. Its style is similar to regional Goryeo-period standing Maitreya bodhisattva images such as those at Gwangcheonsa Temple in Nonsan and Daejosa Temple in Buyeo.

1123605090000.title_en: Three-Story Stone Pagoda of Nognok-ri, Gurye
1123605090000.description: This pagoda stands on a hillside behind Nognok-ri, with its lower part buried so that only one tier of base and three stories are visible above ground. The base has corner pillars and an unusual lotus pedestal with twelve carved petals, while the tower body and roof stones are each made from a single stone. It is considered a late Unified Silla stone pagoda.

1123805190000.title_en: Stone Seated Buddha, Gwanryongsa Temple, Changnyeong
1123805190000.description: This Stone Seated Buddha is enshrined in the Yaksa Hall of Gwanryongsa Temple, one of the major temples of the Silla period. It is believed to have been made in Goryeo by a local artisan who modeled it after the Unified Silla Stone Seated Buddha on Yongseondae in the western valley of the temple.

1123805200000.title_en: West Three-Story Stone Pagoda, Suljeong-ri, Changnyeong
1123805200000.description: This is a typical Unified Silla stone pagoda with a two-tiered base and a three-story body. The base is built in an unusual way with eight stones on both the lower and upper tiers, and the pagoda now retains only the square finial base and an upside-down bowl-shaped ornament at the top.

1123705210000.description: Sungryeoldang was originally the house of General Yi Sunmong (1386–1449), who served in high military and administrative posts during King Sejong's reign. It is a one-story, five-bay by three-bay building with a mixed roof form characteristic of the Yeongcheon area, and it is now used as a lecture hall with a shrine behind it.

1121105220000.description: This painting depicts the actual landscape of Dosan Seowon and was painted by the late Joseon literati painter Kang Se-hwang in 1751. The work includes a handwritten inscription by the artist explaining that Yi Ik asked him to paint Dosan Seowon while ill, and the painting records the arrangement, size, and direction of the buildings in close accordance with reality.

1121105230100.description: Seokbosangjeol was compiled by Prince Suyang at King Sejong's order to pray for the repose of Queen Soheon, and these volumes are early printed copies from the first edition. They were printed with Goryeo metal type (Gapinja), and correction marks and the red seal 'Gyojeong' show that they are corrected proof copies.

1121105230200.description: Seokbosangjeol was compiled by Prince Suyang at King Sejong's order to pray for the repose of Queen Soheon. These two volumes are early printed copies from the first edition, printed with Goryeo metal type (Gapinja).

1121105230300.description: Seokbosangjeol was compiled by Prince Suyang at King Sejong's order to pray for the repose of Queen Soheon. This volume is a woodblock reprint based on an earlier type-printed edition, and later evidence suggests it may have been reproduced at a temple.

1123705240100.title_en: Sama Bangmok, Genealogical Records of the Oksan Clan of the Yeoju Yi Family
1123705240100.description: This volume is a record of the successful candidates in the Sima examination held in 1513 during King Jungjong's reign. It contains the names, courtesy names, places of origin, and fathers of the passers, and includes Yi Eon-jeok among the successful candidates for the licentiate examination.

1123704940000.title_en: Documents of Jeong Tak: Yakpo Collection and Old Documents
1123704940000.description: This group of 13 items consists of writings and documents handed down at a relic hall built to honor Jeong Tak (1526–1605), a mid-Joseon civil official known by the pen name Yakpo. It includes manuscript volumes, royal certificates, letters, and other records associated with Jeong Tak and his descendants. The materials are valuable sources for studying Joseon-period official documents, social conditions, and the Imjin War.

1123804950000.title_en: Bronze Drum of Okcheonsa Temple, Goseong
1123804950000.description: This bronze ritual drum, also called a gongeum or gongeu-banja, was used at a temple to summon the congregation and to mark Buddhist rites. The inscription shows that it was made in 1252, during the 39th year of King Gojong of Goryeo, by the artisan Han Jung-seo. It had originally belonged to Anyangsa Temple in Jirisan before being kept at Okcheonsa Temple.

1123204960000.description: This stone lantern stands at the site of the former Gyesongsa Temple in Gyesong-ri and is thought to date to the early Goryeo period. It is unusual for a stone lantern in having a hexagonal form rather than the more common octagonal shape seen in Silla or square form seen in Goryeo. The lantern was forcibly moved about 200 meters downhill during the Japanese colonial period.

1123204970000.title_en: Three-story Stone Pagoda in Osaek-ri, Yangyang
1123204970000.description: This is a typical Unified Silla period stone pagoda located about 2 km from the Osaek hot springs in Yangyang. It stands on a two-tiered base with a three-story body, and each body stone and roof stone is carved as a single block. The pagoda was restored in 1971 after having collapsed completely.

1123704980000.title_en: Three-story Stone Pagoda in Gusan-ri, Uljin
1123704980000.description: This stone pagoda in Gusan-ri, Uljin, has a three-story body on a two-tiered base. Its overall form follows Unified Silla pagoda styles, but some details are simplified, suggesting that it was built in the late 9th century. The first-story body stone has a long rectangular outline carved on the south side.

1123204990000.title_en: Seven-story Stone Pagoda of Naksansa Temple, Yangyang
1123204990000.description: This pagoda was originally built as a three-story pagoda and was changed into its present seven-story form in 1467, the 13th year of King Sejo of Joseon. At that time, crystal prayer beads and a wish-fulfilling jewel were said to have been enshrined inside. Although it reflects Goryeo-period traditions, its overall form is simplified as a Joseon-period work.

1123805000000.title_en: Daeungjeon Hall of Ssanggyesa Temple, Hadong
1123805000000.description: This main Buddha hall at Ssanggyesa Temple was rebuilt in 1632 after the temple burned during the Japanese invasions. It is a five-bay by three-bay wooden building with a hipped-and-gabled roof and a Dapo bracket system. The hall preserves the form of early Joseon Buddhist architecture and is an important source for its study.

1123705010000.title_en: Hongpae and Baekpae Certificates of Jang Gye and Jang Malson
1123705010000.description: These three civil service examination certificates were granted to Jang Gye and his descendant Jang Malson, ancestors of the Indong Jang clan. Jang Gye's red certificate was issued in 1305 during Goryeo, while Jang Malson's white and red certificates date to 1453 and 1459 in Joseon. The Goryeo certificate preserves an older format and records titles such as jigongeo and dongjigongeo, making it useful for studying the examination system.

1123705100000.title_en: Three-story Stone Pagoda in Giseong-ri, Chilgok
1123705100000.description: This stone pagoda stands at a site long known only as the former site of Beopseongsa Temple. It consists of a two-tiered base with a three-story body, and the remaining finial includes only the base support. The pagoda is thought to date to Unified Silla, and it was restored in 1971 after the upper part was damaged by tomb raiders.

1123305110000.title_en: Five-story Stone Pagoda in Gyesan-ri, Cheongju
1123305110000.description: This pagoda stands in a field on a hill south of Malmijangteo in Gyesan-ri. It has a single-tiered base and a five-story body, with each story made in a different arrangement of stone blocks. It is considered a fine example of a mid-Goryeo pagoda with a well-balanced overall form.

1123305120000.title_en: Seated Iron Buddha of Danhosa Temple, Chungju
1123305120000.description: This seated iron Buddha is now enshrined at Seokjongsa Temple. The figure has a large ushnisha, a crescent-shaped mark on the forehead, and a rather formal treatment of the drapery and seated posture. Its facial features and overall style reflect Goryeo Buddhist sculpture, with some local characteristics added.

1123705130000.title_en: Seated Iron Buddha of Seonwondong, Yeongcheon
1123705130000.description: This seated iron Buddha shows the proportions and rounded volume associated with the style inherited from late Unified Silla into early Goryeo. The face is round, with raised eyebrows, long eyes, a short philtrum, and a tightly closed mouth. The simplified drapery and restrained modeling show the development of Goryeo iron Buddha sculpture.

1123705140000.title_en: Seated Gilt-bronze Bodhisattva of Unbubam Hermitage, Eunhaesa Temple, Yeongcheon
1123705140000.description: This small seated bodhisattva, 1.02 meters high, is enshrined at Unbubam Hermitage of Eunhaesa Temple. It wears an ornate crown decorated with flame patterns, floral motifs, and birds, and the body is richly adorned with bead ornaments. The figure is considered an early Joseon bodhisattva that continues local traditions from late Goryeo in Gyeongsangbuk-do.

1121105150000.title_en: Document Granting a House to Suksin Ongju
1121105150000.description: This document records King Taejo of Joseon granting a house to his daughter, later known as Suksin Ongju. Written in Idu, it gives specific details about the site, orientation, building materials, layout, and number of bays, and states that the descendants may live there forever. It is the earliest Joseon document known for granting a house, and an important source for studying early Joseon property law.

1122205160000.title_en: Musu Inscribed Embankment Construction Stele, Daegu
1122205160000.description: This stele was first discovered in Daegok-dong, Daegu, in 1946, then lost for several years before being found again near Kyungpook National University. It is a long natural stone with a straight-cut lower end and a rounded upper part. Although many characters are damaged, it records the date of construction of a reservoir and the people involved, making it an important source for Silla hydraulic works and social history.

1123805180000.title_en: Multi-story Stone Pagoda and Stone Lantern at Wondangam Hermitage, Haeinsa Temple, Hapcheon
1123805180000.description: This multi-story stone pagoda stands within Wondangam Hermitage at Haeinsa Temple, where the Tripitaka Koreana is kept. The pagoda is made mainly of slate, with a granite base and a ten-story stack of roof stones; it is regarded as an early example of the slate pagoda type. The nearby stone lantern is from roughly the same period and survives with its base, support parts, and roof stone.

1123705240200.title_en: Materials of the Oksan Branch of the Yeoju Yi Clan
1123705240200.description: This collection consists of 13 kinds in 15 volumes of books preserved by the Oksan branch of the Yeoju Yi clan. It includes printed works, legal texts, letters, and writings by figures such as Yi Eon-jeok, Yi Hwang, and Yu Seong-ryong, providing important source material for the study of Joseon-period thought, literature, bibliography, and printing history.

1123705260100.title_en: Autograph Rubbings of the Yeoju Yi Clan Oksan Branch - Haedong Myeongjeok
1123705260100.description: This work is a two-volume compilation of rubbings made by Shin Gong-je from stone inscriptions of famous Korean calligraphers. It brings together calligraphy by Silla, Goryeo, and Joseon figures, including royal handwriting and writings attributed to Choe Chi-won, Kim Saeng, and others, and is valuable for the study of early Korean calligraphy.

1123705260200.title_en: Autograph of the Yeoju Yi Clan Oksan Branch - Wonjo Ojam and Sasan Odae
1123705260200.description: This is a mounted calligraphy work consisting of Yi Hwang's transcription of Yi Eon-jeok's five admonitory texts, together with a set of large-character place-name inscriptions known as Sasan Odae. The pieces preserve Yi Hwang's handwriting and the original calligraphy of the Oksan retreat's scenic place names associated with Yi Eon-jeok.

1121105270000.description: This album contains 25 genre paintings by the late Joseon painter Kim Hong-do. The scenes depict everyday life and work among common people, such as wrestling, blacksmithing, and a village school, in ink and light color on paper.
1121105270000.material: Ink and light color on paper

1123305280000.description: Hanbyeoknu Pavilion was originally built in 1317 to commemorate the elevation of Cheongpung to county status, and the present building dates to a reconstruction in 1634. It is a two-story pavilion with an attached side wing, and the interior preserves plaques written by Song Si-yeol, Kim Su-jeung, and Kim Jeong-hui.

1123605290000.title_en: Five-story Stone Pagoda of Geumbongsan Mountain, Jindo
1123605290000.description: This five-story stone pagoda is thought to have belonged to Haewolsa Temple, which is said to have existed here since the Goryeo period. Its long lower body and irregular forms show a regional late Goryeo style influenced by the Baekje tradition of the Mireuksa and Jeongnimsa pagodas.

1123805300000.title_en: Rock-carved Standing Triad of Tathagata, Gaseopam Temple Site, Geochang
1123805300000.description: This rock carving shows a standing triad of Buddhas cut shallowly into a rock face shaped like a boat, with a halo formed around the figures. The central Buddha and attendant bodhisattvas retain elements inherited from Three Kingdoms-period sculpture, while also showing Goryeo-period formalization.

1123105310000.title_en: Stupa and Stele of Jeongji Guksa, Yongmunsa Temple, Yangpyeong
1123105310000.description: This set consists of a stupa and stele commemorating the life of the monk Jeongji Guksa (1324–1395), located east of Yongmunsa Temple. The octagonal stone stupa was erected by his disciples, and the stele was composed by the scholar Gwon Geun.

1123205400000.description: This stone pagoda was originally located in Gwaeseok-ri, Duchon-myeon, and was later moved to its current site in front of the Hongcheon County Council. It stands on a two-tier stylobate with a three-story body, and the four stone lions set on the upper base give it its distinctive name. The pedestal decoration, stone lions, lotus supports, and three-tiered roofstone supports show the style of the Goryeo period.

1123205410000.title_en: Stone Seated Tathagata Buddha, Mulgelli, Hongcheon
1123205410000.description: This stone seated Buddha is preserved at Daeseungsa Temple in Mulgelli, Hongcheon. Although the face is badly worn, the statue shows a rather flat and compact body compared with 8th-century images, and the elaborate octagonal pedestal reflects a later Unified Silla style. It is regarded as a work from the mid-9th century or later.

1123205420000.title_en: Stone Seated Vairocana Buddha, Mulgelli, Hongcheon
1123205420000.description: This stone seated Vairocana Buddha is one of the Buddhist sculptures preserved at Daeseungsa Temple in Mulgelli, Hongcheon, together with other related remains. The figure has a rounded face, a large topknot, and heavy, rather stiff drapery, while the hands are placed in an unusual mudra. It is considered a typical Vairocana Buddha image of the late 9th century.

1123205430000.description: This Buddhist pedestal remains at Daeseungsa Temple, while the original image and halo are no longer extant. The pedestal is an octagonal, three-tiered form with carved lotus motifs, guardian figures, and a bodhisattva standing figure on the middle section. It is thought to have been made in the 9th century, around the same time as the other Mulgelli Buddhist sculptures.

1123205440000.title_en: Stone Pedestal and Halo, Mulgelli, Hongcheon
1123205440000.description: This set is preserved at Daeseungsa Temple in Mulgelli, Hongcheon, with only the halo and pedestal remaining. The boat-shaped halo is carved with lotus, vine, and flame motifs, and small Buddhas are engraved at nine places with different hand gestures. The octagonal pedestal is also decorated with lotus, guardian figures, and floral motifs, and the whole work is attributed to the late Unified Silla period.

1123205450000.description: This three-story stone pagoda remains at the former temple site in Mulgelli, where many other remains suggest a large temple once stood. It has a two-tiered base and three-story body, with each story made from a single stone for the body and roofstone. Based on its style, especially the simplified base and the reduced roofstone supports on the third story, it is dated to the late 9th century.

1123305460000.description: This standing Buddha image was moved from Eub-ri, Cheongpung-myeon, which was inundated by the construction of Chungju Dam, to the entrance of Daegwangsa Temple beside Cheongpung Lake. Its compact head, square face, heavy drapery, and natural U-shaped folds beneath the waist reflect a style around the 10th century. Although it preserves the strength of Unified Silla sculpture, it is clearly a work of the early Goryeo period.

1123405470000.title_en: Relics of the Kim Jeong-hui Family Lineage
1123405470000.description: These are the relics and related materials preserved in the main family line of Kim Jeong-hui (1786–1856), the late Joseon scholar-official and calligrapher known as Chusa. The group includes personal belongings such as seals, prayer beads, inkstones, and brushes, as well as manuscripts, letters, calendars, and collected albums of his writings. It also includes a portrait of Kim Jeong-hui painted by Yi Han-cheol in 1857.

1123305320000.title_en: Monastic Stupa of Yeongguksa Temple, Yeongdong
1123305320000.description: This octagonal monastic stupa stands on a hill about 200 meters south of Yeongguksa Temple. It is divided into a base, body, and roofstone, with remaining finial elements including a bowl-shaped ornament and a jewel-shaped top. Based on its relationship to the stele of Woncak Guksa at the temple, it is believed to have been made in 1180.

1123305330000.title_en: Three-story Stone Pagoda of Yeongguksa Temple, Yeongdong
1123305330000.description: This pagoda stands in front of the Daeungjeon Hall of Yeongguksa Temple. It has a complete form with a two-tiered base, three-story body, and finial, and the carving on the base and body is relatively simple. It is considered a work of the late Unified Silla period.

1123305340000.title_en: Stele for Woncak Guksa, Yeongguksa Temple, Yeongdong
1123305340000.description: This stele was erected within Yeongguksa Temple to honor the monk Woncak Guksa of the Goryeo period. It consists of a tortoise-shaped base, the stele body, and a headstone; the headstone is carved with clouds and dragons, and the front bears the title "Woncak Guksa Bimyeong." It was built in 1180.

1123305350000.title_en: Three-story Stone Pagoda at Mangtapbong Peak, Yeongguksa Temple, Yeongdong
1123305350000.description: This pagoda stands on the summit of Mangtapbong Peak, about 500 meters east of Yeongguksa Temple. It is made by placing a three-story body on a large granite base shaped from the natural rock, with simplified architectural details. It is believed to date to the 12th century of the Goryeo period.

1123405360000.title_en: Stone Standing Buddha of Medicine Buddha, Pyongchon-ri, Asan
1123405360000.description: This large granite Buddha stands at an old temple site on a hillside in Pyongchon-ri. The figure holds a medicine bowl with both hands, indicating that it represents Bhaisajyaguru, the Medicine Buddha. Its face preserves some features associated with Unified Silla sculpture, while the symmetrical drapery and stiff posture show an early Goryeo style.

1123405370000.title_en: Banner Pole Supports of Eumnae-dong, Asan
1123405370000.description: These two granite pillar stones supported a banner pole used for Buddhist ceremonies at a temple entrance. The lower parts are buried underground, leaving only the paired supports visible, and each pillar has a groove for fixing the pole. They are thought to date to the Goryeo period.

1123405380000.title_en: Banner Pole Supports of Ogan-ri, Hongseong
1123405380000.description: These two stone banner pole supports stand in a cultivated field in Hongseong, an area identified with the former site of Gwanggyeongsa Temple. The pillars narrow upward, have vertical decorative lines on the outer faces, and are joined by a low stone base with a round hole for the pole. They are thought to have been made in the middle Goryeo period.

1122205390000.title_en: Geumgang Ordination Platform of Yongyeonsa Temple, Dalseong
1122205390000.description: This ordination platform at Yongyeonsa Temple enshrines relics of Śākyamuni. It consists of a broad two-tiered base with guardian figures and Eight Classes of Deities carved on it, supporting a bell-shaped body topped by a large jewel ornament. The platform was completed in 1613 during the reign of King Gwanghaegun.

1122205540000.description: This is a detached hall built in 1479 by Park Ilsan, the grandson of Park Paeng-nyeon. The present building was rebuilt in 1614 after the original burned during the Japanese invasions of 1592, and it is also called Ilsiru.

1121105550000.description: This pottery vessel is modeled on a boat and measures 9.1 cm in height and 27.9 cm in length. It was used as a burial object and is understood as an expression of the belief that the dead were transported to the afterlife; it is estimated to date to the 5th to 6th century.

1121105560000.description: This pair of pottery shoes measures 23.5 cm in length and was buried as a funerary object. Unlike the metal shoes found in royal tombs, it closely reproduces the form of actual shoes used at the time and is estimated to date to the 5th to 6th century.

1121105570000.description: These gold earrings, of unknown provenance, are 9 cm long and have a large ring 3.6 cm in diameter. They are decorated with fine gold granulation and delicate dangling ornaments, showing elaborate workmanship.

1121105580000.title_en: Celadon Meiping Vase with Inlaid Cloud, Crane, Peony, and Chrysanthemum Design
1121105580000.description: This Goryeo celadon meiping vase is decorated with inlaid designs of clouds, cranes, peonies, and chrysanthemums. It has a graceful sloping shoulder and a stable broad base, and is estimated to date to the mid-12th century.

1121105590000.description: This lacquer vessel was excavated from Daeseokam-ri, Daedong-gun, Pyeongan-nam-do, and is decorated with polychrome painting on both the inside and outside. It preserves vivid colors and a well-balanced composition of dragons, clouds, mountains, and animals.

1121105600000.title_en: Bronze Seal of Jinshuai Xianyi Baichang
1121105600000.description: This bronze seal is said to have been made in the Jin dynasty and was reportedly excavated in Yeongil-gun together with ten blue glass beads. The seal face is inscribed in clerical script with the characters "Jinshuai Xianyi Baichang."

1123705620000.title_en: Daewoongjeon Hall of Hwanseongsa Temple, Gyeongsan
1123705620000.description: This is the main hall of Hwanseongsa Temple, a Buddhist temple at the foot of Palgongsan Mountain. The present hall was rebuilt in 1635 and again restored in 1897, and it is a five-bay by four-bay wooden structure with a hip-and-gable roof and dancheong decoration.

1123605630000.description: This is a stone rainbow bridge at the entrance to Hyeungguksa Temple. It was built by stacking dressed stones over the stream banks, and the bridge arch and side walls are arranged in a balanced form with decorative dragon-head details.

1123805640000.description: This stone rainbow bridge spans a small stream in the village and is also called Namcheongyo Bridge. It was first built in 1780 and rebuilt in 1892, using natural bedrock at both sides as a foundation and layered granite blocks to form the arch.

1123105650000.title_en: Stone Seated Vairocana Buddha of Simboksa Temple, Pyeongtaek
1123105650000.description: This seated Buddha statue is enshrined in the Neunginjeon Hall of Simboksa Temple. The figure has a rounded face, a low ushnisha, clearly marked three folds on the neck, and a pedestal made of upper, middle, and lower parts; it is estimated to date to the 10th century.

1123305660000.description: This is a full-length portrait of Yu Geun, a mid-Joseon civil official, painted in color on silk. It shows him seated in formal court dress and was painted in 1619, when he was 71 years old.

1123105670000.title_en: Iron Seated Tathagata Buddha of Mangisa Temple, Pyeongtaek
1123105670000.description: This seated iron Buddha statue is at Mangisa Temple in Pyeongtaek and shows the typical style of Goryeo-period Buddhist sculpture. Only the main body remains; the right arm and both hands are later replacements, while the original parts are kept separately in the temple.

1123405680000.description: This group consists of two handwritten items left by independence activist Yoon Bong-gil: a pledge written when he joined the Korean Patriotic Corps, and his résumé and testament. The documents date to 1932 and include a 1-book, 17-leaf manuscript.

1123405680300.description: This group contains 10 kinds of 35 items left by independence activist Yoon Bong-gil, including a pocket watch, wallet with Chinese currency, seal, handkerchief, eyeglass case, diary, founding statement of the Woljinhoe, and the book Nongmin dogbon. The items date mainly to 1932 and preserve materials used by him during his independence activities.

1121105681300.description: This group contains 18 kinds of 30 items associated with independence activist Yoon Bong-gil, including membership records, flags, letters, writing tools, notebooks, printed or handwritten books, and personal belongings. The pieces date from 1920 to 1932 and document his activities in the Woljinhoe and later independence movement.

1123905470200.title_en: Collection of Artifacts from the Kim Jeong-hui Family Lineage
1123905470200.description: This group includes 10 artifacts related to Wolseongwi Kim Han-sin, presumed to have been handed down from Chusa Kim Jeong-hui’s old house, and the front cover and 15 autograph slips of the Shinhaeyeon calendar used by Kim Jeong-hui. The collection is considered valuable as a source for the study of calligraphy history.

1123105480000.title_en: Autograph Works of Yi Hwang - Toegye Seonsaeng Pilbeop and Toegye Seonsaeng Yujeop
1123105480000.description: This set consists of calligraphy models and letters that Toegye Yi Hwang wrote for his disciple Songam Gwon Homan in 1556, the 11th year of King Myeongjong. It includes examples of regular script, semi-cursive script, and cursive script written in different sizes, and the attached letters collected in two volumes.

1123705480200.title_en: Autograph Works of Yi Hwang - Seonjo Yumulcheop
1123705480200.description: This album gathers various writings by Toegye Yi Hwang, including letters to his descendants, drafts of his poems and prose, copies of other authors’ works, and writings of Tang and Song poems, spanning from his youth to old age. The cover title is recorded as "Seonjo Yumul" and the work survives in 18 volumes, although it originally had at least 23.

1123705490000.title_en: Ancient Documents of the Gwon Ju Family Lineage
1123705490000.description: These two documents have been handed down through the chief family line of Wasan Gwon Ju, a scholar of the Yeonsan-gun period. One is a house sale document for a property in Hwanghwabang, Hanseongbu, and the other is a property transfer document.

1121105500000.description: This woodblock-printed book was written by the Confucian scholar Yangchon Gwon Geun during the reign of King Sejong. It is a commentary on the Book of Changes and survives in three volumes, with no preface or postscript in the extant copy.

1121105510000.description: This one-volume music book records scores for hyangak, the Korean court music tradition distinguished from Tang music. It contains 26 song texts with notation, including many Goryeo songs not found in other sources, and is believed to have been compiled in the mid-Joseon period.

1121105520000.description: This is a printed copy of the lower part of volume 19 of the Jajitonggam Gangmok, a historical work compiled by Zhu Xi based on the Zizhi Tongjian. It is regarded as the only surviving movable-type edition of this section and bears an ink stamp indicating previous ownership by Okyeonjae in Andong.

1123705530000.title_en: Chunghyodang, House of the Yean Yi Clan, Andong
1123705530000.description: This house is associated with Yi Hong-in, who died fighting as a righteous army commander during the Japanese invasions of Korea, and it is said to have been built in 1551. The complex has a traditional Andong-style square layout with an inner courtyard, along with a separate pavilion called Ssangsudang.

1121105690100.title_en: Calligraphy by An Jung-geun - Baekindangjung Yu Taehwa
1121105690100.description: This is one of the calligraphic works An Jung-geun wrote in Lushun Prison in February or March 1910, before his death on March 26, 1910. The inscription reads, “In a house of a hundred acts of patience, there will be peace and harmony.” It also bears the note “Written by Great Korean An Jung-geun in Lushun Prison” and a palm print.

1121105690200.description: This is one of the calligraphic works An Jung-geun wrote in Lushun Prison in February or March 1910, before his death on March 26, 1910. The inscription means, “If one does not read for even a day, thorns grow in the mouth.” It also bears the note “Written by Great Korean An Jung-geun in Lushun Prison” and a palm print.

1121105690300.title_en: Calligraphy by An Jung-geun - Yeonnyeonse-se hwa sangsa se-se yeonnyeon in budoong
1121105690300.description: This is one of the calligraphic works An Jung-geun wrote in Lushun Prison in February or March 1910, before his death on March 26, 1910. The inscription means, “Year after year, the flowers are alike; year after year, people are not the same.” It also bears the note “Written by Great Korean An Jung-geun in Lushun Prison” and a palm print.

1121105690400.title_en: Calligraphy by An Jung-geun - Chiak ui ak-sik ja bujok yeoui
1121105690400.description: This is one of the calligraphic works An Jung-geun wrote in Lushun Prison in February or March 1910, before his death on March 26, 1910. The inscription means, “Those who are ashamed of coarse clothing and coarse food are not worth discussing things with.” It also bears the note “Written by Great Korean An Jung-geun in Lushun Prison” and a palm print.

1121105690500.title_en: Calligraphy by An Jung-geun - Dongyang daese saryo hyeon yuji nambae gwianmyeon hwaguk misi u ganggae jeongnyak bugae jin garyeon
1121105690500.description: This is one of the calligraphic works An Jung-geun wrote in Lushun Prison in February or March 1910, before his death on March 26, 1910. The text reflects on the situation in East Asia and says that a man of purpose cannot sleep peacefully while the harmony of the world has not yet been achieved and political plans remain unchanged. It also bears the note “Written by Great Korean An Jung-geun in Lushun Prison” and a palm print.

1122105690600.title_en: Calligraphy by An Jung-geun - Gyeon li sa ui gyeon wi su myeong
1122105690600.description: This is one of the calligraphic works An Jung-geun wrote in Lushun Prison in February or March 1910, before his death on March 26, 1910. The inscription means, “When seeing gain, think of righteousness; when facing danger, give up one’s life.” It also bears the note “Written by Great Korean An Jung-geun in Lushun Prison” and a palm print.

1121105690700.title_en: Calligraphy by An Jung-geun - Yonggongnanyong yeonbo gijae
1121105690700.description: This is one of the calligraphic works An Jung-geun wrote in Lushun Prison in February or March 1910, before his death on March 26, 1910. The inscription means, “An unskilled carpenter cannot work with valuable timber that takes two arms to encircle.” It also bears the note “Written by Great Korean An Jung-geun in Lushun Prison” and a palm print.

1121105690800.title_en: Calligraphy by An Jung-geun - Inmuwonryeo nanseong daeeop
1121105690800.description: This is one of the calligraphic works An Jung-geun wrote in Lushun Prison in February or March 1910, before his death on March 26, 1910. The inscription means, “A person without far-reaching foresight cannot accomplish great deeds.” It also bears the note “Written by Great Korean An Jung-geun in Lushun Prison” and a palm print.

1121105690900.title_en: An Jung-geun’s Manuscript - Onoh-bong is My Brush, Samgang is My Inkstone, the Blue Sky Is a One-Zhang Sheet of Paper on Which I Write the Poetry in My Heart
1121105690900.description: This is one of the calligraphic manuscripts written by An Jung-geun while imprisoned at Lushun Prison in February and March 1910, before his death on 26 March 1910. The inscription gives the date and identifies him as a Korean, and the text expresses his resolve to write the poetry in his heart on a vast sheet of paper.

1121105691000.title_en: An Jung-geun’s Manuscript - After the Cold Has Set in, One Knows That the Pine and Cypress Do Not Wither
1121105691000.description: This is one of the calligraphic manuscripts written by An Jung-geun in Lushun Prison in February and March 1910. The text is a quotation meaning that the pine and cypress are known not to wither only after the weather turns cold.

1123105691100.title_en: An Jung-geun’s Manuscript - Thinking of You a Thousand Li Away, My Eyes Seem to Pierce Through; I Offer This Small Sincerity, So Please Do Not Fail My Affection
1123105691100.description: This is one of the calligraphic manuscripts written by An Jung-geun in Lushun Prison in February and March 1910. The text expresses longing for someone far away and asks that the small sincerity offered in the writing not be rejected.

1121105691200.title_en: An Jung-geun’s Manuscript - Though a Man May Die, His Heart Is Like Iron; When a Righteous Man Faces Danger, His Spirit Is Like the Clouds
1121105691200.description: This is one of the calligraphic manuscripts written by An Jung-geun in Lushun Prison in February and March 1910. The text contrasts physical death with an unwavering heart and describes a righteous person's spirit as lofty as the clouds.

1121105691300.title_en: An Jung-geun’s Manuscript - Learn Broadly from Literature and Restrain Yourself with Ritual
1121105691300.description: This is one of the calligraphic manuscripts written by An Jung-geun in Lushun Prison in February and March 1910. The text advises broad study of writings and self-discipline through ritual propriety.

1121105691400.title_en: An Jung-geun’s Manuscript - The Very Best Rivers and Mountains
