1121105691400.description: This is one of the calligraphic manuscripts written by An Jung-geun in Lushun Prison in February and March 1910. The phrase "the very best rivers and mountains" is written in his hand with the prison-date inscription and palm seal.

1121105691500.description: This calligraphic manuscript was written by An Jung-geun in Lushun Prison after his sentencing to death on 14 February 1910 and before his death on 26 March 1910. It is one of the prison manuscripts that reflect his spiritual world.

1122105691600.title_en: An Jung-geun’s Manuscript - There Is No Lonelier Thing Than Self-Reliance
1122105691600.description: This is one of the calligraphic manuscripts written by An Jung-geun in Lushun Prison in February and March 1910. The text states that there is no greater solitude than self-conceit or overreliance on oneself.

1121105692500.title_en: Calligraphy by Ahn Jung-geun - Eonchungsinhangdeokgyeong manbang gahaeng
1121105692500.description: This calligraphy work was written by Ahn Jung-geun in Lushun Prison in March 1910. It bears the phrase “If one’s words are sincere and trustworthy and one’s conduct is earnest and reverent, then the Way can be practiced even in a barbarian land,” along with Ahn’s inscription and palm印.

1123805692600.title_en: Calligraphy by Ahn Jung-geun - Imjeok seonjin wijeang-ui mu
1123805692600.description: This calligraphy was written by Ahn Jung-geun in Lushun Prison in March 1910, shortly before his death. It reads, “To face the enemy and advance first is the duty of a general,” and includes his inscription and palm印.

1123105692700.title_en: Calligraphy by Ahn Jung-geun - Inmu wonryeo pilyu geunwoo
1123105692700.description: This hanging scroll calligraphy was written by Ahn Jung-geun in Lushun Prison in March 1910 and is thought to have been given to Kamimura Jūden. It bears the phrase “If a person does not plan far ahead, he will surely have immediate worries,” with Ahn’s inscription and palm印.

1123105692800.title_en: Calligraphy by Ahn Jung-geun - Iltong cheonghwa gong
1123105692800.description: This work was written by Ahn Jung-geun in Lushun Prison in March 1910 and appears to have been given to the prison guard section chief Kiyota. It consists of the phrase “To communicate daily with elegant and refined speech,” together with Ahn’s inscription and palm印.

1121105692900.title_en: Calligraphy by Ahn Jung-geun - Hwanggeum baekman nyang bulyeo ilgyoja
1121105692900.description: This calligraphy was written by Ahn Jung-geun in Lushun Prison in March 1910 and was given to Nakamura, the chief of the prison guard section. It reads, “A million nyang of gold is not as good as teaching one child,” and includes Ahn’s inscription and palm印.

1121105693000.title_en: Calligraphy by Ahn Jung-geun - Jisainin salsinseongin
1121105693000.description: This calligraphy was written by Ahn Jung-geun in Lushun Prison in March 1910 and was given to the Japanese journalist Komatsu Motoko. It reads, “A man of principle and benevolence sacrifices his life to accomplish benevolence,” and includes Ahn’s inscription and palm印.

1121105693100.description: This calligraphy work was written by Ahn Jung-geun in Lushun Prison in March 1910, and the recipient is not clearly known. It consists of the three characters meaning “platform for washing the mind,” with Ahn’s inscription and palm印.

1121105700000.title_en: Group of Relics from Goryeong, Former Provenance
1121105700000.description: This is a grouped set of artifacts said to have been excavated from tombs in the Goryeong area of North Gyeongsang Province, the center of Daegaya during the Gaya period. The assemblage includes beads, belt fittings, swords, horse trappings, and other burial goods.

1121105691700.description: This calligraphic work was written by Ahn Jung-geun in Lüshun Prison in February or March 1910, before his death on 26 March 1910. It is one of the group of prison writings in which he wrote moral maxims, quotations from the Analects and Records of the Grand Historian, and occasionally a house name for someone. The work is marked with Ahn’s handprint and his inscription identifying himself as a Korean in Lüshun Prison.

1121105691800.description: This calligraphic work was written by Ahn Jung-geun in Lüshun Prison in February or March 1910. It belongs to the group of prison writings produced before his death on 26 March 1910, and it bears his handprint and the inscription identifying him as a Korean writing in Lüshun Prison.

1121105691900.description: This calligraphic work was written by Ahn Jung-geun in Lüshun Prison in February or March 1910. It is one of his prison writings from the final months before his death, with his handprint and an inscription noting that it was written in Lüshun Prison by Ahn Jung-geun.

1121105692000.description: This calligraphic work was written by Ahn Jung-geun in Lüshun Prison in February or March 1910. It is included among the prison writings he produced before his death on 26 March 1910, and it bears his handprint and identifying inscription.

1121105692100.title_en: Ahn Jung-geun's Calligraphy - If You Wish to Preserve East Asia, First Change Your Political Policy; When the Chance Passes, Regret Is Useless
1121105692100.description: This calligraphic work was written by Ahn Jung-geun in Lüshun Prison in March 1910 and later kept by Orita Tadasu before being donated to Dankook University in 1989. The inscription says that if one wishes to preserve East Asia, one must first change aggressive policy, and that regret is useless once the opportunity has passed. It is written on Xuan paper with Ahn Jung-geun's handprint and his prison inscription.

1121105692200.title_en: Ahn Jung-geun's Calligraphy - Concerned for the Safety of the Nation
1121105692200.description: This calligraphic work was written by Ahn Jung-geun in Lüshun Prison in March 1910 and presented to Prosecutor Yasuoka Seishiro. The inscription reads, 'Concerned for the safety of the nation,' and includes Ahn Jung-geun's prison inscription and handprint. It was later donated to the Ahn Jung-geun Memorial Association in 1976.

1121105692300.title_en: Ahn Jung-geun's Calligraphy - Devoting Oneself to the Nation Is a Soldier's Duty
1121105692300.description: This calligraphic work was written by Ahn Jung-geun in Lüshun Prison in March 1910 and given to a Japanese military police guard, Chiba Toshikichi. The inscription states that devoting oneself to the nation is a soldier's duty, and it includes Ahn Jung-geun's prison inscription and handprint. It was later preserved by the recipient's family and donated to the Ahn Jung-geun Memorial Association in 1980.

1123905692400.title_en: Ahn Jung-geun's Calligraphy - What Heaven Gives, If Not Received, Will Only Bring Misfortune
1123905692400.description: This calligraphic work was written by Ahn Jung-geun in Lüshun Prison in February 1910, before his death. The text reads, 'What Heaven gives, if not received, will only bring misfortune,' and Ahn Jung-geun's handprint appears with the date and prison inscription. It is one of his prison writings from the final period of his life.

1123605710000.title_en: Memorial Stele for Admiral Yi Sun-sin’s Naval Victory, Yeosu
1123605710000.description: This large memorial stele was erected to commemorate the achievements of Admiral Yi Sun-sin. It was originally set up in 1615 and later recovered after having been moved to Seoul during the Japanese colonial period.

1123605720000.title_en: Goryeo Documents of Songgwangsa Temple, Suncheon
1123605720000.description: This group consists of two Goryeo-period documents related to the history and administration of Suseonsa, the earlier name of Songgwangsa Temple. One records the temple’s foundation history, and the other is a slave register for temple-affiliated slaves.

1121105730000.description: This is a woodblock-printed commentary on the Book of Songs and the Book of Documents by the scholar Gwon Geun. It is considered Korea’s first explanatory work on the Confucian classics and was probably printed in 1429–1430.

1121105740000.description: This manuscript records Park Man-jeong’s 65-day inspection trip to Hwanghae Province in 1696 as an amhaeng-eosa, or secret royal inspector. It includes his diary, reports to the king, and related administrative notes.

1123705750000.title_en: Documents Related to the Wooden Amitabha Preaching Image of Daeseungsa Temple, Mungyeong
1123705750000.description: These documents are related to a wooden carved Buddhist hanging image of Amitabha that was moved from Buseoksa Temple to Daeseungsa Temple. They also include records concerning the dispute over the transfer of the object and its earlier temple affiliation.

1121105760000.title_en: Bronze Gong Inscribed with Bongeopsa Temple
1121105760000.description: This large bronze gong, also called a ritual gong, was made in 1217 at Bongeopsa Temple in Duksu. The surface is decorated with concentric bands, lotus petals, cloud motifs, and a flower-bud border, and the inscription records its production date and place.

1121105770000.title_en: Buncheong Ware Inlaid Fish-Design Plate-Shaped Tomb Record with Inscription ‘Jeongtong 5th Year’
1121105770000.description: This buncheong ware vessel is a tomb record that was buried beside a grave to record the deceased person’s life. The rim inscription identifies its production date as 1440, and the interior is decorated with an inlaid fish design.

1123605780000.title_en: Preaching Buddhist Hanging Scroll of Daeungjeon Hall, Heungguksa Temple
1123605780000.description: This large hanging scroll depicts Sakyamuni preaching at Vulture Peak, with bodhisattvas, the Four Heavenly Kings, and attendants arranged around him. It was painted on silk in 1693 by the monk-painters Cheonsin and Uicheon for the nation’s peace and the king’s longevity.

1121105790000.title_en: Five-Story Stone Stupa of Osa-ri, Goesan
1121105790000.description: This stone stupa originally stood on a hillside in Osa-ri village and was nearly taken abroad by a Japanese collector during the Japanese colonial period. It was moved to the Gansong Art Museum and re-erected in 1964 after having collapsed and been scattered during the Korean War. The octagonal base and body are decorated with carvings, and the overall style suggests a work from before the mid-Goryeo period.

1121105800000.description: This Goryeo-period stone pagoda is now housed at the Gansong Art Museum. It originally stood in Mungyeong, Gyeongsangbuk-do, and was recovered by Jeon Hyeong-pil when Japanese collectors tried to move it elsewhere during the colonial period. The pagoda stands on a two-tier base with five stories above, and most parts remain relatively complete.

1123705810000.title_en: Rock-carved Seated Tathāgata Buddha of Gulgulam Hermitage, Gyeongju
1123705810000.description: This rock-carved seated Buddha is located at the top of the twelve cave shrines made by using a natural cave on the high cliff of Gulgulam Hermitage. Its facial features, simplified body, and regular robe folds show a more formalized late Unified Silla style. The carved halo is partly preserved, and the work is thought to date to around the late 9th century.

1123405820000.description: These are the woodblocks used to print Wolinseokbo, and they are the only surviving blocks of this work in Korea. Wolinseokbo was compiled in 1459 by combining Wolin cheongang jigok and Seokbosangjeol, and the surviving blocks consist of 46 plates for volume 21. They were carved in 1569 and later kept at Ssanggyesa Temple in Nonsan before being moved to Gapsa Temple.

1123505830000.description: Pungpazigwan is an old guesthouse (gaeksa) in Jeonju that was originally established before 1471, based on a record that it was repaired using leftover materials from a building project in that year. In Joseon, such guesthouses were used to house envoys and to hold rituals facing the royal palace. Today, the main hall and a few auxiliary buildings remain, and the hall sign reads "Pungpazigwan."

1123605840000.description: This memorial stele records the life and achievements of Yun Hyoson (1431–1503), a Joseon official who served in several high offices and helped compile the Gyeongguk Daejeon and Oryeui ju. It was erected in 1519, with the inscription written by Shin Yong-gae and calligraphy by Shin Gong-je. The stele stands on a turtle-shaped base with a dragon carved on the headstone.

1123105850000.title_en: Collected Calligraphy and Paintings of Two Masters: Toe and U
1123105850000.description: This album brings together writings and paintings by scholars and artists including Yi Hwang, Song Si-yeol, Jeong Seon, Jeong Man-su, Yi Byeong-yeon, Im Heon-hwi, and Kim Yong-jin, arranged in chronological order. It contains eight leaves, including Jeong Seon's Kyesang jeonggeo-do, Yi Hwang's preface to Hoeam seojeolyo, and works by Song Si-yeol, Yi Byeong-yeon, and others. The inner paper is made of mulberry paper, and the album preserves both texts and paintings in good condition.

1123705860100.title_en: Manuscript Copy of Lee Eon-jeok's Seokdaehokmun
1123705860100.description: This manuscript is one of the works personally written by the mid-Joseon Neo-Confucian scholar and statesman Yi Eonjeok between 1547 and 1553. It adds items not discussed in Zhu Xi's Daxue huowen, and it was later lectured on in the royal lectures during King Jeongjo's reign. King Jeongjo also wrote the title page by hand and sent it down to the court.

1122406000000.title_en: Granite Seated Buddha of Yaksaam Hermitage, Gwangju
1122406000000.description: This Unified Silla-period Buddha statue is made of roughly worked granite and is in good condition. It represents Bhaisajyaguru, the Medicine Buddha who is believed to save beings from illness. The figure has a broad upper face, a sloping shoulder line, a thin waist, and sits on an octagonal lotus pedestal composed of separate stones for the upper, middle, and lower parts.

1122206010000.title_en: Stupa of Monk in Dohak-dong, Daegu
1122206010000.description: This stupa, now standing at Donghwasa Temple, was moved there from a site in Dohak-dong where it had fallen over. It has an octagonal base and body, with a three-part platform and a roof stone whose corners rise gently. Based on its style and carving, it is believed to be a work of the early Goryeo period.

1123206020000.title_en: Yulgok Yi I, Manuscript Copy of Gyeokmong yogyol
1123206020000.description: This is the autograph manuscript of Gyeokmong yogyol, written by Yi I in 1577 when he was 42 and living in Haeju after leaving office. It was written in neat cursive on Korean paper and organized into ten chapters from "Iji" to "Cheosae." The book was later presented with a preface added by royal command in 1788.

1123206030000.title_en: Register of Successfu Candidates in the Civil and Military Mixed Examinations
1123206030000.description: This volume is a list of the successful candidates in the civil and military mixed-state examinations held in 1513, the 8th year of King Jungjong's reign. It contains 37 leaves and is printed with Gapinja type, which makes it an important example for the study of early Joseon printing. As an early Joseon roster, it is a rare source for research on major figures of the period.

1123706040000.title_en: King Sejo's Royal Grant to Jeokgae Meritorious Subject Jang Malson
1123706040000.description: This royal document was issued in 1467, the 13th year of King Sejo's reign, to 45 meritorious retainers who helped suppress the Yi Si-ae Rebellion. Jang Malson was awarded the second rank and received this certificate as a Jeokgae meritorious subject. The document lists the names of all the meritorious subjects and bears the royal seal "Simgnigibo."

1123706050000.description: This petroglyph is carved on a rock wall about 3 meters high and 6 meters wide at the entrance to Alter Village. The designs include concentric circles, a cross-like form, and a mask-like face, and they are interpreted as symbols related to beliefs in a sun god and agricultural rites. It is thought to date to the late Bronze Age, around 300 BCE to 0.

1123706060000.title_en: East and West Three-Story Stone Pagodas of Dochonsa Temple Site, Mungyeong
1123706060000.description: These two stone pagodas now stand east and west in front of Daeungjeon Hall at Jikjisa Temple, having been moved from the former Dochonsa Temple site in Mungyeong. Each pagoda has a one-tier base and three-story body, with roof stones whose corners rise lightly. The finial on top was newly made when the pagodas were re-erected in 1976.

1123706070000.title_en: Three-Story Stone Pagoda of Dochonsa Temple Site, Mungyeong
1123706070000.description: This three-story stone pagoda stands in front of Birojeon Hall at Jikjisa Temple and was moved from the former Dochonsa Temple site in Mungyeong in 1974. It has a one-tier base and a three-story body, with each story made from a single stone for the body and roof. Its slim roof stones with upturned corners are characteristic of a late 9th-century Unified Silla pagoda.

1123705860200.description: This is a collection of manuscripts written by Yi Eonjeok (1491–1553), a Neo-Confucian scholar and statesman of the mid-Joseon period. The set was written by Yi himself between 1547 and 1553, and includes a postscript by Noh Su-sin. It is notable for presenting views that differ in part from Zhu Xi's interpretation of the Great Learning.

1123605870000.description: This collection consists of 14 books and 64 sheets of records preserved by Pilyam Seowon, which was founded in 1590 and received royal recognition in 1662. The materials date from 1624 to around 1900 and include seowon registers, student lists, property records, and official notices. They are valuable sources for studying the operation of a Joseon-era private academy as well as local education and socioeconomic history.

1121105880000.description: This portrait depicts Gang Mincheom (963–1021), a famous Goryeo military commander, but the painting itself was copied in 1788 by Park Chun-bin after an earlier original. He is shown seated in full dress, wearing the after-examination cap and holding a tablet, in a half-length composition facing left. The tiger skin on the chair back reflects portrait conventions of the 18th century.

1121105890000.description: This full-length portrait depicts Gang Hyeon (1650–1733), a mid-Joseon civil official and the father of the painter and scholar Gang Se-hwang. He is shown seated on a tiger-skin-covered chair, facing right, wearing official headgear and a green court robe. The work shows characteristic 18th-century portrait techniques in the modeling of the face and garments.

1121105900000.description: This set consists of two portraits of Gang Se-hwang (1713–1791), a leading late-Joseon scholar-painter and calligrapher. One is a self-portrait, and the other is said to have been painted by Yi Myeong-gi. Both are seated full-length portraits on silk, and the self-portrait shows Gang at age 71.

1123105910000.title_en: Woodblocks for Seokssi wonryu eunghwa sajeok
1123105910000.description: These woodblocks were used to print a book published in 1673 by the monk Jiseop at Buleamsa Temple in Yangju, based on a book brought from Ming China by Jeong Duwon in 1631. The work records the life of the Buddha and the spread of Buddhism in India and China in 400 sections, each with a four-character heading and an accompanying illustration. The set consists of 212 blocks, and the names of 18 painters and block carvers are recorded at the end.

1121105920000.description: This is a collection of manuscript writings by the mid-Joseon Confucian scholar Heomok (1595–1682). The set includes three works in 12 volumes: Donghaebi, Geumseok unbu, and Gomun unbu. These materials are important sources for studying Heomok's seal-script style and related calligraphic tradition.

1121105920201.description: This hanging scroll is a large-character seal-script inscription by the Confucian scholar and calligrapher Heomok (1595–1682), a representative figure of 17th-century seal-script calligraphy. It is written in one character per sheet on three joined sheets of paper, and retains four seals by Heomok. A later colophon written in 1791 by the owner Hong Su-bo is attached below the inscription.

1123506080000.description: This Buddhist hall at Wibongsa Temple is believed from its construction style to have been built in the 17th century. The plaque reading "Bogwangmyeongjeon" is said to have been written in 1828, and the hall has a three-bay front, three-bay side plan with a paljak roof and daepo-style bracket complexes. Inside, it has a well ceiling, a canopy above the altar, and well-preserved painted decorations, including a White-robed Avalokitesvara mural on the rear wall.

1123706090000.description: This is a typical Unified Silla stone pagoda with a two-tier base and three-story body. The lower base is carved with the Twelve Divine Generals, the upper base with the Eight Guardian Deities, and the first-story body with the Four Heavenly Kings; the pagoda was repaired in 1974 after nearly collapsing.

1123706100000.description: This pagoda has a two-tier base and a three-story body, with the lower base carved with the Twelve Divine Generals and the upper base with the Eight Guardian Deities. The first-story body is carved with the Four Heavenly Kings, and the form and carving style indicate that it was built in the late Unified Silla period, around the 9th century.

1123106110000.title_en: Stupa Stele of Wonjeung Guksa, Taego-sa Temple, Goyang
1123106110000.description: This stele was erected beside the main hall of Taegosa Temple in 1385 to honor Wonjeung Guksa, a late Goryeo monk who died in 1382. It stands on a tortoise pedestal with a dragon-headed support and is topped with a capstone carved with cloud and dragon motifs; the inscription was composed by Yi Saek and written by Gwon Ju.

1123206120000.title_en: Stupa Stele of Jinghyo Daesa, Heungnyeongsa Temple Site, Yeongwol
1123206120000.description: This stone stele was erected in 944 to commemorate Jinghyo Daesa, who greatly developed Heungnyeongsa Temple. The inscription records his life from ordination to death, and the stele has a tortoise pedestal and a capstone carved with dragons.

1123306130000.description: This portrait depicts Shin Suk-ju (1417–1475), a scholar-official of the early Joseon period, seated and facing to the right in official robes. The painting shows him in the attire of a second-rank civil official and preserves a refined rendering of the face, clothing outlines, and color application.

1123806140000.description: This stele records a Maehyang rite, a Buddhist ceremony in which fragrant wood or incense was buried to honor heaven and earth deities. It was erected in 1387, and the inscription notes that more than 4,100 people joined a religious association to pray for the king's longevity, national prosperity, and the people's peace.

1122306150000.description: This is a Goryeo-period stone standing Buddha carved in relief on a thick granite slab. The figure has a rounded face, short neck, simplified robe folds, and a halo marked with carved flame motifs and bead-like ornaments.

1121105920301.title_en: Heomok, Seal Script Calligraphy of "Aegun Uguk"
1121105920301.description: Written on two sheets of paper, this calligraphy is the largest surviving hanging-board inscription known by the pen name Miseu Heomok (1595–1682). Five of Heomok’s seals are stamped on both sides of the work. It is regarded as a representative example of his large-scale seal-script style, along with the hanging board in the collection of Korea University Museum.

1121105920400.title_en: Heomok, Seal Script Calligraphy of "Hanganmun" and Others
1121105920400.description: In March 1682, Heomok copied his own writings, including the three-part "Hanganmun," "Bulyeomuksaji," and "Hineungiji," in gold ink on eight black silk panels. The work is thought to relate to a 1682 request by Seoin official Lee Jeong-yeong to prohibit Heomok’s seal-script handwriting. Among Heomok’s surviving works, it is the only known example written in gold ink.

1121105930000.title_en: Collection of Buddhist Paintings by Lee Sang-jo
1121105930000.description: This picture book gathers several Buddhist figure paintings by the early Joseon painter Lee Sang-jo (1465–?). The surviving five drawings, rendered only in ink lines on paper without color, are believed to have been prepared as models for later use. They are important materials for studying figure-painting techniques of the early Joseon period.

1123605940000.title_en: Portrait of Choe Deok-ji and Preliminary Sketch on Tracing Paper
1123605940000.description: This set consists of the original portrait of the early Joseon scholar-official Choe Deok-ji (1384–1455) and its preliminary sketch. The portrait, painted in color on silk, shows him seated beside a desk with a book, facing slightly to the right. The sketch on paper is the same size as the original and provides valuable evidence for the portrait-making process.
1123605940000.material: Color on silk; ink on paper

1122105950000.title_en: Embroidered Grass and Insect Folding Screen
1122105950000.description: This eight-panel folding screen is made of black silk with embroidered grass, butterflies, dragonflies, and other insects. More than twenty kinds of plants and insects, including dandelions, pinks, cockscombs, bees, and butterflies, can be identified. It is thought to have been made after the 18th century and to have been used in a palace or a yangban household.

1122105970000.description: This Neolithic bowl was excavated from the shell midden at Yeongseon-dong, Yeongdo-gu, Busan. It has a short spout attached to one side of the rim and raised decorative bands below the rim, with the surface marked by pressed and incised patterns. It is considered an early Neolithic vessel.

1122105980000.title_en: Pottery Horn Cup with Horse-Head Ornament
1122105980000.description: This horn cup with a horse-head ornament was excavated from Tomb No. 7 at the Bokcheon-dong tombs in Dongnae-gu, Busan. Although horn cups were originally made of animal horn, the term also covers vessels copied in clay or metal, and this example is regarded as a superb work among those found in Silla and Gaya tombs. The horse-head attachment and small supporting legs were shaped so that the vessel would not tip over.

1122105990000.description: This is a type of personal firearm used in the mid-Joseon period. It has two barrels, allowing three rounds to be loaded and fired from each barrel, for a total of six shots aimed at once. The barrel is inscribed with the year of manufacture, 1583, and instructions for use.

1123706160000.description: Yeongcheonhyanggyo is a local government-run Confucian school where rites for ancient sages were performed and learning was pursued. Daeseongjeon is the main ritual hall, enshrining the spirit tablets of Confucius and other sages. It was first built in 1435 and later rebuilt and repaired several times; the present building has a five-bay front, three-bay sides, and a gabled roof.

1123706170000.title_en: Gold Crown Ornament from Cheonmachong Tomb (1978-1)
1123706170000.description: This gold crown ornament was found on the lid of a storage box placed near the head side of the coffin in Cheonmachong Tomb. It has a rounded central body with wing-like sides and a shield-shaped lower part, and was decorated with many circular ornaments connected in a row. Its exact function is not known.

1123706180000.title_en: Gold Crown Ornament from Cheonmachong Tomb (1978-2)
1123706180000.description: This gold crown ornament was discovered in a storage box near the head side of the coffin in Cheonmachong Tomb. It is shaped like a large bird with outspread wings, with vine patterns engraved on the body and wings and many round discs linked across the front. Its exact use is uncertain.

1123706190000.title_en: Neck and Chest Ornament from Cheonmachong Tomb
1123706190000.description: This neck and chest ornament was found in the coffin of Cheonmachong Tomb and appears to have been worn around the neck. It is made of gold, silver, jade, and glass, with blue glass beads and metal pieces linked in six rows and large curved jade pendants on both sides. When worn, the whole piece forms a V shape.

1123706200000.description: This glass cup was found in Cheonmachong Tomb; two examples were discovered, though one was too damaged to restore. It is made of transparent blue glass and shows a high level of craftsmanship, with vertical ridges and repeated circular decoration on most of the surface.

1123706210000.description: This ring-pommel sword was found in Cheonmachong Tomb and is an example of a weapon that also indicated the owner's status. The scabbard and hilt were made of wood covered with thin gilt bronze, and the round pommel includes a bird's head that appears to be a phoenix. A separate small scabbard was attached beside the main one.

1123706220000.title_en: Bronze Cooking Vessel with Handle from Cheonmachong Tomb
1123706220000.description: This bronze vessel was used for boiling or warming liquor, food, or medicine and is usually found only in large tombs such as royal tombs. It has a flattened spherical body with a lid, three animal-shaped legs, a goose-head spout, and a hollow handle that probably received a wooden grip. The lid is hinged to the body and topped with a flowerbud-shaped knob.

1123706230000.title_en: Gold Bracelets and Rings from the North Mound of Hwangnamdaechong Tomb
1123706230000.description: These gold bracelets and rings were found in the north mound of Hwangnamdaechong Tomb, a Silla tomb in the Michuwangneung area of Gyeongju. The bracelets include simple bent gold-wire forms and one ornate example decorated with jade, while the rings show different patterns, including lozenge shapes and lattice designs. They provide important evidence for the use of foreign decorative motifs in the period.

1123706240000.title_en: Glass Cup from the North Mound of Hwangnamdaechong Tomb
1123706240000.description: This glass cup was excavated from the north mound of Hwangnamdaechong Tomb, a Silla tomb in the Michuwangneung area of Hwangnam-dong, Gyeongju. It is transparent brown glass with a wood-grain pattern over the whole surface, and its form suggests it was made outside Silla and brought from the West. The cup is largely intact except for slight damage to the base of the stand.

1123706250000.title_en: Silver Crown Ornaments from the North Mound of Hwangnamdaechong Tomb
1123706250000.description: These silver crown ornaments were excavated from the north mound of Hwangnamdaechong Tomb and consist of one bird-wing-shaped ornament and two butterfly-shaped ornaments. They were made by cutting and joining silver sheets, and the surfaces are decorated with punched dot lines and incised marks. The bird-wing-shaped ornament bears engraved characters and symbols on the back, showing distinctive workmanship.

1123706260000.title_en: Gold Goblet from the North Mound of Hwangnamdaechong Tomb
1123706260000.description: This gold goblet was found in the north mound of Hwangnamdaechong Tomb, a Silla tomb in Gyeongju. It follows the form of a footed bowl with a flaring stand, but because it is made of gold and decorated with leaf ornaments, it appears to have been made as a burial item rather than for everyday use. The object is partially dented but is a rare surviving example of a gold footed bowl.

1123706270000.title_en: Silver Cup from the North Mound of Hwangnamdaechong Tomb
1123706270000.description: This silver cup was excavated from the north mound of Hwangnamdaechong Tomb in Gyeongju. The surface is decorated with lotus petals, a turtle-shell pattern, and various fantastic animal motifs, with a phoenix motif placed at the center of the base. The decorative style suggests contacts with foreign cultures.

1123706280000.title_en: Set of Gold and Silver Vessels from the North Mound of Hwangnamdaechong Tomb
1123706280000.description: This set consists of three types of vessels excavated from the north mound of Hwangnamdaechong Tomb: silver bowls with lids, silver bowls, and gold bowls. The silver lidded vessels have rounded bodies with low feet and lids with a ring-shaped knob, while the bowls have low feet and flaring rims. The gold bowls follow the same form as the silver bowls.

1123706290000.title_en: Gold Belt from the South Mound of Hwangnamdaechong Tomb
1123706290000.description: This gold belt, excavated from the south mound of Hwangnamdaechong Tomb, consists of a waist belt and attached pendants. The belt links pierced rectangular plaques with 34 leaf-shaped ornaments, and seven rows of pendants hang below them. Buckles are attached at both ends so the belt can be fastened.

1123706300000.title_en: Gold Crown Ornament from the South Mound of Hwangnamdaechong Tomb
1123706300000.description: This gold crown ornament was excavated from the south mound of Hwangnamdaechong Tomb in Gyeongju. It is made of three gold plates, with the central plate shaped like the character for mountain and the side plates formed like bird wings. Small circular ornaments are attached to the front, while the lower part has no decoration and appears to have been inserted into a crown.

1123706310000.title_en: Silver Crown from the South Mound of Hwangnamdaechong Tomb
1123706310000.description: This silver crown was found in a burial pit near the head end outside the coffin in the south mound of Hwangnamdaechong Tomb. The crown has an unusual three-branch top, with the central branch bent in an arch and the side branches made with silver plates cut into feather-like forms. It is noted as a rare example in the Gyeongju area.

1121106410000.description: This is a woodblock-printed edition of Seonjong Yeonggajib, a work by the Tang-dynasty monk Hyeon'gak explaining the teachings of Seon Buddhism in an accessible way. The colophon states that it was carved and published at Cheongnyongsa Temple in Chungju in 1381 by Damyeo, Gaknul, and others, and the book is well preserved with clear printing.

1121106420000.title_en: Stone Fragment from Pyeongyang Fortress, Goguryeo
1121106420000.description: This stone fragment was carved during the construction of Goguryeo's Pyeongyang Fortress on a relatively flat natural stone. Seven lines of 27 characters remain, and the piece is preserved in a fractured state with nine joined fragments.

1123106430000.description: This small gilt-bronze Buddha image, now displayed at the Hoam Museum of Art in Yongin, is 11.1 cm high. It shows a pensive Bodhisattva in half-seated pose with a three-peaked crown, long side hair, and a separate lotus-decorated footrest; the style is considered to date to the late 6th century and may be a Silla work.

1121106440000.title_en: White Porcelain Vase with Underglaze Blue Pine, Bamboo, and Figure Design
1121106440000.description: This blue-and-white porcelain vase was made in the early Joseon period and is about 47 cm high. Its body is decorated with a pine tree, bamboo, a seated scholar, and a boy holding a gayageum, and the composition is thought to reflect painting styles of the late 16th century.
1121106440000.material: White porcelain with underglaze cobalt blue

1121106450000.title_en: White Porcelain Vase with Iron-painted Cloud and Dragon Design
1121106450000.description: This Joseon-period white porcelain vase is decorated with a cloud and dragon motif painted in iron pigment. Its grayish-white glaze, concave foot, and style suggest production at a 17th-century kiln site in the Gwangju area, and it is considered an important early example of iron-painted white porcelain.

1123306460000.title_en: Celadon Lidded Box with Inlaid 'Sangyakguk' Inscription and Carved Cloud-and-Dragon Design
1123306460000.description: This lidded cylindrical celadon box bears the inlaid inscription 'Sangyakguk,' the name of the government office in charge of medicine in Goryeo. The lid is carved with clouds and cranes, and the piece is thought to have been made in the 12th century for use as a medicine container.

1121106470000.description: This is a large Joseon-period cannon that was ignited and fired by hand. The inscription on the barrel shows that it was made in 1555 during the reign of King Myeongjong, and it is regarded as the largest Korean cannon and the oldest extant cannon with an inscription.

1121106480000.description: This is a small portable hand-cannon used as a personal firearm. The inscription records that it was made in 1579 by Gim Ji, then naval commander of Jeolla Left Province and magistrate of Gyeongsang; it is an early example of a portable cannon.

1123706320000.title_en: Silver Arm Guard from the South Mound of Hwangnamdaechong Tomb
1123706320000.description: This silver arm guard was excavated from Hwangnamdaechong Tomb, a Silla tomb in the Michuwangneung area of Gyeongju. It was found in a burial pit near the head side outside the coffin in the south mound, and measures 35 cm in length.

1123706330000.description: This gold pendant was found in Michuwangneung Tomb in Hwangnam-dong, Gyeongju, and consists of one long strand and three short strands. The long strand is made by linking hollow gold beads with petal ornaments twisted from gold thread and ending with jade-colored beads; it is regarded as one of the most luxurious Silla tomb pendants.

1123706340000.title_en: Inlaid Glass Bead from Hwangnam-dong, Gyeongju
1123706340000.description: This necklace bead was found in Michuwangneung Tomb in Hwangnam-dong, Gyeongju, and the necklace is about 24 cm long. On the small round glass bead, 16 ducks and two human faces are delicately inlaid in multiple colors, and it is noted for its highly skilled workmanship.

1123706350000.description: This sword was discovered in the Michuwangneung area in Hwangnam-dong, Gyeongju, during road construction in 1973. Only the gold fittings remain, since the iron blade and scabbard have decayed; the sword was found near the waist of the buried person and is important evidence for cultural exchange between East and West.

1123706360000.description: This pottery figure was excavated from Tomb No. 3 in Area C among the tombs in front of Michuwangneung in Gyeongju. It is 15.1 cm high and shaped like a tortoise with a dragon-like head and tail, combining animal forms commonly seen in Silla figural pottery with a highly original conception.

1123806370000.description: This Gaya vessel was excavated at an unknown site and is 18.5 cm high and 24 cm long. It has a flaring pedestal with four rectangular openings, a U-shaped horn cup on top, and wheel ornaments attached to both sides.

1121106380000.description: This painted album was made to commemorate a gathering of elderly high officials and includes the banquet scene and portraits of the participants. It was completed in 1720 by court painters for the king and members of the Giseosa office, and contains the preface, poems, postscript, attendance list, and portraits of ten participants.

1121106400000.description: This woodblock-printed Buddhist book, based on a Yuan-dynasty edition printed in 1357, was re-carved and published at Hoeamsa Temple in 1395 by Monk Muhak. It is bound in three volumes and is an important source for early Joseon Buddhist studies and bibliography.

1121106570000.title_en: Rock-carved Standing Buddha at Samcheonsa Temple Site, Seoul
1121106570000.description: This standing Buddha is carved in shallow relief on a screen-shaped rock at the entrance to the Samcheonsa Temple site at the foot of Bukhansan Mountain. It is 3.02 meters high and is considered a representative early Goryeo rock-carved Buddha, despite its somewhat simplified details.

1123306580000.title_en: Stele for Bogak Guksa at Cheongnyongsa Temple Site, Chungju
1123306580000.description: This stele at the former Cheongnyongsa Temple site was erected in 1394 to honor the monk Bogak Guksa Honsu (1320–1392), who was active from the late Goryeo to the early Joseon period. The inscription was written by Gwon Geun, and the calligraphy was written by the monk Cheontaek; the stele is noted for the strength and dignity of its script.

1121106590000.title_en: White Porcelain Bottle with Underglaze Cobalt Blue Plum, Bird, and Bamboo Design
1121106590000.description: This early Joseon white porcelain bottle was made under the influence of Yuan and Ming Chinese ceramics, but it already shows Korean characteristics. It was used as a liquor bottle and is decorated with plum trees, bamboo, and birds painted in underglaze cobalt blue.
1121106590000.material: White porcelain with underglaze cobalt blue

1123606600000.title_en: Documents Related to Choe Hui-ryang’s War Reports from the Imjin War
1123606600000.description: This set of official documents records the battle reports submitted by Choe Hui-ryang, who was then magistrate of Heungyang during the Imjin War, to Admiral Yi Sun-sin and the Jeolla provincial governor. The collection preserves the original format of local wartime reporting and related official replies.

1123706610000.description: These two stone figures are a musician and an offering attendant carved in relief on large granite slabs, now preserved at the Sangju Museum. They are estimated to have been made around the 8th century and are important as material for studying the clothing of the period.

1123506620000.description: Uhwaru is the gate-like pavilion in front of Geukrakjeon Hall at Hwaamsa Temple. The present building was erected in 1611 during the reign of King Gwanghaegun and has been repaired several times since then.

1123306640000.description: Daeungjeon is the main Buddha hall of Ansimsa Temple, which belongs to Beopjusa Temple. The present building is thought to date to the reign of King Injo, based on roof tile inscriptions found during repairs in 1979, and it houses a statue of Śākyamuni Buddha.

1123706650000.title_en: Rock-carved Buddhist Triad in Sitting Pose on Namsan, Gyeongju
1123706650000.description: A triad is carved on the rock face at the western foot of Namsan in Gyeongju, with a main seated figure flanked by two attendant figures. Based on the carving technique and nearby historical associations, it is thought to have been made in the Unified Silla period.

1123706660000.title_en: Stone Seated Tathagata of Samneung Valley, Gyeongju Namsan
1123706660000.description: This stone seated Buddha is carved from granite and stands on the left ridge above Samneung Valley. The figure has a rounded face, small ears, a simple drapery over the left shoulder, and an orderly seated posture on an octagonal lotus pedestal with floral and eye-shaped ornament. Based on these features, it is considered a Unified Silla work from the 8th to 9th century.

1123706670000.title_en: Iron Seated Vairocana Buddha of Hancheonsa Temple, Yecheon
1123706670000.description: This iron Buddha statue is 1.53 m high and is missing its mandorla and pedestal. It shows a calm face, solid body, dignified seated posture, and a style typical of late Unified Silla iron Buddhist sculpture. The drapery is handled naturally on the shoulders but becomes more formal in the folds around the arms and knees.

1122106680000.description: This set consists of relics associated with Gwon Eung-su (1546–1608), a Joseon military officer who fought in the Japanese invasions of Korea. The group includes his portrait, a certificate of meritorious service, a folding screen painting of meritorious retainers, a long sword, royal documents, a ceremonial belt, and two volumes of family records. Among them, the portrait was bestowed by King Seonjo, and the two-volume family record is valuable for the study of poetry and calligraphy.

1123706690000.description: This set comprises relics left by the Joseon military officer Jeong Gi-ryong (1562–1622), who served with distinction during the Japanese invasions. The designated items include a jade belt, a name plaque, a royal letter, two royal certificates on scrolls, and a separate court document. Other related materials, including woodblocks for his biography and additional royal documents issued to his family, are separately designated as cultural heritage materials.

1123806710000.description: This set includes relics associated with Gwak Jae-u, a righteous army commander of the Japanese invasions of Korea, preserved at Chungeui-sa in Uiryeong, Gyeongsangnam-do. The items include a long sword, horse tack, an inkstone and water dropper, a small iron seal with a lion finial, and a white porcelain octagonal bowl with floral decoration. Tradition says the inkstone and water dropper were bestowed by the Ming emperor when Gwak visited Ming China with his father.

1121106720000.title_en: Clothing Excavated from the Tomb of Kim Deok-won
1121106720000.description: This group consists of garments excavated from the tomb of Kim Deok-won (1634–1704), a late Joseon civil official. The collection includes robes, a cheolik, a white outer coat, a lined green robe, a patterned jacket, and other textiles, with a total of 53 types recorded. Because the finds are diverse and well preserved, they are important for studying Joseon clothing history.

1122206730000.description: This stone ice storage was built to store ice and is laid out lengthwise from north to south with a south-facing entrance. It is constructed mainly of granite, with a vaulted stone chamber, ventilation openings in the ceiling, and a drainage channel in the floor. A foundation inscription found during repairs in 1982 showed that it was built in 1730, the 6th year of King Yeongjo of Joseon.

1123706740000.title_en: Three-Story Stone Pagoda of Yugumsa Temple, Yeongdeok
1123706740000.description: This stone pagoda stands in the back courtyard of the main hall at Yugumsa Temple and consists of a two-tiered base with a three-story body. The body and roof stones were each carved from single blocks, and the roof stones have four-stepped supports underneath. Its balanced proportions and relatively restrained decoration suggest a late Unified Silla date.

1123706750000.title_en: Three-story Stone Pagoda at Hwanam-ri, Yeongcheon
1123706750000.description: This pagoda was one of a pair that stood east and west in front of the main hall of the former Hanwangsa Temple. When one side stone of the base was opened during dismantling, a stone seated Buddha statue was found inside.

1123706760000.title_en: Stone Seated Buddha at Hwanam-ri, Yeongcheon
1123706760000.description: This stone seated Buddha was found inside the base stone of the Three-story Stone Pagoda at Hwanam-ri, Yeongcheon, during dismantling and restoration work. It is identified as Vairocana Buddha by the hand gesture, and the pedestal is made of an octagonal middle section with lotus-carved upper and lower parts.

1123706770000.title_en: East and West Three-story Stone Pagodas at Jangyeonsa Temple Site, Cheongdo
1123706770000.description: These two pagodas stand east and west on a low hill beside a stream flowing into the Nakdong River. The west pagoda was restored to its original site in 1979 after having collapsed, and the east pagoda is believed to have had the same two-tiered base.

1123706780000.title_en: East and West Three-story Stone Pagodas at Unmunsa Temple, Cheongdo
1123706780000.description: These two pagodas stand east and west in front of Daeungbojeon Hall at Unmunsa Temple and share the same scale and style. They are built on a two-tiered base with three stories, and the upper base is carved with seated figures of the Eight Classes of Divine Beings.

1123706790000.title_en: Stone Standing Bodhisattva at Gwangdeok-ri, Gimcheon
1123706790000.description: This stone bodhisattva stands by a reservoir embankment in Gammun-myeon, Gimcheon. It represents Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva in relief on granite, with a jeweled crown and a form comparable to early Goryeo stone bodhisattvas.

1123706800000.title_en: Rock-carved Seated Buddha Triad in Sinam-ri, Yeongju
1123706800000.description: This rock-carved Buddhist image was made on all four sides of a boulder, though now only the triad remains clearly visible. The main Buddha and attendant bodhisattvas show the restrained, rounded style associated with early Unified Silla sculpture.

1123706810000.title_en: Stone Seated Buddha at Heukseoksa Temple, Yeongju
1123706810000.description: This stone seated Buddha was excavated from burial near Heukseoksa Temple, and the pedestal and halo are placed separately beside it. The rounded face, stable body, and narrow shoulders reflect the style of late Unified Silla sculpture.

1123706820000.title_en: Three-story Stone Pagoda at Jibosa Temple, Gunwi
1123706820000.description: This pagoda stands within the grounds of Jibosa Temple and has a compact three-story body set on a two-tiered base. The base includes carved animal figures and the Eight Classes of Divine Beings, while the first-story body has a door-shaped niche representing the Buddha's chamber.

1123406490000.title_en: Muin-Inscribed Buddha Stele and Base, Yeonhwasa Temple, Sejong
1123406490000.description: This Buddhist stele and base, kept at Yeonhwasa Temple in Sejong, was discovered in 1961 and is said to have originally stood at the site of Byeongcheonsa Temple nearby. It has carved Buddhist images on four sides of stone slabs, with a separate base made of stone. The inscription indicates the Muin year, which corresponds to 678, suggesting an early Unified Silla date.

1123406500000.title_en: Seven-Figure Buddha Stele, Yeonhwasa Temple, Sejong
1123406500000.description: This stele, made of talc and carved in relief, belongs to the same group as other Buddha steles found in the former Yeongi area. It presents a seven-figure composition centered on a main Buddha, with attendant bodhisattvas, arhats, and guardian figures, and includes lotus and flame motifs on the halo. Based on its style and inscription, it is thought to date to 678 in the reign of King Munmu.

1123506510000.title_en: Documents of the Yeonan Yi Clan
1123506510000.description: This designation covers a group of documents preserved by the Yeonan Yi clan, including materials related to Yi Sung-won from the reign of King Sejong to the reign of King Sukjong. The listed items consist of 18 royal appointment certificates, one meritorious subject register, and six volumes of a mutual oath text. They are valuable sources for tracing the clan history and for studying early Joseon bibliography.

1123706520000.description: This is a collection of Yi Hyeongsang's own manuscripts, preserved in 10 works and 15 volumes. Yi Hyeongsang (1653–1733), a Confucian scholar of the Joseon period, wrote on a wide range of subjects including Neo-Confucianism, ritual studies, history, geography, and poetry. The collection includes works such as Seonhocheon, Akhakpyeongo, Tamna Sunryeoldo, and others.

1121106530000.title_en: Embroidered Four Seasons Potted Plants Screen
1121106530000.description: This embroidered screen, transmitted as a Goryeo-period work, is unusual in being composed of four panels rather than the more common eight to twelve found in Joseon examples. It depicts potted plants and flower vases with grapes, lotus, plum blossoms, and paired butterflies, and includes the Buddhist swastika motif. The embroidery technique and restrained colors show distinctly Korean characteristics.

1121106540000.description: This large 25-strip kasaya measures 240 cm by 63 cm and is divided into bands with four long sides and one short side. The embroidered design places Buddhas, bodhisattvas, scriptures, and venerable monks in separate rows on a plain white silk ground. It is said to date to the early 18th century and is the only surviving example with the entire surface embroidered as a picture.

1123706550000.title_en: Rock-Carved Buddha Triad and Seated Buddha, Nokseok-ri, Chilgok
1123706550000.description: These shallow rock-carved Buddhist images on a large cliff face date to the early Unified Silla period. The main composition is a seated triad with a central Buddha and two attendant bodhisattvas, and a separate small seated Buddha is placed beside the right attendant. The figures preserve a formal style with a prominent halo and flame motifs, and the right attendant bodhisattva is shown in an unusually crossed-ankle posture.

1123306560000.title_en: Stone Lantern with Lion Base in Front of Bogak Guksa's Stupa Site, Cheongnyongsa Temple Site, Chungju
1123306560000.description: This stone lantern was erected in front of the reliquary stupa of Bogak Guksa to pray for his afterlife. Its lower support is carved as a prone lion, which gives the lantern its name, and the upper parts include a square lamp chamber and a roof stone with raised corner flowers. An inscription on the nearby stele suggests that it was built between 1392 and 1393, in the early Joseon period.

1121106920100.description: This printed volume is the seventh fascicle of the Lotus Sutra, a foundational scripture of the Korean Cheontae school that teaches that the path to Buddhahood is open to everyone. It was printed in Goryeo in 1240 based on the commentary text by Jiehuan of the Song dynasty.

1121106920200.description: This printed volume is the seventh fascicle of the Lotus Sutra, a foundational scripture of the Korean Cheontae school that teaches that the path to Buddhahood is open to everyone. It was printed in Goryeo in 1240 based on the commentary text by Jiehuan of the Song dynasty.

1121106930000.description: This is a small-format printed edition of the Lotus Sutra, made in seven volumes and two books for easy carrying. It was printed in 1286 during the reign of King Chungnyeol of Goryeo, and the record at the end shows that it was produced by Jo Geun and Lee Hee-ryeo with Seong Min's record.

1121106940000.title_en: Three Sutras of the Buddha and Patriarchs (1981-1)
1121106940000.description: This woodblock-printed book combines the Sutra of Forty-Two Chapters, the Sutra of the Buddha's Bequeathed Teaching, and the Essentials of Wei-shan. It was printed at Wonamsa Temple in Jeonju in 1361 during the reign of King Gongmin of Goryeo.

1123606940200.title_en: Three Sutras of the Buddha and Patriarchs (2012)
1123606940200.description: This woodblock-printed book combines the Sutra of Forty-Two Chapters, the Sutra of the Buddha's Bequeathed Teaching, and the Essentials of Wei-shan. It was printed at Wonamsa Temple in Jeonju in 1361 based on a Yuan-dynasty edition.

1123106940300.title_en: Three Sutras of the Buddha and Patriarchs (2023)
1123106940300.description: This woodblock-printed book combines the Sutra of Forty-Two Chapters, the Sutra of the Buddha's Bequeathed Teaching, and the Essentials of Wei-shan. It was printed at Wonamsa Temple in Jeonju in 1361 based on a Yuan-dynasty edition.

1121106950000.title_en: Three Sutras of the Buddha and Patriarchs (1981-2)
1121106950000.description: This woodblock-printed book combines the Sutra of Forty-Two Chapters, the Sutra of the Buddha's Bequeathed Teaching, and the Essentials of Wei-shan. It was printed in 1384 during the reign of King U of Goryeo and is said to have been re-carved from a Song-dynasty original.

1121106960000.description: This printed folding edition of the Diamond Sutra was produced in 1363 under the supervision of Namwon-busa Seol Sa-deok and inspector Kim Yeong-gi. It includes the full text of the sutra and illustrated transformed scenes, along with a record of those involved in its production.

1123106970000.title_en: Record of Naong Hwasang and Hymns of Naong Hwasang
1123106970000.description: This woodblock-printed Buddhist book was first published in 1363 and reprinted in 1379 during King U of Goryeo. It is made of two bound volumes on Korean paper, with the sayings of the monk Naong Hwasang Hyegeun collected and edited by his disciples, and the hymns written by Naong Hwasang himself. Among the extant editions, this copy is noted for its especially fine woodblock carving and printing.

1121106980000.description: This is the fifth-volume binding of volumes 6 through 10 of the Śūraṃgama Sūtra, printed from woodblocks on Korean paper. The colophon states that it was published at Cheongnyongsa Temple in Anseong in 1372, with Kim Ho and Lady Choi of Yeongam-gun as patrons. Its printing is not especially clear, suggesting that it is not the first impression.

1121106990000.description: This woodblock-printed copy contains volumes 6 through 10 of the Śūraṃgama Sūtra and is bound as one book on Korean paper. It was printed at Cheongnyongsa Temple in Anseong in 1372 during King Gongmin's reign. It is believed to be a later impression from the same blocks as the related designated copy.

1121107000000.title_en: Precious Instructions of the Forest of Seon (1981)
1121107000000.description: This is a woodblock-printed Buddhist text bound in one volume from two fascicles, printed on Korean paper. A colophon at the end records that it was published at Cheongnyongsa Temple in Chungju in 1378 under King U of Goryeo, with a postscript by the monk Hwanam. Among surviving editions, it is regarded as one of the finest Goryeo printings in terms of carving and impression.

1123307000200.title_en: Precious Instructions of the Forest of Seon (2017)
1123307000200.description: This Buddhist book was printed at Cheongnyongseonsa Temple in Chungju in 1378 during King U of Goryeo. It collects teachings on the Way and virtue of Seon masters, and preserves detailed records about the publication process and the people involved. The edition is considered one of the most refined surviving Goryeo woodblock printings.

1121107010000.title_en: Sutra for Long Life and the Elimination of Sins, Protecting Children
1121107010000.description: This Buddhist scripture teaches methods for removing sins and gaining long life through the power of the Buddha or through practice. It is a woodblock-printed accordion-style book on Korean paper, with a carefully drawn frontispiece illustration at the beginning. Based on the engraving, paper, and printing style, it is believed to have been printed in 1378 during King U of Goryeo.

1121107020000.description: This woodblock-printed Buddhist text was reprinted at Cheongnyongsa Temple in Chungju in 1379 by order of the monk Hwanam. It was produced by Seungjun and Manhoe, and the postscript by Yi Seok records the circumstances of the reprint. The clean carving and clear impression indicate that it was printed directly from newly carved blocks.

1121107030000.title_en: Classification of Buddhist Terms and Numbers (1981-1)
1121107030000.description: This is a woodblock-printed Buddhist reference book that arranges terms and numerical entries from the Tripitaka for easier consultation. It was republished in 1389 by the monk Muhak Daesa, based on an edition compiled by the Yuan-dynasty monk Gasu. The colophon noting Muhak Daesa's publication makes this a rare surviving example.

1123706830000.description: This stone pagoda stands on the site said to have been occupied by a temple called Janggaksa, though there is no definite historical record. It has a typical seven-story form on a two-tier stylobate, and is considered an early Goryeo work that continues the style of Unified Silla stone pagodas.

1121106850000.description: This is Volume 4 of the Jin translation of the Avatamsaka Sutra, with part of the text missing. It is a woodblock-printed scroll on mulberry paper, and is thought to have been printed during the reign of King Sukjong of Goryeo, probably around 1098.

1121106860000.description: This is Volume 28 of the Jin translation of the Avatamsaka Sutra, with the beginning and some sections missing. It is a woodblock-printed scroll on mulberry paper, and is considered a Goryeo-period edition, likely from the reign of King Sukjong.

1121106870000.description: This is Volume 66 of the Zhou translation of the Avatamsaka Sutra, printed from carved woodblocks on mulberry paper. Based on its script, carving style, ink color, and printing condition, it is thought to have been made around 1098 during the reign of King Sukjong of Goryeo.

1121106880000.title_en: Avatamsaka Sutra, Zhou Translation, Volumes 17 and 52
1121106880000.description: These are two volumes, 17 and 52, from the Zhou translation of the Avatamsaka Sutra. Both are woodblock-printed scrolls on mulberry paper and are believed to date from the reign of King Sukjong of Goryeo, based on their script, layout, and printing quality.

1121106890000.description: This is Volume 7 of the Zhenyuan edition of the Avatamsaka Sutra, printed on mulberry paper in scroll format. The first leaf and the binding cord are missing, but the script, woodblocks, ink, and paper indicate a Goryeo printing from the reign of King Sukjong.

1121106900000.description: This is Volume 6 of the Zhou translation of the Avatamsaka Sutra, printed on mulberry paper in scroll format. It is damaged and missing the first seven leaves, and is thought to have been printed in 1098 during the reign of King Sukjong of Goryeo.

1121106910000.description: This woodblock-printed text was produced in the mid-Goryeo period and is preserved in a small silver-gilt box and wooden box. The colophon states that it was carved to quickly overcome the troubles then faced by Choe Chung-heon, Choe U, and Choe Hyang and to pray for their longevity.

1121107030200.description: This Buddhist reference work arranges terms and numerical categories found in the Buddhist canon in an easy-to-search order. The extant copy was based on a Yuan-dynasty edition compiled by Seoam Gasu and was republished in 1389 by Monk Muhak in the late Goryeo period. The volume is considered an early Joseon print and is an important source for the history of Buddhism and book exchange.

1121107040000.description: This Buddhist reference work arranges terms and numerical categories found in the Buddhist canon in an easy-to-search order. The extant edition was republished by Monk Muhak in 1389 during the reign of King Gongyang of Goryeo. The surviving copy lacks the preface found in some other transmitted editions and is regarded as a rare Goryeo-period woodblock print.

1121107050000.description: This scripture teaches the Buddha's words on the deep and valuable kindness of parents. It was printed in 1378, the fourth year of King U of Goryeo, through the donation of Han Cheon, and is a woodblock-printed folding booklet on handmade paper. The work includes text and illustrations of the ten kinds of parental kindness, and also contains Bulseol Bumo Eunjoong Taegolgyeong at the end.

1121107060000.description: This is a woodblock-printed edition of Zhu Xi's book of questions and answers on the Zhongyong, one of the Four Books. It was imported from Yuan in 1371, the 20th year of King Gongmin of Goryeo, and was also carved and printed at Jinju-mok in July of that year. The copy is an important example of a local government-sponsored Goryeo print.

1121107070000.description: This is a woodblock-printed edition of Zhu Xi's book of questions and answers on the Zhongyong, one of the Four Books. It was imported from Yuan in 1371, the 20th year of King Gongmin of Goryeo, and was also carved and printed at Jinju-mok in July of that year. The printing state suggests that this copy was printed somewhat later than the copy held by Korea University Library.

1121107080000.description: This is the personal poetry collection of Min Sa-pyeong, a late Goryeo scholar-official. It was printed in 1370 from woodblocks prepared by Lee Dan with a preface by Yi Saek, and contains prefaces by Yi Je-hyeon and Yi Saek as well as a record of Min's epitaph and chronology. The extant volume is the only surviving copy of the collection.

1121107090000.description: This is the personal poetry collection of Jeong Po, a late Goryeo scholar-official. The surviving copy was printed from woodblocks carved in 1376 by his son Gongwon after he arranged his father's posthumous writings. Several opening leaves are missing, including the preface, and the book is considered a rare late-Goryeo anthology.

1121107100000.description: This anthology was compiled by the Goryeo-period literary figure Choe Hae and preserves prose written in the Silla and Goryeo periods. The extant set consists of 12 volumes in 4 books, and the woodblocks were carved in 1355 during the reign of King Gongmin, though the surviving printing is thought to be from the early Joseon period. It is one of the oldest surviving books in Korea.

1123507180000.title_en: Collected Documents of the Goryim-gun Branch of the Jeonju Yi Clan
1123507180000.description: This collection consists of four old documents dating from 1502 to 1593. They include a deed of property transfer, a family agreement for dividing property, and related agreement documents concerning inheritance and distribution within the family of Yi Hun and his son.

1121107190000.description: This is a woodblock-printed Buddhist book on paper preserving only volume 3 of a work that summarizes and explains the Lotus Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment in eight fascicles. The colophon shows that it was printed in the Goryeo period, probably during the reign of King Gongmin, and the printing and paper are noted for their fine condition.

1121107200000.description: This woodblock-printed Buddhist text is an explanatory work on the Diamond Sutra, printed in two fascicles as one bound volume. The colophon states that it was reprinted at Cheongnyongsa Temple in Chungju in 1378 based on a Yuan-dynasty edition, and the book is considered a rare and important source for Buddhist studies and bibliography.

1123307200200.description: This is a woodblock-printed Buddhist commentary on the Diamond Sutra, published at Cheongnyongsa Temple in Chungju in 1378 as a two-fascicle, one-volume edition. The colophon by the monk Hwanam records the circumstances of its printing and the names of those who participated, making it a valuable source for Buddhist and bibliographic studies.

1121107210000.description: This woodblock-printed Buddhist scripture is a paper edition of the Diamond Sutra translated by Kumarajiva and annotated by Cheonno. The record on the book states that it was published with support from Yu Hwang and Gang In-bu, with Jidam overseeing the printing and Yi Saek writing the colophon; it was later reprinted in the early Joseon period.

1121107220000.description: This set consists of volumes 44 through 50 of the historical work compiled by Kim Busik in 1145. It is a late Goryeo woodblock printing and is the oldest surviving printed copy of the Samguk sagi, with high source value for the study of ancient Korean history.

1123407240000.title_en: Collected Documents of the Seongju Do Clan
1123407240000.description: This collection contains five old documents, including four royal appointment documents and a nokeup issued to Do Eung between 1393 and 1397. The documents are valuable for studying changes in early Joseon administration, royal seals, calligraphy, and documentary formats.

1123507250000.title_en: Collected Documents of the Namwon Yang Clan
1123507250000.description: This collection consists of seven old documents dated from 1355 to 1591, including two Hongpae certificates for passing the civil examinations in the Goryeo period and several Joseon-period examination certificates and appointment documents. They are important materials for studying Goryeo and early Joseon examination certificates and documentary forms.

1121107100200.description: This woodblock-printed book was compiled by Choe Hae (1287–1340), a literary figure of the Goryeo period. It collects prose writings from the Silla and Goryeo periods and consists of six fascicles in two volumes. The blocks were carved in 1355, during the reign of King Gongmin of Goryeo, and the extant printing is believed to be from the early Joseon period.

1121107100300.description: This is a woodblock-printed section of Donginjimun saryuk compiled by Choe Hae (1287–1340). It preserves prose writings from the Silla and Goryeo periods and survives as three fascicles in one volume. It belongs to one of the oldest surviving books in Korea.

1121107100400.description: This woodblock-printed section of Donginjimun saryuk was compiled by Choe Hae (1287–1340). It collects writings from the Silla and Goryeo periods and survives as three fascicles in one volume. The printing records indicate that it was issued at Bujeon-gwan in Bupyeong, and the extant copy shows signs of being printed long after the blocks were carved in 1355.

1121107100500.description: This volume of Donginjimun saryuk contains only the prose section of Choe Hae's collected writings. It is a one-volume set of fascicles 7–9, and the end of volume 7 bears a printing record identifying Jinju-mok as the place of publication. The woodblock style matches that of Choe's collection Jolgobaekcheon, making it an important source for studying woodblock printing and literary history.

1122207100600.description: This is a fragmentary surviving copy of the prose section of Donginjimun, compiled by Choe Hae (1288–1340), and contains fascicles 7–9 in one volume. It preserves only part of the full work, which was arranged into three sections: verse, prose, and parallel prose. The item is noted as a rare surviving example of the Jinju edition.

1123107150000.description: This set includes three portraits of Kim Jungman, a military official of the Joseon period. One larger portrait shows him seated in formal official dress, while the other two are smaller portrait formats, including a meritorious-retainer album leaf and a framed-style portrait. The works are valuable for the study of Joseon portrait painting and the standard form used for meritorious subjects.

1123307160000.title_en: Royal Certificate of Meritorious Retainer for Kim Giltong
1123307160000.description: This royal certificate records the appointment of Kim Gil-tong, then a senior official, as a meritorious retainer of the Left Administration during King Seongjong's reign. It lists the ranks and total number of meritorious retainers in the category, providing material for studying the political groups of the period. Very few certificates of this type survive today.

1123707170000.description: This portrait depicts the upper body of Ju Sebung, a Joseon official and scholar, in formal court dress. He is shown facing left with a simplified face and a stately posture, and the painting is considered an important example of a scholar portrait from the 16th century. The exact date is uncertain, but its style and condition suggest that it is a relatively early work.

1123507260000.title_en: Record of Merit for Chang Gwan, Granted as an Original Contributor to the Founding of the Dynasty
1123507260000.description: This document is a certificate recognizing Chang Gwan as an original contributor to the founding of the Joseon dynasty, issued in 1395 by King Taejo. It is the only surviving individual document issued to an original contributor and records the recipient’s services, official title, and the state seal in several places.

1123407270000.title_en: Document Collection of the Namyang Jeon Clan
1123407270000.description: This collection consists of clan documents transmitted within the Namyang Jeon family, including royal warrants, royal decrees, household registers, and a family instruction. The documents date from 1416 to 1747 and include records on grants of land and slaves, making them valuable for the study of early Joseon documentary forms, family organization, and social-economic history.

1123507280000.title_en: Mrs. Seol’s Encouragement of Goodness Document
1123507280000.description: This illustrated manuscript was written by Mrs. Seol, the wife of Sin Mal-ju, a civil official active from the reign of King Danjong to King Seongjong. It was made to raise alms for the repair of Gangcheonsa Temple in Sunchang, and includes a temple map along with the text of the encouragement document; it is dated 1482 and bears her seal and title.

1123707290000.title_en: Decrees Exempting Yecheon Yongmunsa Temple from Labor Service
1123707290000.description: This royal decree was issued in 1457 to exempt Yongmunsa Temple from miscellaneous labor service. It states that the temple should be reviewed again and further protected, and the document is an important source for studying the temple’s status in early Joseon.

1123707300000.description: Eungjinjeon Hall is a Buddhist worship hall at Bulyongsa Temple in Uljin. The hall enshrines Sakyamuni Buddha flanked by Ananda and Kasyapa, together with the Sixteen Arhats, and its present form reflects several repairs after fires and reconstruction following the Japanese invasions.

1122107310000.title_en: Gilt-bronze Standing Tathagata Buddha from Borisa Temple Site, Uiryeong
1122107310000.description: This gilt-bronze standing Buddha was excavated in 1948 from Borisa Temple in Gaehwa-myeon, Uiryeong, and has been kept by Dong-A University since 1981. The statue is well preserved, with a rounded face, a ribbon-like knot on the chest of the robe, an octagonal pedestal, and stylistic features indicating late Unified Silla period production.

1122107320000.title_en: Screen of the Celebration Banquet for Queen Dowager Jo’s Fortieth Birthday
1122107320000.description: This eight-panel screen depicts the banquet held in 1847 to celebrate the 40th birthday of Queen Dowager Jo, the mother of King Heonjong. It shows the palace buildings, trees, landscape, officials, and military attendants in vivid color, and the final panel records the names and ranks of the participants.

1122107330000.title_en: Screen of King Heonjong’s Wedding Celebration
1122107330000.description: This eight-panel screen depicts the wedding ceremony of King Heonjong and Queen Hyojeong in 1844. The panels include congratulatory text and records of court officials, while the main scenes show the marriage rites and the buildings of Changdeokgung Palace in orderly detail.

1123107330200.title_en: Folding Screen of the Celebration of Hyeonjong’s Royal Wedding and Procession of Congratulations
1123107330200.description: An eight-panel folding screen depicting the court celebration held after King Heonjong’s royal wedding in 1844. The main panels show the congratulatory ceremony at Dondeokjeon Hall of Changdeokgung Palace with court officials assembled in orderly formation, while the last panel includes a roster of the Seonjanggwan Office officials.

1123807340000.title_en: Goryeo Woodblocks of Haeinsa Temple, Hapcheon
1123807340000.description: These are woodblocks preserved at Haeinsa Temple in Hapcheon that contain Buddhist scriptures and writings by famous monks and scholars from the Goryeo period. Unlike the Tripitaka woodblocks carved by the state agency Daejanggam, these were carved by temples or local government offices and are kept in the east and west sagi woodblock halls.

1123707350000.title_en: Goryeo Woodblocks of Buseoksa Temple, Yeongju
1123707350000.description: These woodblocks contain three Goryeo-period versions of the Avatamsaka Sutra: the 40-volume Jingyuan edition, the 60-volume Jin edition, and the 80-volume Zhou edition. They are thought to have been re-carved from a Khitan edition in the 13th to 14th century and are preserved at Buseoksa Temple.

1121107360000.description: This is a woodblock-printed Buddhist book consisting of volumes 3 and 4 of a commentary on the Vimalakirti Sutra. A colophon states that it was printed at Heungwangsa Temple in 1095 during the Goryeo period, though the surviving copy is believed to be a later Joseon re-engraving based on its script, carving, and paper.

1123607370000.description: This woodblock-printed Buddhist history book records the biographies of eminent monks chronologically from the birth of the Buddha to 1334. A postface by Kim Su-on states that it was printed in 1472, and the extant set is complete in 22 volumes bound into seven books.

1123807380000.title_en: The Sutra of the Supreme Vehicle of the Bodhisattva Manjushri
1123807380000.description: This woodblock-printed Buddhist scripture consists of three volumes bound in one book and was completed in 1386. According to the colophon by Yi Saek, it was reprinted in Goryeo from an earlier edition originally printed in 1353, and it is valued as the only known surviving copy listed in major Buddhist canonical catalogues.

1123507390000.title_en: Portrait of Go Hui and Clan Relics
1123507390000.description: This item comprises the portrait of Go Hui, a mid-Joseon military official, together with family documents and relics preserved by the Jeju Go clan of Buan. The set includes 20 kinds and 215 objects spanning materials made from 1522 to 1894, and it is kept and displayed at the Hyochungsa Relics Museum in Buan.

1121107400000.title_en: Volume 8 of the Bodhisattva Precepts Sutra in Dark Blue Paper and Silver Ink
1121107400000.description: This is a hand-copied Buddhist scripture written in silver ink on dark blue paper, consisting of volume 8 of the Bodhisattva Precepts Sutra. A colophon shows that it was produced in 1280 as part of the Tripitaka edition sponsored by King Chungnyeol and carved at the Daejanggam office.
1121107400000.material: Dark blue paper and silver ink

1121107410000.title_en: Lacquered Soapstone Sarira Jar from the Three-Story Stone Pagoda at Biroam Hermitage of Donghwasa Temple, Daegu
1121107410000.description: This soapstone sarira jar was discovered inside the Three-Story Stone Pagoda at Biroam Hermitage of Donghwasa Temple and dates to Unified Silla. It is 8.3 cm high, with a mouth diameter of 8.0 cm and a base diameter of 8.5 cm, and survives only in four broken fragments without a lid. The body bears incised inscriptions and decorative designs, including floral-cloud motifs, and the text records the construction of the pagoda in 863 for King Minae.

1121107420000.description: This stone Buddha triad is associated with the Yeongi region style and is now in the collection of Dongguk University. The seated main Buddha is flanked by two attendant bodhisattvas, and the composition includes carved halos, lotus bases, and vertical robe folds characteristic of the region. It is generally dated to the late 7th century of Unified Silla.

1121107430000.description: This painting of a banana plant beside a rock was painted by King Jeongjo of Joseon. The composition is simple and balanced, and the use of dark and light ink effectively expresses the texture of the rock and the changes in the leaves. The upper left bears Jeongjo’s sobriquet, Hongjae.

1121107440000.description: This chrysanthemum painting was made by King Jeongjo of Joseon. It depicts three wild chrysanthemum blossoms rising beside a rock and grass at the left side of the picture. The work uses light and dark ink to distinguish the rock, petals, and leaves, and is regarded as an important source for the study of Joseon painting.

1121107450100.description: Worin seokbo was compiled in 1459 by combining Worin cheongang jigok and Seokbo sangjeol. This item is a combined copy of volumes 1 and 2, printed during the reign of King Sejo. It contains the opening sections of Worin cheongang jigok and includes the prefaces to Hunminjeongeum, Seokbo sangjeol, and Worin seokbo.

1121107450200.description: Worin seokbo was compiled in 1459 by combining Worin cheongang jigok and Seokbo sangjeol. This item consists of volumes 7 and 8, first printed in the reign of King Sejo. Volume 7 is partly missing and has some restored copying, while volume 8 preserves the later sections of the text.
