1123107450300.description: Worin seokbo was compiled in 1459 by combining Worin cheongang jigok and Seokbo sangjeol. This item consists of volumes 9 and 10, first printed in the reign of King Sejo. Both volumes are damaged and incomplete, and some missing text was recopied to fill the gaps.

1121107450400.description: Worin seokbo was compiled in 1459 by combining Worin cheongang jigok and Seokbo sangjeol. This item consists of volumes 13 and 14, first printed in the reign of King Sejo. Volume 13 is heavily damaged, and volume 14 is missing everything after folio 82, suggesting that the set had been placed inside a pagoda.

1123207450500.description: This printed Buddhist text combines Worin cheongangjigok and Seokbosangjeol, compiled in 1459 during the reign of King Sejo. The extant item is the original first edition of volumes 17-18, preserved as one bound book; volume 17 is complete, while volume 18 lacks the lower part of folio 87. It was found in the back of a Sachaon statue at Inwangmun Gate of Sutasa Temple in Hongcheon.

1121107450600.description: This is a later printed edition reproduced in 1562 at Muryanggul in Sunchang based on the first edition printed in King Sejo's reign. It is a single volume in two fascicles and is the only known extant copy of volume 21. The front of the book includes illustrations of the Buddha's descent from Tusita Heaven and the Nirvana scene under the sala trees.

1121107450700.description: This is a reprinted edition of volume 22 based on the original first edition from King Sejo's reign. It is a single-volume book, measuring about 22.2 cm by 32 cm. It is believed to have been printed in the mid-16th century, before the Japanese invasions of 1592.

1121107450800.description: This is the original first-edition printing of volume 23 from King Sejo's reign. Although the beginning and end are missing, folios 16 through 106 survive and the volume has been repaired with backing paper. It contains verses 497-524 of Worin cheongangjigok together with explanatory text from Seokbosangjeol.

1123607450900.description: This is a printed copy of volume 25 arranged with Worin cheongangjigok followed by explanatory passages from Seokbosangjeol. The first two leaves and part of the volume are missing, but the later section preserves verses 577-583 of Worin cheongangjigok and related text from volume 24 of Seokbosangjeol. The discovery of this volume confirmed that Worin seokbo was composed of 25 volumes.

1123507451000.description: This is the original first printed edition of volume 15 of Worin seokbo, discovered at Guamsa Temple in Sunchang. Unlike the previously known Seongam edition, this copy survives complete in its text, although the front and back covers are missing. It is especially valuable as a complete first-printing copy.

1121107451100.description: This volume of Worin seokbo was newly designated and is one of the 25 volumes believed to have been produced for the full work. It is regarded as an important source for the study of early Joseon Buddhist scriptures and the Korean script, and is noted as the only known surviving copy of this volume. It is also associated with the creation of Hangul and with Korea's early Buddhist hymns.

1123507460000.description: This royal decree was issued on 17 November 1402 appointing Seong Seok-rin as Yeonguijeongbusa and concurrently Pangaeseong yuhusa sa. The document records the appointment with an official seal reading "Joseon-guk wangjiin" and is written in cursive script on thick Korean paper. It is an appointment order given to Seong Seok-rin, a civil official active from the late Goryeo to early Joseon periods.

1121107550000.title_en: Avatamsaka Sutra, Volumes 5–6, Written in Silver on Indigo Paper
1121107550000.description: This manuscript copies volumes 5 and 6 of the 80-volume Chinese translation of the Avatamsaka Sutra by Śikṣānanda. It was written in silver ink on dark blue paper in a folding format, with a gilt title cover and a frontispiece illustration at the beginning of volume 5. It is considered to have been made in the 14th century based on its style and format.

1121107560000.title_en: Śūraṅgama Sutra, Volume 7, Written in Gold on Indigo Paper
1121107560000.description: This manuscript is volume 7 of the Śūraṅgama Sutra, translated in the Tang dynasty by Banzhami. The text is written in gold ink on dark blue paper in a folding format, and the last two sections were rewritten to complete the volume. It is thought to have been made in the 14th century.

1123807570000.title_en: Avatamsaka Sutra, Volume 46, Written in Gold on Indigo Paper
1123807570000.description: This manuscript is volume 46 of the 80-volume Avatamsaka Sutra translated by Śikṣānanda, containing the first half of the chapter "Buddha's Inconceivable Dharmas." It is written in gold ink on dark blue paper and made in scroll form with a frontispiece illustration at the beginning. It is estimated to be a Goryeo work of the 14th century.

1121107580000.title_en: Song of Enlightenment by the Venerable Monk Nammyeongcheon (1984)
1121107580000.description: This woodblock-printed book is a later re-engraved edition based on a metal movable-type edition first printed in 1239 by Choi Yi. The extant copy includes the introductory and colophonic texts by O Yong-cheon-yong and Chu Hwang, which help show its early printing history. It is regarded as an important source for studying early Korean movable-type printing.

1123807580200.title_en: Song of Enlightenment by the Venerable Monk Nammyeongcheon (2012)
1123807580200.description: This woodblock edition of the Song of Enlightenment includes a colophon by Choi Yi dated 1239, stating that the text was re-engraved from a cast-type edition to preserve and transmit it. The surviving copy has handwritten phonetic annotations and shows features of a re-engraved woodblock print based on movable type. It is an important source for studying early Korean printing and Buddhist bibliography.

1121107590000.description: This woodblock-printed edition of the Śūraṅgama Sutra was published by royal order in 1401, the first year of King Taejong. The complete ten-volume text was bound into five books and printed on mulberry-fiber paper. The colophon records the participation of many craftsmen and officials in carving the blocks.

1121107600000.title_en: Korean Translation of the Śūraṅgama Sutra, Volume 1
1121107600000.description: This is the vernacular Korean translation of the Śūraṅgama Sutra, a Buddhist scripture translated by Banzhami and annotated by Zongmi. It is a metal movable-type edition printed on yellow paper made from straw and mulberry bark, and the surviving copy contains only volume 1 of the original ten. It was printed with Eulhae type and became a model for later Buddhist publications.

1121107610000.title_en: Korean Translation of the Śūraṅgama Sutra, Volumes 2 and 5
1121107610000.description: This work is the vernacular Korean translation of the Śūraṅgama Sutra, annotated by King Sejo, Shinmi, Han Gye-hui, and Kim Su-on. It is a metal movable-type edition printed at the Office for the Publication of Sutras in 1461, and only two books containing volumes 2 and 5 survive. The extant copy is a fragment of the original ten-volume set.

1123707470000.title_en: Saddle Used by Choi Mun-byeong, Commander of the Righteous Army
1123707470000.description: This is a horse saddle said to have been used by Choi Mun-byeong, who served as a commander of a righteous army during the Japanese invasions of Korea. It preserves the saddle bow, stirrups, girths, and other fittings, and is noted for its good condition and completeness. The saddle is made with wood, bone, iron, leather, and textile parts.
1123707470000.material: Wood, bone, iron, leather, and textile

1121107480000.title_en: Woodblock of Amitābha Buddha Preaching, Gyeongguksa Temple, Seoul
1121107480000.description: This is a Joseon-period woodblock hanging piece enshrined in the Geungnakjeon Hall of Gyeongguksa Temple in Seoul. It depicts Amitābha Buddha at the center with a total of 13 Buddhist figures and bodhisattvas, including the Eight Great Bodhisattvas of Amitābha and the Four Heavenly Kings. The carving is simple and restrained, and it is valued as one of the few surviving late Joseon woodblock Buddhist images.

1123107490000.title_en: Stupa of Wonjeung National Preceptor, Taegosa Temple Site, Goyang
1123107490000.description: This relic is the sarira stupa of Wonjeung National Preceptor Bowu, a monk of the late Goryeo period. It stands on a three-tiered base with a distinctive finial above the body. Based on the construction of the memorial stele dated 1385, the stupa is thought to have been built after that year.

1123207500000.title_en: Three-Story Stone Pagoda at Geodonsa Temple Site, Wonju
1123207500000.description: This stone pagoda stands in front of the main hall site at the former Geodonsa Temple and consists of a two-tiered base with a three-story body. Its construction, including the two-tiered base, pillar-like carvings, and five-stepped roof support stones, shows the style of the Unified Silla period. It is thought to be a 9th-century work, and the finial has been partially restored.

1121107510000.title_en: Illustrated Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Gyeongwon Edition, Volume 34
1121107510000.description: This manuscript is Volume 34 of the 40-volume Gyeongwon edition of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, copied in silver ink on dark blue paper. The beginning includes a painted transformation scene, and the scroll has a gilt wooden roller and a decorated cover. An inscription states that it was made in 1337 by Gu, the wife of Choe An-do, in prayer for rebirth in the Pure Land.

1121107520000.title_en: Illustrated Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Chapter on Samantabhadra's Practice and Vows
1121107520000.description: This is part of Volume 34 of the Gyeongwon edition of the 40-volume Avataṃsaka Sūtra, copied in gold ink on dark blue paper. It contains the chapter on Samantabhadra's practice and vows, with a transformation painting at the beginning and the text written in gold. An inscription records that it was produced in 1334 by Ansaehan of Yuan to honor his parents' good teachings.

1121107530000.description: This work is a copied manuscript of the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment written in gold ink on brown paper. It is arranged in a folding format and includes a transformation painting at the beginning, along with the Dharma texts of Zhigong and Huineng. The colophon records that it was made in 1357 by Choe Jeok and Kim Cheong for the repose of Gye-hang.

1121107540000.title_en: Illustrated Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Sutra Edition, Volume 37
1121107540000.description: This manuscript preserves part of Volume 37 of the 80-volume Sutra edition of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra translated by Śikṣānanda. It is written and decorated with gold and silver on dark blue paper in a folding format, with a transformation painting at the beginning and the text written within a bordered layout. The exact date and maker are unknown, but it is thought to be a 14th-century work.

1121107620000.description: This is a Korean vernacular translation of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, a Buddhist scripture translated by Banchamildi of the Tang dynasty and explained by Gyehuan of the Song dynasty. It is a movable-type printed book on yellowish paper made from a mixture of straw and mulberry bark, and only Volumes 7 and 8 survive as two fascicles.

1121107630000.description: This is a Korean vernacular translation of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, based on the Tang-dynasty translation by Banchamildi and the Song-dynasty commentary by Gyehuan. It is a movable-type printed edition on yellowish paper, and Volumes 7 to 10 survive in four fascicles.

1121107640000.description: This is a woodblock-printed Korean vernacular translation of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, produced by the Jingdeokgam in 1462 under King Sejo. It is printed on paper made from mulberry bark and straw, and the surviving parts are bound into eight books covering Volumes 2, 3, 4, 6, and 7 to 10.

1121107650000.description: This is a woodblock-printed Korean vernacular translation of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, based on the Chinese text translated by Banchamildi and annotated by Gyehuan. It was produced at the Jingdeokgam in King Sejo's reign using the corrected woodblocks of the Eulhae-type edition, and the surviving set comprises 11 fascicles.

1121107660000.description: This woodblock-printed edition of the Lotus Sutra survives in one bound volume containing Volumes 4 to 7. It was printed on mulberry-bark paper, and the opening volume includes an illustrated frontispiece while the last volume ends with a note by Prince Anpyeong recording the circumstances of its production.

1123107660200.description: This is a woodblock-printed edition of the Lotus Sutra based on a text translated by Kumarajiva and annotated by Gyehuan, with verse and explanatory notes added in Korean. The opening section includes four-page illustrations, and the end of the book preserves colophons by Prince Anpyeong and Yang Yun-son.

1121107670000.title_en: Abridged Record of the Dharma Words of Monk Mongsan (Eonhae)
1121107670000.description: This is a woodblock-printed Korean vernacular edition of selected dharma words attributed to the Yuan-dynasty monk Mongsan. It is believed to have been published by the Jingdeokgam around 1467 and is an important source for the study of early Hangul and Buddhist literature.

1121107680000.title_en: Abridged Record of the Dharma Words of Monk Mongsan (Eonhae)
1121107680000.description: This is a woodblock-printed Korean vernacular edition of selected dharma words attributed to the Yuan-dynasty monk Mongsan, with additional material by Boje Jondeja. It was translated into Korean by Shinmi and is thought to date to around 1472, although no exact publication record survives.

1121111720000.description: This is a Korean vernacular translation and annotated edition of a collection of six dharma talks by Mongsan Hwasang Deok-i and one by the Goryeo monk Naong Hyegeun. It was printed from woodblocks on mulberry paper, and the evidence in the volume suggests it is an original impression from 1467.

1121107670400.description: This book is a Korean vernacular translation of a collection of dharma talks by Mongsan Hwasang Deok-i, annotated with reading marks by the early Joseon monk Sinmi. It was printed in the Gapinjaengongdam edition of 1467 and is valued as an important source for the study of early Korean language and printing history.

1121107690000.description: This is a Korean vernacular translation of a collection of dharma talks by Mongsan Hwasang Deok-i and Naong Hyegeun, annotated by the monk Sinmi. The colophon states that it was printed in 1472, and the volume is composed of leaves from two printings.

1121107700000.description: This is a vernacular translation of Goryeo monk Jinul's work Susimgyeol, together with four related dharma talks. It was printed from woodblocks in 1467 at the Gapinjaengongdam and is an important source for early Hangul studies.

1121107710000.description: This is a Korean vernacular translation of the commentary on the Heart Sutra, compiled in the Joseon period under royal order. It was printed at the Gapinjaengongdam in 1465 and is the only known copy of the first edition.

1121107720000.description: This woodblock print is a vernacular translation and annotated edition of selected commentaries on the Diamond Sutra. It was completed and printed in 1482 using metal type, combining Jungchuk type and Eulhae type.

1121107720200.description: This work is a vernacular translation and annotated edition of selected commentaries on the Diamond Sutra. It was printed in 1482 with metal type, and the Kyujanggak copy preserves volumes 2 through 5.

1123607720300.description: This volume is a vernacular translation of selected commentaries from the Diamond Sutra, printed by metal type in 1482. The colophon states that it was revised under royal command and then issued in 300 copies.

1121107790000.description: This standing gilt-bronze Buddha is 25.4 cm high and is preserved in good condition at the Hoam Art Museum. It is a Unified Silla Buddhist image from the 8th century, with a round face, thick drapery over both shoulders, and an octagonal lotus base.

1121107800000.description: This 28 cm-high gilt-bronze bodhisattva is kept at the Hoam Art Museum. Although part of the neck was repaired and the right hand is missing, it shows a gentle smile, long ears reaching the shoulders, and a graceful, refined body form typical of the late Three Kingdoms to early Unified Silla period.

1121107810000.description: This dragon-head roof tile end was used to protect the ends of eaves or rafters from wind and rain damage. It has a square-cut neck for fitting onto wood, nail holes for fixing it in place, and is mostly gilded, though much of the gilding is now lost.

1121107820000.title_en: Album of Paintings by Gim Hongdo, Byeongjin Year
1121107820000.description: This album by the late Joseon painter Gim Hongdo contains landscape and genre paintings. It consists of 20 leaves painted in ink and light color on paper, and was made in 1796 when the artist was 51 years old.
1121107820000.material: Ink and light color on paper

1121107830000.title_en: Boy Leading a Donkey, by Gim Si
1121107830000.description: This vertical hanging scroll is a genre-and-landscape painting by the mid-Joseon painter Gim Si. Painted in color on silk, it shows a boy forcibly pulling a donkey that refuses to cross a log bridge, with a pine tree and steep rocky peak filling the left side of the composition.

1121107840000.description: This Buddhist painting depicts Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva, who guides beings suffering in hell to the Pure Land. It shows a typical Goryeo two-tier composition, with Kṣitigarbha in the center and eight attendant figures arranged symmetrically below, and uses delicate brushwork and fine coloring.

1121107850000.title_en: Blue-and-white Porcelain Bottle with Cloud and Dragon Design (1984-1)
1121107850000.description: This Joseon white porcelain bottle is 25.0 cm high and was found as a pair with the related bottle. It is decorated with a realistically painted dragon among clouds and is thought to have been made in the first half of the 16th century at a government-run kiln in Gwangju, Gyeonggi-do.
1121107850000.material: White porcelain with underglaze cobalt blue

1123107860000.title_en: Blue-and-white Porcelain Bottle with Cloud and Dragon Design (1984-2)
1123107860000.description: This Joseon white porcelain bottle is 21.5 cm high and was excavated together with the related bottle. It has a thick pale-blue glaze and an underglaze cobalt-blue dragon among clouds, and was probably made in a government-run kiln in the Gwangju area of Gyeonggi-do.
1123107860000.material: White porcelain with underglaze cobalt blue

1122207720400.description: This is Volume 2 of a printed edition of the commentary on the Diamond Sutra by Yabuje, Jonggyeong, and Gihwa. It was begun by order of King Sejo but completed in 1482 at the command of Queen Dowager Jeonghui, who instructed the monk Hakjo to proofread and print it. The main text was printed with metal type called Jeongchukja, while the annotations were printed with Eulhaeja.

1121107740000.description: This is a two-volume, two-book vernacular Korean edition of the Seonjong Yeonggajip, a text on the essentials of Zen practice compiled from the writings of Yongjia Xuanjue and later annotated and arranged by Song-dynasty scholars. The upper volume was first printed in 1464 at the Royal Buddhist Text Printing Bureau, and the lower volume was reprinted in 1495. The colophon at the end was printed with wooden type.

1123807740200.description: This vernacular Korean edition of the Seonjong Yeonggajip was printed in 1464 at the Royal Buddhist Text Printing Bureau, with King Sejo adding reading marks and Sinmi and others translating it into Korean. It is a two-volume, two-book woodblock edition and preserves important early Hangul usage and Buddhist textual history. The extant copy is valued as a particularly fine edition among surviving versions.

1122207740300.description: This is an early printed vernacular Korean edition of the Seonjong Yeonggajip, with King Sejo adding reading marks and Sinmi and others translating it. It is a four-book, two-volume woodblock print made in 1464 at the Royal Buddhist Text Printing Bureau. Although the final four leaves of the lower volume are missing, it is regarded as one of the finest surviving copies and an important source for early Hangul and Buddhist studies.

1121107750000.description: This is a woodblock-printed pocket edition of the Diamond Sutra, produced on thin paper in a folded, accordion-style format. The colophon states that the blocks were carved in 1311 and that the text was printed in 1339 through a donor's sponsorship. It was made for carrying, reading, and memorizing the sutra.

1121107760000.description: This sword has a gold hilt and an iron blade, and the two parts are now separated though they originally belonged together. The hilt is decorated with interlaced dragon motifs, including two dragons on the pommel ring, and the dragon eyes are ornamented with jade. The elaborate decoration suggests that it belonged to a very high-ranking noble of Silla.

1121107770000.description: This set consists of a gilt-bronze latch, a gilt-bronze door ring, and two gilt-bronze nails from the Unified Silla period. The latch has a detachable left side and a keyhole on the left, while the round door ring and nails are carefully made. It is a rare surviving example of Unified Silla door hardware and helps clarify the form of temple and stupa doors of the period.

1121107780000.title_en: Bronze Incense Burner with Silver-inlaid Willow and Waterfowl Design
1121107780000.description: This late Goryeo incense burner is a bowl-shaped ritual vessel with a flaring foot and a disk-shaped base. Its surface is decorated with silver-inlay techniques, including a scene of waterfowl beneath willows and other floral and cloud motifs. A five-line, 34-character inscription is also inlaid on a plaque-shaped ornament.

1121107870000.title_en: Buncheong Jar with Iron-painted Fish Design
1121107870000.description: This Buncheong jar was made in the Joseon period and is 27 cm high. Its surface is decorated with multiple techniques, including white slip, inlay, stamping, and iron painting, with lotus and fish motifs shown in a free and varied manner. It is considered an important example for the study of Joseon-period ceramics.

1121107880000.title_en: White Porcelain Jar with Blue-and-white Carp Design
1121107880000.description: This white porcelain jar was made in the early Joseon period and is 24.7 cm high. The body is painted in cobalt blue with fish swimming among aquatic plants, and lotus vines fill the space around a floral diamond-shaped frame. It is thought to have been made at a government-run kiln in the Gwangju area of Gyeonggi-do.

1121107890000.title_en: Celadon Pillow in the Form of Two Lions
1121107890000.description: This celadon pillow was made in the middle of the Goryeo period. Two lions support the pillow top, and the surface shows a clear jade-green glaze with a soft luster. It is believed to have been produced at the Sagdari kiln site in Daegu-myeon, Gangjin, in the first half of the 12th century.

1123707900000.title_en: Geukrakjeon Hall of Baekheungam Hermitage, Eunhaesa Temple, Yeongcheon
1123707900000.description: Baekheungam Hermitage is said to have been founded in the late Silla period, and the hall was rebuilt in 1643. The building has three bays in front and on the side, a hipped-and-gabled roof, and a bracket system in the Daepo style. Inside, the ceiling is stepped and the altar for the Buddha image is separately designated as a treasure.

1121107910000.title_en: White Porcelain Flat Flask with Inlaid Peony Leaf Design
1121107910000.description: This flat flask was made in the early Joseon period and was used outdoors as a vessel for liquor or water. It has flat opposing sides, a rounded body, and inlaid peony-leaf designs on the two broad faces. It is believed to have been made at a kiln site in the Gwangju area of Gyeonggi-do around the 15th century.

1123507920000.description: This portrait depicts Yi Sang-gil (1556-1637), a civil official of the mid-Joseon period. He is shown seated, wearing official dress and a low official hat, with his hands hidden inside his sleeves. The painting is thought to be a later copy of an original image, but it closely preserves the older model and remains an important reference for portrait studies.

1123207930000.title_en: Reliquary Objects from the Wooden Seated Child Manjushri, Sangwonsa Temple, Pyeongchang
1123207930000.description: These relics were discovered in 1984 inside the National Treasure wooden seated Child Manjushri image at Sangwonsa Temple, Pyeongchang. The group includes two dedicatory inscriptions, records of later repairs, and 23 objects such as books and ritual texts from the early Joseon period. The inscriptions include records from 1466 and 1599 about the making, dedication, and repair of related Buddhist images.

1123407940000.title_en: Stone Four-sided Buddha Statue, Hwajeon-ri, Yesan
1123407940000.description: This stone monument, discovered in 1983, is the only known four-sided Buddha statue from the Baekje period. Each of the four faces is carved with a Buddha image, including seated and standing figures, and the halos and drapery show distinctive Baekje style. It is considered an important work for the study of Baekje art and Buddhist history.

1123607950000.title_en: Three-story Stone Pagoda of Cheongansa Temple, Jangheung
1123607950000.description: This stone pagoda stands to the right of the former main hall site of Cheongansa Temple and is a three-story pagoda on a two-tiered base. It was made in the early Goryeo period and shows transitional features, such as the omission of the central pillar on each face of the base and the thin supports beneath the roof stones.

1123607960000.title_en: Nine-story Stone Pagoda of Unjusa Temple, Hwasun
1123607960000.description: This pagoda stands at the first entrance to the southern valley leading into Unjusa Temple and is built with large stone slabs and a nine-story body. Its unusual forms and carved decoration are characteristic of local Goryeo-period stone pagodas, and it was later upgraded from local heritage status to Treasure in 1984.

1123607970000.title_en: Stone Buddha Shrine of Unjusa Temple, Hwasun
1123607970000.description: This stone shrine is a rare external niche built to house Buddhist images at Unjusa Temple. The rectangular chamber contains two Buddha figures placed back to back, and the structure imitates the form of a wooden building with a paljak roof-shaped stone cap.

1123607980000.title_en: Circular Multistory Stone Pagoda of Unjusa Temple, Hwasun
1123607980000.description: This unusual stone pagoda stands in front of the Stone Buddha Shrine of Unjusa Temple and does not follow the standard square plan of ordinary Korean pagodas. Its body and roof stones are all round, and the remaining six stories suggest that it was originally taller.

1123408000000.title_en: Yeongsanjeon Hall of Magoksa Temple, Gongju
1123408000000.description: Yeongsanjeon is the hall that enshrines a painting depicting the life of Śākyamuni Buddha, and this building is also called Cheonbuljeon because it houses a thousand Buddhas. It was rebuilt in 1651 during the Joseon period and is the oldest surviving building at Magoksa Temple.

1123408010000.title_en: Daeungbojeon Hall of Magoksa Temple, Gongju
1123408010000.description: This main hall of Magoksa Temple enshrines Śākyamuni Buddha together with Bhaisajyaguru and Amitābha. The present building was rebuilt in 1651 during the Joseon period, and its upper-story form and elaborate bracket structure make it an important example of later Joseon architecture.

1123408020000.title_en: Daegwangbojeon Hall of Magoksa Temple, Gongju
1123408020000.description: This is the main hall of Magoksa Temple and stands in line with the temple gate axis. It enshrines Vairocana Buddha and was rebuilt in 1813 after being burned, making it an important example for the study of late Joseon architecture.

1123508030000.title_en: Daeungjeon Hall of Chamdangam Hermitage, Seonunsa Temple, Gochang
1123508030000.description: This hall belongs to Chamdangam Hermitage, one of the hermitages of Seonunsa Temple. The present building dates to the Joseon period and shows a mixed bracket system, with a typical 18th-century multi-bracket structure on the front and a simpler bracket arrangement on the rear.

1123608040000.title_en: Daeungjeon Hall of Jeonghyesa Temple, Suncheon
1123608040000.description: Jeonghyesa Temple is said to have been founded by Boga Guksa or Hyejo Guksa during the reign of King Gyeongdeok of Silla, though the exact history is not known. Daeungjeon Hall is believed to date to the Joseon period, probably the 17th century. It is a three-bay by two-bay wooden hall with a paljak roof, danpo bracket complexes, a wujima ceiling, and remaining polychrome decoration that reflects early Joseon styles.

1122208050000.title_en: Jijangjeon Hall of Bukjijangsa Temple, Daegu
1122208050000.description: Bukjijangsa Temple is traditionally said to have been founded in 485 during the reign of King Soji of Silla. The building was long used as Daeungjeon Hall, but during dismantling and repair in 2011 an inscription was found stating that it had been named Jijangjeon in 1761, and its title was changed accordingly. It is a rare Buddhist hall with an unusual plan, a paljak roof, danpo bracket complexes, and details showing both mid- and late-Joseon techniques.

1121108060000.description: This Joseon-period white porcelain food container measures 22.5 cm in height and has a lid with a floral bud-shaped knop. It has a rounded body, a slightly flaring high foot, and a bluish-white glaze with a soft luster over the entire surface. The form is dignified and balanced, and it is regarded as one of the representative food containers of the early Joseon period.

1121108070000.title_en: White Porcelain Bottle with Inlaid Peony Design
1121108070000.description: This early Joseon white porcelain bottle is 29.6 cm high and has a short neck, flaring mouth, full body, and slightly raised foot. Black inlay is used to form simple scroll designs and two bands around the neck, with a large peony motif on the body. The surface has a pale gray-white tone with a bluish tint, showing the gentle quality associated with the inlaid white porcelain tradition.

1121108080000.description: A Birth Buddha depicts the moment when the Buddha, just after birth, took seven steps and declared, 'Above heaven and below heaven, I alone am honored.' This gilt-bronze figure stands upright on a circular lotus pedestal, with the right hand pointing to heaven and the left hand to earth, and wears a garment only over the lower body. It is considered the only surviving example of a Birth Buddha in Korea and is believed to date to the 6th century.

1121108090000.description: Jagyeongjeon Hall was built in 1867 on the site of Jami-dang as the residence for Queen Dowager Jo, the adoptive mother of King Gojong, when Gyeongbokgung Palace was rebuilt. After being lost to fire, it was rebuilt in 1888 and survives today. It was a living quarters complex for the queen dowager, and the remaining flower-patterned walls and decorative chimneys preserve parts of the original compound.

1121108100000.title_en: Ten-Long-Life Chimney of Jagyeongjeon Hall, Gyeongbokgung Palace
1121108100000.description: This chimney is a projection built into one side of the rear wall of Jagyeongjeon Hall. It is square in form and decorated with ten-long-life motifs, which were made to wish Queen Dowager Jo a long life. Built of brick with a tiled roof and smoke vents on top, it is valued as one of the most beautiful palace chimneys of the Joseon period.

1121108110000.description: These chimneys carry smoke from the ondol rooms beneath Gyotaejeon Hall, the queen's living quarters in Gyeongbokgung Palace. The four surviving chimneys were newly made when the palace was rebuilt in 1866, and their hexagonal walls are decorated with vines, cranes, bats, phoenixes, pine, plum, chrysanthemum, lingzhi, rocks, birds, and deer. The upper part imitates a wooden building and includes small smoke outlets, combining practical function with elaborate decoration.

1121108120000.title_en: Geunjeongmun Gate and Haenggak, Gyeongbokgung Palace, Seoul
1121108120000.description: Geunjeongmun Gate is the south gate of Geunjeongjeon, the main throne hall of Gyeongbokgung Palace, and the haenggak buildings enclose it on both sides. The original gate and corridors were built in 1395, burned during the Japanese invasions of 1592, and rebuilt in 1867. The gate is a two-story building, unusual among the surviving south gates of Joseon dynasty throne halls.

1121108130000.description: Injeongmun Gate is the main gate of Injeongjeon, the throne hall of Changdeokgung Palace. Several Joseon kings, including Hyojong, Hyeonjong, Sukjong, and Yeongjo, ascended the throne here. The present building was built in 1804 and has a simple painted interior ceiling and restrained decoration.

1121108140000.description: Seonjeongjeon was the king's official office, where the king met with officials and discussed state affairs and Confucian studies. Its roof is covered with blue glazed tiles, and it is the only surviving building with such a roof in a palace today. The present building was rebuilt in 1647 using materials from Gwangjeongjeon Hall of Injeonggung Palace.
1121108140000.material: Wood with blue glazed roof tiles

1121108150000.description: Huijeongdang Hall was originally used as a royal sleeping quarters, but from the late Joseon period it served as the king's office. The present building was rebuilt in 1920 after a fire in 1917, using materials from Gangnyeongjeon Hall of Gyeongbokgung Palace. It combines traditional Korean construction with Western-style interior decoration.

1121108160000.description: Daejojeon Hall was the foremost building in the queen's inner quarters and served as a residence for the queen. It was first built in 1405, burned several times, and the present building was rebuilt in 1920 using materials from Gyotaejeon Hall of Gyeongbokgung Palace. The interior shows Western-style flooring, windows, and furnishings.

1121108170000.description: Seonwonjeon was a shrine where portraits of successive Joseon kings were enshrined and memorial rites were performed. The building was originally Chunhwijeon, moved from Gyeongdeokgung Palace in 1656, and renamed Seonwonjeon in 1695. It is a simple and restrained structure that illustrates royal ancestral rites in the Joseon period.

1121108180000.description: Tongmyeongjeon was the main inner hall of Changgyeonggung Palace and was used as the queen's sleeping quarters, though the records show it was mainly used by the queen dowager. The building was first constructed in 1484, rebuilt after fires in the Joseon period, and reconstructed again in 1833 with Yanghwadang Hall. It is the best-preserved inner hall in Changgyeonggung Palace.

1121108190000.title_en: Junghwajeon Hall and Junghwamun Gate, Deoksugung Palace, Seoul
1121108190000.description: Junghwajeon Hall was the main building of Deoksugung Palace, where the king received congratulations and held state ceremonies, and Junghwamun Gate is its main gate. They were built in 1902, burned in 1904, and rebuilt in 1906. The complex is an important source for studying palace architecture from the late 19th to early 20th century.

1123508280000.title_en: Stone Lantern of Geumsansa Temple, Gimje
1123508280000.description: This eight-sided stone lantern stands in front of Daejangjeon Hall at Geumsansa Temple, Gimje. Its pedestal, shaft, fire chamber, roof stone, and finial remain intact, and the floral carving on the roof stone suggests a Goryeo-period work. The lantern is admired for its restrained and simple form.

1123608290000.title_en: Three-Story Stone Pagoda of Geumgoksa Temple, Gangjin
1123608290000.description: This three-story stone pagoda stands at Geumgoksa Temple, Gangjin, on a single-tier base, though parts of the base and body stones are cracked or missing. The first-story body stone has niches on each side, and the roof stones are thick with pronounced eaves. It shows Baekje-style features within a Goryeo-period pagoda.

1123608300000.title_en: Daeungjeon Hall of Bulgapsa Temple, Yeonggwang
1123608300000.description: This Buddhist main hall at Bulgapsa Temple is believed to have been built before the 18th century and repaired in 1764, with another repair in 1909. It is a three-bay-by-three-bay wooden hall with a hipped-and-gabled roof and daepo-style brackets. The building preserves elaborate late Joseon wood carving and decorative details.

1123608310000.title_en: Three-Story Stone Pagoda of Donghwasa Temple, Suncheon
1123608310000.description: This pagoda stands in front of the main hall at Donghwasa Temple, with much of its base buried underground. The roof stones and body stones are each made from a single stone, and the finial components remain almost complete. Its reduced scale and simplified details reflect the transition from late Unified Silla to Goryeo styles.

1123708320000.title_en: Nahanjeon Hall of Seongheolsa Temple, Yeongju
1123708320000.description: This hall enshrines arhats and is set naturally into the terrain at Seongheolsa Temple. It was first built in 1553 and rebuilt in 1634 after the Imjin War. The building has a one-bay-deep gabled roof and detailed carved window decoration showing fish, crab, boy figures, lotus, and birds.

1123708330000.title_en: Daejeokgwangjeon Hall of Girimsa Temple, Gyeongju
1123708330000.description: This hall enshrines Vairocana Buddha and is thought to have been greatly repaired in 1629, during the reign of King Injo. It is a five-bay-by-three-bay wooden hall with a gabled roof and daepo-style brackets. The large scale and rich bracket carving are important evidence for 17th-century temple architecture.

1123708340000.title_en: Daeungjeon Hall of Daebisa Temple, Cheongdo
1123708340000.description: This hall at Daebisa Temple enshrines the Buddha and is estimated to date to around the 16th century. It is a three-bay-by-three-bay wooden building with a gabled roof. Its balanced structure and construction details preserve architectural features of the early to mid-Joseon period.

1123708350000.title_en: Daeungbojeon Hall of Unmunsa Temple, Cheongdo
1123708350000.description: This hall at Unmunsa Temple is thought to have been built during the temple’s fourth reconstruction in 1718. It is a three-bay-by-three-bay wooden building with a hipped-and-gabled roof and daepo-style brackets. The wide bay spacing and restrained ornamentation reflect the architectural style of the Joseon period.

1121108200000.description: Hamnyeongjeon is the living quarters where Emperor Gojong, the first emperor of the Korean Empire, stayed. The original building was built in 1897 and burned during repairs in 1904; the present structure was rebuilt in December of that year. It has a complex L-shaped plan and an unusual roof and bracket composition for a royal bedroom hall.

1121108210000.description: Yeongnyeongjeon is part of Jongmyo Shrine, where the ancestral tablets of Joseon kings and queens are enshrined and rituals are performed. It was originally built in 1421 and later expanded to accommodate the growing number of tablets; the present structure reflects mid-17th-century architecture. Its form, decoration, and colors are restrained and solemn in keeping with its ritual function.

1123108220000.title_en: Rock-carved Standing Buddha at Yeongwolam Hermitage, Icheon
1123108220000.description: This is a large rock-carved Buddha figure carved across the whole face of a natural rock surface. Based on its powerful, spacious composition and the style of the carving, it is thought to date to the early Goryeo period. The figure is shown with the hands joined in a preaching gesture.

1123108230000.description: Yeongsanjeon is the hall that enshrines the seated Buddha and paintings of the eight scenes of the Buddha's life. The present building is a Joseon-period structure and was rebuilt after the temple was destroyed in the Imjin War. Its balanced plan and bracket system are important examples for the study of early to mid-Joseon architecture.

1123108240000.description: Daeungjeon is the main worship hall of Cheongryongsa Temple and is believed to have been rebuilt in the late Joseon period. It has a three-by-four-bay plan, a hip-and-gable roof, and a dense bracket system with elaborate floral decoration. The use of unprocessed round timber pillars is a notable feature.

1123508250000.description: Bogwangjeon is believed to have been built before the 17th century. It is a small Joseon-period Buddhist hall with a front-facing gabled roof and a bracket system that is present on the front but not on the side walls. Decorative elements such as dragon heads and lotus motifs remain inside and on the upper structural members.

1123508260000.description: Daejeokgwangjeon enshrines Vairocana Buddha and is thought to have been rebuilt around the 17th century. It has a five-by-three-bay plan, a gabled roof, and a bracket system extending both above the pillars and between them. The front doors have lattice-patterned windows, and the side bays are enclosed with walls.

1123508270000.description: Daejangjeon was rebuilt in 1635 and moved to its present location in 1922. It originally functioned as a wooden pagoda used to keep Buddhist scriptures, and it now houses Buddhist images instead. The building retains traces of its former pagoda form on the roof and is an important example for the study of wooden pagoda-style architecture.

1121108460000.title_en: Punggidae Observatory at Changgyeonggung Palace, Seoul
1121108460000.description: This stone standard was used to observe wind direction and estimate wind strength by attaching a narrow flag to the top of the pole. It is made of granite and consists of a sculpted base surmounted by an octagonal pillar with cloud designs, a pole hole at the center of the top, and a drainage hole on the side. It is a surviving material witness to Joseon-period weather observation.

1121108470000.title_en: Punggidae Observatory at Gyeongbokgung Palace, Seoul
1121108470000.description: This granite instrument was used in the Joseon period to measure wind direction and wind strength with a flag attached to the top of the pole. The base has a carved pedestal and an octagonal pillar with cloud designs, a pole socket at the top, and a drainage hole on the side. It is considered a surviving example of a Joseon weather-observation device.

1123308480000.title_en: Boseong Beopjusa Temple New Method Astronomical Chart Folding Screen
1123308480000.description: This eight-panel folding screen preserves a copy of the "New Method Astronomical Chart," which depicts the constellations north and south of the ecliptic. The first panel explains the chart in writing and shows the sun, moon, and five planets, while the remaining panels present the star map and the names of the officials involved in its production. It is regarded as the largest and finest known copy of Köegler's astronomical chart.

1121108490000.title_en: Complete Map of the Myriad Countries of the Earth
1121108490000.description: This map is a 1708 Joseon copy made at the Office of Astronomy and Calendars based on an updated version of Matteo Ricci and Li Zhizao's world map from 1602. It presents Europe, Africa, and other parts of the world from a new geographical perspective influenced by Western cartography. The margins and surrounding areas include notes by Ricci, Li Zhizao, and other scholars, as well as diagrams of the hemispheres, eclipses, and celestial structure.

1121108500000.description: This is one extant version of Kim Jeong-ho's 1861 woodblock map, preserved at Sungkonghoe University Museum. The map is divided into 22 folded sections; when assembled, it forms a large nationwide map with roads, administrative units, forts, beacons, and other features marked in detail. This copy is notable for its blue cloth title cover and for containing handwritten map notes and population and production figures.

1121108500200.description: This is a copy of Kim Jeong-ho's 1861 woodblock map preserved at Seoul Museum of History. Like other versions of the map, it is divided into 22 folded sections that together form a large map of Korea with roads, settlements, forts, beacons, and geographic features shown in detail. This copy is distinguished by having 21 bound sections because the Jeju and Chuja islands are combined into one section.

1121108500300.description: This is a copy of Kim Jeong-ho's 1861 woodblock map preserved at the Kyujanggak Institute for Korean Studies, Seoul National University. The map is divided into 22 folded sections and is assembled into a large nationwide map showing roads, administrative units, settlements, forts, beacons, and terrain in detail. It is a rare complete Joseon-period edition, and the text notes that some content was revised after the first printing.

1121108510000.title_en: Gwancheondae Observatory at Changgyeonggung Palace, Seoul
1121108510000.description: This stone astronomical observation platform was built in 1688 during the reign of King Sukjong and was used to install a ganui instrument for observing the positions of celestial bodies. The structure is made of granite, and only the stone base remains today. It is one of two surviving Joseon-period observation platforms in Seoul.

1121108520000.description: This portable sundial was made of stone in 1871 and is based on the latitude of Seoul. The maker's name and the date of production are engraved on it, along with hour lines, the 24 seasonal points, and direction markings for the built-in compass. It is a rare and finely made example that shows the precision of Joseon-period scientific instrument making.

1121108530000.description: This woodblock was used to print the 19th-century map of Hanyang, the capital city known as Susŏn chondo. It is made of three horizontal planks that could be joined to complete one map, and the fine carving itself is considered artistically outstanding. Surviving map woodblocks from Joseon-period printed atlases are very rare.

1121108540000.description: This portable firearm was made in 1432 during the reign of King Sejong. It is the smallest type of chongtong, with a short barrel and a range of about 200 paces, and was used widely because it was easy to carry and fire. The object is preserved in complete condition and is a rare example of Joseon-period casting technology.

1121108550000.description: This is the only surviving example of a Chae Seungjatong cannon, made in 1588 during the reign of King Seonjo. It has six bamboo-like ridges, and the barrel curves slightly from about the fourth ridge from the breech toward the muzzle. It is a portable firearm that was smaller than the Seungjatong.

1121108560000.description: This portable firearm was made in 1591 during the reign of King Seonjo. It is a later form of Seungjatong, with a longer barrel and evenly spaced bamboo-like ridges. The production date, powder amount, and maker are known from records, and its complete preservation makes it an important source for the study of firearms.

1121108570000.description: This weapon is a type of tube cannon called wangu, also known as deanggu. The surviving example was made of bronze in 1845 by Yu Hui-joon and Kim Hyeong-eop during the reign of King Heonjong, and it has a bowl-shaped firing part with bamboo-like ridges. An inscription is preserved on the body, and it is the only surviving large wangu.

1123808580000.description: This medium wangu mortar was discovered in 1985 by a local resident in Donghwa-ri, Hadong-gun, Gyeongsangnam-do. Records indicate that it was made in September 1590 by Imulgeum in Hamgyeong-do and that its range reached about one ri when fired once. It is an important source for the study of firearms development and is also evidence of use during the Imjin War.

1123808590000.description: This medium wangu mortar was recovered by a diver from the sea off Tongyeong-gun, Gyeongsangnam-do, in 1970. Because it was submerged for a long time, the surface is heavily corroded and the inscriptions are difficult to read, but its form and size are very similar to another designated example. It is estimated to date from between 1575 and 1605 and is valued as evidence for naval warfare and the development of firearms.

1123708360000.description: This hall at Daejiksa Temple is said to have taken on the appearance of a temple when Seonghae Daesa built a building and enshrined a Buddhist image in 1689, during the reign of King Sukjong. It is a Buddhist hall expressing the Buddhist paradise of Geungnakjeon, and is considered a rebuilt structure from the mid-Joseon period or later. The building has a 3-bay front, 2-bay side, a gable roof, and a dapo bracketing system, with lotus, turtle, and dragon carvings on the base and stair sides.

1121108370000.title_en: Engraved Stone for the Bokgak Cheonsang Yeolcha Bunyajido
1121108370000.description: This engraved stone is an astronomical chart with constellations carved into stone. Inside a circular sky are 1,467 stars, and below are records explaining the making of the chart and the names of those who participated. It reproduces the original chart first made in 1395, and this version was re-engraved in 1687 after the stone wore down.

1121108380000.description: This water gauge was installed to measure the water level of a stream, following the invention of the rain gauge in King Sejong's reign. The surviving Cheonggyecheon example was improved into a stone pillar during the reign of King Seongjong, and is a granite square pillar with carved graduations for measuring water depth. The marks indicate low, normal, and high water levels so that droughts and floods could be anticipated.

1121108390000.description: This horizontal sundial differs from most sundials in that its time-marked plate lies flat. It is made of white marble and has finely engraved hour lines and seasonal lines on the surface. A record in the Revised Comprehensive Mirror for the Eastern Kingdoms identifies it as a sundial made by Yi Cheong-gyeong in 1636, and it is believed to have been brought back from Qing China in 1645.

1121108400000.description: This sundial is made of black marble and has a flat form with concentric circles and radial lines for reading time. An inscription suggests that it was made in the early 18th century, and its structure and markings indicate that it was newly made at the Office of Astronomy after being modeled on a Chinese example. A related portable sundial is also preserved at the Seoul National University Museum.

1121108410000.description: These two sundials are carved on a single stone in a very unusual combined form. The inscription states that they were made in 1785 using the latitude of Seoul and the angular distance between the ecliptic and equator as reference values. One face is the Ganpyeongilgu, and the other is the Hongaeilgu, both carefully engraved with lines for reading time and seasonal change.

1121108430000.description: This stone pedestal supported a rain gauge used to measure rainfall in the Joseon period, and only the pedestal survives today. The rain gauge itself was invented in 1441 during King Sejong's reign, and this pedestal confirms the former existence of that instrument. It is a rectangular granite block with a central hole for setting the cylindrical metal gauge.

1121108450000.description: Angbuilgu is a hemispherical sundial made in 1434 by Jang Yeong-sil, Yi Cheon, and Kim Jo during King Sejong's reign. The concave bowl-shaped face carries hour lines and seasonal lines, and the shadow cast by the sun indicates the time and the 24 solar terms. These two examples were made in different periods, but both are bronze, finished with black lacquer, and inlaid with silver for the inscriptions and lines.

1121108600000.description: This explosive weapon was invented by Lee Jang-son during the reign of King Seonjo of Joseon and was used in the mid-Joseon period. It is made of parts such as a wooden groove for winding the fuse, a bamboo tube, thin iron pieces, and a lid, and was fired with a type of cannon called a wangu.

1121108610000.description: This is the only breech-loading cannon from the Joseon period that was ignited and fired by hand. Although it had previously been thought to have been introduced in 1592, this artifact shows that it was already in use by 1563. It consists of a mother gun and a smaller child gun used to load and fire the projectile.

1121108610200.description: This small cannon was attached to a bulanggi, a breech-loading gun, and was used to load shot and gunpowder. An inscription on the surface indicates that it was made in 1563 by the artisan Kim Seok-nyeon, and it was excavated from the former site of the military office that managed Joseon weapons.

1121108620000.description: This is a Joseon cannon of the jija type, one of the four standard cannon types named cheon, ji, hyeon, and hwang, and it is the second largest after the cheonja cannon. It was cast in bronze in 1557 and has a structure divided into the muzzle, the packed-powder section, and the wooden plug section.

1122108630000.description: This is another Joseon jija-type cannon, made in 1557 during the reign of King Myeongjong. It retains two handles and a body divided into sections for the muzzle, the powder chamber, and the wooden plug section, and was used with arrows or shot.

1121108650000.title_en: Private Wooden Movable Type and Printing Tools
1121108650000.description: These are wooden movable type pieces and various printing tools used for private publications in the Joseon period. The movable type was used mainly from the reign of King Sunjo through the Japanese colonial period, and the surviving tools include knives, awls, saws, chopsticks for arranging type, an ink brush, an ink board, and a basket.

1121108660000.description: This painting depicts a gathering of members of the Giroso, elderly scholar-officials aged seventy or older, who met to enjoy leisure and friendship. Painted on silk, it shows a meeting held at Namji outside Sungnyemun Gate in Seoul and includes inscriptions naming the participants and the nature of the gathering.

1121108670000.description: This is a painting of a literary gathering set at Dokseodang, an institution for study and training of talented men in Joseon. It is thought to have been made around 1570 and depicts a gathering of nine men, including Jeong Cheol, Yi I, and Yu Seong-ryong, with the landscape and Dokseodang buildings emphasized.

1121108680000.title_en: Miwon Gyhoe-do with Verse by Seong Se-chang
1121108680000.description: This hanging scroll depicts a gyehoe, or gathering of officials for socializing and leisure, associated with the Saheonbu (Board of Censors). The composition places a small meeting scene within a landscape and includes inscriptions recording the participants' names and offices. It is dated to 1540 and is considered the oldest extant gyehoe-do in Korea.

1121108690000.title_en: Hwagwan Gyhoe-do with Verse by Seong Se-chang
1121108690000.description: This hanging scroll portrays a gathering of officials who worked in the military administration, the Hwagwan or Byeongjo. The upper inscription names the work, and the lower section records the participants' official ranks, names, and bon-gwan. A verse by Seong Se-chang shows that it was made in the autumn of 1541.

1121108700000.description: This hanging scroll depicts a gyehoe, or social gathering, of officials from the Hojo, the government office in charge of taxation and finances. The participants are seated in a semicircle on silk, with the central figure emphasized and the others reduced in size to show rank. It was painted around 1550 and reflects the changes in mid-16th-century gyehoe-do painting.

1121108710000.description: This painting shows a gathering of literati of the same office or association, arranged for fellowship and leisure. The meeting scene is set in a landscape with seven people seated inside a pavilion and women seated to the right, while inscriptions originally recorded the title and participants. It is dated to the mid-16th century and represents a transitional stage between early and later Joseon gyehoe-do paintings.

1123708720000.description: This is a portrait of Yi Hyeon-bo (1467–1555), a mid-Joseon civil official and sijo poet. He is shown seated before a desk, wearing a peaked paeraengi hat and a reddish robe, with a ceremonial staff in one hand and the desk held with the other. The painting is said to have been made in 1537 and later copied in 1827.

1121108730000.title_en: Painting of Yuksangmyo Shrine by Jeong Seon
1121108730000.description: This is a documentary landscape painting by Jeong Seon showing Yuksangmyo Shrine in Gyeongjeong-dong, Seoul, with Bukhansan in the background. The upper section lists the 18 officials involved in building the shrine, while the lower section depicts the shrine, trees, and surrounding terrain. It was painted in 1739 and shows Jeong Seon's distinctive style influenced by literati painting.
1121108730000.material: Ink and light color on silk

1123108740000.title_en: Royal Edict Bestowing the Title of Meritorious Subject for Loyal Escort on Yi Chung-won
1123108740000.description: This royal edict was issued in 1604 by King Seonjo to confer a reward and honor on Yi Chung-won. It records his achievements, the privileges granted to meritorious subjects, and his place in the list of recipients as number 12 of the second rank. The document is also valued as a calligraphic work written by Hangeul calligrapher Han Seok-bong.

1123608750100.title_en: Sagyo Jeongbon Jabi Doryang Chambeop, Volumes 7–10
1123608750100.description: This printed Buddhist text is a corrected edition of the Jabi Doryang Chambeop, a repentance ritual text used to confess sins through recitation. It is bound as one book containing volumes 7 through 10, printed from woodblocks on handmade paper. The colophon states that it was published in 1352 under Goryeo King Gongmin.

1123708790000.description: This is a handwritten diary by Gwon Mun-hae (1534–1591), a scholar-official active in the reigns of King Myeongjong to King Seonjo of Joseon. The three-volume set consists of Seonjo Ilgi, Chogan Ilgi, and Sinran Ilgi, and is regarded as an important source for the period before the Japanese invasions of 1592. It records the author’s daily life in detail and provides material on court affairs, local administration, politics, defense, society, education, culture, and geography.

1123708800000.description: This diary was written by Yi Tak-yeong (1541–1610), who served as a military aide under the Gyeongsang governor during King Seonjo’s reign. It consists of two volumes and records events from the outbreak of the Japanese invasions of 1592 through 1598, including reports, circulars, and proclamations related to the war. It is considered a valuable historical source for the study of the Imjin War.

1123708810000.description: These are two items associated with Jang Mal-son (1431–1486), a prominent official of the Joseon period: a sword worn at the waist and a record of the oath-taking banquet for meritorious subjects. The sword was bestowed by the king in recognition of military service in repelling enemy forces at Hoeryeong in Hamgyeong Province. The oath-taking record is an important source for identifying those who took part in suppressing the rebellion of Yi Si-ae.

1121108820000.description: These are printing woodblocks made in 1860 for republishing Gonyeonjeondo, a world map originally produced by the Jesuit missionary Ferdinand Verbiest (1623–1688). The surviving blocks in the collection preserve maps carved on both sides and show the advanced woodblock engraving skills of late Joseon cartography. Three of the original four woodblocks are extant.

1121108830000.description: This bronze celestial globe has a diameter of 24 cm and is thought to have been made by Choe Han-gi. It is marked with meridians and parallels at 10-degree intervals, as well as the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn and the ecliptic with the 24 seasonal terms. It is mounted on a wooden stand with a 360-degree graduated ring.

1123708840000.description: This is a small portable gun designed to be carried by one person and fitted with three barrels so that it could fire three shots at once. An inscription on the grip records the year of manufacture as 1593, along with information on the amounts of gunpowder and bullets and the maker. It is a valuable example for the study of Joseon firearms and military technology.

1123808850000.description: This is a large Joseon-period cannon of the hyeonja type, one of the four kinds of barrel cannon named after Chinese characters. It was found in Gohyeon Bay, Geoje, and an inscription inside the breech indicates that it was made in 1596. The cannon retains its original form and preserves engraved text, making it an important source for the history of Korean firearms.

1121108860000.description: This is the smallest of the barrel-type cannons named after the Chinese characters for heaven, earth, dark, and yellow. It was made for ease of transport, and an inscription indicates a manufacture date of 1587, five years before the Japanese invasions of 1592. Its complete form and dated inscription make it an important object for the study of Joseon firearms.

1122108940200.description: This is an annotated edition of the Brahmā’s Net Sūtra, the scripture that forms the basis of Korean Buddhist precepts, translated by Kumarajiva of Later Qin. It includes three prefaces at the beginning, one dated 1298, and the main text with commentary written in small script below each section. The extant copy appears to have been reprinted in late Goryeo based on a Yuan-dynasty edition.

1121108950000.description: This historical poem was written by Yi Seung-hyu in 1287 and survives in one volume with upper and lower parts. The upper volume presents Chinese history from the mythical age to the Yuan dynasty in seven-syllable verse, and the lower volume treats the history of Korea in two parts. Several missing leaves were copied in by hand in this printed edition.

1123708960000.title_en: Collected Books of the Gwonbeol Clan, Bonghwa
1123708960000.description: This collection preserves books kept by the clan of Gwon Beol, a scholar-official of the Joseon period. The designated set includes 15 titles in 184 volumes, such as family registers of civil-service examinations, official rosters, and Gwon Beol’s own diary. It is considered an important source for the study of early Joseon political, social, and economic history.

1121108970000.title_en: Royal Edict Conferring an Office on Jo Heup (1986-1)
1121108970000.description: This royal edict was issued in 1425 to Jo Heup, a military official active from the reign of King Taejong to King Sejong. It appoints him as Right Army Commander-in-Chief. The document is valuable for studying early Joseon document forms and the personnel administration system.

1121108980000.title_en: Royal Edict Conferring a Rank and Office on Jo Heup (1986-2)
1121108980000.description: This royal edict, issued in 1409, grants Jo Heup the rank of Gajeong daebu and the positions of commander of the Central Army Commander’s Office and inspector of the Office of Military Affairs. It is a single-sheet royal document from early Joseon. The item is important for research on document forms and personnel administration.

1121108990000.title_en: Royal Edict Granting Land to Jo Heup
1121108990000.description: This royal edict was issued in 1401 to reward Jo Heup, then a junior military official, for his service during the Banggan Rebellion, the second struggle among the princes. It granted him state land and slaves. The document is a valuable source for studying early Joseon royal grant documents and rewards for military merit.

1123509000000.title_en: Old Documents of the Buan Kim Clan
1123509000000.description: This collection consists of old documents preserved by the Buan Kim clan in Buan, Jeollabuk-do. It includes royal edicts, land-division records, petitions, and certificates such as meritorious subject registers, selected from among the clan’s family papers. The materials are valuable for studying Joseon-era administration, society, family organization, and economic history.

1123709010000.title_en: Old Documents of the Gwonbeol Clan
1123709010000.description: This collection contains old documents and related materials preserved by the Gwon Beol family line. It includes family records, royal edicts, certificates, petitions, and other documents accumulated over about 570 years, with 15 titles and 274 selected items described here. These materials are important sources for studying early Joseon family organization, politics, and personnel administration.

1121108750200.title_en: Detailed and Corrected Dharma of the Compassionate Bodhimanda Repentance Ritual, Vols. 1–3
1121108750200.description: This woodblock-printed Buddhist text is a collected edition of volumes 1–3 bound into one volume. It was printed on paper from woodblocks originally carved in 1352 under the auspices of Suhan and others, and is thought to have been printed in the early Joseon period. The cover bears the alternate title "Yangmu chammun," and the first section includes an illustrative frontispiece (byeonsangdo).

1121108750300.title_en: Detailed and Corrected Dharma of the Compassionate Bodhimanda Repentance Ritual, Vol. 3
1121108750300.description: This is volume 3 of a Buddhist repentance text used in ritual practice. The Dharmasa copy is an old woodblock-printed edition believed to have been printed around 1352, the same year recorded in the colophon of another volume from the set. It survives in folded-leaf format and retains an early form of the text, though it is incomplete.

1122408750400.title_en: Detailed and Corrected Dharma of the Compassionate Bodhimanda Repentance Ritual, Vol. 6
1122408750400.description: This Buddhist scripture, held by Chonnam National University Library, is a later printing from a woodblock carved in the 10th lunar month of 1352 under the leadership of Suhan and others. The text is in folded-leaf format, and parts of the pages show wear, repairs, and added writing. The copy also preserves ownership marks on the back cover and oral reading marks within the text.

1122208750500.title_en: Detailed and Corrected Dharma of the Compassionate Bodhimanda Repentance Ritual, Vols. 4–7
1122208750500.description: This Buddhist scripture, held by Keimyung University Dongsan Library, was printed later from woodblocks carved in the 10th lunar month of 1352 under the leadership of Suhan and others. It is in sewn book format, and parts of the illustrations and text are worn or damaged, with some added corrections and one missing two-page leaf in volume 7. The copy is notable for preserving a frontispiece and for showing later restoration of a cover title label.

1121108750600.title_en: Detailed and Corrected Dharma of the Compassionate Bodhimanda Repentance Ritual, Vols. 1–5
1121108750600.description: This Buddhist scripture, held by Korea University Library, was printed later from woodblocks made in the 10th lunar month of 1352 under the leadership of Suhan and others. Some parts were supplemented by manuscript corrections, and there are missing sections in the front matter and some leaves, while the cover and title slip were repaired. Even so, it preserves an early form of the Goryeo-period edition and is valuable for studying later restoration and printing history.

1121108760000.title_en: Collected Documents of the Jearyeong Yi Clan, Yeonghae Branch
1121108760000.description: This collection consists of 12 types of documents and 403 items preserved by the head family of the Jearyeong Yi clan, Yeonghae branch. The documents include records of property division, household registers, land and property deeds, petitions, marriage exchange documents, examination papers, notices, and official certificates. They are an important source for understanding the history of the family.

1121108770000.description: This woodblock-printed copy of the Diamond Sutra was commissioned by Kim Jeo of Jeonju and printed in 1357 by Jiseon and Johwan of Deokunsa Temple. It was originally made as a scroll, later folded into book form, and then reassembled into a scroll for placement inside a Buddha statue. The frontispiece illustrates the Buddha expounding the scripture, and the text distinguishes sections by varying the size of the script.

1123708780000.title_en: Woodblocks and Draft Manuscripts of Daedong unbugunok
1123708780000.description: This item consists of the woodblocks and draft manuscripts for Daedong unbugunok, an encyclopedia compiled by Gwon Munhae in 1589. The set includes 667 woodblocks and 3 draft manuscript sets in 27 volumes. The woodblocks preserve the original printing blocks, and the draft manuscripts are incomplete but valuable source materials for the compilation of the book.

1123709020000.title_en: Calligraphic Works of the Kwon Beol Main Family
1123709020000.description: This collection consists of calligraphic works kept by the main family line of Kwon Beol, a scholar-official of the Joseon Dynasty, and includes 8 types in 14 pieces. The designated items include works by Kim Gu, Yi Hwang, Heo Mok, Zhang Donghai, and anthologies of calligraphic pieces from the mid-Joseon period. They are valuable as materials for studying the exchanges of Kwon Beol and his descendants, as well as the poetry and daily life of literati at the time.

1121109030000.title_en: Celadon Meiping Vase with Inlaid Plum, Bamboo, and Crane Design (1986)
1121109030000.description: This Goryeo celadon meiping vase is 38.9 cm high, with a mouth diameter of 5.1 cm and a base diameter of 15.6 cm. It has the typical Goryeo meiping form, with a broad shoulder and a narrow lower body, and is decorated on the front and back with inlaid plum blossoms and bamboo, along with birds, cranes, and grasses in black-and-white inlay. The surface has a clear pale bluish-green glaze and fine crackles throughout.

1121109040000.description: This bronze helmet, 21.5 cm high, was presented in commemoration of Son Kee-chung's victory in the marathon at the 1936 Berlin Olympic Games. It was made in Corinth, Greece, around the 6th century BCE and excavated at Olympia by a German archaeologist in 1875. The helmet is shaped to protect the eyes, nose, and back of the head, and the perforations along the edges suggest that fabric lining may originally have been attached inside.

1123709050000.title_en: Books of the Kim Seong-il Main Family
1123709050000.description: This collection consists of various books and printed materials preserved by the main family line of Kim Seong-il, a scholar-official of the Joseon Dynasty, and 55 types in 261 volumes are designated. It includes printed books published before the Japanese invasions of 1592, such as the Gukjo Oeui and Samgang Haengsildo, as well as manuscript materials such as the Toegye Sajeoncho and Bukbeol Ilgi. The collection is useful for studying pre-war movable-type printing and the history of the Imjin War.

1123709060000.title_en: Documents of the Kim Seong-il Main Family
1123709060000.description: This collection consists of historical documents preserved by the main family line of Kim Seong-il, a scholar-official of the Joseon Dynasty, and 17 types in 242 items are designated. The documents include royal orders, edicts, appointment documents, property division records, letters, and memorial texts, with examples dating from 1564 to 1834. They are valuable for understanding Kim Seong-il's life and the genealogy of the Uiseong Kim clan.

1123709070000.title_en: Three-Story Stone Pagoda at Namsa-ri, Gyeongju
1123709070000.description: This stone pagoda stands at an old temple site and has a three-story body set on a two-tiered base. Most of the structure remains in its original form, with only the north central stone of the upper base restored in 1975. Its refined base carving and more formal upper structure suggest a date in the late 9th century of Unified Silla.

1123709080000.title_en: Three-Story Stone Pagoda at Yongmyeong-ri, Gyeongju
1123709080000.description: This stone pagoda stands on a two-tiered base with a three-story body. Each body stone has pillar-like carvings at the corners, and the roof stones have five-tiered undersides with strongly curved slopes. It is thought to date to the mid-8th century, the height of Unified Silla, and a small bronze Buddha statue was found inside the pagoda when it was dismantled for repair in 1943.

1123709090000.title_en: Flagpole Supports at the Site of Nammansa Temple, Gyeongju
1123709090000.description: These are the stone supports that held a temple flagpole at the entrance of a Buddhist temple. They stand in a rice field about 500 meters from the site of Nammansa Temple, and the lower parts are partially exposed because of cultivation. The supports are plain and simple in form, but the holes for fastening the flagpole include a distinctive cross-shaped hole near the top, and they are considered a mid-Unified Silla work.

1121108870000.title_en: Great Perfection of Wisdom Sutra, Volume 175
1121108870000.description: This is volume 175 of the 600-volume Great Perfection of Wisdom Sutra translated by Xuanzang of the Tang dynasty. It was copied in gold ink on indigo paper in 1055 by Kim Yunbeom for the repose of his parents and the well-being of his family. Although five folios at the beginning are missing, the colophon remains at the end, and it is considered the oldest known surviving Buddhist scripture of this type from the Goryeo period.

1121108880000.title_en: Anthology of the Round-Disc Teachings of the Zen School
1121108880000.description: This book collects 170 statements on Zen from writings by various masters, compiled by Jigyeom, royal preceptor to King Gangjong of Goryeo. The printed copy was made from woodblocks carved at Hwashangsa Temple in 1219 during the late Goryeo period. It is valued as an important source for the study of the round-disc teaching method in the Zen school.

1121108890000.title_en: Song of Enlightenment by Yongga Jingak Daesa, with Commentary
1121108890000.description: This printed book contains the Song of Enlightenment, a seven-character verse work on Zen thought by Huineng, and an explanatory text written by his sister Jingjeo. The surviving edition was printed on paper, and its colophon says it was reprinted by I Simu in 1299 based on an earlier edition first issued in 1089 at Boje Temple. It is highly valued both as a Goryeo-period edition and because Jingjeo’s explanation accompanies the text.

1121108900000.title_en: Annotated Renwang huguo bore jing, Volumes 1-4
1121108900000.description: This is a four-volume printed edition of Jeongwon’s explanation of the Renwang huguo bore jing, an important scripture of Buddhist protection for the state. The surviving copy is printed on paper, and records indicate that a fifth volume of explanatory text once followed it, though it is now missing. Because of its format and textual features, it is thought to be a Goryeo supplement to the Tripitaka produced in the early 11th century.

1121108910000.title_en: Commentary on the Avatamsaka Sutra, Volume 42
1121108910000.description: This is volume 42 of a woodblock-printed edition of Jeongwon’s explanation of Chengguan’s commentary on the Avatamsaka Sutra. It was printed in 1087 from woodblocks sent by Jeongwon of Song to Uicheon of Goryeo, and the original woodblocks were later taken to Japan in 1441. The work is an important source for studying cultural exchange among Song China, Goryeo, and Japan.

1121108920000.title_en: Commentary on the Avatamsaka Sutra, Volumes 28-30 and 100-102
1121108920000.description: This set contains two bound volumes comprising volumes 28-30 and 100-102 of Jeongwon’s simplified explanation of Chengguan’s Commentary on the Avatamsaka Sutra. It was printed in 1087 from woodblocks sent from Song China to Uicheon of Goryeo, and the booklets were later bound and covered with thick outer wrappers. The edition is important for understanding cultural exchange among Song China, Goryeo, and Japan.

1121108930000.title_en: Abbreviated Commentary on the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra, Volume Upper
1121108930000.description: This is the upper volume of a woodblock-printed commentary on the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra by the Tang monk Zongmi. The lower volume is missing, so the publication record has been lost, but the woodblocks and printing style suggest a Goryeo edition made from a Song dynasty model. It is significant as a surviving example of a Goryeo woodblock edition copied from Song materials.

1121108940000.title_en: Commentary on the Brahma's Net Sutra
1121108940000.description: This is a woodblock-printed commentary on the Brahma's Net Sutra by Hyein, based on the translation by Kumārajīva. The edition was printed on paper from woodblocks carved in the late Goryeo period, and a preface written by Guo Tianxi in 1298 indicates that it was likely reprinted from a Yuan dynasty edition. Although the publication record at the end is missing, the work is considered a Goryeo woodblock edition.

1123709100000.title_en: Yongjangsa Temple Site Dangganjiju with Lotus Design, Gyeongju
1123709100000.description: These are the two stone pillars that supported the flagpole at the entrance of a temple for rituals and ceremonies. The temple to which they belonged is uncertain, although the old site of Bomunsa Temple remains to the southeast. Lotus petals are carved within a square frame on the outer upper face of the pillars, an unusual decorative treatment for a dangganjiju.

1123709110000.title_en: Three-story Stone Pagoda of Seokguram Grotto, Gyeongju
1123709110000.description: This pagoda stands on a hill about 150 meters northeast of Seokguram Grotto. Its two-tier stylobate shows a distinctive harmony of circular, octagonal, and square forms, while the three-story body rises above it in square tiers. It is thought to date to the late 8th century.

1123709120000.title_en: Three-story Stone Pagoda of Madong, Gyeongju
1123709120000.description: This pagoda stands in a field on a hill northwest of Bulguksa Temple. It has a two-tier stylobate and a three-story stone body, with each story made from single body and roof stones. The structure is plain and unadorned, typical of the simple and restrained stone pagodas that were widespread around Gyeongju in the late 8th century.

1123709130000.title_en: Rock-carved Seated Tathagata Buddha of Yongjangsa Temple Site, Namsan, Gyeongju
1123709130000.description: This rock-carved seated Buddha is on the stone cliff behind the stone seated Buddha of Yongjangsa Valley, Gyeongju, which is separately designated as a Treasure. The Buddha has snail-shell curls, a gentle face, and a robe with dense parallel-line patterns; the inscription of ten characters remains difficult to read. It is considered a fine work made in the late 8th century.

1123509140000.title_en: Stone Standing Buddhas of Bohwari, Jeongeup
1123509140000.description: These are two stone standing Buddha statues placed side by side on a hillside in Jeongeup, Jeollabuk-do.
