The first volume includes six maps such as a world map, a map of China, a map of Beijing and Hanyang Fortress, and a general map, while the second volume contains provincial maps of Joseon in the style of Jeong Sang-gi’s Dongguk Jido. The third volume contains 16 maps of the provinces of China and differs in composition from most late-Joseon map atlases.

1121115930000.description: This is a map atlas containing county maps of Joseon in the late Joseon period. It consists of two volumes of maps and a third volume of local gazetteer material, and its production date is estimated to be between 1800 and 1804. The maps are drawn on a 20-ri grid, and each province section begins with an "Paldo Bunpyo" map showing the locations of counties and prefectures.

1121115940100.description: This is a colored manuscript map of Joseon covering the whole country, compiled by Kim Jeong-ho in 1834 and now held by the National Library of Korea. It divides the country into 29 north-south tiers and 22 east-west panels, with each map sheet covering 100 ri north-south and 70 ri east-west. The atlas records population, land area, military strength, tax grain, distances to Hanyang, and historical events at places of note.

1123715940200.description: This is a colored manuscript map of Joseon covering the whole country, compiled by Kim Jeong-ho in 1834 and held by Yeungnam University Museum. It divides the country into 29 north-south tiers and 22 east-west panels, and each sheet covers 100 ri north-south and 70 ri east-west. The atlas records local statistics and historical notes, and this copy is notable for its use of different colors for each county and prefecture.

1121115940300.description: This is a colored manuscript map of Joseon covering the whole country, compiled by Kim Jeong-ho in 1834 and held by the Korea University Central Library. It divides the country into 29 north-south tiers and 22 east-west panels, and each sheet covers 100 ri north-south and 70 ri east-west. The copy has the title Giu and features thinly expressed mountain ranges, black dotted county boundaries, detailed red road lines, and distinct coloring by county.

1121115950100.description: This is a colored manuscript atlas made in 1678 showing horse ranches distributed across the country. It includes a map of presented horses, pictorial maps of ranches by district, and a preface by Heo Mok explaining the compilation. The atlas records ranch locations, numbers of cattle, horses, and herders, ranch areas, and the condition of abandoned ranches.

1122115950200.description: This is a colored manuscript atlas made in 1678 showing horse ranches distributed across the country. It was the fourth compiled version of such ranch maps in the Joseon period and was prepared for use by the Sabeoksi in state horse management. The atlas records the actual conditions of ranches, and its pictorial and geographic content makes it an important historical source.

1123815960000.description: This late-Joseon map atlas contains about 32 kinds of maps across 60 leaves. The front part consists of historical maps, followed by maps of special areas such as the capital, and most of the remainder consists of provincial and county maps. The title is thought to mean a map compiled as a reference for understanding Dongguk Yeojiseungnam, and the compilation date is estimated from place names to be the late 17th century.

1123115970000.description: This atlas contains a pictorial map of the Nokdun-do area near the mouth of the Duman River and surrounding regions, compiled into 20 folded panels that open into a large map about 3 meters long. It includes a table of contents, place-by-place notes on households, population, products, military matters, and distances, and an appended preface by Kim Gwanghun and Sin Seonuk. It is painted in ink and color on high-quality paper and is estimated to have been made between 1885 and 1905.

1123115980000.title_en: Map of Hamgyeong-do, Gyeonggi-do, and Gangwon-do
1123115980000.description: This set of provincial maps depicts Hamgyeong-do, Gyeonggi-do, and Gangwon-do in the late Joseon period. Its content and changing place names closely match the provincial maps associated with Sin Gyeongjun made in 1770, suggesting that it is either the original or a very faithful copy of that series. The surviving maps are notable for their vivid colors and great significance in the history of Korean cartography.

1122115990000.description: This provincial map of Gyeongsang-do from the late Joseon period appears to be based on a 20-ri grid-style county map and is similar to the provincial map associated with Sin Gyeongjun. It shows Daemado Island at the lower right, with mountains, seas, administrative centers, forts, and rivers depicted in detail. It is estimated to date from the late 18th century.

1122216000000.description: This 10-panel folding screen presents a pictorial view of Jinju Fortress in Gyeongsang-do in the 19th century. It shows Jinju Inner Fortress, Outer Fortress, the moat, and major buildings outside the fortress, with the names of important structures carefully written in calligraphy. The work combines historical record, pictorial detail, and map-like representation.
1122216000000.material: Ink and light color on paper

1121116010000.description: This map depicts a Sino-centric world view from the late Joseon period and is believed to have been based on the same source as, or a related version of, the royal world map tradition. It reflects the situation of the early 17th century and is especially notable for clearly identifying Hokkaido, which had long been uncertain in Korean maps. It is a rare surviving Joseon-period world map.

1121116020000.title_en: Comprehensive Map of the Ancient and Contemporary Eight Provinces of Joseon
1121116020000.description: This woodblock-printed national map of Joseon was published in 1673. It combines a general map of the country with historical notes on regions so that the ancient and the contemporary can be viewed together. The map is valuable because both the date and the maker, Kim Suhong, are known with unusual clarity.

1121116030000.description: This is a 15th-century woodblock-printed edition of the ten-volume Śūraṅgama Sūtra translated by Paramiti and annotated by Song-dynasty Jinghuan. The extant set has been bound into two books, includes two frontispiece illustrations, and preserves detailed phonetic glosses throughout the text. It is a complete and well-preserved copy copied in the hand of Seong Dalseaeng.

1123716040000.title_en: Bronze Temple Bell and Bell Stand of Eunhaesa Temple, Yeongcheon
1123716040000.description: This Buddhist ritual bell was made in 1646 and used in a temple to gather the monastic community or to conduct ceremonies. The surface is decorated with lotus, phoenix, and cloud motifs arranged within concentric circles, and the back bears an inscription recording the date of manufacture. The accompanying bell stand was made at nearly the same time and is preserved together with the bell.

1123716050000.title_en: Wooden Seated Sakyamuni Triad, Songnimsa Temple, Chilgok
1123716050000.description: This triad enshrined on the pedestal in the Daeungjeon Hall of Songnimsa Temple consists of Sakyamuni Buddha with Manjusri and Samantabhadra Bodhisattvas. The main Buddha is nearly 3 meters tall, and the work is notable for its balanced proportions, stable form, solemn expression, and powerful drapery lines. An inscription found in the reliquary provides the exact date of production and the names of the patrons and sculptors, showing that it was made in 1657 by eighteen sculptors led by Doyu of the Muyeom lineage.

1123716060000.title_en: Stone Seated Amitabha Triad, Songnimsa Temple, Chilgok
1123716060000.description: This triad enshrined in the Cheonbuljeon Hall of Songnimsa Temple consists of Amitabha Buddha with Avalokitesvara and Ksitigarbha Bodhisattvas. It was carved from a soft stone called buseok, quarried in the Gyeongju area, and its hand gesture, with both hands resting palm-down on the knees, is a notable feature often seen in late Joseon stone statues. An inscription in the reliquary identifies it as a work made in 1655 by Doyu of the Muyeom lineage and is important for the history of 17th-century Buddhist sculpture.

1122216070000.title_en: Reliquary Texts from the Wooden Seated Medicine Buddha, Donghwasa Temple, Daegu
1122216070000.description: These are seven kinds of reliquary texts from the Medicine Buddha in the wooden triad enshrined at Daeungjeon Hall of Donghwasa Temple. They include woodblock-printed Buddhist scriptures and sutras copied in silver ink, ranging from the Goryeo period to the Joseon period; some bear dates from 1417 to 1725. The set is valuable for the study of early Joseon popular Buddhism, bibliography, and the history of printing.

1123716080000.title_en: Yongsan Assembly Banner Painting, Seonseoksa Temple, Seongju
1123716080000.description: This hanging banner painting was made in 1702 by Tak-hwi, Beomhae, Seoljam, and others. At the center is Sakyamuni Buddha, with Manjusri and Samantabhadra Bodhisattvas standing to either side, and Ananda and Kashyapa shown above with joined palms. The painting is important as an early example of a Buddhist image expressing the meaning of "holding up a flower and smiling," and of the Sakyamuni image holding a lotus branch.

1123716090000.title_en: Hanging Banner Painting, Bogyeongsa Temple, Pohang
1123716090000.description: This hanging banner painting was first made in 1708 and repaired in 1725. It depicts a single Buddha figure with a lotus branch on a large vertical banner nearly 10 meters high, with elaborate decoration in red, green, and blue. The work is considered an important example of the banner-painting style that spread in Gyeongsang Province in the late 17th and early 18th centuries.

1122216100000.title_en: Amitabha Assembly Painting, Donghwasa Temple, Daegu
1122216100000.description: This Amitabha painting was produced in 1699 by Uigyun and other painters and is divided into three panels. Unlike the common format, it separates the principal Buddha with the Bodhisattvas in one panel and the Arhats and guardian deities in the other two panels, distinguishing the Buddha's teaching scene from the protective retinue. It is the earliest surviving painting by Uigyun and is important for understanding his early style.

1123716110000.title_en: Vairocana Three-Buddha Assembly Painting, Girimsa Temple, Gyeongju
1123716110000.description: This painting, enshrined as the main hanging scroll behind the Buddha in the Daejeokgwangjeon Hall of Girimsa Temple, places the Vairocana assembly in the center, with the Medicine Buddha assembly on the left and the Amitabha assembly on the right. It combines the three-body and three-period types in an unusual form, and is one of the earliest surviving examples of this kind of Buddhist painting in Korea. It was painted in 1718 by a group of court painters including Cheon-o, Geummyeong, Choehun, Jeokjo, Jisun, Johan, and Imhan.

1123716120000.title_en: Yongshan Assembly Painting and Reliquary Objects, Bongnimsa Temple, Yeongcheon
1123716120000.description: This Yongsan assembly painting was made in 1724 by Quaemin, Chejun, and others, who were disciples of Uigyun. It shows Sakyamuni Buddha at the center surrounded densely by Bodhisattvas, disciples, and guardian deities in a classic crowd-filled composition. The package of reliquary objects also preserves a reliquary pouch and other ritual elements, providing important information about the circumstances of the painting's production.

1123716130000.title_en: Painting of the Assembly of the Three Bodies of Vairocana, Silla, and Nosaṇa Buddhas, Unmunsa Temple, Cheongdo
1123716130000.description: This hanging painting is enshrined in Bogwangmyeongjeon Hall at Unmunsa Temple and was made in 1755 under the leadership of Cheoil by a team of 19 monk-painters. Unlike the three-panel format then common for Three-Buddha paintings, it depicts Vairocana, Śākyamuni, and Nosaṇa Buddhas together on a single large hanging scroll with their attendant figures.

1123716140000.title_en: Mural of the Vulture Peak Assembly, Bongjeongsa Temple, Andong
1123716140000.description: This mural, discovered on January 16, 1997, is now preserved after conservation treatment in the temple museum. It depicts the scene of Śākyamuni expounding the Lotus Sutra on Vulture Peak, with the main Buddha seated at the center surrounded by attendants.

1123716150000.title_en: Wooden Seated Amitabha Buddha, Waryongsa Temple, Gyeongju
1123716150000.description: An inscription found inside the statue records that work began in 1466 and was completed in 1474, with many donors participating in its making. The statue is important as a standard example of early Joseon Buddhist sculpture because its date, place of enshrinement, and sculptors are known from the votive text.

1122116160000.title_en: Set of Three Gyehoe Paintings of the Yean Kim Clan
1122116160000.description: This set consists of three gyehoe paintings made from the 16th century to the early 17th century and thought to have been handed down within the Yean Kim clan. They include paintings commemorating gatherings of officials from the Ministry of Personnel, the Military Office, and the Office of the Inspector-General, and are notable for their scenes, figures, and landscapes.

1122216170000.title_en: Letter of Commendation for Hosaeng Meritorious Retainer, Lee Heon-guk
1122216170000.description: This royal commendation was granted to Lee Heon-guk in 1604 for accompanying King Seonjo and the Crown Prince during the Japanese invasions of Korea. It is an important document for studying the history of the Imjin War and the biography of Lee Heon-guk.

1121116180000.title_en: Imperial Seal of the Emperor, Gojong
1121116180000.description: This imperial seal was made in the Korean Empire period for use by Emperor Gojong in state affairs and secret diplomatic correspondence. It is a royal craft object of historical significance, and the seal case and ink pad are preserved together with it.

1121116180200.description: This jade seal with a dragon-shaped knob was one of the ten seals made when the Korean Empire was proclaimed in 1897. It was used to stamp appointments of officials and documents recording the reasons for conferring honors.

1121116180300.description: This gold seal with a turtle-shaped knob was made in 1876 when the royal seals and stamps were remade. It was used on appointment documents for district commanders and is documented in the Uije of the Bureau of Seals and Stamps.

1123116300000.title_en: Royal Calligraphy by King Sukjong: Seven-Character Poem
1123116300000.description: This is a royal calligraphic work by King Sukjong, a seven-character poem written after he examined the collected works of Yi Gyeong-seok and granted it to Yi's descendants. It is regarded as one of the most credible surviving examples of Sukjong's ink calligraphy. It is written on decorated royal stationery and kept in a box engraved with the title "Sukjong Seongje Bomuk."

1123116310100.title_en: Royal Calligraphy by King Yeongjo: Draft of a Memorial Rite Text for Lady Sukbin Choe's Shrine
1123116310100.description: This is the draft of a memorial text written by King Yeongjo for the birthday rite held at the shrine of his biological mother, Lady Sukbin Choe, on November 6, 1726. The manuscript also includes a short congratulatory text for Lady Jeongbin Yi, a concubine of Yeongjo and the mother of the posthumously honored King Jinjong. It is a rare example of a royal ceremonial manuscript directly written on a blank album leaf.

1123116310200.title_en: Royal Calligraphy by King Yeongjo: Draft of the Epitaph for Lady Sukbin Choe's Soreungmyo
1123116310200.description: This is the draft manuscript King Yeongjo wrote in July 1744 for the epitaph of his mother Lady Sukbin Choe's tomb, Soreungmyo. The draft leaves some personal names and dates blank, and the extant epitaph inscription includes additional and revised wording. It is considered an important example of Yeongjo's later calligraphic style in the course of his efforts to honor his biological mother after ascending the throne.

1123116310300.title_en: Royal Calligraphy by King Yeongjo: Album of Precious Writings at Eupgung
1123116310300.description: This album gathers several royal calligraphic works by King Yeongjo. It includes a draft response dated January 16, 1761, as well as verse drafts and other writings, including "Writing for the Jade Hall," composed in 1770 for the crown prince and officials of the Hall of Worthies. The album is valued for its selected contents, late-Yeongjo dates, and well-preserved late Joseon royal mounting.

1123816320100.title_en: Royal Calligraphy by King Jeongjo: Poem for Jeong Min-si Leaving for Honam
1123816320100.description: This is a handwritten seven-character regulated poem composed and written by King Jeongjo in February 1791 for Jeong Min-si, who was being assigned to Honam. The work is mounted on dark pink silk with painted peony, bat, and cloud motifs, and it bears Jeongjo's seals. It is described as one of the finest surviving examples among Jeongjo's calligraphic works in this format.

1121116320200.title_en: Royal Calligraphy by King Jeongjo: Inscription for Munsangjeongsa
1121116320200.description: This is a royal calligraphic poem written by King Jeongjo in September 1798 for Munsangjeongsa, the study of Jeong Min-si. It is written in running script on decorated paper with gold-painted cloud-and-dragon designs and bears Jeongjo's seals. The work is noted for its large size, excellent condition, and exemplary late-style royal mounting.

1123116320300.title_en: Royal Calligraphy by King Jeongjo: Instruction to the Students Entered for the Chrysanthemum Essay Examination
1123116320300.description: This is a draft instruction that King Jeongjo issued on September 9, 1798, after students at Sungkyunkwan failed to understand the topic he had set for the Chrysanthemum Essay Examination. The text is written on three joined sheets of dak paper, with corrections and deletions visible in the manuscript. It is a rare surviving example of a royal directive to students and has historical and scholarly value.

1123716330000.title_en: Dry-Lacquer Seated Amitabha Buddha, Daedunsa Temple, Gumi
1123716330000.description: This seated Buddha statue was made with dry-lacquer technique and remains largely in its original state except for later repair to the ushnisha. X-ray examination showed that the head and body were made of dry lacquer, while the hands were made of wood. The style reflects late Goryeo features of the 14th century and is important as a rare example of dry-lacquer Buddhist sculpture in the Gyeongbuk area.

1123716340000.title_en: Gilt-bronze Amitabha Buddha Seated Statue and Relics from the Buddha’s Belly, Daeseungsa Temple, Mungyeong
1123716340000.description: This gilt-bronze Amitabha Buddha was found to contain inscribed relics and texts in its body. An inscription recording 1301 was discovered inside the head, and the enclosed materials include printed dharani dated 1292 and 1301, as well as a fragrance pouch with ink writing. Based on these finds, the statue is believed to have been made in the early 14th century.

1123716350000.title_en: Wooden Amitabha Buddha Triad Seated Statue, Nammangsa Temple, Sangju
1123716350000.description: An inscription found inside the statue states that it was made in 1645, during the reign of King Injo, with the participation of many donors and under the supervision of Monk Jihi. The triad represents Amitabha, Avalokiteshvara, and Mahasthamaprapta. Its style reflects the early Joseon Buddhist sculpture tradition associated with the Cheongheo school.

1123716360000.title_en: Stone Seated Shakyamuni Buddha, Buseoksa Temple, Yeongju
1123716360000.description: This stone Buddha is enshrined at Jaindang along with other large seated images of similar size. It was moved from Yaksa-gok east of Buseoksa in 1958. The round face, earth-touching mudra, carved robe hems, and the tall triple-tiered pedestal indicate a ninth-century Unified Silla work.

1123716370000.title_en: Wooden Amitabha Buddha Seated Statue, Yongmunsa Temple, Yecheon
1123716370000.description: Two documents found inside the statue record that it was repaired on April 9, 1515, and list the names of the painters, carpenters, and many donors involved. The work was led by the court painter Lee Yeong-mun. Its form shows the transitional style of the early 16th century, retaining some late 15th-century Joseon features while moving toward flatter treatment.

1123716380000.title_en: Assembly Painting at Vulture Peak, Sudasa Temple, Gumi
1123716380000.description: This hanging Buddhist painting was made in 1731 by four monk-painters, including Doik, and depicts Sakyamuni Buddha surrounded by bodhisattvas, Brahma, Indra, the Ten Disciples, the Four Heavenly Kings, and other retinue figures. The composition, restrained colors, ornate patterns, and balanced figure arrangement are characteristic of early 18th-century Buddhist painting.

1122216390000.title_en: Portrait of State Preceptor Jinul, Donghwasa Temple, Daegu
1122216390000.description: This portrait depicts the Goryeo monk Jinul seated on a high chair, wearing a white monastic robe and holding a monk’s staff while turning his body to the right. Although it was based on the same preliminary design as the 1780 portrait of Jinul at Songgwangsa Temple, its fine brushwork and lighter coloring suggest an earlier date. It is regarded as one of the earliest surviving portraits of Jinul.

1123716400000.title_en: Vulture Peak Assembly Hanging Painting, Gilyongsa Temple, Mungyeong
1123716400000.description: This hanging painting was produced in 1703 by six monk-painters led by Suwon. It shows Sakyamuni standing with his right hand lowered and his retinue arranged in an orderly composition, reflecting the style of hanging paintings then popular in the Sangju and Mungyeong area. It is considered one of the representative Vulture Peak Assembly paintings of the Yeongnam region.

1123716410000.title_en: Painting of the King of Sweet Dew, Nammangsa Temple, Sangju
1123716410000.description: This Sweet Dew painting was made in 1701 by monk-painters including Tak-hwi, and it is one of the earliest-dated examples among 18th-century Sweet Dew paintings. The composition is divided into three tiers, with the Seven Buddhas and bodhisattvas placed above, rituals in the middle, and the souls of the dead below. Its labeled scenes are especially valuable for studying changes in Sweet Dew iconography.

1123116220000.description: This album contains calligraphy by Seo Geojeong, who received a Ming dynasty envoy in early 1476, together with the envoy Qi Shun’s poem and Seo’s prose written for the same occasion. It also includes a later colophon from 1736 describing how the album was mounted after being acquired in 1718. The work preserves a rare surviving example of 15th-century Joseon literati calligraphy and records exchanges between Joseon and Ming China.

1122516230000.description: This album contains Seong Su-chim’s calligraphy of Chinese quatrains by Jia Dao, Du Mu, Li Shangyin, and Ouyang Xiu. The sheets were cut and bound into an album, and the work was donated by descendants of Song Myeong-heum. It is valued as a rare surviving example of Seong’s large-character handwriting and for its soft ink style.

1121116240000.description: This scroll preserves Yang Sa-eon’s cursive-style calligraphy of the first poem in Chu Guangxi’s five poems titled "Road to Luoyang." It was originally an album and was remounted as a hanging scroll in modern times. The work is regarded as a representative example of Yang’s large cursive script and shows the free, vigorous style for which he was famous.

1123216250100.title_en: Cursive Script by Hwang Gi-ro - Poem by Li Qunyu
1123216250100.description: This hanging scroll contains Hwang Gi-ro’s cursive transcription of a five-character regulated verse by Li Qunyu. The piece was formerly kept as an album before being remounted, and the lower part has some loss of characters. It is considered a representative work that shows the large-scale, energetic brushwork characteristic of Hwang’s calligraphy.

1121116250200.title_en: Cursive Script by Hwang Gi-ro - Rhymed Poem
1121116250200.description: This work is Hwang Gi-ro’s cursive calligraphy of a rhymed poem composed in response to another person’s verse. The inscription at the end states that Hwang, as the owner of Maehakjeong in Gogseong, wrote it himself, confirming it as an authentic work. The scroll has been remounted in a frame and remains in good condition.

1123116260000.description: In 1614, Kim Hyeon-seong copied nine poems in running script by Lee Jeung, who had been posthumously honored as Prince Acheon and Uigang-gong. The colophon at the end explains that Kim wrote the text because he was acquainted with Lee Jeung’s son, Lee Gyeong-ham. The work is a representative example of Kim’s mature Songxue-style calligraphy and is well preserved apart from the later mounting.

1123116270000.title_en: Seven-character Poem in the Royal Hand of Queen Inmok
1123116270000.description: This hanging scroll contains a large-character seven-character verse written by Queen Inmok, the secondary queen consort of King Seonjo. The royal handwriting is on paper, and a 1966 colophon by calligrapher Bae Gil-gi is attached. Small devotional writing by the monk Jewoldang is also found within the brushstrokes, and the work is notable as a rare surviving original example of a queen’s large-character calligraphy.

1121116280000.title_en: Seven-character Poem in the Royal Hand of King Hyojong
1121116280000.description: This work is King Hyojong’s royal poem written in running-cursive script on paper, with his note at the end saying it was written for a small spring behind his residence. It was mounted as a hanging scroll and bears an attached inscription reading "Authentic Royal Handwriting of King Hyojong." It is regarded as the largest surviving ink trace among known works by Hyojong and a representative example of his royal handwriting.

1121116180400.description: This jade imperial seal with a turtle-shaped handle was made in 1889 and used on documents appointing officials of the Crown Prince’s Lecture Office. The records in Seungjeongwon ilgi and Boin busin chongsu note its production background, storage place, and documented use. It is also valued as a recovered royal artifact with a clear production date.

1121116180500.description: This imperial seal was ordered in 1882 for use together with the national flag when concluding the Korea–United States Treaty of Amity and Commerce. It was made at Muwiyeong with funding from the Hojo, and it is the only surviving example from the six seals produced at the time. It was used on diplomatic documents, appointment papers, commissions, and laws and edicts issued in the name of the Great King.

1123516180600.description: This seal was made in 1897 as one of the ten imperial seals created after Gojong proclaimed the Korean Empire and ascended as emperor. It was used for documents announcing imperial commands and for appointing high officials. The seal’s making process is recorded in detail in Daerye uigwe and its form, material, and use are also noted in Boin busin chongsu.

1121116180700.description: This seal was made on the leap third month 19th day of 1898 as one of the imperial seals of the Korean Empire. It was used on documents announcing imperial commands, and records in Daerye uigwe and Boin busin chongsu confirm its production and use. The seal was later transferred to the Government-General and then to the National Museum of Korea.

1121116180800.description: This seal was made in 1899 when the Office of the Commander-in-Chief was established to oversee the army and navy. It was used on military appointment documents and later transferred from the U.S. military government to the Government-General and then to the National Museum of Korea. The seal preserves the form of a Korean Empire imperial seal with a dragon-shaped handle and a shallow base.

1123416190000.title_en: Wooden Seated Amitabha Buddha of Gaesimsa Temple, Seosan
1123416190000.description: This wooden Amitabha Buddha statue was repaired in 1280 under the supervision of Seungjaeksa, as recorded on a discovered inscription inside the statue. The repair record shows that the statue itself predates 1280. It is considered an early and highly refined example of late Goryeo wooden Buddhist sculpture.

1123716200000.title_en: Wooden Seated Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva of Bongjeongsa Temple, Andong
1123716200000.description: This wooden Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva statue was originally made around 1199 and later repaired in the mid-14th century and again in the early 1750s. The statue was made by joining multiple pieces of wood and has rock crystal inlaid eyes. Its style preserves an early form of Goryeo sculpture influenced by Southern Song Buddhist images.

1121116210000.title_en: Wooden Seated Vairocana Buddha of Jijangam Hermitage, Seoul
1121116210000.description: This wooden Vairocana Buddha statue was made in 1622 and originally belonged to a triad enshrined in the main hall of Jijangam Hermitage. A dedicatory inscription states that it was produced for a royal Buddhist project sponsored by Queen Jangnyeol to pray for the royal family and deceased relatives. The statue is one of a set of eleven images and is now kept at the National Museum of Korea.

1123716420000.title_en: Bongjeongsa Temple Buddhist Painting of the Vulture Peak Assembly, Andong
1123716420000.description: This hanging scroll is a Vulture Peak Assembly painting made in 1710, during the reign of King Sukjong of Joseon. It follows the general iconography of such paintings in Gyeongsang Province, but the attendant bodhisattvas on both sides are rendered relatively large, and the composition tightly fills the screen around the central Buddha, Śākyamuni.

1123716430000.title_en: Bongjeongsa Temple Amitābha Buddha Preaching Painting, Andong
1123716430000.description: This Buddhist painting, made in 1713 by Doi and others, is considered a model for late Joseon Amitābha preaching paintings. It places Amitābha Buddha at the center with bodhisattvas, Brahmā, Indra, the Ten Great Disciples, pratyekabuddhas, the Four Heavenly Kings, and the Eight Vajra Deities arranged around him.

1123716440000.title_en: Yongmunsa Temple Ten Thousand Buddhas Painting, Yecheon
1123716440000.description: This rare Ten Thousand Buddhas painting was made in 1709 by the monk-painters Domun, Seoljam, Gyesun, and Haeyeong. It shows the orderly arrangement and firm brushwork characteristic of early 18th-century painting, and it is especially notable as an early surviving example of this type.

1123716450000.title_en: Bronze Bell of Gwangheungsa Temple, Andong
1123716450000.description: This bronze bell was made in 1583, during the reign of King Seonjo of Joseon. It is an important example of a transitional bell form from the mid-Joseon period, and its inscription records the makers and the temple where it was cast.

1121116460000.title_en: First Edition of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra of Kāśyapa Goes to the Buddha
1121116460000.description: This is a printed copy from the first carved edition of the Tripiṭaka, printed in the 11th century. It is valuable for comparative study of the first carving and later recarved editions, and it is also important as a rare surviving example recovered from within a Buddhist statue.

1123716470000.description: This woodblock was carved at Buseoksa Temple in June 1219, during the reign of King Gojong of Goryeo. It records auspicious and inauspicious days by month for use in choosing proper dates, and is among the earliest surviving woodblocks with a clearly known date, place, and carver.

1123716480000.title_en: Stupa Monument of Buddhist Master Jajik at Gyeongcheong Seonwon, Myeongbongsa Temple, Yecheon
1123716480000.description: This stone stele was erected in 941 by order of King Taejo of Goryeo to honor the monk Jajik Seonsa, who lived from 882 to 939. Its inscription includes an Idu-language document and valuable information on the early Goryeo administrative writing system, while the monument itself survives in a largely intact state.

1121116490000.title_en: Wooden Seated Amitābha Buddha and Votive Inscription, Gaeunsa Temple, Seoul
1121116490000.description: This wooden seated Amitābha Buddha is regarded as an outstanding late Goryeo Buddhist sculpture for its refined face, balanced form, and strong linear treatment. The image preserves a votive inscription dated 1274, which suggests that the statue was made no later than the early 13th century.

1121116500000.title_en: Buddhist Scriptures from the Inner Reliquary of the Wooden Seated Amitabha Buddha, Gaeunsa Temple, Seoul
1121116500000.description: This group consists of old transcribed and woodblock-printed Buddhist scriptures placed inside the wooden seated Amitabha Buddha statue at Gaeunsa Temple in Seoul. It includes many rare editions of the Avatamsaka Sutra produced between the 9th and 13th centuries, and is important for the study of bibliography, calligraphy, Avatamsaka Sutra editions, and Buddhist history.

1123416510000.title_en: Painting of Śākyamuni Buddha and the Buddhas of the Three Ages, Gapsa Temple, Gongju
1123416510000.description: This Buddhist painting was made by Uigyeom, a leading painter active mainly in Jeolla, Gyeongsang, and Chungcheong provinces in the first half of the 18th century. The work is a large three-panel composition showing preaching scenes, and the reliquary items from 1730 have also been preserved.

1122516520000.description: This rain gauge pedestal was installed when the Naval Command Headquarters was located in Tongyeong. The front is inscribed with the characters "Cheugwudae" and the date "Sinmi second month," so it has been interpreted as having been made in 1811 or 1871; the pedestal stone and base remain preserved.

1123316530000.description: This woodblock-printed book is a reprint of a movable-type edition, and its layout and letter forms suggest that the original type used was the Heungdeoksa type that printed the Jikji. Although the original metal-type edition no longer survives, the book is important evidence for late Goryeo metal-type printing and for the study of Buddhist scholarship.

1123316540000.description: This arithmetic text was printed with the Gyeongoja type cast in the early Joseon period under the handwriting of Prince Anpyeong. It survives in a complete state without missing leaves, and includes a colophon recording the casting of the Gyeongja and Gapin types in King Sejong's reign.

1123316550000.description: This edition of Im Hui-il's commentary on the Laozi was printed with the Gyeongoja type, the second metal type cast in Joseon after the Gyemija type. It survives in complete form without missing or damaged leaves and is valuable for the study of early Joseon metal-type printing and bibliography.

1123716560000.title_en: Three-story Stone Pagoda at Beopsusa Temple Site, Seongju
1123716560000.description: This three-story stone pagoda stands within the Beopsusa Temple site in Seongju, which was founded during King Aejang's reign of Silla. The pagoda is 5.8 meters high and has an upper and lower two-tier base with a three-story body; based on its style, it is thought to date to the 9th century.

1121116570000.title_en: Certificate of Merit for Yi Hyeong as a Wongong Meritorious Subject and Its Case
1121116570000.description: This certificate was issued in November 1411 to Yi Hyeong, who served and supported King Taejong during his years as crown prince. It is the second Wongong merit certificate issued after the one granted to Yi Seong-gye, and is an important source for studying early Joseon merit subjects and certificate formats.

1123116580000.description: This is a woodblock-printed volume of the Goryeo Buddhist canon, believed to have been carved in 1247 and printed around that time during the reign of King Gojong of Goryeo. It is considered the same edition as existing designated volumes 55 and 64, but Volume 42 is the only known surviving copy. The text also shows later Korean annotations in the form of gugyeol marks.

1123116590000.description: This woodblock-printed edition was published in 1583 based on the calligraphy of Seokbong Han Ho. It is regarded as the only surviving first edition and was widely circulated in the Joseon period for beginner-level Chinese character and handwriting study. It is also an important source for research in Korean language, bibliography, and calligraphy history.

1123616600000.title_en: Wooden Seated Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva and Reliquary Objects of Songgwangsa Temple, Suncheon
1123616600000.description: This wooden seated Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva statue at the Avalokitesvara Hall of Songgwangsa Temple was made in 1662. A dedication inscription on a garment and a separate white silk cloth records the donors, including court attendant No Ye-seong, and identifies the sculptors as the mid-17th-century masters Hyehui and Geummun. The associated reliquary objects are also valuable materials for the history of clothing, textiles, dyeing, and folklore.

1123616610000.title_en: Reliquary Buddhist Texts from the Wooden Seated Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva of Songgwangsa Temple, Suncheon
1123616610000.description: These are important Buddhist scriptures found among the reliquary objects enshrined inside the Wooden Seated Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva of Songgwangsa Temple, Suncheon. Among them, the most significant is the printed edition of the Great Floral Adornment Sutra with Commentary, a rare 15th-century impression of the Goryeo Tripitaka. The group was designated separately for preservation as independent reliquary texts.

1123116620000.title_en: Letter Collection of Great Master Dahui Pujue
1123116620000.description: This is a woodblock-printed edition of the letter collection of the Song-dynasty Chan master Dahui Zonggao. It was reprinted in Goryeo in 1387 using the Jingansan Miaoheam edition as the base text, and the volume includes gugyeol annotations and a colophon by Yi Saek. It became widely used as a study text in Joseon and is the only surviving Goryeo edition of this work.

1123116630000.title_en: Commentary on the Awakening of Faith in the Mahayana, Volumes Upper and Lower
1123116630000.description: This woodblock-printed book is a commentary by the Tang-dynasty monk Fazang on the Awakening of Faith in the Mahayana. It is a late Goryeo printing in two volumes and two books, with gugyeol annotations in the text. Because no colophon survives, the exact date is unknown, but the printing style suggests a late-Goryeo edition.

1123616640000.description: This is a manuscript copy of Fengyayi, a 15-volume compilation of annotated poetry edited by Liu Li. Although an inscription indicates printing in 1442, the surviving copy is judged from the textual evidence to have been produced around 1553. It is the only complete surviving copy in Korea and is an important source for poetry, book history, and the study of early Joseon metal type printing.

1121116650000.title_en: Silver-Ink Avatamsaka Sutra on Mulberry Paper, Standard Edition, Volume 4
1121116650000.description: This is a surviving fragmentary volume, Volume 4, from a 14th-century Goryeo manuscript of the 80-volume Avatamsaka Sutra written in silver ink on mulberry paper. The cover is decorated with lotus motifs, and the main text is carefully written in calligraphy. It is one of only a small number of extant silver-ink sutra manuscripts in Korea.

1123716660000.title_en: Wooden Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva Triad, Cheongnyangsa Temple, Bonghwa
1123716660000.description: This wooden triad consists of a Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva image and two attendant figures, totaling three statues. An inscription discovered inside the statue indicates that it was made in 1578. The work is valued as an important example for understanding late Joseon Buddhist sculpture and the stylistic transition after the Imjin War.

1123616670000.description: This handscroll is a transcription by the monk Seosan Daesa Hyujeong (1520–1604) of selected sayings from the Song-dynasty Chan masters Mazu, Baizhang, Huangbo, and Linji. The title on the work varies, but the last inner title, "Jeongseon Sagaryok," is used as its name. Its free and vigorous brushwork is noted for its similarity to the style of Yang Saeon.

1123116680000.description: This calligraphy album contains a cursive-script transcription by the Joseon scholar-calligrapher Lee Jijeong (1588–1650) of a poem set titled "Chweyeong Gugyeol." The colophon shows that it was written in 1647 for a recipient named Hwan-eojeong jujin. The work is valued for its lively and forceful brushwork and as a rare surviving example of his calligraphy.

1123116690000.title_en: Jo Mun-su Piljeok Wi Sim Sujae Seo
1123116690000.description: This album preserves the calligraphy of Jo Mun-su (1590–1647), one of the representative scholar-calligraphers of the early 17th century. It includes passages written in regular script, running script, and semi-cursive script, and the colophon states that it was written in 1647 for a man named Sim, a student. The work is notable for its excellent quality, clear date, and well-preserved condition.

1121116700000.description: This bound album contains poetry written by Jo Sok (1595–1668) in July 1646 while he was serving as magistrate of Byeokseong. The texts are written in varying sizes of cursive script, and the colophon records that he wrote it during his leisure time in Byeokseong. It is notable as a single-volume work that clearly shows his characteristic style.

1121116710000.description: This work is a large-format cursive-script rendering by Yun Sun-geo (1596–1668) of the poem "Muigugokga." It survives as a ten-panel folding screen and is regarded as one of his representative works. Its broad composition and rapid brushwork are considered important in the development of 17th-century large-format cursive script.

1123116720100.description: This album contains calligraphy by Song Jun-gil (1606–1672), including a copy of Zhu Xi's "Hagojjae Myeong" and a transcription of his father-in-law Jeong Gyeong-se's "Ugok Japyeong 20jeol." The first part shows a neat running script influenced by Toegye Yi Hwang, while the second part shows Song's characteristic running-cursive style. It is dated after 1666 and represents his later calligraphic style.

1122516720200.title_en: Song Jun-gil Haengcho Seojeung Song Byeong-ha
1122516720200.description: This handscroll is a large-format running-cursive calligraphy work by Song Jun-gil (1606–1672), written as a gift for his grandson Song Byeong-ha. The text is a seven-character regulated verse by Yang Shi of the Song dynasty, and the colophon dates it to the spring of 1669. It is the largest surviving piece among Song Jun-gil's works and is well preserved.

1123116800000.description: This album contains seven-character regulated verses written in running-cursive script by Pyoam Gaksehuang (1713–1791) in the winter of 1790. The colophon includes a record about jeongcheongji, a paper produced in southern Korea, providing an important late Joseon reference on paper production. It is one of the few extant works by Gaksehuang with a clearly documented date and provenance.

1123116810000.title_en: Lee Hanjin Seal-and-Clerical Script Calligraphy Album, Gyeongsan Jeon Palssangjeolcheop
1123116810000.description: This album contains several five-character regulated verses written in seal script and clerical script by Gyeongsan Lee Hanjin (1732–1796?) in the winter of 1790, when he was 59. The seal script follows the thin, even-stroked style associated with Li Yangbing, while the clerical script combines features of famous Eastern Han stele models such as the Lique Stele and Cao Quan Stele. It is regarded as one of the best preserved examples showing Lee Hanjin’s mature calligraphic style.

1123816820000.title_en: Yu Hanji Clerical Script Calligraphy Album, Giwoncheop
1123816820000.description: This album contains seven-, five-, and four-character antithetical verses written in a variety of clerical-script styles by Yu Hanji (1760–1834) in the first half of the 19th century. It also includes seal-script writing in an ancient-script manner, and displays a wide range of models from Eastern Han clerical inscriptions such as the Lique Stele, Yiying Stele, Shichen Stele, Zhang Qian Stele, Cao Quan Stele, and Hesheng Stele. The work shows that Yu Hanji had studied Han clerical script broadly and deeply.

1121116830100.title_en: Jeong Yagyong Running-cursive Calligraphy Album, Dasan Sageongcheop
1121116830100.description: This album contains seven-character regulated verses praising the four scenery elements around Dasan Chodang—the tea stove, medicinal spring, standing stone, and artificial rock garden—written by Jeong Yagyong (1762–1836) during his exile in Gangjin. The album preserves calligraphy from after his Gangjin period and reflects the distinctive style he developed in exile. The title slip is written in clerical script.

1123116830200.description: This three-volume album contains writings made by Jeong Yagyong in 1810 after his wife sent him several worn pieces of skirt fabric while he was exiled in Gangjin. He cut the fabric and wrote moralizing passages for his two sons, and the surviving volumes include prefaces dated July and September 1810. The album also preserves his characteristic post-exile running-cursive style, and one volume includes seal script and clerical script rarely found in his other works.

1121116840000.title_en: Shin Wi Regular Script Thousand Character Classic
1121116840000.description: This album contains the Thousand Character Classic written by Ziha Shin Wi (1769–1845) in 1837, when he was 69. It is one of the few extant examples of his calligraphy in this form, and shows the mature style of his late years. The script is based on Ouyang Xun, with a softness and elegance comparable to the style of Wong Fanggang.

1121116850100.title_en: Kim Jeonghui Regular Script Inscription, Moksogeosa Jachan
1121116850100.description: This work is a self-praise text for Kim Yukgeun written in regular script by Chusa Kim Jeonghui (1786–1856). It is dated to around 1837–1840 based on Kim Yukgeun’s late-life aphasia and year of death. The calligraphy combines the structural basis of Ouyang Xun with the influence of Chu Suiliang and Yan Zhenqing.

1121116850200.title_en: Kim Jeonghui Clerical Script Pair of Hanging Scrolls, Hogo Yeongyeong
1121116850200.description: This pair of hanging scrolls expresses Kim Jeonghui’s long-standing interest in metal and stone inscriptions and classical texts. The calligraphy presents the clerical-script view he advocated, using an unconventional structure and dry, rough brushwork to realize an archaic simplicity. It is considered one of the representative examples of his paired works in clerical script.

1123116730000.title_en: Autograph Album by Yi Hajin, Cheongeummuljeon
1123116730000.description: This autograph album preserves calligraphic works by Yi Hajin (1619–?), a Joseon scholar-official and noted calligrapher. It contains ten volumes of writings in various script styles, including inscriptions, large-character works, poems, classical passages, and anecdotes about admired objects and fragrant plants. The album also bears several of Yi Hajin’s seals.

1123116740000.title_en: Autograph Album of Seogye Yi Setaeng, Seogye Yumul
1123116740000.description: This three-volume album contains autograph writings by Seogye Park Sedang (1629–1703) given to his disciple Yi Jeongsin. The first volume includes self-composed poems and writings on nature, while the second and third volumes mostly contain letters sent to Yi Jeongsin, with a few addressed to Nam Gu-man and Park Tae-bo. Most of the texts were written between 1679 and 1702 and were not included in Park Sedang’s collected works.

1123116750000.title_en: Autograph Album by Park Taeyu, Baekseok Yumulcheop
1123116750000.description: This single-volume album contains calligraphic works by Park Taeyu (1648–1686) in a variety of scripts and sizes, including regular, semi-cursive, cursive, clerical, and large-character writing. The pieces show influences from Yan Zhenqing and from the calligraphic style associated with Park’s father, Park Sedang, as well as references to Wang Xizhi and Huaisu. It appears to have been written as a model for someone’s study of calligraphy.

1121116760000.title_en: Poems in Ancient Scripts by Yun Sun
1121116760000.description: This hanging scroll was written by the master calligrapher Baekha Yun Sun in March 1737, when he was 58 years old. It is written in a range of regular, semi-cursive, and cursive scripts and is regarded as representative of his later calligraphic style. The scroll is accompanied by four colophons by later figures, which comment on the strengths and limitations of Yun Sun’s calligraphy.

1121116770100.title_en: Calligraphic Inscription in Running Script by Yi Gwangsa
1121116770100.description: This calligraphic inscription was written by the eighteenth-century calligrapher Won-gyo Yi Gwangsa in the summer of 1746, when he was 42 years old. It is based on the running style of Wang Xizhi but also shows Yi Gwangsa’s distinctive personal brushwork. Aside from minor loss to the first two characters, the work is in good condition and includes a later viewing note by Unwon.

1121116770200.title_en: Autograph Album by Yi Gwangsa, Wongyo Beopcheop
1121116770200.description: This forty-folio album contains calligraphic works by Yi Gwangsa, also known as Wongyo, in seal script, clerical script, regular script, running script, and cursive script. It was written on silk in different colors, using ink and gold pigment, and includes phonetic glosses for the seal-script passages. The album is a representative example of Yi Gwangsa’s autograph album format and calligraphic theory.

1121116780000.title_en: Clerical Script Inscription of Gyeongjae Jam by Song Munheum
1121116780000.description: In the summer of 1751, Song Munheum wrote Zhu Xi’s "Gyeongjae Jam" for Yeoil at his brother Song Myeongheum’s residence, using clerical script. The text is arranged in 44 lines, with four characters per line in its present mounted form, and the underlying paper shows that it was originally written as an eight-character banner format. The calligraphy is based on the Cao Quan Stele and is noted for its smooth and elegant brushwork.

1121116790000.title_en: Seal Script Album of Wonryeongpil by Yi In-sang
1121116790000.description: These three volumes preserve seal-script writings by Nongho-gwan Yi In-sang on Chinese and Korean poems and prose. The album includes a variety of seal-script styles, from forceful square forms to slender jade-stick seal script and more expressive dry-brush writing. It was written on paper and is said to be one of the most substantial surviving collections of Yi In-sang’s calligraphy.

1123816860000.title_en: Wooden Seated Amitabha Buddha of Wolmyeongam Hermitage, Jinju
1123816860000.description: This wooden seated Amitabha Buddha was made in 1612 by the sculptor Hyunjin, who led four sculptor-monks including Hakmun, Myeongeun, Uineung, and Taehun. The votive inscription indicates that it was likely created at the same time as the seated Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva at Sanggaldae. It is considered an important work for studying the stylistic changes in Hyunjin’s Buddhist sculptures in the first half of the 17th century.

1123816870000.title_en: Wooden Seated Sakyamuni Buddha Triad of Eungseoksa Temple, Jinju
1123816870000.description: This triad, enshrined in the Daeungjeon Hall of Eungseoksa Temple, consists of Sakyamuni Buddha in the center with Bhaisajyaguru Buddha and Amitabha Buddha on either side. According to the inscription, the images were dedicated in 1643 after the temple was rebuilt following a fire, and sculptor-monks such as Cheongheon, Beophyeon, and Wontaek participated in their production. The main Buddha is made slightly larger than the attendants, emphasizing its central role.

1123816880000.title_en: Wooden Seated Sakyamuni Buddha Triad of Cheonggoksa Temple, Jinju
1123816880000.description: This wooden triad in the Daeungjeon Hall of Cheonggoksa Temple consists of Sakyamuni Buddha in the center, with Manjusri Bodhisattva on the left and Samantabhadra Bodhisattva on the right. No contemporary record of its production survives, but a 1750 document records the image as having been made in the year of Eulmyo, which points to 1615. The main image is a large-scale work with a stable composition and is considered an important example for studying Hyunjin’s style.

1123816890000.title_en: Wooden Seated Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva Triad and Ten Kings, Cheonggoksa Temple, Jinju
1123816890000.description: This set of 21 wooden figures was dedicated in 1657 for the Eopgyeongjeon Hall of Cheonggoksa Temple. It includes a seated Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva triad with Domyeong Venerable and Mudok Ghost King, together with the Ten Kings, ghost kings, judges, and guardian figures. The figures are notable for their distinctive, unified style and high sculptural quality.

1123816900000.title_en: Wooden Seated Amitabha Buddha of Simwusa Temple, Geochang
1123816900000.description: This wooden seated Amitabha Buddha was made in 1640 by the sculptor-monks Cheongheo and Beophyeon. According to the votive inscription, it had originally been enshrined at Yeonsusa Temple in Deogyusan. The image is characterized by a dignified face, a stable seated posture, and drapery treatment typical of Cheongheo’s work.

1123816910000.title_en: Wooden Seated Amitabha Buddha of Beopinsa Temple, Hamyang
1123816910000.description: This wooden seated Amitabha Buddha was made in 1657 by Yeonggyu and Jonung. It is enshrined in the Geuknakbojeon Hall and is a well-balanced image with a long torso, broad shoulders, and a stable seated posture. The votive inscription and reliquary materials were once identified, and the work is regarded as a comparatively refined example of mid-17th-century Buddhist sculpture.

1123816920000.title_en: Pensive Sakyamuni Buddha in the Assembly of Vulture Peak, Anjeongsa Temple, Tongyeong
1123816920000.description: This large hanging Buddhist painting was produced in 1702 by the chief monk painter Gwangheum with Hongteuk and Gakhwan, and was later repaired in 1934 by Gyehong. It depicts Sakyamuni Buddha in the center with Manjusri and Samantabhadra, and includes Dabo Buddha, Amitabha Buddha, Ananda, and Kashyapa. The composition follows a form commonly used in late Joseon hanging paintings of the Vulture Peak assembly.

1123816930000.title_en: Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva Painting and Ten Kings Paintings, Okcheonsa Temple, Goseong
1123816930000.description: This set of Buddhist paintings was made in 1744 under the leadership of the monk painter Hyoan with 11 painters participating. It originally consisted of one Ksitigarbha-and-Ten Kings painting and eight Ten Kings paintings, and the missing Second King painting was recovered from France in 2016 and returned to the temple. The set represents a standard 18th-century format for underworld paintings.

1123816940000.title_en: Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva Painting of Unheungsa Temple, Goseong
1123816940000.description: This hanging painting was made in 1730, when the chief monk-painter Uigyeom worked with Haengjong and Chaein to produce it together with other Buddhist paintings for Unheungsa Temple. It depicts Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva seated on a rocky outcrop, with Sudhana, a dragon king and dragon princess, a vase, a blue bird, and blue bamboo arranged around the figure.

1123816950000.title_en: Suspended Buddhist Banner Painting of Ssanggyesa Temple, Hadong
1123816950000.description: This large hanging banner was made in 1799, although the original production record no longer survives and the date is known from a later repair inscription. It presents only a standing, bodhisattva-like Buddha holding a lotus flower with both hands, wearing a jeweled crown and ornate ornaments.

1123816960000.title_en: Gamrowangdo (Sweet Dew Painting) of Ssanggyesa Temple, Hadong
1123816960000.description: This Buddhist painting was produced in 1728 by Myeongjeong, Choiu, Wonmin, Cheoyeong, Sinyeong, and Yeongho. It is organized into an upper and lower section, with buddhas and bodhisattvas descending through clouds above and ritual scenes, hungry ghosts, and the dead arranged densely below.

1123816970000.title_en: Gamrowangdo (Sweet Dew Painting) of Haeinsa Temple, Hapcheon
1123816970000.description: This painting was made in 1723 by Singam, Sinu, and Deukchong. It retains many features of earlier Joseon-period Gamro paintings, with the upper section emphasizing the descent of the Seven Buddhas and Amitabha Triad, and the lower sections showing ritual scenes and various forms of death.

1123816980000.title_en: Bronze Bell of Samseonam Hermitage, Jinju
1123816980000.description: This bronze bell was found in 1951 while a farmer was opening farmland in Saksil village, Sogok-myeon, Jinju, and is now enshrined at Daewoongjeon Hall of Samseonam Hermitage. It is a Goryeo-period bell with a dragon-shaped knob, four flanged panels, and simple decoration, and it is especially valuable because its place of discovery is known.

1123816990000.title_en: Bronze Bell of Anjeongsa Temple, Tongyeong
1123816990000.description: This large bronze bell was originally cast in 1580 for Yongcheonsa Temple in Damyang and later moved to Anjeongsa Temple. The inscription records the date, the temple, and the artisans involved, and the bell is decorated with lotus panels, four sound-pads, and Buddhist inscriptions.

1123817000000.title_en: Bronze Bell of Gyeongamsa Temple, Geochang
1123817000000.description: This bell was cast in 1630 as a bell for Gyeonamsa Temple and is now enshrined in the main hall of Gojeonsa Temple. Its body includes rare reliefs of a seated Buddha and a pagoda between the sound-pads, along with lotus, Sanskrit characters, and a dedicatory inscription that records the temple history and the casting process.

1123817010000.title_en: Bronze Bell of Ssanggyesa Temple, Hadong
1123817010000.description: This large bronze bell is displayed at the Ssanggyesa Temple Sacred Relics Museum and is dated only by the cyclical year sinsa, which indicates 1641. It is decorated with four sound-pads, circular bands of Sanskrit inscriptions, bodhisattva figures, and memorial tablets, and is regarded as an important early Joseon bell.

1122217020000.description: This is a unique combined edition of the literary collection of Jeong Do-jeon (1337–1398), a scholar-official of the late Goryeo and early Joseon periods. It was compiled from the 1465 Andong edition and the 1487 Gangneung edition, and includes a preface by Gwon Geun. Later editions are described in the record, including a 1791 re-edited printing from Daegu.

1122217030000.title_en: Collected Poems of Meng Haoran with Critical Notes by Xu Xi
1122217030000.description: This is a Joseon-period woodblock-printed edition of the poetry collection of Meng Haoran, a representative poet of the High Tang period. It was printed in Namwon in 1445 from a source edition annotated by Liu Chenweng (Xu Xi) and corrected by Cheng Peng. The record notes the number of poems by section and states that it was independently engraved from a manuscript prepared for carving.

1122217040000.title_en: Newly Printed and Detailed Methods of Calculation
1122217040000.description: This is an early Joseon movable-type edition of a major arithmetic textbook, printed with Eulhaeja metal type in the first half of the 16th century. The work is based on a 1373 Chinese edition and survives as a complete 2-volume, 1-book copy. It was an important textbook for the examination of specialists in mathematics in Joseon.
1122217040000.material: Metal movable type printed book on paper

1122217050000.title_en: Early Printed Avadāna Mahāvibhāṣā Śāstra, Volume 38
1122217050000.description: This is a woodblock-printed volume from the early Tripiṭaka Koreana, produced in the 11th or 12th century. The volume is relatively intact from beginning to end, though the printing quality is not high. It is described as the only publicly known surviving Korean complete copy of this volume.

1122217060000.title_en: Early Printed Collection of the Great Vehicle Characteristics Treatise, Volume 2
1122217060000.description: This is a manuscript-like printed Buddhist text from the early Tripiṭaka Koreana, with the lower volume surviving as a single scroll. The text explains key doctrines of Mahayana Buddhism and includes later corrected readings when compared with a re-engraved version. It is described as the only publicly known Korean copy and is in relatively good condition.

1122217070000.title_en: Commentary on the Flower Garland Sutra
1122217070000.description: This is a surviving volume from the Korean importation of a Song-dynasty woodblock edition of a commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sutra. The volume is 41 fascicles in extent and is described as being in relatively good condition, with paper, format, and printing features noted in detail. The record states that the woodblocks were later transferred to Japan and that the edition is an important witness to the transmission of Buddhist texts among China, Korea, and Japan.

1123117080000.title_en: Commentary on the Heart Sutra with Correct Exegesis (Eonhae)
1123117080000.description: This is a Joseon-period vernacular Buddhist text printed in 1495 from woodblocks first carved in 1464 at the Gangyeong Dogam by royal command. It is based on Fayang's abridged commentary and Zhongxi's 'Correct Exegesis,' and the Korean translation is printed alongside the Chinese text. Compared with an earlier preserved copy, this edition omits some prefatory material and includes a later preface by Hakjo.

1123117090000.description: This pavilion was built in 1794 as the northeast corner turret of Hwaseong Fortress during the reign of King Jeongjo. Although intended for wartime use, it was designed with both stone and wood and also functions as a pavilion, and it was later repaired in 1848 and several times after the Japanese colonial period. The record emphasizes its unusual plan and roof form and its balance of military purpose and landscape composition.

1123117420000.title_en: Jongjagak Hall of Sungneung Royal Tomb, Guri Donggureung
1123117420000.description: This jongjagak hall is the ritual building for Sungneung, the tomb of King Hyeonjong and Queen Myeongseong of Joseon, and was built in 1674. It is the only surviving 8-bay jongjagak among the Joseon royal tombs and preserves the hipped-and-gabled roof form. It is considered an important example for studying the royal tomb system of the 17th century.

1123117430000.title_en: Jongjagak Hall of Mokneung Royal Tomb, Guri Donggureung
1123117430000.description: This jongjagak hall serves the tomb complex of King Seonjo, Queen Uiin, and Queen Inmok at Mokneung in Guri Donggureung. The present building was relocated in 1630 and combined from earlier tomb facilities, and it is the only surviving doweled-bracket style jongjagak among Joseon royal tombs. It preserves the appearance of the 1630 relocation and is valued for its architectural and historical significance.

1123717440000.title_en: Daeungjeon Hall of Bulguksa Temple, Gyeongju
1123717440000.description: Daeungjeon is the main Buddha hall of Bulguksa Temple in Gyeongju, a temple first founded in the Silla period and rebuilt several times during Joseon after being destroyed in the Imjin War. The present hall is a one-story building with a hipped-and-gabled roof and late Joseon multi-bracket construction. It stands in front of Dabotap Pagoda to the east and Seokgatap Pagoda to the west.

1123717450000.title_en: Stone Retaining Walls of Bulguksa Temple, Gyeongju
1123717450000.description: These are the structured stone retaining walls at the Daeungjeon and Geuknakjeon areas of Bulguksa Temple. They include the walls connected with Cheongungyo and Baegungyo, as well as the lower walls around Jahamun and Beomyeongnu, and show a distinctive frame-like masonry technique using dressed stone members and natural stone infill. The walls are an important example of Silla stone architecture from the 8th century.

1123417460000.title_en: Lecture Hall of Nogang Seowon, Nonsan
1123417460000.description: This lecture hall belongs to Nogang Seowon, a Joseon-period seowon established in 1675 to honor Yun Hwang and educate local scholars. The hall is a large 5-bay by 3-bay structure with a front veranda and a central main hall flanked by rooms, arranged on a straight axis with the academy's gates and shrine. It is notable for preserving an older and more orderly seowon layout.

1123817470000.title_en: Silver Gilt Bronze Amitabha Triad and Buddhist Relics, Tongdosa Temple, Yangsan
1123817470000.description: This Amitabha triad was made in 1450, according to an inscription found inside the statue. The set consists of an Amitabha Buddha seated in the center with Avalokiteshvara and Mahasthamaprapta standing as attendants, along with 48 relic items from the inner cache. The work is important for the study of late Goryeo to early Joseon Buddhist sculpture and its foreign-influenced style.

1123717480000.title_en: Wooden Seated Amitabha Buddha and Buddhist Relics, Bongamsa Temple, Mungyeong
1123717480000.description: This wooden seated Amitabha Buddha was made in 1586 by the sculptors Naun and Beopjeong, as recorded in the dedication inscription found inside the statue. The figure is about 51.5 cm high and is accompanied by 26 inner-cache relic items in 14 groups. It is an important dated example for the study of late 16th-century Joseon Buddhist sculpture and sculptors.

1123217490000.title_en: Wooden Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva Triad, Sinheungsa Temple, Sokcho
1123217490000.description: This wooden Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva triad was made in 1651, a date and production details confirmed by a dedicatory text found inside the statues. The record distinguishes the figures responsible for carving and for finishing work such as gilding and painting, making it an important source for understanding Buddhist sculpture production in the mid-17th century. The triad is also valued as a representative work of the sculptor Muyeom and his workshop tradition.

1123617260000.title_en: Wooden Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva Triad and the Ten Kings, Hwasun Ssangbongsa Temple
1123617260000.description: This set consists of 21 wooden Buddhist images, including the seated Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva, attendants, the Ten Kings, and related guardian figures. An inscription found in the set shows that it was made around 1667 by the sculptor monk Unhye and his group. The figures preserve the sculptural style of Unhye and old polychrome decorative patterns, making them important for the study of late Joseon painted Buddhist sculpture.

1123717270000.title_en: Daeseongjeon Hall of Gyeongju Hyanggyo Confucian School
1123717270000.description: Gyeongju Hyanggyo is a large hyanggyo in Gyeongsangbuk-do, and its layout is considered a standard example along with Naju Hyanggyo. Daeseongjeon Hall has a clear repair history, and records found in the building confirm its rebuilding date and the craftsmen who took part. The hall retains old construction techniques in its bracket sets, doors and windows, and timber frame.

1123117280000.description: This is a portrait of Heo Jeon (1797–1886), a late Joseon scholar-official whose courtesy name was Iro and pen name was Seongjae. According to the family tradition, the portrait was painted by royal command while he was alive. It was later moved from the family collection and is now preserved separately.

1123817290000.title_en: Wooden Seated Vairocana Buddha Triad, Seongjusa Temple, Changwon
1123817290000.description: This set is a 17th-century wooden triad centered on Sakyamuni Buddha, with Bhaiṣajyaguru Buddha and Amitābha Buddha seated on the left and right. An inscription records that the work began in spring 1655 and was completed and consecrated in autumn that year. It is an important early work for studying the sculptor monk Nokwon and the development of mid-17th-century Buddhist sculpture.

1123817300000.title_en: Wooden Seated Sakyamuni Buddha Triad and Pedestal, Gwanryongsa Temple, Changnyeong
1123817300000.description: This wooden triad consists of Sakyamuni Buddha in the center, flanked by Bhaiṣajyaguru Buddha and Amitābha Buddha. An inscription under the main Buddha's pedestal shows that the images were started in the tenth month of 1629 and completed in the fifth month of 1630. Eight sculptor monks took part, including Hyeonjin, and the work is important for understanding early 17th-century Buddhist sculpture and sculptor lineages.

1123817310000.description: This Gamnoroeui painting was made in Geumdaeam in Hamyang and was originally intended to be enshrined at An'gukam. Its composition follows the usual 18th-century format, with the Seven Buddhas, the guide bodhisattva, Ksitigarbha, the ritual platform, hungry ghosts, ritual monks, and scenes of various kinds of death. According to the inscription, it was made in 1726 by three painters, Chaein, Ilmin, and Taehyeon.

1123817320000.description: According to the inscription, this Gamnoroeui painting was produced in 1729 by Seongjeung as both examiner and chief painter, together with other painters including Ssinjeong, Hanyeong, Inhaeng, Seogwan, and Gukyeong. Unlike many late Joseon Gamnoroeui paintings, it omits the ritual altar and ritual-action scene, and it places a building symbolizing the Pure Land in the upper right. The painting is thought to have been modeled on the now-lost 1724 painting formerly kept at Jikjisa Temple.

1122117330000.title_en: Bronze Temple Bell, Gukcheongsa Temple, Busan
1122117330000.description: This bronze temple bell was made in 1666 and is a rare surviving Joseon-period example from the 17th century. It has an inscription on the back naming the temple, the donors, and the artisans, including the master metalworker Taeung. The bell is important for studying Joseon-period bell casting techniques and the artisan community of the late 17th century.

1123817340000.title_en: Bronze Temple Gong of Naewonsa Temple, Yangsan
1123817340000.description: This temple gong is a bronze ritual instrument used in Buddhist temples to announce meals or summon people, rather than for the major morning and evening services used with temple bells. The front is decorated with concentric bands, a lotus-flower motif, and cloud designs, and the side bears an inscription recording its casting in 1091 at Geuminsa Temple.

1123817350000.title_en: Bronze Incense Burner with Silver Inlay of Tongdosa Temple, Yangsan
1123817350000.description: This incense burner is a gobae-shaped incense burner with a flaring body and trumpet-shaped stand, a form characteristic of Goryeo-period ritual utensils. Its surface is richly decorated with silver-inlaid arabesque, lotus, and Sanskrit designs, and the lower edge bears an inscription naming the donor and indicating its offering to Tongdosa Temple.

1121117360000.description: This is volume 53 of the 60-volume Jin translation of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, a fundamental scripture of the Huayan school of Buddhism. It is a Goryeo woodblock-printed temple edition on one scroll, with the text of chapter 34, "Entering the Realm of Reality, Part 10."

1123817370000.description: This Buddhist book was engraved and printed in August 1497 at Hyeonam Hermitage on Yongchulsan in Jinan, Jeolla-do. It explains the six realms of rebirth and the ten realms, and the volume includes publishing records, donor names, and the names of the engravers.

1121117380000.description: This bridge, also called Jeoban Bridge, was used as an important route connecting Hanyang, the Joseon capital, with the southeastern regions. It was begun in 1420 and completed in 1483, and the structure originally had 64 stone piers shaped to reduce the resistance of flowing water.

1123817390000.title_en: Stone Ice Storage of Yeongsan, Changnyeong
1123817390000.description: This stone ice storage is a Joseon-period ice house built of granite. It has a high entrance and a rounded exterior that slopes downward toward the rear, with a square interior built of roughly dressed large stones.

1121117400000.description: This observatory platform was installed on the site of Gwancheongam, the Joseon government office in charge of astronomy, meteorology, and calendrical work. Built in 1434, it was used for observing the sky and is a valuable source for the history of astronomical observation in Korea.

1123117410000.title_en: Jeongjagak Hall of Geonwonneung Royal Tomb, Guri
1123117410000.description: This T-shaped memorial hall stands in front of Geonwonneung, the tomb of King Taejo, founder of the Joseon dynasty. The original hall was built in 1408, and records show repeated repairs during the Joseon period, including a major renovation in 1764 that is reflected in its current appearance.

1123117100000.description: This defensive structure stands beside Hwaseomun Gate in Hwaseong Fortress and was built in 1796, the 20th year of King Jeongjo's reign. It projects from the northwestern fortress wall in three stories, with the lower chiseong built of squared stone and the upper levels constructed with brick and equipped with gun holes, arrow slits, and a pavilion roof.

1123817110000.title_en: Murals of Yeongsanjeon Hall, Tongdosa Temple, Yangsan
1123817110000.description: These murals are painted throughout the interior and exterior walls of Yeongsanjeon Hall at Tongdosa Temple, with 52 surviving wall surfaces inside and 17 on the exterior. Most of the interior paintings depict scenes from the "Illustrated Account of the Origins and Transformations of Sakyamuni" and the "Lotus Sutra" "Appearance of the Jeweled Stupa" chapter, and they are thought to have been made during the hall's reconstruction in 1714-1716. The murals are considered important examples of late Joseon temple wall painting.

1123817120000.description: This is a collection of poetic criticism compiled and published by Seo Geo-jeong. It contains prefaces by Gang Hui-maeng and Kim Su-on and postfaces by Choe Suk-jeong and Yang Seong-ji, and it was first printed in Miryang in 1477.

1123817130000.title_en: Commentary on the Awakening of Faith in the Mahayana
1123817130000.description: This is a Buddhist text printed with metal type in 1457 during the Joseon period. It is a commentary on the "Awakening of Faith in the Mahayana" and survives as a single extant copy in three volumes and one book, although part of the first volume is missing.

1123317140000.title_en: Brahmajala Sutra of the Bodhisattva Precepts in Gold Ink on White Paper
1123317140000.description: This handwritten Buddhist manuscript was copied in gold ink on white paper in 1364, during the Goryeo period. It contains the text of the Brahmajala Sutra of the Bodhisattva Precepts, a frontispiece illustration, a record of its production, and a record of its later enshrinement in Japan.

1123617150000.title_en: Wooden Seated Sakyamuni Triad of Seodongsa Temple, Haenam
1123617150000.description: This group of three wooden seated Buddha statues was made in 1651 and later repaired and repainted in 1804. The central Sakyamuni Buddha is flanked by Yaksa Buddha on the left and Amitabha Buddha on the right, forming a triad arrangement typical of late Joseon Buddhist sculpture.

1122317160000.description: This surviving volume is an edition of a major Chinese materia medica work printed with metal movable type in the Joseon period. The copy preserves volume 17 of the 30-volume work and is believed to have been printed around 1577 based on internal records.

1123717170000.description: This woodblock-printed book was first compiled and published in 1434 under King Sejong's order. It presents biographies, poems, and praises of exemplary filial sons, loyal subjects, and chaste women, and this item is the filial-son volume.

1123517180000.title_en: Clay Seated Sakyamuni Buddha Triad and Buddhist Relics, Dongguksa Temple, Gunsan
1123517180000.description: This clay triad consists of Sakyamuni Buddha with his two principal disciples, Kasyapa and Ananda. It is the only large-scale clay Sakyamuni Buddha triad over 150 cm high that includes Kasyapa and Ananda as attendant figures. The associated relic deposits are considered important materials for studying the construction techniques, contents, and materials of the reliquary tube.

1123417190000.title_en: Wooden Seated Sakyamuni Buddha Triad and Buddhist Relics, Donghaksa Temple, Gongju
1123417190000.description: The construction votive text found in the relic deposits records the exact date of production as 1606, along with the makers and other participants. This makes the work an important reference for the study of Buddhist sculpture in the mid to late Joseon period. The iconography accurately shows the Sakyamuni Buddha triad form that became popular after the Japanese invasions of Korea, and the inscription identifies the image names precisely.

1123417200000.title_en: Buddhist Texts from the Buddhist Relics of the Wooden Seated Sakyamuni Buddha Triad, Donghaksa Temple, Gongju
1123417200000.description: These Buddhist texts were found in the relic deposits of the Wooden Seated Sakyamuni Buddha Triad enshrined in the Daeungjeon Hall of Donghaksa Temple. All of them are printed editions produced before the Japanese invasions of Korea, and seven important titles in eight volumes were separately designated as heritage items. The set includes rare, valuable, and complete editions such as the Wonkak sutra, the Suramgama sutra vernacular translation, and the Lotus Sutra vernacular translation.

1363217210000.title_en: Wooden Seated Amitabha Buddha Triad, Sinheungsa Temple, Sokcho
1363217210000.description: The construction votive text found in the relic deposits identifies the exact date of production as 1651, along with the maker and other participants. This makes the triad an important reference for the study of Buddhist sculpture in the mid-17th century. The work shows balanced proportions and a restrained, refined form, reflecting the sculptural skill of the maker Muyeom.

1123617220000.description: This group-portrait painting follows the standard form of late 16th-century gyehoe paintings, with a title inscription, painting, poems, and a list of participants. The date of production, August 1591, can be confirmed from the inscription and the recorded career dates of the people listed. It is also important because the original owner and transmission history are known, and the mounting appears to preserve its original state.

1123217230000.title_en: Relic Stupa and Stele of Hae-su Gwaneum Gongjung Saritap, Naksansa Temple, Yangyang, and Relics
1123217230000.description: The relic stupa was built in 1692, making it an important benchmark for dating similar late Joseon stone monuments. It is a rare surviving example of a Buddhist stupa for relics, and its form and details show similarities to royal tomb lanterns of the Joseon period. The stele and the assembled relic deposits are valuable as a complete set, and the silk cloths among the relics are also important for textile history.

1123117240000.description: Bak Sa-ik (1675-1736) was a civil official of the late Joseon period.
