They also provide valuable evidence for studying the format of Joseon-period letters and the king’s style of rule and thought.

1123119240000.description: This legal text was compiled by Jeong Do-jeon in the early years of Joseon to establish basic principles for governing the new state, drawing on the six-ministry system of the Zhouli. It later served as a foundation for subsequent law codes, including Gyeongje Yukjeon and Yukjeon Deungnok, and ultimately for the Great Code of State Administration. As the only surviving early Joseon printed edition, it is an especially important source for the study of books and law codes.

1121119250000.title_en: Sarira Reliquary Set Dedicated by Yi Seonggye, Excavated from Geumgangsan Mountain
1121119250000.description: This set of sarira reliquaries was offered by Yi Seonggye and others shortly before the founding of Joseon and was discovered in 1932 inside a stone casket at Wolchulbong in Geumgangsan Mountain. The assemblage includes white porcelain bowls, silver-gilt reliquaries in pagoda and octagonal-hall forms, and bronze bowls, many of which bear inscriptions identifying the patrons, purpose, and makers. These inscriptions, along with the clear findspot and date of production in 1390 and 1391, make the set an important historical and craft record.

1123119260000.title_en: Annotated Anthology of Ten Selected Poems by Renowned Worthies
1123119260000.description: This printed anthology was compiled with the needs of civil-service examination candidates in mind and was edited by Gwon Ram. It selects 10 seven-syllable regulated verses each from 30 poets of China and Silla, with annotations added to the texts. Printed locally in Miryang, it is an important example of an early Korean-made anthology of Chinese and Korean poetry with Korean selection and commentary.

1123119270000.title_en: Portrait and Portrait Case of Park Dong-hyeong
1123119270000.description: This set includes full-length and half-length portraits of Park Dong-hyeong, who was honored for his role in capturing a rebel leader during the 1728 Musin Rebellion. The portraits show the conventional form of a meritorious subject portrait, including official dress, a formal seated pose, and realistic facial treatment. The portrait cases are believed to have been made together with the portraits.

1123819440000.title_en: Miryang Pyochungsa Three-story Stone Pagoda Excavated Artifacts
1123819440000.description: This assemblage was discovered in the core of the stone foundation during the dismantling and repair of the three-story stone pagoda at Pyochungsa Temple in 1995. It includes 20 gilt-bronze Buddhist statues from the Unified Silla to Goryeo periods, various offerings placed inside the pagoda, and an early Joseon repair record stele dated 1491. The group is significant because many Buddhist statues from different periods were found together at a clearly identified excavation site.

1123719450000.title_en: Daeungjeon Hall of Daedunsa Temple, Gimpo
1123719450000.description: This Buddhist hall stands on a raised stone terrace built to match the sloping ground in front, with a granite stairway at the center. It is a typical Joseon-period dapo-style building with a hipped-and-gabled roof, round pillars on natural stone bases, and bracket complexes that reflect the architectural features of the 17th to 18th centuries. Interior elements such as the coffered ceiling, ornate canopy, and surviving dancheong patterns are also preserved.

1122219460000.description: This album contains Hangul letters sent to Princess Sukhwi, the fourth daughter of King Hyojong, by King Hyojong, King Hyeonjong, King Sukjong, Queen Inseon, Queen Myeongseong, and Queen Inhyeon. The album originally consisted of two volumes, titled Gwon and Gon, and the surviving volume preserves 36 letters in all. It is an important source for studying royal Hangul correspondence of the Joseon period.

1123319470000.description: This album brings together Hangul letters sent to Princess Sukmyeong, the third daughter of King Hyojong, by King Hyojong, King Hyeonjong, Queen Jangryeol, and Queen Inseon. It originally contained 66 letters, though one opening is now separately mounted and another is missing, with a photograph preserved. The work is valued as a key source for studying royal Hangul correspondence and the transition from old-style script to palace script in the 17th century.

1123219480000.description: This Buddhist ritual manual collects the origins, rites, and procedures of the Suryuk Muchae Pyeongdeungjae ceremony. Based on the colophon by Kim Suon, it was printed under royal supervision in 1470 by Queen Jeonghui to pray for the repose of King Sejo, King Yejong, and King Deokjong. It is the oldest extant edition of this ritual text and of related works such as the Beopgyeseongbeom Suryuk Seunghoe Sujae Uigwe and the Suryuk Muchae Pyeongdeungjae Chwaryo.

1121119490000.title_en: Haeoek jeonsin cheop by Jeong Seon
1121119490000.description: This album is a representative late work by Jeong Seon, painted in 1747 when he was 72 years old. It consists of 38 leaves, including 21 landscape paintings and accompanying titles, prefaces, poems, and colophons. The album shows Jeong Seon's varied brushwork and pale blue-green ink wash in depictions of Geumgangsan.

1121119500000.description: This album contains true-view landscape and figure paintings of scenic places in Seoul and along the Han River. It is believed to have been begun in 1741 and completed in 1759, and it preserves both the artistic features of Jeong Seon's painting style and historical views of landscapes that have since been altered or lost. The work is also notable for retaining records of its production and mounting.

1121119510000.title_en: Pungak Naesan Chongramdo by Jeong Seon
1121119510000.description: This single painting depicts the inner valleys of Geumgangsan and is believed, from its brushwork and style, to date to the 1740s. It makes unusually extensive use of green, yellow, red, and white pigments to express the full autumn scenery of Inner Geumgang. The painting also labels major landmarks and buildings, making it one of the most detailed surviving depictions of the area.

1123419600000.title_en: Woodblocks for the Eonhae Commentary on the Sutra on the Profound Kindness of Parents
1123419600000.description: These are the woodblocks used to print the vernacular annotated version of the Buddhist sutra explaining requital of the boundless kindness of parents and the eradication of sins. They are 13 blocks, and the version held at Seosaemsa is believed to have been carved in 1563 at Sinshimsa on Dongnimsan Mountain; it is the oldest surviving eonhae edition of this scripture.

1123419610000.description: These woodblocks were recarved in 1565 at Bowonsa Temple on Gayasan Mountain based on the Gosan Hwaamsa edition originally transcribed by Seong Dal-saeng in 1443. Of the original 112 blocks, one block is missing, and 111 blocks are preserved at Seosan Gaesimsa Temple.

1123419620000.description: These woodblocks were printed in 1584 at Gaesimsa Temple on Gayasan Mountain. The work, written by Bojo Guksa Jinul in 1205, warns beginner Buddhist practitioners against improper conduct; all 8 blocks survive intact and are in excellent condition.

1123419630000.title_en: Woodblocks for the Daojia Lunbian Mouzi Lihuolun
1123419630000.description: These woodblocks were carved in 1580 at Bowonsa Temple on Gayasan Mountain. The text, generally known as Mouzi Lihuolun, discusses doubts that people had about Buddhism; of the original five blocks, four survive at Gaesimsa Temple.

1123419640000.description: These woodblocks were carved in 1584 at the present location of Gaesimsa Temple. The text explains the six realms of rebirth in Buddhism, and all 6 blocks survive in a complete set; it is regarded as the most complete pre-Imjin War edition among surviving woodblocks of this work.

1123419650000.title_en: Woodblocks for Yeosu Siwang Saengchiljae Uichanyo
1123419650000.description: These woodblocks were carved in 1577 at Bowonsa Temple on Gayasan Mountain and are now held at Gaesimsa Temple. The ritual manual is for the yesujae ceremony, and 26 blocks survive, preserving 55 leaves including the main text and related ritual sections.

1123419660000.description: These woodblocks were carved in 1621 at Gayasa Temple in Deoksan, Chungcheong-do, to print a Buddhist text on cultivating meditation through the six-syllable mantra. Five blocks survive, and the inscription records the date and place of carving, the donors, and the carver.

1123419670000.title_en: Woodblocks for the Five Great Mantras
1123419670000.description: These woodblocks were printed in 1604 at Gangdangsa Temple on Gayasan Mountain, apparently another name for Bowonsa Temple. They preserve only the section for Susugwok Deung Dharani from the five mantras, with 9 blocks surviving complete; they are valuable for the study of Sanskrit letters and Korean transcription.

1121119520000.description: This dated landscape painting depicts the old house of Kim Sang-yong of the Andong Kim clan in Cheongpunggye, at Baegaksan in Seoul, as it appeared in 1739. It is regarded as a representative example of Jeong Seon’s true-view landscape painting, with a carefully structured composition, confident brushwork, and light coloring that gives the scene a sense of vitality.
1121119520000.material: Ink and light colors on paper

1121119530000.title_en: Painting of the Thatched Cottage on Mount Lu by Jeong Seon
1121119530000.description: This large painting combines landscape and figure painting to depict the historical story of Bai Juyi, who built a thatched cottage and lived in retirement on Mount Lu. It represents Jeong Seon’s style of formal landscape painting based on the Southern School tradition, and it is notable for being executed in color rather than monochrome ink.

1121119540000.title_en: Celadon Bottle with Incised Ring Design
1121119540000.description: This 12th-century Goryeo celadon was made in the form of a two-handled ritual bronze vessel. The body, neck, foot, handles, and incised circular motifs imitate a metal prototype closely, and the vessel is especially noteworthy for its refined workmanship and excellent state of preservation.

1121119550000.title_en: Celadon Ding-form Incense Burner with Relief Taotie Design
1121119550000.description: This 12th-century celadon incense burner has a ding-shaped form, a greenish glaze close to celadon, and delicate decoration. Its shape and details reflect the influence of bronze vessels, and it is considered a representative example of a three-legged ding-form incense burner from the peak period of Goryeo celadon.

1123719560000.description: This large hanging scroll is a post-Buddha painting nearly four meters high, made in 1749. It was stolen from Yongcheonsa Temple around May 2000 and recovered in August 2014. The painting is valued for its well-composed depiction of the Vulture Peak assembly centered on Sakyamuni Buddha, with calm coloring and refined brushwork.

1123719570000.description: This Buddhist painting was made in 1686 and was stolen from Daebisa Temple on December 24, 1988 before being recovered in August 2014. The work is notable for its balanced composition, orderly arrangement of figures, and harmonious use of red and green colors, and the inscription records that four painters participated in its production.

1123719580000.title_en: Samjang Bosaldo of Bomunsa Temple, Yecheon
1123719580000.description: This Buddhist painting was created in 1767 and was stolen from Bomunsa Temple on June 5, 1989 before being recovered in August 2014. It is distinguished by the harmony of figure drawing, brushwork, and color, and by its unusual emphasis on Ksitigarbha and beliefs about the underworld within a painting of the Three Bodhisattvas.

1123619590000.title_en: Printing Woodblocks for the Lotus Sutra (2017-1)
1123619590000.description: These woodblocks are a 1561 re-engraving of the Gaboja edition of the Lotus Sutra made at Cheonggwan-sa Temple on Mt. Jije in Jangheung, Jeolla-do. Of the original 246 blocks, 245 survive today, and the set is regarded as the oldest extant edition of this text of its kind.

1123619120000.description: This set of 17 woodblocks is preserved at Songgwangsa Temple. The first 16 blocks contain chapters 1 through 64 of Jonggyeong Chwalyo, while the last block contains chapter 65 together with the fifth chapter and publication note of Cheongnyang Dapsunjongsim Yobeommun. The colophon records that it was newly carved in 1531 at Eunjeokam Hermitage near Songgwangsa.

1123619130000.title_en: Woodblock Edition of Cheongnyang Dapsunjongsim Yobeommun
1123619130000.description: This set consists of two woodblocks preserved at Songgwangsa Temple. The text for chapters 1 through 4 is carved on these two blocks, while chapter 5 and the publication note are carved on the end of the Jonggyeong Chwalyo blocks. The publication record shows that it was printed in 1531 at Songgwangsa.

1123619140000.title_en: Woodblock Edition of Cheonji Myeongyang Suryuk Japmun
1123619140000.description: This set of 38 woodblocks is preserved at Songgwangsa Temple and is in relatively good condition, though some characters are worn. The publication note records that it was carved in 1531 at Songgwangsa. Among surviving editions of Cheonji Myeongyang Suryuk Japmun from the Joseon period, this is the earliest extant version and one of the few for which the original woodblocks survive.

1123419150000.title_en: Woodblock Edition of Darma Daesa Gwan Simnon
1123419150000.description: This set of eight woodblocks is preserved at Gaesimsa Temple. The last block contains chapter 22 of Darma Daesa Gwan Simnon together with chapter 17 of Doga Nonbyeon Mojari Hwakron, and the publication note records a new carving in 1580 at Bowonsa Temple near Gaya Mountain. It is the only surviving woodblock set for this work in Korea.

1123419160000.title_en: Woodblock Edition of Darma Daesa Hyeolmyeoknon
1123419160000.description: This set of seven woodblocks is preserved at Gaesimsa Temple. Some blocks contain more than one chapter, and one curved block was carved to fit its shape. The publication note records a new printing in 1579 at or near Bowonsa Temple by Gaya Mountain, and this is the only extant woodblock set for the work.

1123719170000.description: Yaongjeong is a pavilion built in 1566 by Gwon Sim-eon to commemorate his father, Gwon Ui. It preserves much of its original early form, including roof tiles and dancheong, and is considered valuable for the study of pre-Imjin War architecture. The building has a roughly T-shaped plan with a main hall, an ondol room, and a front raised floor.

1123519180000.title_en: Wooden Seated Sakyamuni Buddha Triad, Munsusa Temple, Gochang
1123519180000.description: This triad consists of Sakyamuni Buddha in the center, flanked by Medicine Buddha and Amitabha Buddha. An inscription and temple plaques indicate that it was made in 1654 by 15 sculptors led by Hae-sim. It is an important reference work for the study of late Joseon Buddhist sculpture and was later repaired in 1844.

1123719190000.title_en: Dry-lacquer Seated Medicine Buddha and Relics, Cheongnyangsa Temple, Bonghwa
1123719190000.description: This dry-lacquer seated Buddha was made by repeating layers of hemp cloth and lacquer over a modeled core, then carving the finished form. Scientific testing of the cloth layers dates the image to between the late 8th and mid-10th century, making it one of the earliest surviving dry-lacquer Buddhist images in Korea. The assemblage also includes 19 categories of reliquary objects, including votive documents, a reliquary tube, scriptures, and mandalas.

1123319360000.title_en: Portrait of Choe Seok-jeong and Its Container
1123319360000.description: This is a full-length seated portrait of Choe Seok-jeong (1646–1715), who wore an official hat and a green court robe with a rank badge. He is shown seated on a chair with his hands tucked inside his sleeves, with a leopard skin on the chair and his feet on a footrest. It is considered a rare early-18th-century portrait that reflects a move away from the stiff figure style of 17th-century meritorious-retainer portraits.

1122419370000.title_en: Royal Edict of Promotion for Shin Yeo-ryang
1122419370000.description: This document was issued by King Seonjo in 1604 to recognize Shin Yeo-ryang’s military service and promote him from Jeolchungjanggun, a third-rank dangsanggwan, to Gaseon Daebu, a second-rank official. It is a royal edict of commendation and promotion.

1122419380000.title_en: Royal Secret Seal Decree for Shin Yeo-ryang
1122419380000.description: This document was issued by King Seonjo in 1605 to Shin Yeo-ryang when he was appointed as commander of the Naval Command of Jeolla Right Province. It is a royal decree that uses a secret seal.

1123719390000.description: This is a commentary on the Śūraṃgama Sūtra compiled by Yuan-dynasty monk Wei Ze. It appears to have been printed at Gangyeongdogam between 1461 and 1471 using Eulhae-ja metal type cast in 1455, and it survives as a complete set of 10 volumes in 3 booklets in good condition.

1123719400000.title_en: Early Printed Copy of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Ju-bon Volume 41
1123719400000.description: This is the 41st volume of the early printed copy of the 80-volume Huayan Sutra translation by Śikṣānanda. It is a rare surviving volume of the lost early printed edition and is important for studying the textual lineage of the original edition and its differences from the later recon-engraved edition.

1123319410000.title_en: Stone Seated Buddha Triad and Stone Standing Buddha, Bijeung-ri, Cheongju
1123319410000.description: The seated triad was carved from a single stone with a halo, a Buddha, and bodhisattvas arranged around a square lion throne. The main Buddha sits in the gesture of fearlessness and wish-granting, and the style of the attendant bodhisattvas reflects Buddhist sculpture from the mid-6th century.

1123119420000.title_en: Daeungbojeon Hall of Yongjusa Temple, Hwaseong
1123119420000.description: This is the main Buddha hall of Yongjusa Temple and has undergone several repairs, but it largely retains its original appearance except for exterior dancheong. It is a three-bay by three-bay building with a dapo-style hipped-and-gabled roof and shows the characteristics of 18th-century Buddhist temple architecture.

1122119430000.title_en: Re-engraved Copy of the Four-part Vinaya, Volumes 47–50
1122119430000.description: This book is a Joseon-period printed copy made from the Haeinsa Tripitaka woodblocks, which were originally compiled in Goryeo under King Gojong 31. Although it consists of only one booklet containing volumes 47–50, it is notable as the first publicly disclosed early Joseon bound printed edition in complete condition.

1123819680000.description: This folding booklet contains the Diamond Sutra, the Samantabhadra Chapter of the Flower Garland Sutra, the Sutra of Forty-Two Sections, the Sutra of the Buddha's Last Teaching, the Admonitions of Weishan, the Great Buddha's Crowned Shurangama Mantra, and the Marici Dhāraṇī, among other Buddhist texts popular in Goryeo. It is a rare surviving example in Korea, and the colophon and donor list provide specific evidence for the date of publication and the people involved. It is valued as an important source for the study of Goryeo-period Buddhist scriptures.

1121119690000.description: This work is a manuscript copy of the first part of Seogyeol, a calligraphic theory text written by Yi Gwangsa (1705–1777), one of the leading calligraphers of the late Joseon period. It consists of three booklets labeled Geon, Gon, and Bu, and the last page of the Gon volume includes a note dated June 1, 1764, addressed to his eldest son, Yi Geung-ik. It is a rare calligraphic theory work from Joseon and an important source for studying the history and system of Korean calligraphic theory.

1121119700000.title_en: Kim Hong-do, Horseback Listening to the Orioles
1121119700000.description: This painting shows a scholar riding a horse with a page attendant, stopping to look toward a pair of orioles singing in a willow tree. Through delicate linework, soft brushwork, expressive faces, and a bold sense of space, it conveys the lyrical feeling that Kim Hong-do sought in his genre paintings. The poem written on the painting by fellow artist Yi In-mun also gives it added historical value.

1121119710000.title_en: Kim Hong-do, Figures from Historical Anecdotes
1121119710000.description: This eight-panel painting depicts anecdotes involving historical figures such as Zhu Xi, Emperor Guangwu, Wang Xizhi, and Tao Yuanming. It was probably originally made as a folding screen and is relatively well preserved. By rendering Chinese classical subject matter in a distinctive Korean style, it represents an important late work by Kim Hong-do and holds a significant place in the history of Korean painting.

1121119720000.title_en: Kim Hong-do, Zhang Guolao Riding Backward on a Donkey
1121119720000.description: This Daoist and Buddhist figure painting depicts Zhang Guolao, an immortal of the Tang dynasty, riding backward on a donkey while reading a book. It closely follows accounts in the Xianzhuan, showing him with white hair, a white donkey, and a bat attendant. The work is notable for its varied brushwork and colors, and for the contemporary appraisal by Gang Se-hwang that accompanies it.

1121119730000.description: This painting by Shin Yun-bok, who stood alongside Kim Hong-do as a major late Joseon genre painter, depicts a woman in full figure. She wears a large wig, a wrap-style jeogori, and a full skirt, with restrained yet elegant coloring that contrasts with the still pose. As a full-length beauty painting, it is one of the few surviving examples before the 19th century and became an important model for later beauty portraits.

1121119740000.description: This is a white porcelain seal made for use by Saongwon, one of the central offices responsible for food and meals in the Joseon royal court. Unlike ordinary official seals, it features a lion-shaped attachment rather than a cord holder, and the lion is finely carved and decorated with blue and copper pigments. It is significant as a rare surviving official seal and an exceptional example of Joseon white porcelain craftsmanship.

1121119750000.description: This rectangular case was made to store Buddhist scriptures, including the Tripitaka, in scroll form during the Goryeo period. It is made of conifer wood with iron nails joining the parts, then covered with cloth, bone ash, lacquer, and mother-of-pearl inlay. As the only surviving mother-of-pearl sutra case in Korea, it is an especially rare and important example of Goryeo lacquerware.

1123419760000.title_en: Tae-shrine and Steles of King Myeongjong, Seosan
1123419760000.description: This tae-shrine and its steles were established in 1538, the year King Myeongjong was born, according to royal ritual. The complex is said to have remained in its original location with its surrounding landscape relatively well preserved, unlike many other Joseon royal taeshrines that were moved or altered. It is also valuable as historical evidence for Joseon royal taesil rites and for the study of taeshrines in Korean art history.

1121119770000.title_en: Stone Seated Buddha with Square Pedestal, Gyeongju
1121119770000.description: This stone seated Buddha statue was made in the 9th century during Unified Silla. It shows the right shoulder bare and the earth-touching gesture, and although the middle and lower parts of the pedestal are damaged, the figure is otherwise well preserved. Its balanced proportions, full modeling, and finely carved fan-shaped drapery show the high level of Unified Silla Buddhist sculpture and its connection to the main Buddha image of Seokguram Grotto.

1121119780000.description: This is a pair of hanging scrolls written by Kim Jeong-hui in 1856, the year of his death, as a late work for a person known by the pen name Haengnong. The text comes from a poem by the Ming-dynasty writer Wu Zhongqian and praises a simple but satisfying life. Written in clerical script on powdered Chinese paper, it is a representative late work showing Kim Jeong-hui's mature calligraphy and outlook on life.

1121119790000.description: This pair of hanging scrolls presents the phrase "Calling the bright moon, we become three friends; happily sharing a mountain with plum blossoms" in clerical script. The second panel states that it was written in the style of the Shu clerical script, referring to an old Chinese stone inscription style. The work shows Kim Jeong-hui's scholarship combined with art and is regarded as a representative example of his free and varied brushwork.

1121119800000.description: This work is a horizontal hanging scroll written in clerical script on powdered paper and mounted with silk. The main inscription gives the two characters "Chimgye" on the right, while the left side contains a long colophon in running script, explaining that Kim Jeong-hui combined regular and clerical script after long reflection. It is considered a representative example of his broken-script style and is important for understanding his scholarship, art, and character.

1123219810000.title_en: Geungnakbojeon Hall of Sinheungsa Temple, Sokcho
1123219810000.description: Geungnakbojeon Hall was rebuilt in the mid-18th century as a three-bay by three-bay pavilion-style wooden hall with a hip-and-gable roof. It served as an important royal temple in the Yeongdong region during the 18th and 19th centuries, and its platform, stairs, windows, and bracket system are well preserved. Carvings such as peony and lion motifs on the platform and taeguk and dragon-head designs on the stair side stones are rare examples.

1121119820000.title_en: Afterword to Seowon Gyeopilgyeol by Kim Jeong-hui
1121119820000.description: This handwritten work by Kim Jeong-hui criticizes the self-preface to Seogyeol and Jeonpyeon written by the late Joseon calligrapher Yi Gwang-sa. It is an important source for the study of Korean calligraphic theory because it emphasizes the need to verify calligraphy through metal and stone inscriptions. The volume also includes three ink landscape paintings, which show Kim Jeong-hui's taste in literati painting.

1121119830000.description: This album contains 16 ink orchid paintings and seven calligraphic works by Kim Jeong-hui, made as a gift for his regular mounting specialist, Yu Myeong-hun. It is the only known album in which he gathered only orchid paintings, and the orchids are rendered in a wide variety of compositions and brush methods based on his own approach to painting orchids. The inscriptions also reflect his broad learning and add to the work's importance in the history of painting.

1122419930000.title_en: Buncheong Ware Inlaid Grave Marker with 'Gyeongtae 5th Year' Inscription for Yi Seonje
1122419930000.description: This grave marker was made for Yi Seonje (1390–1453), a former Hallim Academy scholar-official who served as a rank-2 official in the reign of King Sejong. It is a rare early Joseon funerary object with a distinctive tablet-like form assembled from four clay slabs, and it was repatriated to Korea in 2017 after being smuggled out in 1998.

1121119940000.description: This Buddhist painting is thought to have been made in 1580, based on an inscription record. It depicts Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva with Mudok Gwisang and Domyeongjonja at the center, surrounded by the Ten Kings of the Underworld and their attendants.

1123219950000.title_en: Jungdae Jeokmyeol Bogung, Odaesan Mountain, Pyeongchang
1123219950000.description: This Buddhist hall has a rare double structure, with separate inner and outer buildings. The outer building reflects the common late Joseon style of the 19th century, while the inner building preserves older construction techniques similar to early and mid-Joseon buildings.

1123719960000.title_en: Vairocana Buddha Painting, Bogyeongsa Temple, Pohang
1123719960000.description: This painting was made in 1742 by the Buddhist painters Naehyeon, Milgi, and Seokjam, who worked in the Gyeongbuk region during the late Joseon period. It is a large line-drawing Buddhist painting on hemp ground, with Vairocana Buddha at the center and Manjushri, Samantabhadra, and the Four Heavenly Kings arranged around him.

1122319970000.title_en: Painted Folding Screen of Pyeongyang Castle
1122319970000.description: This eight-panel folding screen shows Pyeongyang as it flourished in the late Joseon period. It is believed to date earlier than most surviving Pyeongyang Castle paintings, and may have been made as early as the late 18th century.

1123619980000.title_en: Wooden Seated Trinity of Śākyamuni Buddha, Ssanggyesa Temple, Jindo
1123619980000.description: This three-image Buddhist sculpture set was made in 1665 by nine sculptor-monks led by Heejang. It consists of a central seated Śākyamuni Buddha flanked by two bodhisattvas, and the dedicatory texts and reliquary containers were found largely intact.

1122219990000.title_en: Wooden Seated Trinity of Amitābha Buddha, Donghwasa Temple, Daegu
1122219990000.description: This large wooden Buddhist sculpture set was made in 1629 under the direction of Hyunjin, with five sculptor-monks participating. It consists of a seated Amitābha Buddha flanked by standing Avalokiteśvara and Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattvas, and preserves its original form and pedestal.

1121120000000.title_en: Kim Hong-do, Three High Ministers Would Not Be Exchanged for It
1121120000000.description: This eight-panel folding screen was painted by Kim Hong-do in 1801, when he was 57 years old. It combines landscapes and genre scenes to depict the pleasures of rural life, with houses, fields, guests, servants, farmers, and a fisherman shown throughout the composition.

1121119840000.title_en: Album of the Three Purities by Yi Jeong
1121119840000.description: This album was painted by Yi Jeong (1554–1626) in Gongju on December 12, 1594. It contains 54 leaves of paintings and calligraphic material, including his ink bamboo paintings as well as paintings of plum blossoms and orchids. The album also includes colophons by contemporaries and later scholars, which help clarify its date of production and transmission.
1121119840000.material: Ink and gold on dyed silk

1121119850000.title_en: Album of Landscapes and Birds and Flowers by Yi Jing
1121119850000.description: This album contains 18 paintings by Yi Jing (1581–?) and 37 pieces of writing by well-known literati of the time, including Yi Sik and Yi Myeong-han. Based on the colophons, it was made around 1642, when Yi Jing was about 62 years old. It is a combined album of painting and calligraphy and is valued as an important dated work for the study of Joseon period painting.

1121119860000.title_en: Scroll of the Road to Shu by Sim Sa-jeong
1121119860000.description: This large landscape handscroll was painted by the literati painter Sim Sa-jeong in August 1768, one year before his death. It depicts the dangerous journey to Shu, based on Li Bai's poem "Hard Is the Road to Shu." The work shows a long, continuous landscape composition rendered with varied colors and detailed brushwork.

1121119870000.title_en: Album of Genre Paintings by Kim Deuk-sin
1121119870000.description: This album consists of eight genre paintings by the late Joseon court painter Kim Deuk-sin (1754–1822). Strongly influenced by Kim Hong-do, the album focuses on everyday scenes and carefully captures the gestures, gaze, and emotions of the figures. Its simplified backgrounds and selective use of shading highlight Kim Deuk-sin's own distinctive style.

1121119880000.title_en: Brahmajala Sutra, Bodhisattva Precepts Chapter in Gold on Dark Blue Paper
1121119880000.description: This manuscript is a transcription of the Bodhisattva Precepts Chapter of the Brahmajala Sutra, an important text used as a basis for Bodhisattva precept assemblies and ordination ceremonies. Although it lacks a colophon giving the exact date of copying, the manuscript can be dated to the early Joseon period based on internal evidence and the note left by the monk Daeyeon. It includes a small frontispiece painted in gold, showing the Buddha preaching the precepts and emanated Buddhas.

1121119890000.description: This book was printed in 1403 with small and medium-sized movable type cast in the Gyeongoja year type. It is a Joseon-period compilation of exemplary Song dynasty memorials and proclamations, arranged as models for formal court documents. The extant copy is rare and is an important source for the study of early Joseon movable-type printing.
1121119890000.material: Movable type printed book on paper

1123519900000.title_en: Gamnowangdo Painting Inscribed for Daegoksa Temple
1123519900000.description: This Buddhist hanging scroll was painted in 1764 by Cheisang and 12 other monk painters. Although part of the inscription is damaged, the painting is thought to have been enshrined at Daegoksa Temple in Uiseong, Gyeongsangbuk-do. It depicts the Seven Buddhas, bodhisattvas, ritual scenes, hungry ghosts, and souls in a balanced composition with gentle colors.

1123719920000.title_en: Investiture Document for Yi Suk-gi as a Meritorious Subject
1123719920000.description: This royal document was issued to Yi Suk-gi in June 1472, one year after he was enfeoffed as a meritorious subject for assisting King Seongjong's accession. It records political developments and participants related to Seongjong's enthronement and supplements details omitted from official histories. The document preserves its original form and is important for the study of late 15th-century meritorious-subject certificates.

1121120010000.description: This pair of earrings was excavated in 1949 from Tomb No. 52 in Hwango-dong, Gyeongju. They are typical Silla earrings of the 5th–6th century, made in three parts: the main hoop, middle ornaments, and terminal ornament. The workmanship is delicate, with fine granulation and a pen-nib-shaped pendant.

1125020020000.description: This manuscript records the official duties, activities, and Jeju-related history written by Yi Ik-tae, who served as magistrate of Jeju from 1694 to 1696. It also includes travel accounts, poems, and records of drifting incidents involving Koreans and Japanese, including the rare account of Kim Dae-hwang's drift voyage to Vietnam and return. The book is significant as an early local gazetteer of Jeju and for understanding Joseon-era policies on castaways.

1123120030000.title_en: Wooden Seated Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva of Bulamsa Temple, Namyangju
1123120030000.description: This wooden seated Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva was completed in 1649 by the sculptors Muyeom and four others. The inscription records that it was originally made for Myoryeonam Hermitage at Daedunsan and was later re-gilded and moved to Bulamsa Temple in 1907. Its balanced proportions and natural volume are characteristic of Muyeom's sculpture.

1121120040000.title_en: Wooden Seated Shakyamuni Buddha of Chilbosa Temple, Seoul
1121120040000.description: This wooden seated Shakyamuni Buddha is believed to be one of the eleven Buddha images made in 1622 and enshrined at Jasusa and Insusa, royal temples supported by Queen Jangnyeolwanghu and the royal family. It was produced by master sculptors including Hyeonjin, Suyeon, Eungwon, and Ingyun, and shows features of their combined styles. The figure is seated in the earth-touching gesture and has a sturdy, dignified form.

1123720050000.title_en: Banner Painting of the Buddha at Beopjusa Temple, Gunwi
1123720050000.description: This banner painting was completed in 1714 by the monk-painters Ducho and eight others. The large vertical composition shows a standing Buddha figure wearing a crown and holding lotus flowers, with an unusual arrangement that includes dragon kings and dragon maidens at the lower part of the image. The work is an important source for the study of late Joseon Buddhist iconography.

1123420060000.title_en: Banner Painting of Vairocana Buddha of Daeryeonsa Temple, Yesan
1123420060000.description: This banner painting of Vairocana Buddha was made in 1750 by four monk-painters, including Chungmyeong and Sa-hye. The composition places Vairocana Buddha at the center, with Manjushri and Samantabhadra on the sides and Ananda and Kashyapa arranged above and below in a five-deity format. It is a rare surviving example of a Vairocana banner painting made before the 19th century.

1123720070000.title_en: Banner Painting of the Vulture Peak Assembly of Nammjangsa Temple, Sangju
1123720070000.description: This banner painting was completed in 1788 for the Buddhist ritual known as Yeongsanjae, with leadership by the monk-painter Sanggyeom and participation by 21 other monk-painters. Despite its large size, it arranges Shakyamuni Buddha and his retinue in a balanced composition with vivid colors and decorative elements. The accompanying record of the ritual process is an important source for understanding the painting and the broader Buddhist activities of the time.

1121120080000.description: This bronze drum was made around 1218, as indicated by the inscription, and was donated by six military officials for enshrinement at Gyeongseonsa Temple. Its surface is decorated with concentric circles, a lotus-seed motif at the center, 16 lotus petals, and cloud-patterned border designs. It is an important early example of a Goryeo bronze drum with a sound hole on the side.

1123420090000.title_en: Record of Merit for Jang Cheol, a Distinguished Contributor in Pacifying the First Strife of Princes
1123420090000.description: This license was issued in November 1398 to Jang Cheol (1359–1399), then Vice Minister of the Central Hall, as one of the 29 meritorious retainers recognized for suppressing the First Strife of Princes. It records the purpose and process of their appointment, their merits and offices, and the rewards granted, using a mix of Classical Chinese and Idu notation. It is the only confirmed early Joseon license for a Distinguished Contributor in Pacifying the First Strife of Princes and is valued for its historical, linguistic, and bibliographic significance.

1123720100000.description: This roof-end tile is a Silla-period round eave tile widely known as the “Smile of Silla,” said to have been excavated from Sajong-ri, Gyeongju. It was purchased in Japan in 1934, later taken out of the country, and returned to Korea in 1972. Unlike ordinary mold-made tiles, it was shaped by hand, and it is regarded as the only known hand-formed face-patterned roof end tile.

1123620110000.title_en: Wooden Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva Triad and Ten Kings of Mokpo Dalseongsa Temple
1123620110000.description: This Buddhist sculpture group was made in 1565 by five sculptor-monks led by Hyang-eom and consists of the Ksitigarbha Triad, the Ten Kings, and attendants and messengers, for a total of 19 figures. The main altar holds the Ksitigarbha Triad, with the Ten Kings arranged on the side walls of the hall. It is the only surviving pre-Imjin War group in Korea that preserves both the Ksitigarbha Triad and the Ten Kings, and both the original dedication text and later repair texts survive.

1121120120000.title_en: Painting of the Bhaisajyaguru Buddha Triad Inscribed 'Hoeamsa Temple'
1121120120000.description: This painting was made in 1565 as one of 400 Buddhist paintings commissioned by Queen Munjeong to pray for King Myeongjong’s longevity and for the birth of an heir. It was created for the inauguration of Hoeamsa Temple in Yangju, and its record states that the works included gold-ink and color paintings of Buddhas and bodhisattvas. The composition places Bhaisajyaguru in the center with the Sunlight and Moonlight Bodhisattvas on either side, and it survives today as the only extant example in Korea from that original set.
1121120120000.material: Gold ink and color on silk

1123120130000.title_en: Sarira Stupa of Sujongsa Temple, Namyangju
1123120130000.description: This stone sarira stupa at Sujongsa Temple in Namyangju is preserved together with the temple’s octagonal five-story stone pagoda and a three-story stone pagoda. When the stupa was dismantled and repaired in 1939, a set of sarira reliquaries was discovered and is now designated separately as a Treasure. The stupa is a fully preserved early Joseon work, and its date, decorative quality, and memorial function for Princess Jeonghye show the development of royal Buddhist belief and funerary form in the period.

1123220140000.description: These woodblocks were carved in 1658 at Sinheungsa Temple in Gangwon Province for a printed edition of three works: the Buldingsim Dharani Sutra, the Table of Jejineonjip, and Jejineonjip. The first carving was done in 1569 at Ansimsa Temple, but the original blocks no longer survive, making the Sinheungsa recarving the oldest extant edition. The set is notable for its rare combination of Hangul, Chinese characters, and Sanskrit, and it is an important source for studying language, Buddhist ritual, and regional religious culture in the 16th and 17th centuries.

1121120150000.title_en: Goryeo Painting of the Thousand-Armed Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva
1121120150000.description: This Goryeo Buddhist painting depicts Avalokitesvara in the form of the Thousand-Armed, Thousand-Eyed Bodhisattva, an image symbolizing compassionate salvation. The figure sits on a lotus pedestal placed on a rock, with a large circular halo filling the upper part of the composition and Sudhana worshipping below. It is the only known extant painting of this subject from the Goryeo period and reflects the refined style, rich color, and use of gold typical of Goryeo Buddhist paintings.

1123620160000.title_en: Great Dharani Sutra of the Heart of Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva (2019)
1123620160000.description: This esoteric Buddhist sutra teaches that copying, carrying, or reciting the text with the aid of Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva’s spiritual power can remove misfortune. The copy held by Myodeoksa Temple was printed in 1425 by Yun Hui and others, who prayed for the rebirth of their deceased parents in paradise and for blessings for themselves and their families. It survives as a rare small-format edition in three volumes and one booklet, and is significant for the study of early Joseon Buddhism and woodblock printing.

1122220170000.title_en: Bronze Tiger-shaped Belt Hook Excavated from Wooden-coffin Tomb No. 1 at Sindae-ri, Gyeongsan
1122220170000.description: This bronze tiger-shaped belt hook was excavated in 2007 from Wooden-coffin Tomb No. 1 at Sindae-ri, Gyeongsan, North Gyeongsang Province. It is commonly known as a tiger-shaped belt hook (hohyeong daegu) and was used as an ornament attached to clothing or sword hilts. It is valued as one of the best-preserved examples among the few known tiger-shaped belt hooks.

1121120180000.title_en: Gilt-bronze Crown Excavated from Tomb No. 32 at Jisan-dong, Goryeong
1121120180000.description: This gilt-bronze crown was excavated in 1978 from Tomb No. 32 at Jisan-dong, Goryeong, and its date to the 5th century has been confirmed by the excavation context and associated finds. It was made by hammering a thin copper sheet and gilding it, and it has a distinctive form with an X-shaped pattern incised by dotted lines on the broad central plate. It is regarded as a representative crown of the Daegaya period.

1122120190000.title_en: Bronze Seven-headed Bell Excavated from Tomb No. 22 at Bokcheon-dong, Busan
1122120190000.description: This bronze bell was excavated during the 1980–1982 excavation of Tomb No. 22 at Bokcheon-dong, Busan. It is a rare example showing that ritual traditions involving bronze bells continued into the Gaya period. The object is notable for its unique form and for the skill shown in its hollow casting and finish.

1122120200000.title_en: Iron Armor Excavated from Tomb No. 38 at Bokcheon-dong, Busan
1122120200000.description: This set of iron armor was excavated in the fifth excavation of Tomb No. 38 at Bokcheon-dong, Busan, in 1994–1995. It consists of a vertical-plate helmet, neck guard, and vertical-plate cuirass, and it is the only known complete set of this type excavated together. Because the excavation context and date are clear and the preservation is good, it is an important reference for the chronology and construction of ancient Korean armor.

1123420210000.title_en: East Three-story Stone Pagoda at Seongjusa Temple Site, Boryeong
1123420210000.description: This pagoda is one of four surviving pagodas at the Seongjusa Temple Site in Boryeong. It is considered to have been built in the late Unified Silla period by the same craftsman who made the other two three-story pagodas at the site. The pagoda stands 4.1 meters tall and shows the characteristic form of late Unified Silla stone pagodas, including a two-tiered base and carved door panels on the first-story body.

1121120220000.title_en: Set of Buddhist Ritual Offerings Excavated from Ingaksa Temple, Gunwi
1121120220000.description: This set of 18 objects was excavated in 2008 from the eastern remains of the first building site at Ingaksa Temple in Gunwi. It consists of metal ritual utensils and ceramics, including a gilt-bronze lion-shaped incense burner, incense container, purification bottle, bronze gong, and a gilt-bronze kalaviṅka figure. The ceramics are thought to be Chinese wares and were found stacked together, making the assemblage valuable for dating the associated metal objects and for studying late Silla to early Goryeo material culture.

1121120230000.title_en: Newly Compiled Anthology of Answers to the Three Examinations, Vols. 5–6
1121120230000.description: This book is a themed compilation of model answers from the three stages of the Yuan imperial examinations, newly edited in 1341 by Liu Renchu. The designated item consists of vols. 5–6 of both the Goryeo and Joseon editions, preserving only the answers. Printed with metal movable type, it is an important comparative source for studying late Goryeo and early Joseon printing and the transmission of metal-type editions.

1123620240000.title_en: Geungnakbojeon Hall of Cheoneunsa Temple, Gurye
1123620240000.description: Geungnakbojeon is the main Buddha hall of Cheoneunsa Temple, located on the southwestern slope of Jirisan Mountain. It was rebuilt in 1774 during the reign of King Yeongjo and enshrines Amitabha Buddha as the principal deity. The hall is a three-by-three bay building with a multi-cluster bracket system and a hipped-and-gabled roof, and its interior dancheong is well preserved and representative of late Joseon tradition.

1123820410000.title_en: Excavated Iron Horse Armor and Ring-Pommel Long Sword from Haman Magapchong Tomb
1123820410000.description: This set consists of an iron horse armor and a ring-pommel long sword excavated from the Magapchong tomb in Haman in 1992. The horse armor includes the helmet, neck-and-chest armor, and body armor, and its nearly complete preservation is rare among known Gaya horse armors. The two objects were buried on the left and right sides of the deceased and are considered important evidence for understanding Gaya burial customs, ironworking, and mounted warfare.

1121120420000.title_en: Set of Ring-Pommel Long Swords from Hapcheon Okjeon Tomb No. 3
1121120420000.description: This set of four ring-pommel long swords was excavated from Hapcheon Okjeon Tomb No. 3 during the 1987–1988 excavation by the Gyeongsang National University Museum. All four swords feature dragon-phoenix motifs and show highly refined metalworking techniques. Because the burial context is secure and the preservation is excellent, they are regarded as representative works of Three Kingdoms metalcraft.

1123820430000.title_en: Pair of Gold Earrings from Hapcheon Okjeon Tomb No. 28
1123820430000.description: This pair of gold earrings was excavated during the 1985–1986 investigation of Hapcheon Okjeon Tomb No. 28. It is an important example of fifth-century Gaya earrings because the find context is clear and the original form can be understood well. The earrings are especially notable for their long-chain structure and elaborate hanging ornaments.

1121120440000.title_en: Pair of Gold Earrings from Hapcheon Okjeon Tomb No. 4
1121120440000.description: This pair of gold earrings was excavated from Hapcheon Okjeon Tomb No. 4 during the 1991 excavation by the Gyeongsang National University Museum. They were found in the original wearing position and remain complete as a pair. The earrings combine several advanced techniques, including granulation, filigree, and repoussé, and are considered an important example of sixth-century Gaya metalwork.

1123820450000.title_en: Pair of Gold Earrings from Hapcheon Okjeon Tomb No. 6
1123820450000.description: This pair of gold earrings was excavated from Hapcheon Okjeon Tomb No. 6 during the 1991–1992 survey by the Gyeongsang National University Museum. They were found near the head of the deceased in the southern part of the wooden chamber, and the burial context is clear. The earrings show a mixed style that combines Silla-type intermediate elements with Gaya-style pendant decorations, illustrating exchange in the Gaya region during the sixth century.

1123220460000.description: Gyeongpodae is a long-established pavilion associated with many poets and scholars from the Goryeo and Joseon periods. It was first built in 1326, during the reign of King Chungsuk of Goryeo, and records of relocation and later repairs have been preserved. The pavilion is a five-bay by five-bay structure and is valued for the continuity of its historical record.

1123720470000.description: Bangchojeong has relatively well-preserved records of its construction history, including repair, reconstruction, and ridge-beam inscriptions. Although some members have been replaced in later repairs, the overall structural system follows the late Joseon style. It retains the appearance it had when it was rebuilt in 1788.

1123720480000.description: Hansujeong preserves many features of a traditional pavilion despite its small site, including its landscaped setting and the surrounding water features and trees. Its location was carefully chosen for its function, and its creation reflects the particular meaning given to it by the Andong Gwon clan. The pavilion is also notable for the diversity of its plan and structural form.

1123520330000.title_en: Bronze Sword and Bronze Dagger Mold from Galdong, Wanju
1123520330000.description: This set consists of two stone molds excavated from Tomb No. 1, a pit tomb at Galdong in Wanju. One mold is for a narrow bronze sword, and the other has designs for both a bronze sword and a bronze dagger on each side. The molds are important evidence for bronze-production technology in the Honam region during the early Iron Age.

1123520340000.title_en: Decorated Bronze Mirrors from Galdong, Wanju
1123520340000.description: This set consists of two bronze mirrors excavated from pit tombs No. 5 and No. 7 at Galdong in Wanju. They are rare examples recovered through formal excavation and are considered late examples of decorated mirrors from the early Iron Age. The fine surface patterns and near-complete condition make them valuable for studying bronze-casting technology of the period.

1123120350000.title_en: Unhangak, Bokdogak, and Ianchung Hall of Hwaryeongjeon Shrine, Suwon
1123120350000.description: Hwaryeongjeon was built in 1801 to enshrine the portrait of King Jeongjo after his death, and these three buildings form its core complex. Unhangak, Bokdogak, and Ianchung are arranged in a U-shaped plan, showing a late Joseon arrangement for a royal memorial shrine. The interior layout and joinery also reflect the architecture of late Joseon ritual buildings.

1123120360000.title_en: Daewoongjeon Hall of Chiljangsa Temple, Anseong
1123120360000.description: Daewoongjeon Hall at Chiljangsa Temple was rebuilt in 1790 and moved in 1828. It is a representative late Joseon Buddhist hall in the Gyeonggi area, with a three-bay front and side, a gabled roof, and a bracket system used only on the front and back. The building also preserves rare remaining examples of decorative dancheong and stonework from the period.

1123620370000.description: Geumseonggwan was an official guesthouse where the royal tablet was kept and the rite of manggwollye was performed during the Joseon dynasty. Its overall scale and framework are thought to have retained the form of the 1617 renovation, while later repairs in 1775 and 1885 are reflected in the wooden framework and bracket details. The main hall is especially notable for its large size and its hipped-and-gabled roof, which is unusual for an official guesthouse.

1123720380000.description: This is a two-volume set of seonsaeng-an, or registers of officials who served in an office, consisting of an older register compiled in 1523 and a later register compiled in 1741. The records list successive magistrates and related details such as appointment dates, audience attendance, and honors received. It is an important source for studying administration, personnel history, and local history from the Goryeo period through 1910.

1123720390000.description: This is a two-volume set recording the names of governors who served in Gyeongsang Province from the Goryeo period through the Joseon dynasty. One volume was first compiled in 1426 by Ha Yeon, and the other was later compiled in 1622 based on that earlier version. Together they preserve a long, continuous record of provincial governors over more than 800 years.

1121120400000.title_en: Reprinted Edition of the Mahayana Dharmadhatu-viśeṣa-śāstra
1121120400000.description: This Buddhist text was woodblock-printed from blocks carved in 1244 and is believed to have been printed in the late Goryeo to early Joseon period. It survives in a rare folded-leaf format and contains the standard bibliographic elements of a Buddhist scripture. The text is valuable for studying Buddhist history, bibliography, and the printing and circulation of Goryeo reprint editions.

1123720490000.description: This pavilion is built on a natural rock outcrop without cutting or levelling the bedrock, and it includes an ondol heated room, a rare feature for a pavilion. Its interior structure uses a 5-ryang framework in which the main beam and side beam are set at the same height from the inner post. Historical records of its construction and rebuilding, its plan suited to an official pavilion, and its late Joseon structural style give it strong historical and scholarly value.

1123720500000.description: This is a 17th-century building that well reflects the architectural features of local yangban scholar-officials. Its restrained form, with minimal ornament including the balustrade and lower wall, expresses the upright character of a Confucian scholar. It preserves the appearance of its 17th-century rebuilding relatively well and retains the overall integrity of the building.

1123720510000.description: The pavilion’s historical value can be seen from the many poems inscribed by visiting writers and artists, and its central ondol room reflects a local architectural tradition. The front window arrangement is unusual, with a small auxiliary window in the center and paired doors on both sides that open and stack inward. This is a rare example of a pavilion with such a window type and folding-door system.

1123720520000.description: This hexagonal pavilion is an important example for studying traditional construction techniques because its floor, ondol room, and storage spaces are skillfully divided within the plan. It also combines round and square columns in a balanced way and uses different floor heights to connect naturally with the exterior space. Its unusual wooden bracket and roof framing over a hexagonal plan make it especially significant.

1122220530000.description: Built around 1604 by Nokpo Lee Jong-mun, this pavilion-style detached house has a distinctive T-shaped plan formed by a main hall and attached rooms. It is unusual not only for its plan but also because the master and servants lived in the same building. As an early to mid-Joseon pavilion-type annex with notable spatial composition, details, and design, it has strong historical, architectural, and scholarly value.

1123620540000.description: This pavilion was founded in the mid-to-late 15th century by families who settled in the area, rebuilt around 1635 after the Japanese invasions, and later repaired to its present form. It served as a meeting place for the local village association and is a rare example of a hyangyak pavilion. Its large scale, high floor, unusual plan with a partitioned central rear room, and varied architectural devices make it an important witness to the development of Korean pavilion architecture.

1123520550000.description: This pavilion was built in 1686 and repaired in 1884 and 1888. It is located in a natural cave formed by bedrock, with the building fitted into irregular rock gaps. Its use of curved upper beams, a coffered ceiling, a rock crevice as an entrance, and the dramatic contrast between darkness and light during entry show an unusual architectural form, and its roof finishes also reflect local building practice.

1123120560000.description: This Buddhist scripture is one part of a ten-volume edition of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, printed from woodblocks carved in 1401. It is important for the study of Joseon-era Buddhist scripture printing and Middle Korean because it preserves examples of script annotations and old orthographic forms such as rare consonants used before the late 15th century. The text is also valuable because its proofreading marks suggest it was printed no later than the 15th century.

1123720250000.title_en: Samjang Bodhisattva Painting of Daedunsa Temple, Gumi
1123720250000.description: This Buddhist painting was made in 1740 and originally enshrined at Daedunsa Temple together with paintings of the Vulture Peak Assembly, Indra, King of the Underworld, and Amitabha. It is the only surviving work from that group and depicts a gathering of Cheonjang, Jiji, and Jijang Bodhisattvas with their attendants in a carefully organized composition. It is also important for studying the development of 18th-century Buddhist iconography and painting style in Gyeongsangbuk-do.
1123720250000.material: Ink and mineral pigments on silk

1123720260000.title_en: Gwaebul Painting of Jikjisa Temple, Gimcheon
1123720260000.description: This hanging Buddhist painting was made in 1803 and is the earliest known surviving gwaebul of the 19th century. It shows a standing main deity in bodhisattva form wearing a jeweled crown and holding lotus blossoms with both hands, with smaller Buddhas and bodhisattvas arranged above. The work is notable for its large scale and for reflecting a transitional style in early 19th-century Buddhist painting.
1123720260000.material: Ink and mineral pigments on silk

1121120270000.description: This metal-type printed book comprises volumes 1 and 2 of the collected works of the late Goryeo writer Yi Sung-in (1347–1392), known by the pen name Doeun. It was compiled by Byeon Gye-ryang and printed after King Taejong ordered the publication of Yi's works in 1406. The surviving copy is incomplete, but it is valuable for studying early Joseon metal movable type and the Guemja typeface.

1123720280000.title_en: Set of Earthenware Jars with Lead Glaze and Stamped Design
1123720280000.description: This set consists of two earthenware jars, a large jar and a small jar, made in Unified Silla during the 8th century. They are coated with a greenish lead glaze and decorated with stamped patterns over the mouth and body. As an unusually large and elaborate example of lead-glazed earthenware, the set is an important source for studying Unified Silla ceramic production.

1121120290000.description: This long handscroll landscape painting was created by Yi In-mun, a court painter active in the late 18th and early 19th centuries. It depicts the traditional theme of endless mountains and rivers, combining idealized scenery with figures, villages, cliffs, and broad plains. The work is notable for its extended panoramic composition and for showing Yi In-mun's distinctive style.

1122220300000.title_en: Newly Compiled Anthology of Korean Poetry, Vols. 9-11 and 31-39
1122220300000.description: This metal-type printed book is a surviving copy of selected volumes from Yu Hui-ryeong's 70-volume anthology of Korean poetry, compiled from ancient times to the author's own era. It was likely printed around 1542 using the Byeongja type, which was newly cast based on the 1516 edition of the Zizhi Tongjian. The text differs in many places from other transmitted versions and is an important source for the history of 16th-century Korean book publication.

1123520310000.title_en: Stone Seated Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva of Chamdangam Hermitage, Seonunsa Temple, Gochang
1123520310000.description: This stone seated Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva image was made in the late Goryeo to early Joseon period and reflects the hooded Ksitigarbha type that was popular in Buddhist painting. Its gentle expression, rounded lips, jeweled orb, and finely carved hood and sash details closely follow late Goryeo bodhisattva styles. The stone pedestal, which may or may not have been made with the statue, also shows clear stylistic features of the middle Goryeo period.

1123120320000.description: This astronomical instrument combines the traditional East Asian theories of the celestial sphere and the flat heaven on a single circular device. It was made in 1787 by the scholar Yu Geum as a Joseon reinterpretation of the astrolabe transmitted through China. The instrument shows the development of mathematics and astronomy in 18th-century Joseon and is notable for its precise metalwork.

1121120570000.description: This is a fengshui treatise widely used as one of the subjects in the Onmyo-ga examination for officials of the Office of Astronomy. It is organized into two volumes with 22 chapters in total, and was probably printed in the Taejong reign based on the use of a specific metal type. Because few copies were printed and surviving examples are rare, it is considered important for history, scholarship, and bibliography.

1121120580000.title_en: White Porcelain Jar with Underglaze Cobalt Blue Plum, Bird, and Bamboo Design
1121120580000.description: This lidded jar is an early Joseon white porcelain vessel painted with plum blossoms, birds, and bamboo in underglaze cobalt blue. Its form and decoration suggest production at a government kiln, and the brushwork shows varied tonal effects that give the design a lively, pictorial quality. It is significant as an example of early Joseon blue-and-white porcelain made before the style fully developed independently from Chinese influence.
1121120580000.material: White porcelain with underglaze cobalt blue

1123820590000.title_en: Pottery Cylindrical Pedestal with Turtle Ornament and Short-necked Jar from Bokcheon-dong Tomb No. 11, Busan
1123820590000.description: This set consists of a cylindrical pedestal with a turtle appliqué and a short-necked jar excavated from Tomb No. 11 at Bokcheon-dong, Busan. The pedestal and jar were found together in a nearly complete condition, making them a rare example of a Gaya ritual vessel group. The turtle ornament on the pedestal is the only known turtle appliqué among Three Kingdoms terracotta figures.

1121120600000.title_en: Gilt-bronze Buddhist Statues Excavated from the Five-story Stone Pagoda of Muryangsa Temple, Buyeo
1121120600000.description: This group consists of one gilt-bronze seated bodhisattva and three gilt-bronze seated Amitabha Triad statues, all found during dismantling repair of the five-story stone pagoda at Muryangsa Temple in 1971. One statue is an early Goryeo bodhisattva, while the other three are early Joseon Amitabha Triad images with Avalokiteshvara and Ksitigarbha as attendant figures. The group is important for studying the history of Buddhist sculpture and the enshrinement of images inside pagodas.

1122120610000.description: This atlas of maps, likely made between 1738 and 1753, depicts villages and military strongpoints in Hamgyeong Province, the northern Gwanbuk region. Each sheet presents detailed pictorial rendering, and the margins record information such as distance from Hanyang, household numbers, troop numbers, and post stations. It is notable for directly linking beacon-fire stations with solid lines and for indicating their distances numerically.

1123520620000.description: This is the civil-service examination pass certificate granted to Choi Gwang-ji after he passed the civil examination in 1389, the first year of King Chang. The document is written with the title and the date of issuance, and bears the seal of the King of Goryeo. It is a very rare surviving Goryeo official document and the only known Goryeo hongpae with an imperial-style seal and complete formal structure.

1123820630000.title_en: Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch
1123820630000.description: This is a woodblock-printed edition of the text compiled by the disciple Fahai from the teachings of Huineng, the sixth patriarch of Chinese Chan Buddhism. The Korean edition was printed at Seonwonsa Temple in Ganghwa in 1300 after being accepted by Hyegam Guksa Manhang. It is regarded as the oldest surviving copy of this scripture in Korea and an important source for the study of Goryeo woodblock printing and the history of Korean Seon Buddhism.

1122120640000.description: This large standing jar was made in the late 17th to early 18th century and stands 52.6 cm high. Although there were minor cracks at the rim and shoulder that were repaired, the vessel is almost complete and well preserved. Its stable form, pale bluish-white glaze, and refined technique suggest production at a government kiln in the late Joseon period.

1123820810000.title_en: Necklace Excavated from Tomb No. 76, Daesong-dong, Gimhae
1123820810000.description: This necklace was excavated in 2011 from a wooden coffin tomb dating to the late 3rd to early 4th century at Daesong-dong, Gimhae. It consists of 2,473 beads, including crystal, agate, and glass beads, and is notable as a well-documented prestige ornament representing Geumgwan Gaya.

1123820820000.title_en: Crystal Necklace Excavated from Tomb No. 270, Yangdong-ri, Gimhae
1123820820000.description: This necklace was excavated in 1992 from a pit wooden-coffin tomb during a survey by Dong-Eui University Museum. It is made of 146 crystal beads in various shapes and colors, and is regarded as a prestige ornament of Geumgwan Gaya.

1122120830000.title_en: Necklace Excavated from Tomb No. 322, Yangdong-ri, Gimhae
1122120830000.description: This necklace was excavated from a wooden-coffin tomb during a 1994 survey by Dong-Eui University Museum. It is composed of 574 beads made of crystal, agate, and glass, including many curved and faceted crystal beads.

1121120840000.title_en: Album of Paintings of the Gyeongjin Embassy to the Qing Court
1121120840000.description: This album was made to present the progress of the 1760–1761 Gyeongjindongjisa mission to King Yeongjo. It includes landscape paintings, records of sites in Beijing and Shanhai Pass, diagrams showing the placement of tablets, and colophons explaining the images.

1121120850000.description: This is the manuscript of Malmoi, the first Korean-language dictionary, compiled under the Joseon Gwangmunhoe with participation by Ju Si-gyeong and his disciples. Only one volume survives, and it contains headwords from "g" to "gyaljuk" in a specially prepared manuscript format.

1123420860000.title_en: Manuscript of the Comprehensive Korean Dictionary
1123420860000.description: This is a set of manuscript proof sheets prepared by the Joseon Language Society between 1929 and 1942. The materials were seized by the Japanese police in 1942 and later rediscovered in 1945, helping lead to the publication of the Comprehensive Korean Dictionary in 1957.

1121120870000.title_en: Autograph Manuscript of Queen Hyoeui and Letter Box, Volume of Records of Mansaekgun jeon and Gwak Jayi jeon
1121120870000.description: Queen Hyoeui of Joseon personally copied Korean translations of the biographies of Mansaekgun and Gwak Jayi after having them translated for her in 1794. The set includes the manuscript volume and a paulownia wood box, both preserved as a rare example of royal vernacular calligraphy.

1123220880000.description: This is a large lecture hall of Gangneung Hyanggyo, measuring 11 bays by 2 bays. Originally built in the early Joseon period and later repaired and rebuilt in the 17th century, it preserves the tradition of a long hall used as a hyanggyo lecture building.

1123520650000.description: This pavilion at Seonunsa Temple was first built in 1620 as Daeyangnu and rebuilt in 1752 after it was destroyed by fire. It is a single-story wooden structure with a gabled roof, nine bays on the front and two bays on the side. Its large scale and mixed structural methods show the changing organization of late Joseon Buddhist temple space.

1123620660000.title_en: Wooden Seated Amitabha Buddha, Baekyangsa Temple, Jangseong
1123620660000.description: This wooden seated Amitabha Buddha was made in 1607 by the sculptor monk Hyeonjin and two others, with the base and associated inscriptions also dating from that year. It was created to pray for the enlightenment of deceased kings, queens, and royal ancestors after the wars of the late 16th century. The image and its base preserve records that are important for the study of 17th-century Buddhist sculpture.

1123720670000.title_en: Wooden Seated Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, Gwaneumseonwon, Namjangsa Temple, Sangju
1123720670000.description: This wooden seated Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva is considered a work of the 15th century, early Joseon, based on its aristocratic face, drapery, jewelry, and rounded topknot. Because surviving examples of early Joseon Buddhist sculpture are very rare, it is regarded as an important benchmark work. Inscriptions found during later re-gilding in 1701 and 1841 provide historical evidence about the image's production and repairs.

1123720680000.description: This main Buddha hall was built in the late 17th century and has survived through several repairs. It is a late Joseon Buddhist hall with a dignified five-bay front. The interior decoration, including old dancheong painting on the ceiling and phoenix paintings on the sloped ceiling panels, is especially notable.

1123720690000.description: This pagoda is thought to have been built in the late Unified Silla or early Goryeo period. It follows the brick-like masonry pagoda style concentrated in the Gyeongbuk region. Its niche on only one side of the first story and the floral carvings on the niche posts are distinctive features.

1123120700000.title_en: Drawings of the Main Government Office of the Jangyongyeong Guard Unit
1123120700000.description: This set consists of architectural drawings of the main office of Jangyongyeong, the royal guard unit established by King Jeongjo, drawn in 1799 and 1801. It includes one colored view and two plan drawings, and records the layout and changes of the compound in detail. The set is an important visual source for understanding the location, scale, and arrangement of the former Jangyongyeong office in Seoul.

1123720710000.title_en: Stone Seated Maitreya Buddha Triad, Jangchanggok Valley, Namsan Mountain, Gyeongju
1123720710000.description: This triad consists of a seated Maitreya Buddha in the center and standing attendant bodhisattvas on the left and right. It is widely known as a symbolic work showing Maitreya belief and practice in the Three Kingdoms period, and it is considered the earliest surviving Korean seated Buddha image of this type. The central Buddha and the attendants are rendered with gentle faces and detailed ornaments and robes.

1123820720000.title_en: Wooden Seated Amitabha Triad and Relics, Wondangam Hermitage, Haeinsa Temple, Hapcheon
1123820720000.description: This triad at Wondangam Hermitage consists of an Amitabha Buddha with the teaching mudra, Avalokiteshvara wearing a crown with a transformation Buddha, and a head-shaved Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva. It is thought to have been made in the late 15th century, based on the form of the images and the associated votive inscription. The bundle also includes 8 groups of buried relics, which help document the production background and later history of the triad.

1123820730000.title_en: Avatamsaka Sutra (True Edition) from the Reliquary of the Wooden Amitabha Triad of Wondangam Hermitage, Haeinsa Temple, Hapcheon
1123820730000.description: This is the 23 fascicles corresponding to the "True Edition" section among the relic texts enshrined in the wooden Amitabha Triad at Wondangam Hermitage, Haeinsa Temple. It was printed in the late 14th to early 15th century from woodblocks carved in the mid-13th century and preserved in several later bindings. The text provides important evidence for the printing culture of Haeinsa and for the condition and preservation of the Haeinsa Goryeo woodblocks.

1123820740000.title_en: Avatamsaka Sutra (Jeongwon Edition) from the Reliquary of the Wooden Amitabha Triad of Wondangam Hermitage, Haeinsa Temple, Hapcheon
1123820740000.description: This item is the five fascicles corresponding to the "Jeongwon Edition" among the relic texts enshrined in the wooden Amitabha Triad at Wondangam Hermitage, Haeinsa Temple. It was printed in the late 14th to early 15th century from woodblocks carved in the mid-13th century, and the fascicles are largely complete and in relatively good condition. The work is valued as source material for studying Haeinsa's printing culture and the preservation state of the Haeinsa Goryeo woodblocks.

1123820750000.title_en: Individual Dhāraṇī from the Reliquary of the Wooden Amitabha Triad of Wondangam Hermitage, Haeinsa Temple, Hapcheon
1123820750000.description: This is a single small-format fascicle of dhāraṇī among the relic texts enshrined in the wooden Amitabha Triad at Wondangam Hermitage, Haeinsa Temple. It was printed in the 15th century from woodblocks carved in 1375, and was discovered in 2017 inside the wooden Amitabha Buddha statue. The first page includes a figural illustration dated and identified with the carver Jeon Seong-cheok, making it an important source for the study of Buddhist illustrations and Goryeo Buddhist art.

1123420760000.title_en: Seated Wooden-Seated Clay Shakyamuni Buddha Triad and Four Standing Bodhisattvas, Gongju Gapsa Temple
1123420760000.description: This group consists of seven Buddhist statues made in 1617 by nine sculptors, including Haengsa. The set includes three seated Buddhas and four standing bodhisattvas, and it is regarded as the largest and finest surviving example of a seven-figure Buddhist ensemble made after the Japanese invasions. The statues were formed using clay over a wooden armature, and the reliquary offerings provide the exact date and names of the makers.

1121120770000.title_en: Relic Texts from the Seated Clay Shakyamuni Buddha Triad and Four Standing Bodhisattvas, Gongju Gapsa Temple
1121120770000.description: These are eight relic texts discovered inside the clay statues at Gapsa Temple, including one handwritten copy of the Diamond Sutra and seven printed works. The prints date from the late Goryeo period to the mid-16th century and are thought to have been placed inside the statues before their making in 1617. They are important as a set for studying the texts, bindings, and printed editions used in Buddhist statue reliquaries.

1123720780000.description: Yeonsujeon Hall was built during the Joseon period to commemorate a king's entry into the Giroso, the office for retired officials, and it is considered the only surviving example that retains its original form. Its dancheong and wall paintings are notable for their high-quality gilded polychrome decoration and for the rich use of motifs associated with the Korean Empire. The building is important evidence for changes in commemorative architecture and royal ceremonial style in the late Korean Empire.

1121120790000.title_en: Easy Guide to the Prevention of Epidemics (Eonhae), 2020
1121120790000.description: This medical book was compiled in 1525 by royal physicians Kim Sunmong, Yu Yeongjeong, and Park Segeo by order of the king, and was printed in Chinese text with Korean vernacular explanation. The National Hangeul Museum copy bears a royal-gift seal and an inner presentation note showing that it was bestowed in January 1578 to Kim Jip by the chief state councilor Yoon Du-su. It is considered the earliest known extant edition of its kind and is very rare.

1122120800000.title_en: Screen of the Picture of the Gathering of Old and New Meritorious Retainers
1122120800000.description: This record painting depicts the banquet held at the Office of Meritorious Subjects in November 1604, when old and new meritorious retainers gathered together during King Seonjo's reign. The work includes the names of the participants and shows the ceremony in a compact bird's-eye composition. It is considered the only known painting of this subject and an important example of early 17th-century documentary painting.

1123720970000.description: This hall of Gyeongju Hyanggyo was rebuilt in 1614 and has been repaired in the 18th and 19th centuries. It is a gabled wooden building with five bays in the front and three bays on the side, and it is the largest surviving single Myeongnyundang hall at a hyanggyo in Korea, excluding guesthouse-type examples.

1123720980000.title_en: East and West Wings and Sin Sammun Gate of Gyeongju Hyanggyo
1123720980000.description: The east and west wings were rebuilt in 1604 and remain through later repairs in 1829 and 1995. Together with the main hall, they form the ritual area of Gyeongju Hyanggyo, and the Sin Sammun Gate, rebuilt in 1602, is a three-bay gabled gate that preserves older forms in its layout and details.

1123620990000.title_en: Daeseongjeon Hall of Changpyeong Hyanggyo, Damyang
1123620990000.description: The present form of Changpyeong Hyanggyo was completed in 1689 after several rebuildings and repairs. Its Daeseongjeon Hall shows a distinctive bracket system and decorative details, including unusual false brackets and finely carved panels.

1123621000000.title_en: Myeongnyundang Hall of Changpyeong Hyanggyo, Damyang
1123621000000.description: The present layout of Changpyeong Hyanggyo was completed in 1689 after repeated reconstruction. Myeongnyundang Hall is a gabled wooden building with four bays on the front and three on the side, and it is notable for its open front and exposed timber structure.

1123621010000.description: Suncheon Hyanggyo was established in 1407, and the present Daeseongjeon Hall can be dated to 1649 from an inscribed ridge-beam record. It is a five-bay by three-bay building with an open front porch and a bracket structure that reflects the style of the mid-17th century.

1123721020000.title_en: Jeonghakdang Hall of Kumo Seowon, Gumi
1123721020000.description: Jeonghakdang Hall of Geumo Seowon was rebuilt in 1602. The hall preserves older construction methods, including the use of round columns even in the ondol room area, large members, and restrained ornament.

1123721030000.title_en: Sanghyeonmyo Shrine of Geumo Seowon, Gumi
