1123721030000.description: Sanghyeonmyo is a three-bay by three-bay gabled shrine rebuilt in 1602. It has no front bay for a porch, and its walls and doorways are set between the front and rear columns to secure a larger interior space.

1123721040000.title_en: Mandaeru Pavilion of Byeongsan Seowon, Andong
1123721040000.description: Mandaeru is a pavilion at Byeongsan Seowon that was built before 1717. It preserves the functions expected of a seowon pavilion while making effective use of the landscape, and it is noted for its restrained design and structural simplicity.

1123721050000.description: Dosanseodang was built in 1561 during the reign of King Myeongjong of Joseon. It is valued as a building that well embodies the architectural ideal pursued by scholars in the 16th century, with a simple interior of maru, ondol room, and kitchen within a minimal three-kan by one-kan plan. After Toegye's death, the seodang was left in place and a seowon was built behind it, making it a rare example where a memorial site and a seowon remain together in one compound.

1123721060000.description: Nongunjeongsa is a site where scholars from Yeongnam studied under Toegye in their youth, and its original form has been well preserved. It is a notable example of an educational building that retains the form of a single-unit house, with an '工'-shaped plan centered on the main building and side spaces at the front and back ends. Its design is based on the idea of Beopyeon, the monk artisan who oversaw the construction of Dosanseodang, and it was completed by his disciple Jeongil.

1123321070000.description: Ijidang originated from the school established by Jo Jeong in Okcheon in the late 16th century, and was renovated around 1674 under the leadership of Kim Man-gyun, with the left pavilion added and the name given by Song Si-yeol. It is a composite structure that combines the functions of a seojae and a pavilion, with a U-shaped plan and two-story pavilions on both side wings. The building overlooks the Seohwa Stream and the surrounding rocks and hills, and its form reflects the simple and refined style of late Joseon architecture.

1123721080000.title_en: Rock-carved Maitreya Buddha Seated Figure, Bongamsa Temple, Mungyeong
1123721080000.description: This rock-carved Buddha at Bongamsa Temple in Mungyeong was made in 1663 and is identified in historical records as the work overseen by the monk Hwajeokdang Uicheon. It is a large seated Maitreya Buddha carved on a rock face, with a clearly modeled face, simple robes, and the yogic seated posture, and it is also important for the study of Buddhist painting and Maitreya iconography in the late Joseon period. Because its date, patronage, and iconography can be verified through documents, it is a key reference work for rock-carved Buddhas of the period.

1123821090000.description: This bronze drum was made in 1190 for Miryukwon, as shown by the inscription on its side. Miryukwon is believed to have been a name used for the former Injewon in Gongju for a short time during the Goryeo period. It is a typical Goryeo bronze drum with three knobs, an open back, and lotus and flower-boss ornamentation, and it is an important example for understanding bronze casting techniques of the 12th century.

1123821100000.title_en: Painted Banner for the Assembly on Vulture Peak and Hanging Case, Okcheonsa Temple, Goseong
1123821100000.description: This hanging Buddhist banner and its case were made in 1808 by the chief painter Seongsu Pyeongsam and 18 other monk painters. The banner depicts the Vulture Peak Assembly with Sakyamuni Buddha, the two attendant disciples Ananda and Kashyapa, and six Buddha figures, and its inscription clearly identifies the subject. The case is lacquered and decorated with metal fittings, and it preserves records of the production date and makers inside.
1123821100000.material: Ink and color on silk; lacquered wood case

1123821110000.description: These woodblocks were recarved in 1603 at Neunginam Hermitage in Jirisan using a printed edition from the Shinhungsa or Songgwangsa line as the base text, and they have been preserved as a complete set of 22 blocks at Ssanggyesa Temple in Hadong. The text, compiled by the Tang monk Zongmi, summarizes the essential points of his Seonyeonjeonjip and discusses the classification of Chan practice and the relationship between Seon and Gyo. The blocks are an important source for studying pre-1636 Buddhist printing, the people involved, and the relationship between Neunginam and Ssanggyesa.

1123821120000.title_en: Combined Woodblocks for Wondon Seongbulron and Ganhwa Georuilron
1123821120000.description: These woodblocks were carved in 1604 at Neunginam Hermitage in Jirisan and later moved to Ssanggyesa Temple, and the full set of 11 blocks survives. They contain Ginhul's two works, Wondon Seongbulron and Ganhwa Georuilron, which explain his thought in question-and-answer form and emphasize meditation based on gwanhwa. The blocks are well preserved and are important as a pre-1636 example of Buddhist woodblock printing.

1123220890000.title_en: Gangneung Hyanggyo East Wing, West Wing, and Front Corridor
1123220890000.description: These three buildings belong to Gangneung Hyanggyo. The east and west wings are each five bays long and flank the main courtyard in front of Daeseongjeon, while the front corridor stretches horizontally across the front of the main hall. They preserve older architectural features such as carefully made lattice windows, bracket arms, and carved braces.

1123120900000.description: This is the main worship hall of Suwon Hyanggyo, rebuilt at its present site in 1795 after the hyanggyo was moved with the relocation of the town center. It is a 20-bay building with a large, formal structure and refined late Joseon carpentry techniques. The building is notable for the detailed records of its construction in the Hwaseong Seongyeok Uigwe.

1123120910000.description: This Daeseongjeon was rebuilt in the mid-17th century after being destroyed during the Japanese invasions. It keeps the traditional form of a Confucian shrine hall with an open front porch and a gabled roof. The building preserves older construction methods and is an important example for studying mid-Joseon architecture.

1123120920000.description: Punghwaru is a large gate pavilion at the front of Anseong Hyanggyo, used both as a pavilion and as the main entrance. It is the largest surviving gate pavilion of a Joseon-period hyanggyo, with an 11-bay front and a single-bay side. Its structure reflects careful use of timber and construction techniques characteristic of the 17th century.

1123820930000.description: This lecture hall of Danseong Hyanggyo was completed in the 1720s after the hyanggyo had long functioned mainly as a shrine. It preserves an unusual pavilion-like plan and a rare roof and framing arrangement. The building is considered historically and academically important because of its uncommon form.

1123820940000.description: Miryang Hyanggyo is a representative example of a side-by-side layout, with the shrine hall and lecture hall placed in parallel. The Daeseongjeon was rebuilt in 1602 after being destroyed in wartime and later moved, while reused members such as columns and brackets preserve older Joseon-period construction methods. It is especially notable because the shrine hall and lecture hall face in different directions.

1123820950000.description: This lecture hall was rebuilt in 1618 after the Japanese invasions and remains one of the better-preserved hyanggyo buildings in Gyeongsangnam-do. It keeps the typical large lecture-hall plan with side rooms and retains bracket forms characteristic of the 17th century. The structure also shows reinforcement methods suited to its size.

1123720960000.title_en: Sangju Hyanggyo Daeseongjeon, East Wing, and West Wing
1123720960000.description: This group consists of the main worship hall and its east and west wings at Sangju Hyanggyo. The east and west wings were rebuilt in the early 17th century and have kept their original placement and general structural form. The complex is notable for its formal layout and for adapting well to the sloped site.

1123721170000.title_en: Scripture Cabinet of Daedunsa Temple, Gumi
1123721170000.description: This pair of Buddhist scripture cabinets was made in 1630, as recorded in an inscription on the back. The inscription also names the craftsmen involved in the making of the cabinets, making it a rare and important example for the study of late Joseon Buddhist woodcraft. Paintings of the Four Heavenly Kings are placed on the inside of the doors, suggesting that the pair originally stood beside the altar in the main hall.

1123121180000.description: This is a surviving woodblock-printed copy of the Yuan dynasty legal code first published in 1346. It is the only known extant copy of a Yuan legal text and the only example identified in the world, making it a highly important source for the study of late Goryeo and early Joseon legal history and bibliography.

1124521190000.description: Geungnakbojeon is the main Buddhist hall of Biamsa Temple in Sejong. It is a Joseon-period hall built on a side-three-bay plan with a side depth of two bays, reflecting architectural changes after the wars of the late 16th century.

1123421200000.description: Daeungjeon Hall at Gapsa Temple was rebuilt shortly after the Imjin War and has undergone several repairs since then. The hall preserves the form of a 17th-century multi-bracketed gabled Buddhist hall, including its five-bay front, three-bay side, and roof structure.

1123721210000.title_en: Beomjongnu Pavilion of Daegoksa Temple, Uiseong
1123721210000.description: This two-story bell pavilion was rebuilt sometime between 1644 and 1683 after being burned down during the Japanese invasions. It is a Joseon-period pavilion with a three-by-three bay plan and shows an eclectic mixture of bracket styles and structural features.

1123621220000.description: This stele was originally erected after 1281 to honor Choe Seok, a magistrate known for his integrity, and was rebuilt in 1617 by Yi Sugwang after earlier destruction. The current stele has a rounded top, a large relief inscription on the front, and a pedestal carved with lotus designs.

1123621230000.title_en: Amitabha Buddha Preaching Painting and Relic Objects, Baegyangsa Temple, Jangseong
1123621230000.description: This hanging scroll was painted in 1775 by Seokmin and ten other monk-painters when the Amitabha Buddha image in Geungnakjeon Hall was repaired. The painting was stolen in 1994 and recovered in 2006, and its reliquary objects were also preserved, making it an important source for the study of late-18th-century Buddhist paintings and relic deposits.

1123521240000.title_en: Gilt-bronze Shoes from the Buried Tomb No. 1, Bongdeok-ri, Gochang
1123521240000.description: This pair of gilt-bronze shoes was excavated in 2009 from Stone Chamber No. 4 of Tomb No. 1, the largest of the large mound burials at Bongdeok-ri, Gochang. The shoes were found almost intact on both feet of the buried individual and are decorated with various openwork motifs such as dragons, human-faced bird figures, paired birds, monsters, and lotus patterns.

1122621490000.title_en: Stone Seated Amitabha Buddha of Sinheungsa Temple, Ulsan
1122621490000.description: This seated Amitabha Buddha is the main Buddha image of an Amitabha triad enshrined in Daeungjeon Hall at Sinheungsa Temple. It was made in 1649 from bolseok, a white mineral stone, and the votive inscription records that the stone was quarried in Eocheon (present-day Ocheon-eup, Pohang) and transported by boat to the temple. It is known as the only dated Buddha image made by the sculptor Yeongsaek (also written Yeongi) using bolseok in Gyeongsang-do.

1121121500000.title_en: Vairocana Buddha Triad Great Banner Painting of Heungcheonsa Temple, Seoul
1121121500000.description: This great banner painting was produced in 1832 by the monk-painter Hwadam Sinseon and 16 other painters. It was made to pray for the longevity of King Sunjo, the queen, and members of the royal family, with many royal figures and court ladies participating as donors. The composition depicts the Vairocana Buddha Triad with iconographic variations, and the work preserves its votive contents, banner case, and related records.

1121121510000.title_en: Gyeonggeundang Hall and Okcheopdang Hall, Jongchinbu Office
1121121510000.description: These are the main buildings of Jongchinbu, the government office in charge of the royal clan, rebuilt in 1866 during the reign of Heungseon Daewongun. Gyeonggeundang served as the main hall for princes and royal clan members, while Okcheopdang was built at a lower rank and connected by a corridor. They preserve the layout and construction methods of a late Joseon central government office and retain much of their original material through relocation and reinstallation.

1122221520000.title_en: Seonhwadang Hall, Gyeongsang Provincial Government Office, Daegu
1122221520000.description: Seonhwadang was the main hall of the Gyeongsang Provincial Government Office, where the magistrate of the highest provincial rank carried out official duties. It was rebuilt in 1807 and has largely preserved its original form despite later repairs and some alteration. The building also retains features such as a rain gauge stand and flagpole holder that help show the office complex’s layout and functions.

1123121530000.description: Sueojangdae is located on a strategic peak on the west side of Namhansanseong Fortress, overlooking both the inside and outside of the fortress. The present building was rebuilt in 1836, after a two-story command post had been built in 1751 and named the West Command Post. It is a two-story military structure that has retained its form since the 19th-century rebuilding and is associated with visits by several Joseon kings.

1123121540000.description: Yeonmugwan was founded in 1625 during the reconstruction of Namhansanseong Fortress and became the main building of Sueocheong, the central military command established in 1626. It was later used as the headquarters of Sueocheong and as the office of the governor of Gwangju after the abolition of the local command in 1795. The building’s records document several repairs, and its structure reflects its military function.

1123121550000.description: This guesthouse hall was built before 1363, making it the oldest extant guesthouse building in Korea. Although it was repaired, relocated, and reused over time, it preserves late Goryeo building techniques such as jar-shaped beams and bracket composition. It was later used as a school building before being moved to its present location.

1123221560000.description: Chilsadang is a government office hall in the Gangneung Daeodobu office complex and was used as the office of the local magistrate during the Joseon period. It was rebuilt in 1632, expanded and repaired in 1726, and rebuilt again after a fire in 1867. The building has an unusual plan with different floor levels and a distinctive bracket structure and decorative details.

1122221330000.description: Sumajeon Hall at Donghwasa Temple in Daegu is recorded as first built in 1465 and rebuilt in 1702 after the Japanese invasions of 1592. It is a one-bay Buddhist hall with a dapo bracket system and a gable roof, and it is noted as the only surviving example in Korea of this combination. The structure preserves a rare roof framework and bracket arrangement that suggests reuse of members from an earlier building.

1123721340000.description: Suun Japbang is a handwritten Korean-language cookbook in Chinese characters compiled by Kim Yu and his grandson Kim Ryeong of Andong. It contains 122 entries on food preparation and related matters, including liquor, vinegar, pickles, sauces, sweets, soups, noodles, and methods for sowing and storing vegetables and fruit. The book is valued as a unique manuscript that reflects the food culture of Joseon yangban households and the traditions of the Andong area.

1121121350000.title_en: Buddhist Ritual Offering Implements Excavated from the Site of Yeongguksa Temple, Seoul
1121121350000.description: This set of Buddhist ritual offering implements was recovered in 2012 beneath the foundation of Building Site No. 5 at the presumed center of the former site of Yeongguksa Temple in Seoul. The group includes a vajra, a bell, an incense burner, an incense container, spoons, a stand, a lidded jar, and a water vessel, all of which were found together. A later excavation identified the site as Yeongguksa Temple, showing that the objects were used there in the Goryeo period.

1122421360000.title_en: Wooden Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva Triad and the Ten Kings, Deoklimsa Temple, Gwangju
1122421360000.description: This set of wooden Buddhist statues was made in 1680 by the sculptor monk Saenan, as shown by dedicatory inscriptions found inside the images. It consists of the Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva triad and statues of the Ten Kings and attendants, forming a large underworld hall ensemble. The group is important as an early work of Saenan and as a representative example of late 17th-century Joseon Buddhist sculpture.

1123621370000.title_en: Wooden Shakyamuni Triad and Sixteen Arhats, Neunggasa Temple, Goheung
1123621370000.description: This group of wooden Buddhist statues in the Eungjin Hall of Neunggasa Temple was produced in June 1685 under the leadership of the sculptor monk Saenan and his associates. The set includes the Shakyamuni triad and sixteen arhats, with dedicatory inscriptions preserved inside the images. It is significant for its unusual iconographic arrangement and for its importance in understanding Saenan's workshop and artistic lineage.

1123821380000.title_en: Wooden Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva Triad and the Ten Kings, Eunhasa Temple, Gimhae
1123821380000.description: This set of wooden Buddhist statues was made in 1687 for the Ten Kings Hall of Seorimsa Temple, the predecessor of present-day Eunhasa Temple in Gimhae. The ensemble includes the Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva triad, the Ten Kings, and attendant figures, and it survives in nearly complete form. It is an important dated work by the sculptor monk Saenan and shows the characteristic style of his school.

1123621390000.title_en: Wooden Shakyamuni Triad and Four Bodhisattvas, Hwaeomsa Temple, Gurye
1123621390000.description: The statues enshrined in Geakwangjeon Hall at Hwaeomsa Temple were made in 1703 as a large-scale set led by the sculptor monk Saenan after the hall was rebuilt. The ensemble consists of a Shakyamuni triad and four standing bodhisattvas, and the dedicatory inscription records the participation of many sculptor monks. It is a late work of Saenan and is notable for its large scale, balanced composition, and important iconography.

1121121400000.description: The Denny Taegukgi is a Korean national flag once owned by Owen Nickerson Denny, a U.S. diplomat who served as a foreign adviser to King Gojong. It is believed to date to 1890 or earlier and was donated to Korea by a descendant in 1981. The flag is important as one of the earliest surviving Taegukgi and as evidence for the early form and making of Korea's national flag.

1123221570000.title_en: Seonhwadang Hall, Gangwon Provincial Government Office Site, Wonju
1123221570000.description: Seonhwadang Hall was the main hall of the Gangwon provincial government office in the Joseon period, where the centrally appointed magistrate conducted official duties. It is notable for preserving the original Pojeongmun Gate, making it the only former provincial government office that retains the hierarchy of its entrance space in situ.

1123821580000.description: Giseonggwan Hall served as the guesthouse of Geoje Hyeon and later Geoje Dohobu from its construction in 1665 until the early 20th century. Documentary remains found during dismantling repairs in 1974 provide important evidence for studying the construction of late Joseon local government buildings, and the hall is unusual for its different roof treatment on the front and rear sides.

1121121590000.description: Angbuilgu is a hemispherical sundial, and the surviving example from the National Palace Museum of Korea is one of about ten known in Korea. Its inscription uses a latitude value first recorded in sources from after 1713, so the object is estimated to date to after that year; it has a silver-inlaid dial, engraved seasonal divisions, and a base decorated with dragon and cloud motifs.

1121121600000.description: Angbuilgu is a hemispherical sundial, and this example in the Gyeongju National Museum is one of about ten known in Korea. It closely resembles the National Palace Museum example but differs in the direction of the inscription and the form of the base, which is decorated with dragon, cloud, and turtle-head motifs.

1121121610000.description: Angbuilgu is a hemispherical sundial, and this example in the Sungsin Women's University Museum is one of about ten known in Korea. It closely resembles the other two designated examples and has a silver-inlaid dial, engraved seasonal divisions, and a base decorated with dragon, cloud, and turtle-head motifs.

1123721620000.title_en: Gilt-bronze Medicine Buddha Standing Statue, Bunhwangsa Temple, Gyeongju
1123721620000.description: This gilt-bronze standing Buddha at Bunhwangsa Temple was made in 1609 and later repaired with gilt in 1775. It is significant as the only and largest surviving gilt-bronze standing Buddha of the late Joseon period, and inscriptions found during repair work confirm its creation date and history.

1123621630000.title_en: Celadon Incense Burner with Lion-shaped Lid
1123621630000.description: This Goryeo incense burner consists of a celadon body and a lion-shaped lid, and four complete examples survive as two sets. They were recovered from the Taean shipwreck, a vessel that sank while carrying 12th-century celadon from Gangjin toward Gaegyeong, and they show an unusual and highly distinctive lion form.

1121121640000.title_en: Wooden Seated Tathagata Buddha Statue, Jogyesa Temple, Seoul
1121121640000.description: This wooden seated Buddha statue was made in the 15th century Joseon period and was originally enshrined at Dogapsa Temple in Yeongam, Jeollanam-do. It was moved in 1938 to serve as the main Buddha of the Joseon Buddhist General Headquarters, now Jogyesa Temple, and is valued for its historical role in modern Korean Buddhism and its refined early Joseon style.

1121121650000.description: This is the earliest extant collection of sijo lyrics in Korea, compiled from 580 songs that had been orally transmitted up to the late Joseon period. It is attributed to Kim Cheontaek and is valued as an early anthology of traditional song lyrics and as an important source for the history of Korean literature, music, and Hangeul calligraphy.

1123821660000.description: This is a woodblock-printed book made from blocks carved in 1335 at Gyerimbu in Gyeongju. It is the earliest known surviving edition of the same text and contains colophon information on the printing, block carvers, and local figures involved in the publication.

1121121670000.description: This is an early woodblock edition of Im Yosu's annotated commentary on the Chunqiu and Zuozhuan, carved and printed in 1431 in Cheongdo, Gyeongsang-do. The extant copy is rare and survives in 50 volumes, with detailed publication information preserved in the colophon and title page format.

1123521680000.title_en: Screen with Old and New Method Astronomical Charts
1123521680000.description: This eight-panel folding screen presents a traditional East Asian star chart and a Western-style astronomical chart side by side, along with an additional sun, moon, and five planets chart. It was painted in color on silk and is thought to date to the late 19th century based on the use of imported green pigment.

1121121690000.description: This album brings together 14 letters written in Hangeul by King Jeongjo, from his years as crown prince to his reign, along with two large-calligraphy pieces. It shows changes in his handwriting over more than 50 years and is valuable for the study of Joseon royal culture and Hangeul calligraphy.

1121121700000.description: This is a rare 16th-century movable-type edition of the core legal code that defined the Joseon state system. The volumes correspond to the first three sections of the code and are the only known domestic copy of this part in this edition.

1123121710000.description: This is a rare 16th-century movable-type edition of the Joseon legal code. The surviving volumes correspond to the fourth through sixth sections, covering military, penal, and public works regulations, and are the only known domestic copy of this part in this edition.

1123721720000.title_en: Mubyeonru Pavilion of Oksanseowon Confucian Academy, Gyeongju
1123721720000.description: Mubyeonru is the main gate pavilion of Oksanseowon Confucian Academy in Gyeongju, said to have been built when the academy was first established in 1572. It is a two-story wooden structure that has remained on its original site and preserves dated roof tiles that record later repair campaigns.

1123221810000.description: This Buddhist painting was made in 1755 by the chief monk-painter Taejeon and nine other monk-painters. After being taken out of Sinheungsa Temple, it spent more than 70 years overseas and was recently returned from the United States. It was originally enshrined in Geukrakjeon Hall at Sinheungsa for the performance of Yeongsanjae rituals.

1123721820000.description: Cheongamjeong Pavilion is a pavilion in the grounds of the Chungjae head family of the Andong Gwon clan in Bonghwa, North Gyeongsang Province. Historical records indicate that it was built in 1526 by Gwon Beol, and later repaired and altered in the 17th and 18th centuries. It is regarded as an early example of the scholar-official pavilion culture built for private rest and study.

1123721830000.title_en: Anyangru Pavilion of Buseoksa Temple, Yeongju
1123721830000.description: Anyangru Pavilion is the gate pavilion in front of Muryangsujeon Hall at Buseoksa Temple, a UNESCO World Heritage temple in Yeongju. The present pavilion was built in 1576 after an earlier building named Gangeungak was destroyed by fire in 1555. It is a two-story pavilion that serves as the main entrance to the Muryangsujeon area.

1123721840000.title_en: Beomjonggak Pavilion of Buseoksa Temple, Yeongju
1123721840000.description: Beomjonggak Pavilion is the bell pavilion of Buseoksa Temple in Yeongju, located on the temple's central approach axis. According to records, it was rebuilt in 1747 after a fire in 1746. It is a two-story pavilion with a bell, wooden fish, and cloud plate inside the upper level.

1123121850000.description: Sungnyeoljeon Shrine was first established in 1638 to honor King Onjo, the founder of Baekje, in connection with events during the Manchu invasion of 1636. It was moved to its present site in 1661 and later received the shrine name 'Sungnyeoljeon' during King Jeongjo's reign. The present building preserves the original form of a 17th-century state shrine.

1123221860000.description: Chanjeolsa Shrine was built in 1685 to honor the Six Martyred Ministers and other loyal subjects executed under King Sejo. It later received the shrine title 'Chanjeol' and was moved to its current location in 1705. The complex includes a lecture hall, east and west quarters, and a pavilion, resembling a Confucian academy layout.

1123321870000.description: Secheonjae Shrine Hall was first built in 1691 by Park Se-pil of the Chungju Park clan's Gangneung branch. It served as a place to memorialize three generations of ancestors and to educate descendants. The building retains its simple plan and restrained decoration, representing a typical shrine hall of the Chungcheong region.

1123621880000.title_en: Double Loyalists' Memorial Gate, Yesan Song Clan, Goheung
1123621880000.description: This memorial gate was erected in 1704 to honor Song Daerip and his son Song Sim of the Yeosan Song clan, both of whom served with merit and died for their country during the Imjin War and the Manchu invasion. The structure has a hipped roof and an elaborate mixed bracketing system rare for a memorial gate. It preserves plaques and architectural details associated with its original construction and later repairs.

1123621890000.title_en: Chuwondang Hall, Gangjin, Hae Nam Yun Clan
1123621890000.description: This ritual hall was built around 1649 by Yun Seondo to honor Yun Sa-bo and his son Yun Gyeong, the founding ancestor and branch founder of the Hae Nam Yun clan's Deokjeong-dong line. It has been repaired several times and preserves a wide ritual floor, as well as clan documents and woodblocks kept inside, including the 1702 genealogy woodblocks.

1123621900000.title_en: Yeongmodang Hall, Gangjin, Hae Nam Yun Clan
1123621900000.description: This ancestral ritual hall was built in 1737 and repaired in 1813 to enshrine the spirit tablets of Yun Gwang-jeon, Yun Dan-bong, and Yun Dan-hak of the Hae Nam Yun clan. Its layout and details, including fish-shaped ornamentation and a ventilated raised roof over the service wing, provide useful evidence for regional 18th-century architecture.

1123521910000.description: This shrine was built in 1771 to enshrine the spirit tablets of Yi Han, the progenitor of the Jeonju Yi clan, and his wife. Located behind Gyeonggijeon Shrine, it shows the typical form of a late Joseon clan shrine and reflects strong state involvement in its construction, management, and rituals.

1123721920000.description: This ritual hall was rebuilt in 1484 near the grave of Son So to protect the tomb and pray for the deceased's repose; it was later repaired in 1595 and 1786. Its L-shaped plan, gabled roof, and attached auxiliary roof preserve architectural features of the 15th century and document its transformation into a Confucian ritual building.

1123521930000.description: This building is thought to have been constructed around 1749 and survives together with the magistrate's office and pavilion, making it a rare example for studying the daily life of a local magistrate. It has a U-shaped plan and combines a main block and side wings arranged to separate official, living, and service spaces.

1123721940000.title_en: East and West Three-story Stone Pagodas of the Former Yeombulsa Temple Site, Gyeongju
1123721940000.description: These two three-story stone pagodas were built in the first half of the 8th century at a temple site believed to have been founded in the early 8th century and abandoned in the 12th century. The east pagoda was once moved in 1963 but returned to its original location in 2009, and the west pagoda was also restored on site after excavation.

1123121950000.title_en: King's Merit Certificate for Son So
1123121950000.description: This is a certificate of meritorious service granted in 1467 to Son So, a member of the Gyeongju Son clan, for his role in suppressing the Yi Si-ae Rebellion. It records the recipient, his achievements, rewards, the list of meritorious retainers by rank, and the issue date, and it survives in its original mounting condition.

1123721960000.description: This agricultural manual was compiled in China in 996 by Han Eok and covers seasonal farming methods, livestock raising, food processing, medicine, hygiene, commerce, and tools. The designated copy is an early Joseon metal-type edition printed with mixed type, and it is considered one of the oldest known extant editions.

1123421410000.title_en: Taegukgi with Kim Gu’s Inscription and Signature
1123421410000.description: This silk Taegukgi was made in 1941 and bears a handwritten inscription and signature by Kim Gu, then chairman of the Provisional Government State Council, dated March 16, 1941. Kim Gu gave it to the Belgian priest Charles Meeus, and it later passed through the family of An Changho’s wife before being donated to the Independence Hall of Korea in 1985.

1121121420000.description: This Taegukgi was discovered in 2009 during the dismantling and restoration of Chilseonggak Hall at Jingwansa Temple in Seoul, together with 19 independence-related newspapers and pamphlets. It is thought to have been made around 1919, and it is especially notable for having been painted with a Taeguk and four trigrams over a Japanese flag.

1123721430000.description: These stone banner-pole supports stand at the south entrance of Bunhwangsa Temple in Gyeongju and are generally attributed to the Unified Silla period. The supporting base stone has an unusual turtle-shaped form, and the overall layout suggests that the banner pole once stood here for the temple’s use.

1123121440000.description: This martial arts manual was compiled by Han Gyo under royal order, based on Qi Jiguang’s Jixiao Xinshu, and was printed from woodblocks in 1598. It explains and illustrates six weapons, with Korean explanations added in hangul, and is regarded as the earliest extant Korean martial arts book.

1122221450000.title_en: Commentary on the Awakening of Mahayana Faith, Volume Lower
1122221450000.description: This is the lower volume of the 1461 woodblock edition printed from the Gangyeong Dogam blocks during the reign of King Sejo. It is the only known surviving copy of a Joseon-period edition of Fazang’s commentary on the Awakening of Mahayana Faith.

1121121460000.description: This scroll is volume 175 of the Goryeo first Tripitaka edition, printed from woodblocks carved in the 11th century. It is the only known extant copy of this volume in Korea and is an important source for studying the creation and circulation of the early Tripitaka blocks.

1123521470000.title_en: Exemption Certificate for Muwisa Temple, Gangjin
1123521470000.description: This official royal document, issued on August 10, 1457, ordered that Muwisa Temple in Gangjin be exempted from certain labor obligations. It retains King Sejo’s seal and signature marks and is an important source for studying early Joseon state documents and Buddhist policy.

1123221480000.title_en: Wooden Seated Manjushri Bodhisattva, Bohyeonsa Temple, Gangneung
1123221480000.description: This wooden seated Bodhisattva image is thought to have been made in the late Goryeo to early Joseon period, although the exact date is not known. A repair record found inside the sculpture shows that it was repaired in 1599 by the sculptors Seokjun and Won-o, and the image is noted for its elegant form and distinctive crown and hair arrangement.

1123122130000.title_en: Gilt-bronze Seated Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva, Cheongnyongsa Temple, Anseong
1123122130000.description: This gilt-bronze seated Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva statue was made in the late Goryeo period, in the 14th century. It wears a jeweled crown and dharma robe, sits in full lotus posture on a pedestal, and makes a preaching gesture with both hands. The crown and pedestal are later replacements, and the work is important as a rare gilt-bronze example of a bodhisattva type usually made in wood.

1122122140000.description: This book is the section of the 30-volume commentary on the Buddhist scripture Suramgama-sutra corresponding to volumes 9 through 15. It was printed at the Gangyeongdogam in 1462, during King Sejo's reign, as shown by the publication record at the end of each volume. The copy is complete, well preserved, and notable as a rare extant printed edition of this work.

1121122150000.title_en: Heohae Calligraphy of the Thousand Character Classic by Yi Hang-bok
1121122150000.description: This manuscript is a Thousand Character Classic copied by Yi Hang-bok in 1607 for the education of his six-year-old grandson Yi Si-jung. The text is written in regular script, with a postface in running-cursive script dated the same year. It is valued as an early surviving autograph copy and as an important source for the history of calligraphy and the Korean language.

1121122160100.title_en: Royal Seals, Royal Books, and Investiture Documents of the Joseon Dynasty (2023-1)
1121122160100.description: This designation covers ritual seals, books, and investiture documents used in the Joseon royal court from 1392 to 1910 when conferring titles, posthumous names, temple names, and honorific names on kings, queens, and other royals. They were enshrined in the royal shrines of Jongmyo, where the seal cases and book cases were kept separately. The group is significant for its long historical continuity, documentary value, and artistic quality as court ritual objects.

1121122160200.title_en: Royal Seals, Royal Books, and Investiture Documents of the Joseon Dynasty (2023-2)
1121122160200.description: This designation covers ritual seals, books, and investiture documents used in the Joseon royal court from 1698 to 1908 when conferring titles, posthumous names, temple names, and honorific names on kings, queens, and other royals. They were originally enshrined in the royal shrines of Jongmyo as part of the court's ritual system. The group is important as documentary evidence for Joseon and Daehan Empire court ceremonies and as examples of court art made by skilled official craftsmen.

1121122160300.title_en: Royal Seals, Royal Books, and Investiture Documents of the Joseon Dynasty (2023-3)
1121122160300.description: This designation covers two royal seals made in 1420 and 1676 as part of the Joseon court's ritual system for conferring titles and honorific names. Such seals were used for investiture ceremonies and were enshrined in the royal shrine of Jongmyo. They are valuable as examples of court ritual objects and as historical records of Joseon royal authority.

1121122170000.description: This calligraphy album was compiled in 1943 by the modern calligrapher and connoisseur O Se-chang at the age of 80. It contains 1,136 calligraphic works by 1,136 people, ranging from Jeong Mong-ju to Yi Do-yeong, spanning about 600 years from the late Goryeo period to the modern era. The volume is important as a major source for the history of Korean calligraphy and for studying historical writing styles and the social background of the writers.

1122622180000.description: This Buddhist painting was made in 1565, during the reign of King Myeongjong, and its date is precisely recorded in the painting inscription. It depicts Amitabha Buddha at the center, with Avalokitesvara, Ksitigarbha, and the Eight Great Bodhisattvas arranged symmetrically around him. The work preserves elements of late Goryeo painting while also showing the color-centered style characteristic of 16th-century Joseon Buddhist painting.
1122622180000.material: Ink and color on hemp cloth

1123822050000.description: Jabangnu at Okcheonsa Temple was first built in 1664 as the main gate facing the dharma hall, and it was rebuilt in pavilion form in 1764. The building stands 7 bays by 3 bays and is used as an entrance pavilion, with side entrances on both sides rather than passage beneath the gate tower. It preserves plaques reading "Okcheonsa" on the front and "Jabangnu" on the back.

1123722060000.description: Daesanru was first built in 1602 as a pavilion and study where Ubok Jeong Gyeong-se retired, lived in seclusion, and pursued learning, and it was later remodeled into its present form in 1778. It functioned as a center for study and exchange within the head family of the clan. The complex consists of a connected single-story study hall and a two-story pavilion arranged in a 丁-shaped plan.

1123122070000.description: Bongguksa Temple was founded under royal patronage to pray for the repose of the two princesses of King Hyeonjong of Joseon. Tree-ring analysis shows that the main timber members of Daegwangmyeongjeon date to the late 17th century, indicating that the hall was built with the temple's original foundation. The hall is a 3-bay by 3-bay Buddhist sanctuary with an imcheong-style bracket structure and a double-eaved gable roof.

1123522080000.title_en: Pyeonun Hwasang Stupa, Silsangsa Temple, Namwon
1123522080000.description: This stupa commemorates Venerable Pyeonun and reflects offerings and remembrance of the monk. An inscription on the stupa body provides information on the line of transmission, the person commemorated, and the date of construction, showing that it was made around 910. Its form is closely related to a ritual incense burner (hangwan), and it has a rare circular plan.

1122522090000.description: These two Hangeul letters were written by the early Joseon military officer Na Singeol to his wife, Mme. Sinchang Meng, and were discovered in 2011 in her tomb in Geumgo-dong, Yuseong District, Daejeon. The content expresses longing for his mother and children, asks that clothing such as a military uniform be sent, and requests that household and farming matters be handled well. Based on the use of the old Hamgyeong Province name "Yeongan-do," the letters are thought to date to the 1490s.

1123822100000.title_en: Wooden Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva Triad and the Ten Kings, Gwanryongsa Temple, Changnyeong
1123822100000.description: This set of 17 wooden Buddhist statues was completed in March 1652 by sculptor monks led by Eunghye and enshrined in the Myeongbujeon Hall at Gwanryongsa Temple. The group includes a wooden Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva triad, the Ten Kings, a Judge, one Ghost King, and two Vajra Guardians. The accompanying votive text matches the extant images, and the group is considered a representative work of Eunghye.

1121122110000.title_en: Painting of Vairocana Buddha as a Triple Body Mandala, Cheongnyongsa Temple, Seoul
1121122110000.description: This large hanging scroll was commissioned in 1806 by Court Lady Choe of Wongtongsa Temple for the long life of King Sunjo and Queen Sinjeong, and was painted by five monk-painters including Min Gwan. It depicts the triple-body Buddhas—Vairocana, Rocana, and Śākyamuni—across the full screen, with attendant Buddhas placed slightly in front of the main image. The painting also introduces new iconographic elements associated with early 19th-century Seoul and Gyeonggi Buddhist painting.

1121122120000.description: This painting commemorates a gathering of government officials who practiced saga-dokseo at Doseodang from 1516 to 1530 during King Jungjong's reign. The work is believed to have been painted around 1531 and is one of the earliest extant examples of a Doseodang gathering painting. It shows the Doseodang area and the participants' boat outing on the Han River, and its inscription records the names and personal details of 12 attendees.

1123722270000.title_en: Clay Four Heavenly Kings of Jikjisa Temple, Gimcheon
1123722270000.description: This set of four Clay Four Heavenly Kings was enshrined in the Heavenly Kings Gate of Jikjisa Temple. An inscription and related texts show that it was made in 1665 by the sculptor Dan-eung and his group, and the statues preserve unusual details such as a bamboo banner pole, an irregular pagoda, and a blue lion on the lute of the northern guardian.

1123622280000.title_en: Wooden Four Heavenly Kings of Neunggasa Temple, Goheung
1123622280000.description: This set of four Wooden Four Heavenly Kings was likely made around 1666, based on records found during the dismantling and repair of the Heavenly Kings Gate. It is regarded as one of the earliest surviving wooden Four Heavenly Kings from the 17th century and as an important transitional work between clay and wooden sculpture.

1123622290000.title_en: Wooden Four Heavenly Kings and Boksang Texts of Bulgapsa Temple, Yeonggwang
1123622290000.description: This designation includes four Wooden Four Heavenly Kings and 33 kinds of reliquary texts totaling 46 volumes. The statues are dated to the late 17th century, while the texts span the Goryeo to Joseon periods, and the reliquary texts are preserved together with the images because they are historically and religiously meaningful.

1125122300000.title_en: Clay Four Heavenly Kings of Sutasa Temple, Hongcheon
1125122300000.description: This set of four Clay Four Heavenly Kings was made in 1676. It is noted for its balanced pose, vivid facial modeling, excellent detail, and the survival of eight yaksha attendants, as well as an unusual lion-like sacred beast held by the western guardian.

1123422310000.title_en: Clay Four Heavenly Kings of Magoksa Temple, Gongju
1123422310000.description: This set of four Clay Four Heavenly Kings was clearly made in 1683, as recorded in an inscription inside the eastern guardian. It is a late-17th-century clay work associated with the Dan-eung school and is important for studying changes in the style of Four Heavenly Kings sculptures.

1123822320000.title_en: Honghammu Gate of Haeinsa Temple, Hapcheon
1123822320000.description: Honghammu Gate is the one-bay Iljumun gate at Haeinsa Temple. It is a gabled-roof wooden structure with a multi-bracket system and unusually large proportions for an Iljumun, and its bracket composition preserves the sturdy character of the early Joseon period.

1123822330000.title_en: Iljumun Gate of Yongchusa Temple, Hamyang
1123822330000.description: This Iljumun gate was built in 1711 and is the only surviving structure that preserves traces of the former Jangsu-sa site in the Yongchu Valley area. It is a one-bay hip-and-gable-roof wooden gate with a multi-bracket system and unusually large proportions for its type.

1123622340000.title_en: Iljumun Gate of Taeansa Temple, Gokseong
1123622340000.description: This Iljumun gate was originally built in 1521 as the Jogye Gate, as confirmed by a ridge beam inscription discovered during repair work. It is a one-bay gabled-roof wooden gate with a multi-bracket system, and the surviving structure shows later Joseon-period repair features.

1123622190000.title_en: Wooden Seated Sakyamuni Buddha Triad, Donghwasa Temple, Suncheon
1123622190000.description: This wooden triad of seated Sakyamuni Buddha was completed in 1657 by seven sculptor-monks led by Gyechan and enshrined in the Daeungjeon Hall of Donghwasa Temple. The votive texts found within the images record the date, makers, and division of labor in detail, making the work an important source for the study of Buddhist image production. It also preserves its original enshrinement place and shows the simplified style that emerged in the mid-17th century Joseon period.

1123622200000.title_en: Daeungbojeon Hall of Baegryeonsa Temple, Gangjin
1123622200000.description: Daeungbojeon is the main Buddha hall of Baegryeonsa Temple and was rebuilt in 1762 after a fire in 1760. It is valued as a representative example of the decorative trend in 18th-century Buddhist architecture and preserves many records related to its reconstruction. The hall also reflects the temple’s long Buddhist history from the late Goryeo through the Joseon period.

1121122210000.title_en: Kim Jeong-hui, "Buliseon Nando" (Orchid of Nonduality and Seon)
1121122210000.description: This is regarded as Kim Jeong-hui’s last work using the orchid motif, painted in the 1850s. The artist rendered the orchid with the brushwork of calligraphy and inscribed poems and texts around the image in several different scripts. The work is significant for combining Kim’s scholarly and artistic interests with Buddhist ideas of non-discrimination.

1122122220000.title_en: Vulture Peak Assembly Painting of Gobulsa Temple, Gijang
1122122220000.description: This Buddhist painting was made in 1736, as recorded in the inscription on the painting. It depicts Sakyamuni Buddha preaching the Lotus Sutra at Vulture Peak, with attendants including Manjusri, Samantabhadra, Ksitigarbha, the Four Heavenly Kings, and the Ten Disciples arranged around the central figure. The altar inscription includes prayers for the longevity of the king, queen, and crown prince.

1123122230000.title_en: Bronze Bell of Bogwangsa Temple, Paju
1123122230000.description: This bronze bell was cast in 1634 by T'aepo, together with artisans including Sangnyun and Seonjam, using 300 geun of bronze, as stated in its casting inscription. It reflects a transitional stage in Joseon bell-making while preserving the form of earlier bells from the 15th and 16th centuries. The bell is notable for its twin-dragon knob without a sound tube and for the use of Lantsa script in its Sanskrit mantras.

1123622240000.title_en: Clay-Modeled Four Heavenly Kings, Hwaeomsa Temple, Gurye
1123622240000.description: These four guardian kings were made during the reconstruction of Hwaeomsa Temple after the Japanese invasions, probably between 1632 and 1636. Standing nearly 5 meters high, they were built with a wooden armature and covered with clay, and they are seated on chairs rather than standing. They are important for showing the scale, technique, and dynamic modeling of early Joseon clay sculpture.

1123622250000.title_en: Clay-Modeled Four Heavenly Kings, Heungguksa Temple, Yeosu
1123622250000.description: These four guardian kings were likely made around 1645, when the main gate complex of Heungguksa Temple was being completed after the temple’s reconstruction following the Japanese invasions. Built on a wooden framework and covered with clay, the figures are seated and show the robust form typical of early 17th-century sculpture in the region. The temple floor below them is modeled with waves and a turtle, a rare feature linked to the temple’s coastal setting and naval history.

1123322260000.title_en: Clay-Modeled Four Heavenly Kings, Beopjusa Temple, Boeun
1123322260000.description: These four guardian kings were made in the mid-17th century, during the reconstruction of Beopjusa Temple under Monk Byeokam Gakseong after the Japanese invasions. They are the largest surviving Four Heavenly Kings figures in Korea, standing 5.7 meters high, and are unusual for being represented in a standing form. The figures also contain historical references in the form of Qing and Joseon officials placed beneath their feet.

1123121730000.description: This painting shows the taesil, or placenta chamber, of King Jangjo, the posthumous title of Crown Prince Sado, together with the surrounding landscape. It was made around 1785, when the taesil was elevated with additional stone structures. The composition combines map-like place names and routes with landscape painting elements such as mountains, trees, and streams.

1123121740000.description: This painting depicts the taesil where King Sunjo's placenta was interred and the surrounding terrain. It shows key sites around Songnisan, including Beopjusa Temple, and marks roads and geographic features in a map-like manner. The taesil was later elevated with added stone structures in 1806, and the work is thought to date from that time.

1123121750000.description: This painting depicts the taesil where King Heonjong's placenta was buried and the surrounding landscape in Eunsan, Yesan. It appears to have been painted around 1847, when the taesil was elevated with additional stone structures. Unlike other taebongdo paintings, it uses a more landscape-oriented style with little map-like depiction.

1121121760000.description: This seated Bodhisattva statue was made in the late Goryeo to early Joseon period using the dry-lacquer technique. It wears an ornate crown and holds its hands in the preaching mudra. The work is notable for its large size, detailed decoration, and the excellent preservation of its original appearance.

1121121770000.title_en: Gilt-bronze Amitabha Buddha Triad and Reliquaries
1121121770000.description: This gilt-bronze triad was made in 1333, as recorded in the inner reliquary dedication text. It consists of Amitabha Buddha with Avalokiteshvara and Mahasthamaprapta as attendants, and preserves many inner relic objects as well. The sculpture is important for understanding the style, iconography, and production of 14th-century Goryeo Buddhist images.

1123721780000.description: This royal taesil was first installed in 1521 according to Joseon court rites for enshrining a placenta. It was later elevated in 1546, repaired in 1680, and its stele was rebuilt in 1711. The present site consists of the taesil, the stele, and related stone structures.

1122221790000.description: This is a woodblock-printed Buddhist text explaining the key ideas and terms to be considered when interpreting the Lotus Sutra. The extant copy is a damaged set of volumes 3-4, printed in 1461 by the Gangyeongdogam as a re-engraved edition of the 1102 original from Daehungwangsa Temple. It is a rare surviving copy and provides evidence for early Joseon annotation practices.

1123821800000.title_en: Set of Shape-Based Pottery Excavated from Haman Malayisan Tomb No. 45
1123821800000.description: This set consists of five shape-based earthenware vessels: two house-shaped vessels, one deer-shaped horn cup, one boat-shaped vessel, and one lamp-shaped vessel. They were excavated together from a Gaya tomb dating to the first half of the 5th century. The group is significant because such a clearly provenanced set of shape-based pottery from a Three Kingdoms-period tomb is extremely rare.

1123522510000.title_en: Geumgangmun Gate of Songgwangsa Temple, Wanju
1123522510000.description: This temple gate was likely built before 1649, based on records related to Songgwangsa Temple and the date of the Four Heavenly Kings statues enshrined there. It is a rare example of a Buddhist temple gate built on the straight axis between the Iljumun Gate and the Cheonwangmun Gate after the Imjin War, and it uses a daepo-style paljak roof rather than the more common gabled form.

1123322520000.title_en: Cheonwangmun Gate of Beopjusa Temple, Boeun
1123322520000.description: This gate is thought to have been built in the early 17th century during the reconstruction of Beopjusa Temple after the Jeongyu Jaeran. Tree-ring analysis of the gate posts and the Four Heavenly Kings statues found construction dates converging on 1619 and 1620, and the building preserves a very large scale and an unusually elaborate structural system.

1123822530000.title_en: Cheonwangmun Gate of Tongdosa Temple, Yangsan
1123822530000.description: The gate was rebuilt in 1714 after being destroyed by fire in 1713, and a record from 1716 as well as an inscription on the enshrined Four Heavenly Kings statues confirm this date. It is a 3-bay by 2-bay gate with a gabled roof and a two-tier beam structure, and its detailed bracket system shows mid-Joseon-period architectural features.

1123622540000.title_en: Sacheonwangmun Gate of Songgwangsa Temple, Suncheon
1123622540000.description: The gate was rebuilt in 1612, as confirmed by a reconstruction inscription and an inscription discovered during dismantling and repair work in 2004. It is a 3-bay by 3-bay daepo-style gabled gate with a central internal post, and it retains its early 17th-century location and form.

1123622550000.title_en: Cheonwangmun Gate of Hwaeomsa Temple, Gurye
1123622550000.description: The gate is believed to have first been built in the late Goryeo period and was rebuilt in 1636 after being destroyed in the Imjin War. It is a 3-bay by 3-bay double-eaved gabled gate with a daepo-style bracket system, and it contains the temple’s Four Heavenly Kings statues.

1123622560000.title_en: Cheonwangmun Gate of Bulgapsa Temple, Yeonggwang
1123622560000.description: A record from 1725 shows that the gate was built before that year. The gate was later moved and then returned to its original site after excavation in 2009, and it is a 3-bay by 2-bay gabled gate with a distinctive beam-and-post structure supporting the Four Heavenly Kings statues.

1123722570000.title_en: Cheonwangmun Gate of Bogyeongsa Temple, Pohang
1123722570000.description: The gate was rebuilt between 1761 and 1767 after an earlier reconstruction in 1679, as shown by surviving records. It is a single-story paljak-roof gate with a central passage, and it has a uniquely carved supporting beam with lion figures, the only known example of its kind among temple gates in Korea.

1123722580000.title_en: Cheonwangmun Gate of Jikjisa Temple, Gimcheon
1123722580000.description: The gate is thought to have been built sometime between the late Goryeo and early Joseon periods, and it survived the 1596 fire that destroyed much of the temple complex. Its present form is believed to predate the new Four Heavenly Kings statues made in 1665, and it shows a transitional bracket arrangement between 17th- and 18th-century styles.

1123622350000.description: This one-bay Iljumun gate at Ssanggyesa Temple in Hadong is said to have been built in 1641. It is a double-eaved hip-and-gable-roof structure with a dense bracket system, and the plaques on the front and back were written by Haeang Kim Gyu-jin.

1122222360000.description: This gate at Yongyeonsa Temple in Dalseong was built in 1695, as recorded in the building inscription and later repair record. It is a one-bay hip-and-gable-roof structure with a double-eaved roof and a bracket system, and the front plaque was written by Hoesan Park Gidon.

1123622370000.description: The exact date of construction is unknown, but records show that this gate existed before the 1802 reconstruction of Songgwangsa Temple. It is a one-bay gable-roof structure with a double-eaved roof and a bracket system, and several plaques and carved details reflect local features.

1121122380000.title_en: Celadon Ewer with Incised Parrot Design
1121122380000.description: This Buddhist ritual water vessel, or jungbyeong, was made in the 12th century in Goryeo celadon. Parrots are incised on three sides of the body, and the original cover for the spout survives, which is rare among extant examples.

1121122390000.title_en: Gold Belt Excavated from Geumnyeongchong Tomb, Gyeongju
1121122390000.description: This gold belt was excavated in 1924 from Geumnyeongchong, a Silla stone-chamber tomb with wooden coffin. It was found on the body of the buried person and preserves the typical Silla belt components, including belt fittings and pendants with unusual details.

1121122400000.title_en: Gold Belt Excavated from Seobongchong Tomb, Gyeongju
1121122400000.description: This gold belt was excavated in 1926 from Seobongchong, a Silla stone-chamber tomb with wooden coffin. It was found worn on the buried person and is important for understanding the development of Silla gold belts because of its decorative fittings and long pendants.

1123822410000.title_en: Bokjae Seonsaengjip (Collected Works of Jeong Chong)
1123822410000.description: This is the first printed edition, produced in 1446, of the collected writings of Jeong Chong, a founding meritorious subject of Joseon. It contains poetry, prefaces, records, official writings, and inscriptions, and also preserves information on the people involved in its publication.

1123722420000.title_en: Wooden Seated Shakyamuni Buddha and Relic Contents from Seonchalsa Temple, Andong
1123722420000.description: This wooden seated Shakyamuni Buddha was made in 1622 by master sculptor Hyeonjin and other leading monk sculptors of the time. A dedicatory inscription found in the reliquary shows that it was made at the request of Queen Consort Yu of King Gwanghaegun, and a personal garment of hers was also discovered inside.

1121122430000.description: This annotated edition is based on Wang Bo’s text on the Buddha’s enlightenment and Daocheng’s commentary on it. It covers the life of Śākyamuni from birth and growth to awakening and nirvana, and the surviving copy is a rare, complete Goryeo-period woodblock print.

1123722440000.title_en: Stone Sculpture of the Three Bodhisattvas and Wooden Statues of the Ten Kings from Songnimsa Temple, Chilgok
1123722440000.description: This set of Buddhist images was completed in 1665 by sculptors including Seungil and installed in Myeongbujeon Hall at Songnimsa Temple. It is notable as the only known sculptural example in Korea of the Three Bodhisattvas, a subject more commonly preserved in paintings, and it preserves evidence of later repairs and replacement figures.

1123422450000.description: This Buddhist bronze gong bears a 36-character inscription stating that it was made in 1162 for Cheonsuwon in Aju (present-day Asan). The inscription and form make it an important dated example of a bronze gong with a narrow rear sound hole, called geumgu.

1122122460000.title_en: Geumgang Banya Gyeong Soneun Chanryo Jeohyeonrok (2024)
1122122460000.description: This Buddhist text is an explanation of the Diamond Sutra based on the Chinese translation by Kumarajiva and the commentary tradition of Zongmi, with a simplified Korean annotation added in the Korean manuscript tradition. The surviving volume records its production in 1373 under the direction of Eungbong Hye-nyeong and is an early printed copy of a rare Goryeo edition.

1122122470000.description: This five-volume section belongs to a ten-volume Buddhist ritual manual used for repentance and aspiration for rebirth in the Pure Land. The surviving copy was printed in 1483 from woodblocks originally carved in 1474 under royal patronage, and it includes extensive handwritten phonetic and recitation notes.

1123822480000.description: This five-volume section belongs to a ten-volume Buddhist ritual manual used for repentance and aspiration for rebirth in the Pure Land. The copy was printed from Joseon-period woodblocks first carved in 1474 under royal patronage and preserves handwritten recitation notes and later additions to the list of donors.

1121122490000.description: This government-compiled gazetteer was assembled between 1757 and 1765 to support local administration in the late Joseon period. It contains 55 volumes of county and provincial gazetteers together with maps, and is valued as the only surviving complete copy.

1125122500000.title_en: Daejeokgwangjeon Hall of Sutasa Temple, Hongcheon
1125122500000.description: This main Buddhist hall at Sutasa Temple is a late Joseon building with a three-bay front and side plan, double eaves, and a multi-bracket hipped-and-gabled roof. It retains structural features of the mid-Joseon period and was rebuilt in 1636 after the temple had been destroyed.

1122506190001.title_en: Folding Screen of the Court Examination at Geunjeongjeon and Matching Poems
1122506190001.description: This eight-panel folding screen records a court examination held at the former site of Gyeongbokgung Palace in 1747 to celebrate and commemorate the conferral of a new honorific title on Queen Inwon, the widow of King Sukjong. It also includes King Yeongjo’s composed poem and the matching poems written by 50 officials, and its contents correspond exactly with entries in the Veritable Records of King Yeongjo and the Daily Records of the Royal Secretariat.

1122506190002.description: This work is the section of the Chinese historical text Zizhi Tongjian covering volumes 81 to 85, compiled in metal movable type at Jujaso in 1436. It is a rare surviving printed copy corresponding to Jin annals 3 through 7, and is considered an important source for the study of politics, history, and bibliography.

1122506190003.title_en: Woodblocks for the Ritual Manual of the Water and Land Dharma Assembly
1122506190003.description: These woodblocks were produced at Unmunsa in 1515 under the direction of the monk Gakseon, with donations from many patrons, and have remained at the temple ever since. They are complete surviving woodblocks for the Buddhist ritual compendium also known as Jungnyemun, and the inscription on the final block confirms the date and place of production.

1122506190004.title_en: Woodblocks for the Great and Comprehensive Perfect Enlightenment Sutra (2025)
1122506190004.description: These woodblocks for the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra were made at Unmunsa in 1588 under the direction of the monk Seokheon, based on the commentary by the monk Dohrim and with carving by several craftsmen. The blocks are complete, preserve production details on the side edges and end pieces, and remain at the temple today.

1122506190005.title_en: Woodblocks for Beopjib Byeolhaengnok Jeolyo Byeongip Sagi
1122506190005.description: These woodblocks were produced at Unmunsa in 1588 under the direction of the monk Seokheon and preserve the Buddhist treatise known as Jeolyo, together with the author’s added notes. They are complete surviving blocks, and the final block records the date and place of production.

1122506190006.description: These woodblocks for Chijeom Gyeonghun were produced at Unmunsa in 1588 under the direction of the monk Hongin, with text preparation, polishing, and carving carried out by several people. They are complete surviving blocks and preserve production details, donor names, and section markings.

1122509040003.title_en: Stele for Great Master Byeokam at Hwaeomsa Temple, Gurye
1122509040003.description: This stele was erected in 1663, three years after the death of the monk Byeokam, to honor his achievements in restoring and developing Buddhism after the Japanese and Manchu invasions. The inscription was written by Yi Gyeong-seok, the calligraphy by O Jun, and the title at the top by Jo Gye-won.

1122509030001.title_en: The Writings of Great Master Dahui Baoguo (2025)
1122509030001.description: This is a later printed copy made from woodblocks carved in 1418 under the leadership of the monk Sinin. It is a rare 11-line, 20-character edition of Dahui’s Chan Buddhist writings, and it also preserves a colophon by the monk Seongmin that is not found in official records or private collections.

1122412240001.title_en: Wooden Avalokitesvara Triad, Heungcheonsa Temple, Seoul
1122412240001.description: This wooden Avalokitesvara triad was made in 1701, and the dedicatory inscription identifies the makers, including master sculptor Beopjam, as well as its original enshrinement at Jikjoam Hermitage of Sinheungsa Temple in Imsil. It is a rare triad composed of Avalokitesvara, Sudhana, and the Dragon King of the Sea, and it is an important source for studying late Joseon Buddhist sculpture and Avalokitesvara triad worship.

1122412240002.title_en: Painting of the King of Sweet Dew, Yongjusa Temple, Hwaseong
1122412240002.description: This hanging painting was made in 1790 for the water-and-land rite held at Yongjusa Temple, which King Jeongjo founded for the soul transfer of his father, Crown Prince Jangheon. The composition places the descent of Buddhas and bodhisattvas in the upper section and the liberation of wandering spirits in the lower section, while also showing the influence of genre painting and narrative illustration of the late 18th century.

1122412240003.title_en: Gilt-bronze Standing Bodhisattva from Seonlimwon Temple Site, Yangyang
1122412240003.description: This gilt-bronze bodhisattva was excavated in 2015 from a presumed monk's quarters area at the Seonlimwon Temple Site in Yangyang. It is a rare and large surviving excavated bodhisattva with its halo and pedestal preserved, and its separate detachable components and stylistic features are characteristic of bodhisattva images of the 9th century.

1122412240004.title_en: Lacquered Box with Mother-of-Pearl Chrysanthemum Vine Design
1122412240004.description: This late Goryeo lacquered box was returned from Japan in 2023 and is made in the characteristic moksim jeopi technique of applying cloth and ash over a wooden core before attaching mother-of-pearl and finishing with repeated coats of lacquer. Its surface is decorated with 770 chrysanthemum vine motifs, along with other inlaid patterns such as hemp-leaf, tortoise-shell, and linked-bead designs.

1122502270001.title_en: Hanging Painting of the Vulture Peak Assembly, Yugasa Temple, Dalseong
1122502270001.description: This hanging painting was made in 1784 for the Buddha-and-bodhisattva assembly called the Vulture Peak Assembly, as recorded in its inscription. It presents the seated Sakyamuni Buddha as the main image with Vairocana Buddha and Rocana Buddha placed smaller in the upper section, and it is a rare example of a small-format hanging painting with this iconographic arrangement.

1122504240001.title_en: Commentary on the Avatamsaka Sutra, Volume 118
1122504240001.description: This is volume 118 of the 120-volume commentary on the Avatamsaka Sutra by the Song monk Jingyuan, based on the explanations of the Tang monk Chengguan. The woodblocks were carved in 1086-1087 and later transmitted to Goryeo, making this a valuable witness to the compilation and circulation of the canon associated with Uicheon.

1122504240002.description: This volume belongs to the collected works of Jeong Do-jeon, the scholar-official of the late Goryeo and early Joseon periods. It preserves the prefaces and publication records of the first and second printings, making it an important source for understanding the book's publication and transmission history.

1122504240003.title_en: Collected Works of Dongguk Yi Sang-guk, Volumes 18-22 and 31-41
1122504240003.description: This is a surviving fragment of the collected works of Yi Gyubo, a scholar-official of the Goryeo period, and was reprinted in 1251 after collation at the offices responsible for the printing of the Tripitaka. Although only sixteen volumes survive here, the set is the oldest and rarest extant edition and is an important bibliographic source.

1123722670000.title_en: Gaunru Pavilion of Gounsa Temple, Uiseong
1123722670000.description: Gaunru Pavilion is a Buddhist pavilion at Gounsa Temple in Uiseong, a temple traditionally said to have been founded in the Silla period. Documentary sources indicate that the pavilion was built in 1668, and it has remained in place with only partial repairs. It is a rectangular two-story pavilion with a hipped-and-gabled roof that preserves architectural features of the mid-to-late Joseon period.

1121122680000.description: This book is a Confucian work that organizes the contents of classical learning by topic and summarizes 148 items likely to appear on the civil service examination. It is a rare Joseon-period printed edition produced with small-type Gyeongja metal type, and it is notable for having the full text, preface, and table of contents preserved. The work is an important source for the history of early Joseon printing and bibliography.

1123322690000.description: This portrait depicts Gwon Sang-ha (1641–1721), regarded as a leading successor to the learning of Song Si-yeol, and it has been enshrined at Hwanggang Yeongdang in Jecheon for more than 300 years. Dressed not as an official but in ceremonial black robes, he is shown as a pure Confucian scholar. The painting is dated to 1719 and is attributed on the work itself to the court painter Kim Jin-yeo.

1123622700000.title_en: Wooden Seated Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva Triad and the Guardian Kings, Yeonggwang Bulgapsa Temple, with Relic Interments
1123622700000.description: This group of wooden Buddhist sculptures was completed in 1654 by the sculptor-monk Muyeom and his associates and enshrined in the Myeongbujeon Hall of Bulgapsa Temple. The set includes 27 figures, and the number surviving today matches the original making it an unusually complete Joseon-period assembly of Underworld deity images. Relic interments and dedication texts found inside the images provide important evidence for the workshop lineage of Muyeom and his school.

1123622710000.title_en: Iron Seated Vairocana Buddha of Eungjeoksa Temple, Haenam
1123622710000.description: This seated iron Buddha image is believed to have been made in the late Silla to early Goryeo period. It preserves features associated with 9th-century Silla style, including a rounded face, realistic body proportions, and the hand gesture of Vairocana Buddha. Although the knees are missing, the remaining parts are largely intact and show a high level of technical and artistic refinement.

1123722720000.description: Yonggyejeong Pavilion is a two-story pavilion structure in Pohang completed in 1696 by members of the Yeogang Yi clan. It originally served as a place for study and later took on the role of a gate pavilion for a local seowon before becoming a meeting place for the clan. The building preserves architectural features of the 18th century and is closely related to the surrounding Ddeokdong Forest.

1123722730000.description: Bunokjeong Pavilion was built in 1820 to honor the virtues and achievements of Kim Gye-yeong. It has an unusual T-shaped plan with a raised floor hall and ondol rooms arranged to suit the view of the stream and surrounding landscape. The pavilion is associated with numerous inscriptions, plaques, and historical records by literati including Kim Jeong-hui.

1123722740000.title_en: Five-story Stone Pagoda of Bogyeongsa Temple, Pohang
1123722740000.description: This five-story stone pagoda stands in front of Jeokgwangjeon Hall at Bogyeongsa Temple in Pohang and is about 4.6 meters high. Records indicate that the pagoda was erected in 1023 during the Goryeo period, and parts of it were later replaced while the overall form was preserved. Its carved door and lock design on the first-story body reflects the Buddhist beliefs and pagoda style inherited from Unified Silla into Goryeo.

1122509030002.title_en: Draft Manuscript of Bukhakui by Park Jega
1122509030002.description: This manuscript of Bukhakui was written by Park Jega after his visit to Beijing in 1778. It presents reform ideas and practical measures for social, economic, and administrative change, divided into inner and outer sections. The volume is especially valuable because it is a near-original draft in Park Jega’s own hand and also preserves a preface in the hand of Park Ji-won.

1122509030003.description: This is a woodblock-printed edition of Yegi Jipseol, a commentary on the Book of Rites by the Yuan-dynasty Neo-Confucian scholar Chen Hao. It is believed to be a reprinted edition produced in Sangju in 1391 based on an earlier Chinese edition. The book is an early surviving example in Korea and is an important source for the history of printing and textual transmission.

1122509030004.description: Byeokyeok Sinbang is a medical text compiled by Heo Jun in 1613 by royal command. It records his observations, theories, and treatment methods for an epidemic disease that spread during King Gwanghaegun’s reign, likely scarlet fever. The extant copy was printed with wooden movable type and includes a royal presentation record showing that it was bestowed in 1614.

1122509030005.title_en: Gilt-bronze Avalokitesvara and Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva Statues with Reliquary Deposits, Haeinsa Temple, Hapcheon
1122509030005.description: This pair of gilt-bronze seated Bodhisattva statues and their reliquary deposits were originally made in 1351 for Buprimsa Temple in Seongju. The set consists of two statues and 252 associated relic items, and the inscription confirms the production date and original dedication. It is an important example for the study of late Goryeo Buddhist sculpture, especially the combined worship of Avalokitesvara and Ksitigarbha.

1122509030006.title_en: Stone Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva Triad and the Ten Kings, Seongjusa Temple, Changwon
1122509030006.description: This group of stone Buddhist sculptures was completed in 1681 by the sculptor monk Seungho and other artisan monks for Seongjusa Temple. The dedication inscription records 31 figures in total, and all 31 survive today without loss. It is a representative late Joseon work in fossil stone and an important source for the study of Ksitigarbha and Ten Kings iconography.

1122509040001.description: This pair of mirror stands was made in 1627 and once enshrined in the Daeungjeon hall of Jeondeungsa Temple. Each stand supports a mirror on a lion-shaped base, and the underside bears an inscription naming the makers and the date. It is an important reference work for 17th-century wooden craft and Buddhist ritual furnishings.

1122509040002.title_en: Bronze Pure Water Bottle Excavated from Heungjeon-ri Temple Site, Samcheok
1122509040002.description: This is a set of two bronze ritual water bottles excavated in 2016 from the east courtyard building area of the Heungjeon-ri Temple Site in Samcheok. A pure water bottle was a Buddhist vessel used to hold clean water for offering to the Buddha. The objects are well preserved and are important examples for the study of Unified Silla Buddhist implements.

1122510290001.description: This portable Angbuilgu is a handheld sundial made in 1908 during the Korean Empire. It has a hollow hemispherical face, a central gnomon, and a compass for aligning the instrument north-south before measuring time. The underside bears the date and maker’s name, making it an important scientific-historical object.

1122510290002.title_en: Goryeo Five Hundred Arhats Painting (Plate 329, Wonsangjuseonja)
1122510290002.description: This is one panel from a set of 500 Five Hundred Arhats paintings made in 1235 during the period of the Mongol invasions of Goryeo. It depicts the 329th Arhat, Wonsangjuseonja, seated on a broad rock and looking up at a dragon in the upper left. The inscription records the date of production, the patron Kim Huin, and the donor Yi Hyeokcheom, making it an important source for the study of Goryeo Buddhist painting.

1122510290003.title_en: Sejong Biamsa Suso Amitabha Buddha Seated Statue
1122510290003.description: This seated Amitabha Buddha statue is thought to have been made in the mid-16th century on the basis of its stylistic features, since no dedicatory inscription survives. It was fashioned as a dry-lacquer-like clay image with a wooden framework, using a method in which the outline was made in wood and only small amounts of clay were used for details. The work is valuable as a rare surviving 16th-century Buddhist sculpture and as an important source for the study of Joseon-period clay Buddhist images.

1122510290004.description: This is the first woodblock-printed edition of the poetry collection of Han Su (1333–1384), a late Goryeo civil official and writer. It also includes a preface by Gwon Geun, an epitaph by Yi Saek, and a royal directive from King U, providing important material for understanding Han Su's life, thought, learning, and character. As the earliest surviving edition of the work, it is a valuable source for bibliography and the history of private literary collections.

1122511030001.description: Gwangheungsa is said to have been founded by the monk Uisang in the Unified Silla period, and its Unginjeon Hall is believed to have been built before 1647 based on a roof tile inscription recording a repointing in that year. The hall survived the major fires of 1827 and 1946 and later came to function as the main Buddha hall after the original Daeungjeon was lost. It is a large Joseon-period Buddhist hall with a valuable traditional structural system and preserves a seated group of clay Buddhist statues and sixteen arhats.

1122512230001.description: This album was made to commemorate longevity banquets held for Shin Jungeom on his 80th birthday, celebrated by his sons Shin Sik and Shin Seol beginning in 1601. It contains calligraphy by Heo Mok and Han Ho, four paintings including the earliest surviving version of a longevity banquet painting, poems by leading figures of the time, a list of attendees, and a later colophon. The work is an important source for the history of mid-Joseon calligraphy, painting, and literature.

1122512230002.description: This Buddhist painting records its date of production as 1560 and states that it was made for the royal family's longevity and prosperity of descendants under Queen Munjeong.
