It depicts the moment when Śākyamuni expounds the Lotus Sutra on Vulture Peak, with the main Buddha placed at the center and attendant figures such as the six bodhisattvas, Indra and Brahma, the Four Heavenly Kings, and the Eight Classes of Divine Beings arranged around him. It is a representative early Joseon-period group composition of the Vulture Peak assembly and an important reference for the iconography of this subject.

1122512230003.description: This is volume 3 of the seven-volume Korean metal-type edition of the Lotus Sutra, printed in 1450 by royal order during King Sejong's reign. It is the earliest surviving edition among the extant metal-type printings of this text, produced with the first cast Jia-yi type on Korean-made paper. The volume preserves the contents of three chapters and retains original features such as the dark-blue cover, making it an important source for the study of royal publications, printing history, and Korean linguistics.

1122512230004.title_en: Bronze Bell of Hwaeomsa Temple, Gurye
1122512230004.description: This bronze bell was cast in 1711 by the bell founder Yun Jongbaek with Kim Wonhak, Han Cheonseok, and others, as recorded in the inscription on the bell body. Although it was originally made for Unheungsa Temple, it was later moved to Hwaeomsa Temple, where it is confirmed to have been present by the 1925 repair record and an old glass-plate photograph. It is a large late-Joseon bell with a well-preserved form, and the bell body also preserves records of repairs in 1925 and 1955.

1122608250004.title_en: First Edition of the Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Volume 3
1122608250004.description: This is Volume 3 of the first printed edition of the Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, a 100-volume work translated into Chinese by Xuanzang of the Tang dynasty. It preserves seokdeok gugyeol notation from the Goryeo period, making it an important source for the study of Korean language, Buddhist scholarship, and bibliography. It is the only known surviving copy of this volume in the first Tripitaka edition.

1122608250005.title_en: Royal Appointment Decree for An Seong
1122608250005.description: This document, issued on 22 April 1414 by King Taejong, appoints An Seong as Provincial Inspector of Gangwon-do. It is written in cursive script in seven lines and bears the seal "Joseon Gukwang Jiin". The document is valuable for showing the earlier use of the term wangji and the administrative system before the completion of the Gyeongguk Daejeon.

1122609090001.title_en: Daegwangjeon Hall of Sinhansa Temple, Geumsan
1122609090001.description: This Buddhist hall was originally built in the 16th century, with records showing repairs in 1638 and 1840. Dendrochronological analysis identified many major timbers dating to 1583, confirming an early construction date. It is a five-bay front, three-bay side dapo-style gabled hall with distinctive structural features and mixed framing methods.

1122512230005.description: This Buddhist painting depicts Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva on Potalaka Mountain, as described in the Avatamsaka Sutra, when Sudhana meets the bodhisattva during his southern pilgrimage. The bodhisattva sits by the waterside in half-lotus posture, and Sudhana is shown bowing with joined hands before a vase with willow branches. It follows the standard late Goryeo Water-Moon Avalokitesvara iconography, with refined decorative patterns and restrained, elegant use of gold and color.

1122512230006.title_en: Vulture Peak Assembly Painting with the Inscription 'Yeongchuksa'
1122512230006.description: This Buddhist painting has a dated inscription showing that it was made in 1742, by the monk-painter Hyesik, and originally enshrined at Yeongchuksa Temple. It portrays the moment when Śākyamuni Buddha preaches the Lotus Sutra on Vulture Peak, with attendant bodhisattvas, Brahma, Indra, disciples, the Eight Legions, pratyekabuddhas, Buddhas of other directions, attendants, and the Four Heavenly Kings arranged around the main image. The work reflects the characteristics of early-18th-century Buddhist painting in the Yeongnam region and shows the painter’s individual style.

1122601230002.title_en: Daeungjeon Hall of Cheongwonsa Temple, Anseong
1122601230002.description: This temple hall was likely originally built by the late Goryeo period, and the existing building is dated by structural analysis and tree-ring study to the mid-15th century. It is a three-bay by three-bay hall with a gabled roof, and it combines multi-bracket form on the front with bracket-arm form on the rear. The building is important for showing the transition from earlier bracket systems to later bracket-arm systems in Korean architecture.

1122602250001.title_en: Amitabha Preaching Painting of Hyeondeungsa Temple, Gapyeong
1122602250001.description: This Buddhist painting is dated by an inscription to 1759 and records its maker Ogan and its original place of enshrinement, Hyeondeungsa Temple. It depicts Amitabha Buddha preaching in the Western Paradise, with bodhisattvas, arhats, the Eight Vajra Beings, and the Eight Legions arranged symmetrically around the central figure. It is the earliest known Amitabha preaching painting from the Seoul-Gyeonggi area.

1122602260004.title_en: Stone Seated Vairocana Buddha of Jingusaji Temple Site, Imsil
1122602260004.description: This stone Buddha image is thought to have been made in the late 9th century, during the later period of Unified Silla. Although there is no exact date, its form, pedestal, artistic style, and comparison with the stone lantern at Jingusaji Temple Site support this dating. The statue retains most of the Buddha body and pedestal, and it is notable as a rare 9th-century stone seated Vairocana Buddha in the Jeolla region.

1122602250002.title_en: Stone Seated Śākyamuni Buddha Triad and Buddhist Relics from Singheungsa Temple, Yangsan
1122602250002.description: This stone triad was completed in 1682 by the sculptors Seungho, Suyeon, Bojang, Inwon, and Cheohaeng and enshrined at Singheungsa Temple. An inscription found inside the right attendant bodhisattva records its creation and identifies the set as an 'Assembly of Vulture Peak' triad. The group is made of soapstone, and the accompanying reliquaries and inserted objects are important materials for understanding late-17th-century Buddhist consecration rites.

1122602250003.title_en: Draft Manuscripts of Pak Ji-won's Yeolha Ilgi
1122602250003.description: This set preserves draft materials from the earliest stage of Pak Ji-won’s Yeolha Ilgi, a travel account written after his journey to Beijing and Jehol. The manuscripts show how the text was revised and supplemented by Pak Ji-won’s descendants and literati, and they are important for studying the bibliography and transmission history of the work. As a representative late-Joseon practical-learning text, the set also has high historical value.

1122602260001.title_en: Chimgyeru Pavilion of Songgwangsa Temple, Suncheon
1122602260001.description: This pavilion is thought to have existed by the 14th century because a poem by Yi Saek is recorded under its name in the Sinjeung Dongguk Yeoji Seungnam. The present building was rebuilt in 1668 by Monk Hyemun, and tree-ring analysis confirms that the main timbers were cut in 1687. It is a large, three-bay, gabled pavilion used for monastic study and is important for understanding late-Joseon pavilion architecture.

1122602260002.description: This pavilion at Bongjeongsa Temple in Andong was built in 1680 and is now known as Manseru. It was repaired in 1818 and has survived to the present with little alteration. Inscriptions inside the building record its construction and repair history, making it important for understanding the changing history of the temple and the pavilion.

1122602260003.description: This two-story pavilion at the center line of the main hall at Yongjusa Temple was built in 1790, during King Jeongjo's reign. It is a pavilion with five bays in the front and three bays on the side, with an upper-story lecture hall and a lower story allowing entry from below. Its layout and structure reflect the architectural expression of temple authority and the mixed use of Buddhist and Confucian elements.

1122604230001.title_en: Celadon Bowl with Inlaid Twin-Dragon and Chrysanthemum Design
1122604230001.description: This celadon bowl, thought to have been made in the 13th century, is decorated on both the interior and exterior with inlay and incision. The interior has a pair of dragons surrounded by wave patterns, and the exterior includes chrysanthemum motifs and scrolling floral designs. It is considered a high-quality example of 13th-century celadon and is thought to have been used by the royal court or a related government office.

1122604230002.title_en: Portrait of Yu Hyo-geol and Its Chest
1122604230002.description: This portrait depicts Yu Hyo-geol (1594–1627), who was honored as a second-grade military merit subject after helping suppress Yi Gwal's rebellion. He is shown wearing a sa-mo hat and official robe, seated with both hands joined in front, and the portrait follows the general form of 17th-century meritorious subject portraits. The object includes the chest that originally held the portrait, which adds to its significance.

1122606230001.title_en: Punch’ong Bowl with Incised Fish Design
1122606230001.description: This punch'ong vessel is believed to have been made in the Jeolla region in the 15th to 16th century. It was formed by beating a wheel-thrown body into flat planes, then decorated with incised designs over a white slip surface. The fish-and-wave motif and geometric patterns are distinctive, and the piece was returned to Korea from abroad in 2018.

1122606240001.title_en: Wall Paintings of Daeungjeon Hall, Beomeosa Temple, Busan
1122606240001.description: These four wall paintings in the main hall of Beomeosa Temple depict a spatial Buddhist world centered on the Vairocana triad, the Medicine Buddha triad, and the Amitabha triad. The set also includes paintings of Avalokiteshvara and Bodhidharma with Huike on the side walls, forming a coherent group of themes and iconography. They preserve their original form and are important for studying 18th-century Buddhist painting in the Yeongnam region.

1122606240002.title_en: Wall Painting of Avalokiteshvara, Daeungbojeon Hall, Naesosa Temple, Buan
1122606240002.description: This wall painting is located on the back wall behind the main altar of Daeungbojeon Hall at Naesosa Temple. It depicts Avalokiteshvara in white robes welcoming Sudhana, based on the Avatamsaka Sutra, and includes Amitabha in the bodhisattva's crown. It is considered an important example for studying the style associated with the Uigyeom school and the iconography of Korean Water-Moon Avalokiteshvara paintings.

1122606240003.title_en: Wooden Standing Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva and Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva, Wibongsa Temple, Wanju
1122606240003.description: These two wooden standing bodhisattva statues were made in 1605 for enshrinement at Wibongsa Temple's Bukam Hermitage and are part of a set of four bodhisattvas originally made to accompany a triad. They were carved by five sculptors led by Won'o, an early master active in the years after the Imjin War. The statues were stolen in 1989 and returned in 2016, and the crowns and hand-held attributes were remade for their restoration.

1122606240004.title_en: Yeosu Heungguksa Temple Je-seokcheon and Cheonryong Paintings
1122606240004.description: These two hanging scroll Buddhist paintings were made in 1741 and originally formed a pair as separate mid-tier guardian paintings for the main Buddha hall. They were produced under the direction of the monk-painter Geungcheok, who inherited the style of Uigyeom, and are important as a dated work showing an earlier stage before Je-seokcheon and Cheonryong imagery became combined in one composition.

1122607070001.description: Geukrakjeon is the main Buddhist hall of Hyeondeungsa Temple and was rebuilt in 1765 after a fire in 1763. Documentary records and physical evidence confirm that much of the main timber dates to the original reconstruction, and the hall is a representative surviving Joseon-period Buddhist hall in northern Gyeonggi Province.

1122607070002.description: Birojeon at Gagyeonsa Temple is believed to have been rebuilt in 1499, based on the rebuilding record and its architectural details, with later repairs carried out in the 16th century, the 17th to 18th centuries, and in modern times. It is valuable for its early Joseon-period bracket system, old-style roof form, and the reuse of earlier stone foundations and base stones.

1122607070003.description: Yeongsanjeon at Seonunsa Temple was rebuilt in 1821 as a single-story hall after an earlier two-story hall had been destroyed and then rebuilt several times since the late 15th century. It preserves records of its changes and retains structural members from the former two-story building, making it important for the study of Buddhist hall architecture.

1122607070004.description: Wontongjeon was rebuilt in 1828 after repeated destruction by fire and is documented as having also served as a royal prayer hall during the Joseon period. The hall has a rare plan with a front projection, an open three-sided arrangement except for the rear, and decorative details such as floral lattice doors and blue-toned dancheong.

1122607070005.description: Eungjindang was built in 1504 and repaired in 1623, and it houses the Wooden Seated Sakyamuni Triad and Clay Fifteen Arhats and the Buddhist paintings of Sakyamuni and the Sixteen Arhats. The building preserves old construction techniques such as its bracket system, carved rafters, and support structure, giving it high historical and artistic value.

1122607070006.description: Eungjinjeon was rebuilt as Yeongsanjeon in 1649, enshrined with 500 arhats in 1729, and later renamed, while remaining largely intact to the present. It is a rare multi-bracket Buddhist hall with distinctive middle-Joseon structural features and late-Joseon decorative details on the bracket arms and roof ornaments.

1122607070007.description: Muryangsugak at Yeongcheonam Hermitage was rebuilt in 1786, as shown by the ridge-beam record and a dated inscription found during restoration work. It is an inbeopdang hall that combines living quarters and worship space, with a raised platform, inner shrine, and loft-like arrangement that reflect the practical and religious use of a mountain hermitage.

1122607070008.description: Seolseondang Hall is a monk’s living and practice hall at Janggoksa Temple in Cheongyang. Dendrochronological analysis conducted during dismantling repairs in 2021 suggests that it was rebuilt or newly built in 1569. The hall was originally smaller and was later expanded in stages, and its detailed bracket and beam work shows architectural features of both the mid-Joseon and later Joseon periods.

1122607070009.title_en: Seolseondang Hall and Dormitory, Naesosa Temple, Buan
1122607070009.description: Seolseondang Hall and the dormitory at Naesosa Temple were built in 1640 during the temple’s post-war reconstruction, with repairs in 1821 and an extension to the dormitory in 1893. The complex preserves the changing living space of monks and consists of two gabled buildings connected into a distinctive U-shaped plan. Its structural layout reflects adaptation to the sloping site and a clear hierarchical arrangement.

1122607070010.description: Jeonghyewon Hall at Sungnimsa Temple is believed to have been built in 1644, after earlier reconstruction work in the 1590s. The building was later enlarged as a monk’s living quarters, but its original timber framework has been largely preserved. Its bracket system and decorative beam ends show the stylistic features of 17th-century temple architecture in the southwest coastal region.

1122608070001.title_en: Daeseongjeon Hall, Yean Hyanggyo Confucian School, Andong
1122608070001.description: Daeseongjeon Hall is the main shrine building of Yean Hyanggyo in Andong. The hall is documented as having been repaired in 1572, and later repairs in 1723 are also recorded; the present building has kept its basic scale with little change. It is a three-bay by three-bay gabled hall with an open front porch and features uncommon post and window arrangements for a hyanggyo building.

1122608250001.title_en: Iron Seated Tathagata Buddha, Jingusa Temple Site, Imsil
1122608250001.description: This iron seated Buddha is estimated to have been made in the late 9th to early 10th century. Although the hands and part of the body are damaged, the balanced proportions, refined carving, and elegant drapery preserve the original form well. The figure shows late Unified Silla features and is an important transitional example of iron Buddhist sculpture leading into the Goryeo period.

1122608250002.title_en: Album of Landscape and Figure Paintings by Yi Gyeong-yun
1122608250002.description: This album contains landscape-and-figure paintings attributed to Yi Gyeong-yun, a leading mid-Joseon literati painter. It also includes a colophon and inscribed poems written by Choe Rip in 1598–1599, which record the album’s compilation and earlier ownership. The volume preserves rare evidence of how paintings were collected, mounted, and appreciated in the Joseon period.

1122608250003.title_en: Wooden Seated Jecheon, Sanggwonsa Temple, Pyeongchang, and Reliquary Objects
1122608250003.description: This seated Jecheon figure enshrined at Sanggwonsa Temple is thought to have been made in the Joseon period, before 1645, and was later repaired in 1645 and 1862. It wears a decorated robe and sits on a chair, showing features that combine late Goryeo and early Joseon Buddhist sculpture styles. The reliquary objects found in its body provide important evidence for its history and relationship to the temple’s other wooden Buddhist images.

1122608260002.description: This is volume 1 of Sambong Seonsaengjip, the collected works of Jeong Do-jeon. The edition was printed in Andong in 1465 by Jeong Mun-hyeong using materials from the earlier edition, and it preserves poems and editorial materials such as prefaces and colophons. It is an important source for studying the publication and transmission of an early Joseon literary collection.

1123821130000.title_en: Woodblocks for the Sutra of Complete Enlightenment
1123821130000.description: This set of woodblocks was used to print the Buddhist scripture known as the Sutra of Complete Enlightenment, a text explaining Mahayana doctrine and the stages of practice through a dialogue between the Buddha and twelve bodhisattvas. The extant set, kept at Ssanggyesa Temple in Hadong, consists of 335 complete blocks and was recarved in 1611 at Neunginam Hermitage on Jirisan based on a metal-type edition printed with Eulhaeja type. The blocks include engraved volume and leaf numbers on the side surfaces, and later replacement blocks were added where some were damaged.

1121121140100.description: Goryeosa is the official history of Goryeo, compiled in 1451 and regarded as one of Korea’s two major dynastic histories. This item is an Eulhaeja metal-type edition printed in 1482 and preserved at the Kyujanggak Institute for Korean Studies, Seoul National University. The set originally had 139 volumes in 46 cases, though some volumes here are replaced with manuscript copies and several parts are missing.

1121121140200.description: Goryeosa is the official history of Goryeo, compiled in 1451 and regarded as one of Korea’s two major dynastic histories. This copy, held by the Kyujanggak Institute for Korean Studies, Seoul National University, is an Eulhaeja metal-type edition from 1482. It survives as 98 volumes in 32 cases, with 41 volumes missing from the original 139-volume work.

1121121150100.description: Goryeosa is the official history of Goryeo, compiled in 1451 and regarded as one of Korea’s two major dynastic histories. This copy, held by the Kyujanggak Institute for Korean Studies, Seoul National University, is a woodblock edition recarved from the Eulhaeja metal-type text and printed in 1613. It is a complete 139-volume set in 85 cases and was printed for the Taebaeksan royal archive.

1121121150200.description: Goryeosa is the official history of Goryeo, compiled in 1451 and regarded as one of Korea’s two major dynastic histories. This copy, held by the Kyujanggak Institute for Korean Studies, Seoul National University, is a woodblock edition recarved from the Eulhaeja metal-type text and printed in 1613. It is a complete 139-volume set in 85 cases and was printed for the Odaesan royal archive.

1121121150300.description: Goryeosa is the official history of Goryeo, compiled in 1451 and regarded as one of Korea’s two major dynastic histories. This copy, held by Yonsei University, is a woodblock edition recarved from the Eulhaeja text, printed in 1613, and later reprinted in the 17th or 18th century. It survives as a 139-volume set in 33 cases, with one later manuscript supplement in volume 122 and 123.

1122121150400.description: Goryeosa is the official history of Goryeo, compiled in 1451 and regarded as one of Korea’s two major dynastic histories. This copy, held by Dong-A University Museum, is a woodblock edition recarved from the Eulhaeja text, printed in 1613, and later reprinted in the 17th or 18th century. It survives as a 139-volume set in 75 cases, with the order of some front matter differing from the Kyujanggak archive copies.

1123721160000.title_en: Supreme Bliss Assembly Hanging Painting of Nammangsa Temple, Sangju, and Associated Buddhist Relics
1123721160000.description: This large Buddhist hanging painting, over 11 meters high, was made in 1776 by Yuseong and about 23 other monk-painters active in Gyeongsang Province. The painting has survived with its original coloring and mounting more fully than many similar works, though it was damaged after being used in a rainmaking ritual. The associated relics include a sacred pouch, a bronze mirror, and a storage box, all of which are preserved together with the painting.

1123621250000.title_en: Gilt-bronze Shoes Excavated from Jeongchon Tomb, Naju
1123621250000.description: A pair of gilt-bronze shoes excavated in 2014 from the third wooden coffin in Tomb No. 1 of Jeongchon Tomb, a large tumulus from the Three Kingdoms period in Naju. They are notable for being preserved almost intact, including a dragon-head ornament attached to the instep, the only known example among surviving Three Kingdoms-period gilt-bronze shoes. The shoes are thought to date to the late 5th century and show decorative motifs such as hexagonal patterns, dragons, human-faced bird bodies, beast designs, and lotus patterns.

1123521260000.title_en: Wooden Seated Sakyamuni Triad and Painted Clay Sixteen Arhats from Songgwangsa Temple, Wanju
1123521260000.description: This Buddhist sculpture group was made in 1656 and is the largest known example among Joseon-period Arhat statues in terms of scale and number. It consists of three wooden Buddha images, sixteen clay Arhats, attendant figures, and related deities, and combines wood, clay, and polychromy in its production. The work also preserves records of the participating sculptors and the production process, making it important for the study of late Joseon Buddhist sculpture.

1123721270000.title_en: Buddhist Sedan Chairs of Bulgyeongsa Temple, Uljin
1123721270000.description: These are two Buddhist sedan chairs made in 1670 for ritual use in carrying Buddhas, relics, scriptures, and other objects of worship. They are the most completely preserved examples among known late Joseon Buddhist sedan chairs, and the production records identify the patron, donors, and makers. The chairs are notable for their wooden curved roofs, phoenix carvings, rail decorations, and the hanging of bronze mirrors on the beaded curtains.
1123721270000.material: Wood with bronze, brass, tin, and iron fittings

1123321280000.description: This is a portrait of Song Siyeol (1607–1689), the Neo-Confucian scholar and statesman, and had been enshrined for more than 300 years at Hwanggang Yeongdang in Jecheon. The painting depicts him not as an official but as a scholar wearing a square cap and simui, and inscriptions identify it as based on an original portrait drawn by Kim Chang-up. The work is believed to be based on a sketch made in 1680 and was later completed in the early 18th century.

1123521290000.description: Hanfungnu is a Joseon-period government pavilion in Muju that was praised in historical records as one of the best scenic pavilions in the Honam region. Although its original construction date is unknown, records show that it existed by the early Joseon period and was rebuilt after being burned during the Japanese invasions of 1592. The present building is a two-story pavilion with a hip-and-gable roof and reflects the formal style of late Joseon government architecture.

1123121300000.title_en: Saritae Pagoda at Hoeamsa Temple Site, Yangju
1123121300000.description: This pagoda at the Hoeamsa Temple Site is a large and well-preserved relic-pagoda founded through royal patronage in the early Joseon period. It is understood to have enshrined the true relics of Sakyamuni, and its form, carvings, and ornamentation reveal many features of royal Buddhist stone sculpture. The structure consists of an octagonal multi-tiered base, a spherical body, and an upper finial, with dragon, qilin, floral, vine, and guardian-deity motifs carved throughout.

1123721310000.title_en: Daeungjeon Hall of Songnimsa Temple, Chilgok
1123721310000.description: This is the main Buddha hall of Songnimsa Temple, rebuilt in 1649, and is notable for its rare five-bay front among surviving late Joseon Buddhist halls. The building preserves an older floor plan with the Buddha platform and back wall arranged in a way that reflects earlier temple architecture. Its bracket system and structural details also show regional characteristics associated with the Palgongsan area.

1122221320000.title_en: Geukrakjeon Hall of Donghwasa Temple, Daegu
1122221320000.description: Geukrakjeon Hall of Donghwasa Temple was first built in 1600 in the Geumdangam area and is the surviving upper wooden structure of a hall rebuilt in 1622. It retains the original stone base and foundation stones from the Silla-period temple layout, preserving an old-style plan without shifting the columns. The hall is also valued for its early Joseon architectural features and the craftsmanship shown in its bracket system and structural composition.

1122317860000.title_en: Wooden Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva Triad and the Ten Kings, Jeondeungsa Temple, Ganghwa
1122317860000.description: This set consists of the Wooden Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva Triad and the Ten Kings, along with attendant figures, for a total of 31 pieces. An inscription in the production record gives a clear date of 1636 and shows that the images were made under the direction of the monk-sculptor Suyeon, with many donors and sculptors participating. The triad and attendants were originally produced for the Mingjeon Hall at Jeondeungsa Temple.

1122317870000.title_en: Wooden Amitabha Buddha Seated Statue, Cheongnyeonsa Temple, Ganghwa
1122317870000.description: This Wooden Amitabha Buddha Seated Statue shows the refined and elegant style associated with Goryeo Buddhist sculpture. Although no production record survives, its facial features, robe folds, and overall form closely resemble works dated to the first half of the 13th century. It was likely made in Kaegyeong and later enshrined as the main Buddha image of Cheongnyeonsa Temple.

1121117880000.title_en: Set of Exhumed Relics from the Eight-sided Five-story Stone Pagoda at Sujongsa Temple, Namyangju
1121117880000.description: This set includes a miniature Buddhist shrine, 18 Buddha and bodhisattva images, and associated relic objects. Inscriptions and a dedicatory text suggest that the items were made in the late 15th century and around 1628. The assemblage is important for the study of early Joseon Buddhist iconography and royal Buddhist patronage.

1123117890000.title_en: Clay Seated Sakyamuni Buddha Triad, Cheongryongsa Temple, Anseong
1123117890000.description: This clay Buddha triad was made in 1603, in the early Joseon period when large clay Buddhist images became popular after the Japanese invasions. The main Buddha has a wooden pair of hands and is shown with the right hand touching the earth and the left hand forming a preaching gesture. The inscription in the body cavity identifies the chief sculptor as Gwangwon.

1123117900000.title_en: Gilt-bronze Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva Seated Statue, Yongmunsa Temple, Yangpyeong
1123117900000.description: This gilt-bronze Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva Seated Statue is a representative example of the gilt-bronze bodhisattva images that spread widely in the 14th century during the late Goryeo period. It has a round face, realistic features, a jeweled necklace, and a triangular inner-robe ornament that is characteristic of the type. Apart from a later replacement of the crown, the statue is well preserved and finely modeled.

1123117910000.title_en: Wooden Amitabha Buddha Triad, Sinreuksa Temple, Yeoju
1123117910000.description: This Wooden Amitabha Buddha Triad was made in 1610, and the production record identifies the maker and date. The central Buddha is seated, while the attendant bodhisattvas stand on either side, following a layout inherited from earlier Buddhist sculpture traditions. The triad is notable for its long proportions, distinct robe treatment, and the presence of the sculptor Inil.

1123117920000.title_en: Birojana Three Bodies Hanging Buddhist Painting, Bongseonsa Temple, Namyangju
1123117920000.description: This hanging Buddhist painting depicts the three bodies of Vairocana Buddha and their attendants. The upper portion centers on Vairocana, with Nairatmya? no, Norsana (Sambhogakaya) and Sakyamuni arranged to the right and left, and the lower section includes bodhisattvas, Brahma, Indra, the Ten Great Disciples, and other attendant figures. It was made in 1735 to pray for the repose of Lady Kim, a concubine of King Sukjong.

1123117930000.description: This bronze bell was originally enshrined at Bongseonsa Temple and was later moved to Hyeondeungsa Temple during the Japanese colonial period. It was cast in 1619 and follows the Chinese-style bell tradition seen in late Goryeo and early Joseon royal bells. The bell is notable for its floral and wave designs and for the inscription recorded in regular script on the body.

1122121970000.description: This is volume 88 of the 120-volume Avatamsaka Sutra Commentary written by the Northern Song monk Jingyuan (1011–1088) on the Avatamsaka Sutra Commentary by Tang monk Chengguan (738–839). The extant copy is a Goryeo woodblock print, and the source text was transmitted to Goryeo through the efforts of Uicheon and later brought from Song China in 1087. It is the only known surviving copy of this volume in Korea from the same edition.

1121121980000.description: This 22-volume, 14-volume-set edition of Bulseo yeokdae tongjae was printed in 1472 from woodblocks recut in Korea after a Ming edition of 1430. The work is a Buddhist history compiled by the Yuan monk Nianchang, covering stories and biographies of eminent monks from the Buddha's birth to 1334. The copy preserves the complete set and includes a postface by Kim Su-on dated June 1472.

1121121990000.title_en: Earliest Tripitaka Edition of Yogacarabhumi-sastra, Volume 66
1121121990000.description: This is volume 66 of the 100-volume Yogacarabhumi-sastra, translated into Chinese by Xuanzang. It is the only known surviving copy of this volume from the first carved Tripitaka edition, and the text preserves saengdok kugyeol reading marks used in Korea. The volume is incomplete at the front, but it is an important source for the study of Korean language, Buddhism, and bibliography.

1121122000000.description: This oath document was written on December 13, 1931, by independence activist Lee Bong-chang (1901–1932) as a pledge to carry out an anti-Japanese act. It was submitted to the Korean Patriotic Corps, the anti-Japanese organization founded by Kim Gu. Lee signed it on the same day and later carried out the Tokyo bombing attempt in January 1932.

1123622010000.title_en: Iljumun Gate of Seonamsa Temple, Suncheon
1123622010000.description: This one-bay gate at Seonamsa Temple is said to have been rebuilt in 1540, though its original construction date is unknown. It has a gabled roof, multi-bracket style supports, and a simple T-shaped structural frame, and it survived the destruction of the Imjin War and the Manchu invasion. It is an example of mid-Joseon temple architecture.

1123722020000.title_en: Bonghwangmun Gate of Bongamsa Temple, Mungyeong
1123722020000.description: This one-bay gate at Bongamsa Temple is thought to date to before 1723, although no record of its original construction survives. It has a gabled roof, multi-bracket style supports, and a distinctive H-shaped arrangement of transverse beams. The structural treatment is considered unusual and specific to this gate.

1123622030000.title_en: Iljumun Gate of Cheoneunsa Temple, Gurye
1123622030000.description: According to temple records, this gate at Cheoneunsa Temple was built in 1723. It has a one-bay hipped-gabled roof, multi-bracket style supports, and a structural frame made up of two main columns and four auxiliary columns. It is notable for its elevated bracket system and for a stone sill placed between the main pillars.

1122222040000.title_en: Bonghwangmun Gate of Donghwasa Temple, Daegu
1122222040000.description: This one-bay gate at Donghwasa Temple was first built in 1633 and moved to its present location in 1965. It has a hipped-gabled roof, multi-bracket style supports, and a mixed structural form using main columns and auxiliary columns. The gate also has a coffered ceiling and dragon-head ornaments inside.

1123422590000.title_en: Geumakbojeon Hall of Munsubsa Temple, Seosan
1123422590000.description: Geumakbojeon Hall at Munsubsa Temple in Seosan was rebuilt in the 1630s, based on wood dating and radiocarbon analysis of its major structural members. The hall has a 3-by-3 rectangular plan with a gabled roof and dapo-bracket construction, and it preserves features and interior polychromy that show changes from the 17th to 19th centuries.

1121122600000.title_en: Screen of Seowon Ageumdo by Kim Hongdo
1121122600000.description: This six-panel folding screen was painted by Kim Hongdo in 1778 and depicts the Seowon Ageum gathering, a literary and artistic salon associated with Wang Shen and famous Chinese literati. It includes a colophon by Kim Hongdo's teacher Kang Seghwang, which records the completion date and comments on the painting.

1123522610000.title_en: Bronze Bell of Daeboksa Temple, Namwon
1123522610000.description: This bronze bell bears an inscription showing that it was cast in 1635 by the monk-craftsman Jeongu with seven others. It was first made for Yeongwonsa Temple and later moved to Daeboksa Temple after the original temple was abandoned. The bell preserves Goryeo-style decorative elements while also showing the distinctive character of early Joseon bell casting.

1121122620000.title_en: Album of Bukeonsuhoe Gathering by Jeong Seon
1121122620000.description: This album was made in 1716 to commemorate a longevity banquet and gentry gathering held at Bukwon in Zhangui-dong for Yi Gwangjeok. It includes the painting Bukwonsuhoedo, the list of participants, poems, and colophons, and is important as an early work by Jeong Seon and as a record of a gichohoe gathering in album format.

1123722630000.title_en: Vulture Peak Assembly Painting of Jangryuksa Temple, Yeongdeok
1123722630000.description: This Buddhist painting was made in 1764, and its inscription identifies nine painters including Duhun, Jaeok, and Jeonsu. It depicts Sakyamuni preaching the Lotus Sutra on Vulture Peak, with bodhisattvas, disciples, Indra, Brahma, and other deities arranged around the central Buddha in a circular composition.

1123722640000.title_en: Ksitigarbha and the Ten Kings Painting of Jangryuksa Temple, Yeongdeok
1123722640000.description: This Buddhist painting was made in 1764, and its inscription identifies nine painters including Jeonsu, Jaeok, and Duhun. It shows Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva and the Ten Kings, with 31 figures arranged symmetrically and the six bodhisattvas of light placed in the upper register.

1123622650000.title_en: Wooden Amitabha Triad of Mokuam Hermitage, Muan
1123622650000.description: This wooden triad was made in 1614, as indicated by an inscription on the base of the main image, and was produced by the sculptor monk Gaksim. It consists of Amitabha Buddha, Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva, and Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva, and is a large early-17th-century example of Joseon Buddhist sculpture.

1123522660000.title_en: Daeungjeon Hall of Munsusa Temple, Gochang
1123522660000.description: Daeungjeon Hall of Munsusa Temple in Gochang was rebuilt after the Imjin War, with records indicating major rebuilding in 1607 and further reconstruction in 1653. It is a 3-by-2 bay Buddhist hall with dapo-style brackets, a hipped-and-gabled roof form, and traditional polychrome decoration that preserve important Joseon-period architectural features.
